Amidst growing awareness of the need for future making projects that decentre the role of 
top-down and profit-driven institutions, this Handbook offers an update on the premises and 
practices of participatory design. Designing here is not a goal or artifact-oriented task to be 
completed, but ongoing engagement in the resource-differentiated locations, contested politics, 
relations, knowledges, and collective practices through which transformative possibilities are 
materialized. As reflected in these writings, the field itself is opening to include sites of design 
innovation beyond the parochial boundaries of the hyper-developed world, including pluriversal 
social movements aimed at unsettling, reparation, transition, and regeneration. As a sign of the 
field’s maturity, and consistent with its commitment to learning in doing, these chapters offer more 
in the way of critical reflection on troubles encountered than on their neat resolution. It is precisely 
for this reason that the Handbook will be an invaluable resource for researchers, teachers, students, 
and practitioners interested in the history and present of the field, as well as those already engaged 
in projects of participatory design who are looking for renewed inspiration.
Lucy Suchman, Professor Emerita of Sociology, Lancaster University, UK



ROUTLEDGE INTERNATIONAL 
HANDBOOK OF CONTEMPORARY 
PARTICIPATORY DESIGN
This handbook offers a comprehensive overview of key themes and agendas in contemporary 
Participatory Design across diverse disciplines, continents, communities, and practices. Building 
on Participatory Design’s core values of empowerment and democracy, the handbook explores 
how the field is developing and diversifying to address contemporary societal challenges in a 
global community.
Participatory Design actively engages peoples, groups and other actors in collaborative design 
processes to explore and co-create their everyday technologies, practices, and environments. 
In doing so, Participatory Design aims to address social justice and agency by including 
diverse actors in the collective shaping of alternative futures. Participatory Design embraces 
a diverse collection of principles and practices aimed at making technologies, environments, 
organisations and institutions more responsive to human and planetary needs. In this volume, a 
multidisciplinary and international group of highly experienced and recognised experts present 
an authoritative review of the contemporary field and discuss the diverse opportunities and 
challenges that arise from pivotal issues in Participatory Design, including scaling, collectives, 
sustainability and more-than-human, decolonisation, emerging technologies and AI, new 
approaches, methods and engagement beyond academia.
The handbook advances contemporary research, theory and practice and highlights case studies 
that demonstrate how Participatory Design can bring about game-changing shifts in diverse contexts. 
The volume is an invaluable resource for students, researchers, scholars, and professionals who 
seek to utilise Participatory Design research and practice to enrich, support and transform complex 
contemporary conditions towards inclusive, sustainable and transitional futures.
Rachel Charlotte Smith is Associate Professor of Human-Centred Design at Aarhus University, 
Denmark. Her research focuses on everyday digital transformations and sustainable technology 
futures through Participatory Design and Design Anthropology. She co-chaired PDC 2016 in 
Denmark and is Chair of the PDC Advisory Board 2020–2024.
Daria Loi  is Chief Experience Officer at Astral and Founder at Imperfecta, USA. Her work 
combines design strategy and participatory research with the goal of enriching people’s everyday 
lives. She was Conference Co-Chair for PDC 2010 in Australia, Co-Chair of the PDC Advisory 
Board 2020–2022, and Beyond Academia Chair for every PDC since 2014.

Heike Winschiers-Theophilus is Professor in Software Engineering at the Namibia University 
of Science and Technology, Namibia, and UNESCO Chair in Digital Technology Design with 
Indigenous People. Collaborating with local communities, she conceptualised community-based 
co-design, grounded in principles of Participatory Design, Afrocentricity and Ubuntu. She 
co-chaired PDC 2014 in Namibia and PDC 2024 in Malaysia.
Liesbeth Huybrechts is Associate Professor in the Faculty of Architecture and Arts at the Univer-
sity of Hasselt, Belgium. Based on Participatory Design, Design Anthropology and spatial trans-
formation processes, her research applies design and politics for/with participatory exchanges 
between human and material/natural environments. She co-chaired PDC 2018 in Belgium and is 
Co-Chair of the PDC Advisory Board 2022–2025.
Jesper Simonsen is Professor of Participatory Design at Roskilde University, Denmark. He has 
over 30 years of experience conducting participatory design projects and was Programme Chair of 
PDC 2008, General Chair of PDC 2012, and Chair of the PDC Advisory Board 2014–2019. His 
books include The Routledge International Handbook of Participatory Design (2013).

Yoko Akama is a design researcher and educator in the School of Design, RMIT University, 
Naarm, Kulin Nation (now called Melbourne, Australia). She is a recipient of several national 
and international awards and research funding for collaborative work with self-determining In -
digenous nations and regional communities preparing for disaster. Her practice explores ways to 
enhance qualities of inter-relating, embrace differences and pursue plurality. While she has lived, 
studied and worked in the UK, the US and Australia, her Japanese heritage and ongoing work with 
collaborators in and from Asia-Pacific continues to guide her practice. She brings this practice to 
research, teaching and various platform leadership through Designing Entangled Social Innova-
tion in Asia-Pacific (http://desiap.org/) network.
Raphael Arar heads design at One Project, an organisation focused on co-designing and scaling 
new economic and governance systems that are equitable, ecological and effective. He previously 
led design for learners at Khan Academy, worked on the ethical considerations of AI at IBM Re -
search and designed over a hundred apps with Apple. As an educator, Raphael has taught media 
arts and theory at USC, San José State University, California Institute of the Arts and the Pacific 
Northwest College of Art. Raphael also serves as a Board Member at Leonardo, the International 
Society for the Arts, Sciences and Technology. Raphael’s artwork has appeared internationally 
in museums, conferences and galleries, including the Moscow Museum of Applied Art, the In -
ternational Symposium on Electronic Art (ISEA) and the Boston Cyberarts Gallery. His design 
work focuses on developing transdisciplinary methods to cultivate mutual learning and has been 
featured in TED, Forbes, Wired and other outlets.
Susanne Bødker is Professor of Human-Computer Interaction at the Department of Computer 
Science, Aarhus University. She is known for her theoretical and empirical work on second-wave 
Human-Computer Interaction, computer mediated activity, and Participatory Design.  She has 
co-managed Aarhus University’s interdisciplinary center for Participatory IT research and headed 
the ERC Advanced Grant Common Interactive Objects (CIO) for the past 5 years. In 2024, she 
received the ACM SIGCHI Lifetime Research Award. Bødker was engaged with the Utopia pro-
ject in the early 1980s and has taught and published on Participatory Design ever since. Recent 
CONTRIBUTORS

Contributors
xiv
publications include the Springer Synthesis Lectures introductory book Participatory Design 
(Bødker, Dindler, Iversen and Smith 2022).
Claus Bossen  is Professor of Digital Design and Information Studies and co-heads the 
Science-Technology-Studies Centre, Aarhus University. His research focuses on the processes of 
technology design, development, implementation, appropriation and post-design. With a back-
ground in anthropology, he is keen to get close to people and their everyday practices of imagin -
ing, developing and taking technologies into use. Drawing on the fields of Participatory Design, 
Science-Technology-Studies and Computer-Supported Cooperative Work, he has conducted re -
search upon Information Technologies including Electronic Health Records within the healthcare 
domain, as well as research on how to evaluate Participatory Design projects. Recently, he has 
focused on data and data work in healthcare investigating the often unnoticed and invisible efforts 
invested in generating, processing and taking data into use. Efforts that reshape established profes-
sions’ task portfolio and lead to the emergence of new occupations.
Andrea Botero is DA in Arts and New Media, Aalto University. After graduating as a Designer at 
Universidad Nacional de Colombia, she obtained an MA in Strategic and Product Design at Aalto 
University. She works as Associate Professor at the School of Arts, Design, and Architecture at 
Aalto University and Adjunct Professor of the Faculty of Architecture and Design at Universidad 
de los Andes, Colombia. She is interested in the possibilities and contradictions inherent in partici-
pating in the design of tools, services and media that allow more relational and affective interac -
tions between people and between them and their environments.
Pablo Calderón Salazar is a Colombian designer, researcher and educator based in Madrid. 
He is currently an assistant professor at the School of Architecture & Design of IE University 
(Spain), after being engaged as a postdoc researcher at LUCA School of Arts (Belgium) until 
2023, working to articulate an interdisciplinary approach to  situated creative practices. His cur -
rent research builds upon his practice during the last decade, where he has explored the potential 
roles of designers – and creative practitioners at large – in triggering, supporting and enabling 
socio-ecological transitions. He has published several academic papers and contributed to numer-
ous non-academic publications, and his more recent project,  L’Agence Saint-Gilloise, represents 
an active creative practice dealing with designing social narratives in/and/for public space.
Rachel Charlotte Smith is Associate Professor at the Department of Digital Design and Informa-
tion Studies at Aarhus University, Denmark. Her research focuses on sustainable human futures 
between emerging digital technology and everyday life. Through long-term participatory research 
projects, she engages in exploring and transforming everyday practices and co-designing inclusive 
and responsible technologies in diverse contexts, such as emerging technologies in education, fu-
ture mobility in urban environments and future heritage and memory-making practices with mar -
ginalised communities. Smith contributes to theoretical and methodological advancements in and 
across Participatory Design and Design Anthropology. Recent publications include the Springer 
Synthesis Lectures introductory book Participatory Design (Bødker, Dindler, Iversen and Smith 
2022) and many journal Special Issue in the field. She co-chaired PDC’2016 in Aarhus, Denmark, 
and is Chair of the PDC Advisory Board 2020–2024.
Laura Cortés-Rico is a PhD student in Information Science at Cornell University. She is an Elec-
tronic Engineer from Universidad Nacional de Colombia and a Magister in Systems Engineering 

Contributors
xv
and Computing from Pontificia Universidad Javeriana. Her research interest is in historical mem-
ory building through a digital technology lens in contexts of peace-seeking and conflict from 
bottom-up approaches, where these memories have a phenomenological connotation related to 
the body and the territory. Her work in these contexts has focused on putting traditional textile 
knowledge into dialogue with computer and information sciences from material and political per-
spectives. She is also a co-founder and CTO at PiCoLab, a Colombian company committed to the 
design of contextual interactive experiences.
Vincenzo D’Andrea, is Associate Professor in the University of Trento, Department of Computer 
Science and Engineering. D’Andrea is teaching courses on Participatory Design, Information Sys-
tems, Ethics for IT and Social Innovation. His main research interest is Participatory Design of ICT, 
which he has been actively involved in 2005. D’andrea has been a member of the steering commit-
tee of the bi-annual Participatory Design Conference (PDC) and is co-programme chair of PDC 
2024. Among other techniques, his works explore the use of playful activities and theatre-based 
practices in Participatory Design. D’Andrea is currently involved in ECOEMPOWER, a European 
research project on energy communities, and was responsible for P4P (Participatory Design for 
Public Good), aiming at innovating the touristic offer of a valley in Trentino by including the resi-
dents’ knowledge and competences.
Chiara Del Gaudio is a designer, researcher and Reader in the School of Industrial Design, Car -
leton University, Canada. Her work focuses on political design, power and conflict within design 
processes, participatory and collaborative design approaches and explores the possibilities for 
design processes for transformative justice and self-determination. She has been part of the Partici-
patory Design Community since 2014, having edited special issues on Participatory Design – “Ex-
ploring Participatory Design as a Strategy to Act within the City” (2016) and “Autonomía: Design 
Strategies for Enabling Design Process” (2018) for the Strategic Design Research Journal, organ-
ised the Participatory Design Conference in 2020 as programme chair. She has been a member of 
the PDC Advisory Board since 2020.
Christian Dindler is Associate Professor of participatory interaction design and co-director of 
the Interaction Design Research programme at the Department of Digital Design and Informa-
tion Studies at Aarhus University. In his research, Christian focuses on the ethics of designing 
digital technology in practice and how users and designers can be empowered to better address 
the ethics of design. Christian has published research papers at the PDC conference since 2008 
and has co-authored the Springer Synthesis Lectures introductory book Participatory Design. He 
has taken part in organising several PDC conferences and led Participatory Design projects within 
areas such as schools and museums with a particular focus on how children can be empowered to 
critically and constructively engage with digital technology.
Betsy DiSalvo, is Associate Professor in the School of Interactive Computing, Georgia Insti -
tute of Technology, USA. DiSalvo is an expert in learning sciences, Participatory Design and 
human-centred computing. She directs the Culture and Technology Lab (CAT Lab), which in-
vestigates the impact of culture on technology use and production and applies that knowledge to 
developing novel socio-technical environments and tools. The CAT Lab works with a wide range 
of community organisations using participatory methods to understand and design technology for 
minoritised groups. DiSalvo’s Participatory Design efforts have led to the development of multiple 
award-winning educational games and the development of DataWorks and Glitch Game Testers, 

Contributors
xvi
both research platforms investigating novel technology workplaces. She received her PhD from 
Georgia Tech in Human-Centred Computing in 2012 and previously worked in the Learning Re-
search and Development Center at the University of Pittsburgh.
Katrien Dreessen holds a PhD in the social sciences (KULeuven, Belgium). Her PhD research 
provided an understanding of the importance of backstage design activities and the relational qual-
ities of the designer in setting up long-term Participatory Design with non-expert users in open 
spaces (e.g. Fablabs, maker spaces, Living Labs and City labs). She worked for more than ten years 
as a design researcher at the research unit “Inter-Actions” (LUCA, School of Arts/KULeuven) and 
was involved in several design research projects. She now works as the participation officer for the 
city of Genk (Belgium), putting some of her research into practice.
Pelle Ehn is Professor Emeritus at the School of Arts and Communication, Malmö University, 
Sweden. He has for more than 50 years been involved in the research field of collaborative and 
Participatory Design and in bridging design and information technology. Research projects in -
clude DEMOS from the seventies on information technology and workplace democracy, UTOPIA 
from the eighties on user participation and skill-based design, ATELIER from the turn of the 
century on architecture and technology for creative environments, and as his last research engage-
ment Malmö Living Labs, an open environment for democratic design experiments. His often 
collaborative publications include Emancipation and the Design of Information Systems  (1974), 
Computers and Democracy (1987), Work-Oriented Design of Computer Artifacts  (1988), Mani-
festo for a Digital Bauhaus  (1998), Design Things (2011), Making Futures (2014), Democratic 
Design Experiments (2015), Design/Politics  (2017) and Participatory Design and Learning as I 
Found It (1970–2015) (2017).
Mette Agger Eriksen is now applying co-design approaches outside academia. She is former As-
sociate Professor at The Royal Danish Academy in Denmark. Prior to this she was a PhD scholar 
and co-design researcher at School of Arts and Communication, Malmö University, from 2003 to 
2016. The PhD was on Material Matters in Co-Designing. With roots in Participatory Design, she 
was closely aligned with Malmö Living Labs from the start and was actively involved in projects 
associated with the Neighbourhood Lab from 2014 to 2016, especially InnovationPlatform Malmö 
Sydöst and URB@Exp. Together with Pelle Ehn, she also developed a cross-disciplinary course 
on Co-design – Design, Participation, Democracy. Mette has been an active participant in the 
Participatory Design Conference community since 2004.
Laura Forlano, a Fulbright award-winning scholar, is a disabled writer, social scientist and design 
researcher. She is Professor in the departments of Art + Design and Communication Studies in the 
College of Arts, Media, and Design and Senior Fellow at The Burnes Center for Social Change 
at Northeastern University, USA. Forlano’s research is focused on the aesthetics and politics at 
the intersection between design and emerging technologies. She uses participatory workshops, 
collaborative games, exhibitions, speculative videos, prototypes and performances to imagine al -
ternative futures for living with data and computation. She is the author of Cyborg (with Danya 
Glabau, MIT Press 2024) and an editor of three books: Bauhaus Futures (MIT Press 2019), digi-
talSTS (Princeton University Press 2019) and From Social Butterfly to Engaged Citizen  (MIT 
Press 2011). Forlano is also an Affiliated Fellow at the Information Society Project at Yale Law 
School. She received her PhD from Columbia University.

Contributors
xvii
Christopher Frauenberger  is Professor for Human-Computer Interaction at the Interdisciplinary 
Transformation University (IT:U), Linz, Austria. He investigates and designs interactive digital 
technology in a wide range of contexts, with groups who are often marginalised in mainstream 
innovation landscapes, for example, autistic children or the elderly. His primary mode of scientific 
enquiry is through design, in particular participatory practices that seek to involve stakeholders in 
imagining and creating alternative technological futures. Other modes of research through design 
he is interested in including forms of speculation as a means to critically engage with the inter -
action of digital technology with society. Theoretically, he builds on philosophical perspectives 
related to posthumanism, to conceptualise our increasingly entangled relationships with technol-
ogy, unearthing the ethical, epistemological and ontological implications of designing technology.
Penny Hagen is Director Tangata Tiriti at the Auckland Co-Design Lab, a public sector learning 
and innovation unit focused on equity and intergenerational wellbeing in Aotearoa New Zealand. 
Working across Australia and Aotearoa New Zealand, Penny has supported cross-sector teams and 
communities to respond to complex social issues by connecting policy and evidence to the lived 
realities and aspirations of communities in place. Penny has a PhD in Participatory Design, and 
her work takes a systems approach to wellbeing, integrating approaches from health, design, youth 
wellbeing, systems, adult learning and evaluation. Penny is the design representative on the Min-
istry for Social Development Ethics committee, a member of the Understanding Police Delivery 
Independent Panel, and Ngā Aho Kaupapa Whānau. She is a strong advocate of social design and 
ethics practices that are of Aotearoa, supporting local practices and networks.
Sara Heitlinger is a UKRI Future Leaders Fellow and Senior Lecturer in Computer Science at the 
Centre for Human–Computer Interaction Design at City, University of London, UK. She leads the 
four-year More-than-Human Sustainable and Inclusive Smart Cities (MoSaIC) project, exploring 
co-designing smart cities for flourishing interspecies cohabitation with industry, in policy and in 
ways that work for urban communities. She is co-editor (with Marcus Foth and Rachel Clarke) 
of Designing More-Than-Human Smart Cities: Beyond Sustainability, Towards Cohabitation 
(Oxford University Press, 2024). In her work she employs creative approaches from the arts and 
humanities to collaborate across different sectors and with marginalised communities to co-design 
urban futures with emerging technologies.
Niels Hendriks, PhD, is affiliated with LUCA School of Arts, Belgium, serving as a design re -
searcher and lecturer in product design. He also leads the “Inter-Actions Research Unit” and coor-
dinates the “Caring and Design Research” cluster (https://caring.anddesignresearch.com/), which 
emphasises participatory research for methodology sharing, educational strategies and reflections 
with marginalised communities. This cluster addresses taboo topics like sexual expression in resi-
dential care and collaborates with various user groups, including children with autism, individuals 
with intellectual disabilities and those with dementia. Hendriks’ work focuses on participatory 
methods and holds a systemic view of the interaction between artefacts and users within the care 
ecosystem. He manages several national projects and a European doctoral network, HOMEDEM, 
on design and care for people with dementia and their caregivers.
Per-Anders Hillgren is Professor in Interaction Design at the School of Arts and Communi -
cation at Malmö University, Sweden, where he coordinates the research platform Collaborative 
Future-Making. He initiated and coordinated Malmö New Media Living Lab that later evolved 

Contributors
xviii
to become Malmö Living Labs. Per-Anders has also been the project manager for Living Lab the 
Neighbourhood and has been active in the Participatory Design research community with several 
publications in PDC proceedings and the Co-Design Journal. Besides his long-standing engage -
ment in co-design processes, his research interest has increasingly been directed towards critical 
imagination and how basic assumptions, norms and structures can be challenged to widen the 
perspectives on what can constitute sustainable and inclusive futures.
Liesbeth Huybrechts is Associate Professor and works in the areas of Participatory Design, de -
sign anthropology and spatial transformation processes in the research group Arck, University of 
Hasselt, Belgium. She has developed a research interest in the design for/with participatory ex-
changes and processes of capacity building between human and the material/natural environment 
and the “politics” of designing these relations. She explores this in several research (fundamental, 
EU and in commission of governments, public and private organisations) and educational projects 
and in her work on the level of coordination and policy. Examples are the EU projects Traders, 
Critical Heritage and Reworlding and the Living Lab De Andere Markt https://deanderemarkt.

xxv
This book provides a state-of-the-art overview of the developments, diversity and spread of con -
temporary Participatory Design research and practice. It presents a comprehensive review of Par-
ticipatory Design over the past decade (2012–2023).
Participatory Design embraces a diverse collection of principles and practices aiming to make 
technologies, tools, environments, businesses and social institutions more responsive to human 
and planetary needs. It brings together a multidisciplinary and global community of researchers, 
social scientists, software developers, designers, managers, practitioners, communities, activists 
and citizens. This diverse community advocates and has adopted distinctively participatory ap -
proaches to the development of information and communication artefacts, systems, services and 
technology, as well as other designed artefacts and environments.
While it is a stand-alone publication, this handbook builds directly upon the first Routledge 
International Handbook of Participatory Design from 2013. Edited by Jesper Simonsen and Tony 
Robertsen, the 2013 handbook reviewed two decades (1990–2012) of Participatory Design re -
search and its foundations, values and political legacy since the early 1970s. The publication pro-
vided a solid and authoritative overview of the research field as it had matured internationally, 
while covering core theoretical issues in Participatory Design: heritage, ethics, ethnography, meth-
ods, tools and techniques and communities, as well as exemplary cases in practice that continue 
to be highly relevant today.
Based on the widespread interest and use of the 2013 handbook, we had discussions in 2022 
about producing an updated edition to include a review of contemporary literature and develop -
ments in the field. Participatory Design over the past decade, however, has developed dynamically 
into numerous diverse and novel arenas, making such a task impossible. Consequently, we agreed 
to produce a new Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design  and build upon the founda-
tions of the 2013 handbook, from its theoretical approaches, concepts and definitions. This new 
handbook therefore reviews contemporary Participatory Design and presents theoretical, meth -
odological and practical developments in the field from the past decade (2013–2023). The con -
temporary themes presented include notions of scaling, collectives, sustainability, decolonisation, 
emerging technologies, new approaches and methods, teaching and Participatory Design beyond 
academia. This handbook, together with the 2013 edition, offers readers an updated and authorita-
tive overview of Participatory Design since the establishment of this research field.
PREFACE

Preface
xxvi
The handbook is edited by recent generations of Participatory Design researchers and practi-
tioners who are actively engaged in contemporary areas of research and practice and have been a 
part of shaping the community within the past decade – as chairs of Participatory Design confer -
ences (PDCs) and members of the PDC Advisory Board (see http://pdcproceedings.org). The PDC 
Advisory Board, established and initiated at PDC 2014, includes chairs of PDC conferences along 
with elected senior and junior members to support the field by advising, sharing experiences and 
organising calls for the biennial PDC conference series – and now also by editing this new Hand-
book of Contemporary Participatory Design.
Consistent with participatory practice itself, this book has been developed through a collabora-
tive process of review and feedback. To build and reflect on the legacies, cornerstones, and key 
developments in the field of Participatory Design, the process included senior expert advisers who 
are major players in the field but also authors involved in the 2013 handbook and in core journals 
and publications. Since its inception, the ambition behind this book has been to bring together 
a vibrant global Participatory Design community – of senior as well as junior interdisciplinary 
voices – to enable them to jointly shape new contributions, take stock and set directions for the 
contemporary field within complex societal and changing global landscapes. The book is there -
fore itself the result of a participatory process, with contributions from 42 co-authors across the 
globe with first-hand knowledge of the discourses that have shaped the field over the last decade. 
Abstracts and chapter drafts were discussed and reviewed at a full-day hybrid workshop held at 
Aarhus University in 2022 and again in a full-day online seminar in 2023. Drafts for each chapter 
have been reviewed and circulated among the contributors, senior expert advisers and external 
reviewers to ensure quality, consistency and cross-referencing.
We extend our gratitude to the highly esteemed Senior Expert Advisors who gave their invalu-
able experience and knowledge from decades of Participatory Design research and practice to 
develop this work and to give their feedback and reflective reviews of the chapters. The Senior 
Expert Advisors are Research Emeritus Jeanette Blomberg (IBM Research), Professor Susanne 
Bødker (Aarhus University), Professor Emeritus Pelle Ehn (Malmö University), Professor Emeri-
tus Finn Kensing (Copenhagen University), Professor Emeritus Janet McDonnell (Central St Mar-
tins University of the Arts London) and Professor Emeritus Lucy Suchman (Lancaster University).
As editors we have enjoyed our numerous discussions, reflections and exchanges of draft mate-
rial with authors and expert advisers. We hope that readers of the book will not only be inspired 
by the contemporary developments and trajectories it offers but also feel compelled to share the 
insights it provides while engaging in the concerns and actions raised by contemporary Participa-
tory Design.

1
CONTEMPORARY 
PARTICIPATORY DESIGN
An Introduction
Rachel Charlotte Smith, Liesbeth Huybrechts,  
Heike Winschiers-Theophilus, Daria Loi and Jesper Simonsen
Participatory Design research, theory and practice have diversified and evolved in novel directions in 
the past decade. This introductory chapter explores how contemporary Participatory Design is diver -
sifying and developing to address societal challenges in a global community, both within and outside 
of academia. While building on Participatory Design’s core values of participation, empowerment and 
democracy, the chapter offers an overview of key challenges and agendas in contemporary Participa -
tory Design across diverse disciplines, continents, communities and practices.
Participatory Design is widely known for focusing on the direct involvement of people in the 
co-design of the technologies they use and for its emphasis on collaborative design processes, driven 
by the participation of the people affected by the technology designed. Over the past decade, Par -
ticipatory Design has evolved to include a diverse set of contexts and agents across scales and time. 
Drawing together highly relevant concerns from a vibrant and global Participatory Design community, 
this introduction highlights four emergent agendas for Participatory Design, namely politicising, diver-
sifying, relationality and transforming. These agendas create new directions for Participatory Design, 
based on the foundational aspects of the field as well as contemporary shifts and trajectories. Based 
on the evolving theory, methods and practice, we propose a definition of contemporary Participatory 
Design that supports shared local and global trajectories towards sustainable and transitional futures.
In addition to exploring new directions, the chapter provides an overview of the contributions in 
this handbook. It contributes a resource and inspiration for students, researchers, scholars and profes -
sionals for leveraging Participatory Design research and practice to enrich, support and transform their 
global communities within highly challenging, complex and contemporary contexts.
DOI: 10.4324/9781003334330-1

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
2
Contemporary Conditions and Participatory Design
What is contemporary Participatory Design? And what does Participatory Design have to offer to 
a contemporary changing world? This Handbook investigates how Participatory Design research 
and practice address a vast range of societal challenges in a fast-changing and complex world. 
Current global crises – from existential to societal, environmental, technological and political – are 
increasingly acute and raise key questions about the role, responsibility and impact of the field. We 
are confronted with threats to democracy and wars that are raging across the world, destabilising 
geopolitics and global orders; with crises of poverty, food availability, and human, social and cul-
tural displacement; with crises in economic representation and equality; with the disruptive impact 
of information technology’s accelerated complexities on work and daily life; with health crises and 
epidemics; and, crucially, with accelerating and growing climate and environmental crises. Navi-
gating such complex conditions and operating within such a messy world are daunting prospects, 
and collaborative design and research are deeply entwined with these shifting politics and tensions. 
To explore the possibilities of designing alternative futures in the context of human, societal and 
planetary crisis, the chapter first looks closer at what characterises the contemporary conditions of 
Participatory Design. It provides brief historical insights into the growth of the field of Participatory 
Design before introducing four agendas for Participatory Design that contribute to a definition of 
contemporary Participatory Design.
According to anthropologist Paul Rabinow (2008), the contemporary is an open moment in which 
transition towards change is within reach. Quoting his words, at particular moments, the contemporary 
holds an almost expectant promise of being “on the verge of something momentous or extravagant” 
(2008, p. 12). The sense of being on the verge of either breakthrough or disruption is discernible in 
repeated events through history. Turning towards the future, efforts can be made in “making possibility 
into potential for change rather than lateral difference” (Faubion et al., 2016, p. 374). Participatory De-
sign has engaged in multiple waves of social and technological advancement – from the 1970s influx of 
information technology and automation of the workplace that initiated early Scandinavian research pro-
jects with the labour unions (Nygaard and Bergo, 1975; Kensing and Greenbaum, 2013), to the internet 
revolution and global spread of digital technology and social media platforms in the 1990s and 2000s, 
and the current diffusion of emergent data-intensive, hyper-connected, intelligent technologies and sys-
tems into most aspects of everyday life. When they occur, these moments and waves of change foster 
the emergence of new trajectories and phenomena, calling for a reconsideration of how research, design, 
technology and knowledge relate to each other and operate. The contemporary therefore provides a pos-
sibility
 – a promise and the hope for a better future. In reflecting on current crises of human existence, 
Fry (2018) argues however, for the determining role of design in taking on the accelerating defuturing 
conditions of unsustainability. The amplified socio-ecological consequences of our modes of growth 
and material and technological development have actively created the conditions to deprive humans 
and more-than-human species of a (better) future. Designing is doubly implicated in these challenges, 
as cause and potential, and such a context increasingly calls for the design community to take action – to 
broaden its gaze, to reach out across disciplines and communities and to reimagine as well as engage in 
the complexity of design as part of a world-shaping force (Fry, 2018, p. 3; Bannon et al., 2018).
Historical moments like these thus hold the struggle of change and transition because they not 
only require a move away from established practices and well-known traditions but also hold hope 
and anticipation for creating alternative futures by transcending existing conditions (Ehn, 1988;  
Simonsen and Robertsen, 2013). In Donald Schön’s (1987) conceptualisation of design as reflec-
tive practice, the complex conditions of real-world problems are always characterised by the un -
certainty and messiness of indeterminate situations. Problems of real-world practices present 

Contemporary Participatory Design
3
themselves not as well-formed structures but only through our dialogic engagement and continuous 
conversational acts of problem setting and problem solving with the situation at hand. This ontological 
process of reflective design practice, Schön argues, constitutes the making of worlds (Schön, 1987).  
In Participatory Design, the dynamic processes of designing are characterised, not by the individual de-
signer but, by collective reflective design practices between multiple participants who collaboratively 
shape their future practices and worlds. Widely known for focusing on the direct involvement of people 
in the codesign of the technologies they use and concerned with how collaborative design processes can 
be driven by such a direct involvement, Participatory Design embraces a diverse set of emancipatory prin-
ciples and practices aimed at making technologies, tools, environments, business and social institutions 
more responsive to human needs (Simonsen and Robertsen, 2013; Bødker et al., 2022, see definitions of 
contemporary Participatory Design below on pp. 8–10). Through its strong foundational commitments 
to democracy, empowerment and emancipation (Bødker et al., 2022), Participatory Design research-
ers, practitioners and participants work together to develop alternatives through small- and large-scale 
democratic design experiments. The designer(s) thus include diverse participants, citizens and collectives, 
computer scientists, ethnographers, urban planners, and beyond, and skilful Participatory Design practi-
tioners from multiple domains and levels of expertise, who work together in critical and inclusive ways.
Inspired by the pragmatic philosophy of John Dewey (1938), the field draws on a perspective of 
democratic and active engagement from the bottom up. This process is driven by the drawing together 
of heterogeneous interests and by assemblages of sociotechnical material into controversial things 
where matters of concern can be openly raised (Bannon and Ehn, 2013, p. 57; Binder et al., 2002). In 
these assemblages, the changing social, economic, technical and political landscapes can be confronted 
from different socio-technical positionalities and designerly stances, to give space to diverse voices and 
politics in technological and societal innovation. Foregrounding the politics of participation, to give 
voice to those traditionally excluded from decision-making processes through equalising power rela-
tions and mutual learning (Kensing and Greenbaum, 2013), and how such design processes themselves 
can be designed to support ‘genuine’ participation (Bødker et al., 2004) thus are core concerns.
Contemporary Participatory Design theory and practice are increasingly faced by and concerned 
with the acceleration of complex relations between technologies and human and more-than-human 
worlds. Integrating diverse disciplines, from human–computer interaction, interaction design, and 
design studies to architecture and urban planning, sociology, anthropology and other human sci -
ences, the field has expanded to include a widening set of domains and global contexts. The focus 
in Participatory Design today has extended far beyond defined organisations, communities, and 
tools and technologies into diverse and pluralistic collectives and complex technologies and sys -
tems at different scales that are continuously shifting and morphing. This diversification makes 
contemporary Participatory Designers’ roles increasingly ambiguous. As a result, a series of funda-
mental shifts have impacted the field, creating the need for continuous reflection and evolvement:
• Technologies have become more complex to engage with and design at numerous different 
scales, due to their exponential growth, opaqueness and omnipresence.
• Participation has become more challenging as groups and collectives have become diversified, 
dispersed and versatile.
• Contexts have become both more diverse and interconnected and simultaneously less easy to 
situate and grasp culturally, geographically and conceptually.
• Knowledge and knowledge production have become more pluriversal as different epistemolo-
gies, ontologies and a multiplicity of worlds are acknowledged. 
• Design(ers) are increasingly facing the need for action and responsibility in addressing funda-
mental and future concerns of people, societies, species and the planet.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
4
The vast complexity and uncertainty that the world confronts us with calls for action and 
strengthens the belief that Participatory Design can and must leverage its position from which it 
can act and support radical change. 
What paths, agendas and responsibilities, then, do we see for Participatory Design as we 
move forward? In this chapter, we present four participatory agendas to guide future actions in 
the field. We propose these agenda as a synthesis of this handbook’s diverse contributions and 
of how Participatory Design has diversified and evolved over the past decade into multiple new 
directions. Themes presented in the book include scaling, collectives, more-than-human, decolo -
nisation, emerging technologies, new methods and approaches, and Participatory Design beyond 
academia, along with exemplary cases on living labs, dementia and education, to name a few. 
Some themes, such as more-than-human and decolonisation, are newer to Participatory Design, 
yet they obviously connect to foundational concerns of the field. Other themes, such as the forma-
tion of collectives in urban spaces, the reconfigurations of participation into new domains, and the 
politics and democratisation of emerging technologies, have developed over time in Participatory 
Design research and hence build on the strong existing base of theory, methods and practice. We 
precede our description of the four agendas with a brief overview of key milestones in the history 
of Participatory Design. The overview shows how Participatory Design’s political roots have de -
veloped alongside shifting societal and technological concerns, into a vibrant global community 
of researchers and practitioners that continues to evolve the field.
A Brief Historical Overview
Participatory Design has come a long way since its Scandinavian inception in the 1970s, with its 
focus on workplace democracy and workers’ self-determination and empowerment against the 
influx of information technology. The history of critical engagement with the democratisation 
of technological innovation across Europe and the United States (e.g. Suchman, 1987) is woven 
into this book’s chapters, as well as numerous existing resources that provide valuable overviews 
of the history and legacy of Participatory Design, including the 2013 Handbook (see Simonsen 
and Robertsen, 2013; Kensing and Greenbaum, 2013; Ehn, 1998, 2018 ; Kensing, 2003; Halskov 
and Hansen, 2015; Björgvinsson and Keshavarz, 2020; Bødker et al., 2022). Drawing on Bødker 
et al.’s (2022) outline of four eras of Participatory Design, as well as Ehn (2018), we provide a 
brief overview of four key historical eras in Participatory Design evolution. These are conceptual-
ised as waves to indicate how each era is characterised by particular discourses and concerns that 
continue to exist as undercurrents of the field (see Kuhk et al., 2019).
Participatory Design grew in the 1970s as what has been conceptualised as the first wave of 
Participatory Design (1970–1985), foregrounding democracy at work (Bødker et al., 2022; Ehn, 
2018). These early Participatory Design projects were anchored in Scandinavia in political engage-
ments for workplace democracy and linked to the NJMF Norwegian Iron and Metal Workers’ Un-
ion (Nygaard and Bergo, 1975). This design turn has been coined as work-oriented design (1980s), 
nurturing famous projects such as DUE (Kyng and Mathiassen, 1997) and UTOPIA (Bødker et al., 
1985; Ehn, 2014). Bringing design practice to software development in this era forged a shift from 
expert to activist researchers in the fight for workers’ self-determination. 
The second wave of Participatory Design (1985–1992) involved a more widespread focus on 
participation and users in Participatory Design (Bødker et al., 2022), while placing the cooperative 
design of computer systems and critical computing on the agenda (Ehn, 2018). Work by Suchman 
(1995) and Lave and Wenger (1991) describes a growing attention to learning by participating in 
communities of practitioners, leading to new series of contextual design methods and approaches 
for understanding users and use in local contexts (e.g. Simonsen et al., 2014; Bødker et al., 2022).

Contemporary Participatory Design
5
This critical lens has expanded to many experimentations in the digital design field, frequently 
referred to as the second design turn, or a digital Bauhaus (2000s) (Ehn, 1998, 2018).
The third wave (2010s) focused on marginal and cosmopolitical design collectives for publics in 
the making (Ehn, 2018). While Participatory Design in this era still engaged with the political, it in-
creasingly focused outside of formal organisational structures (Huybrechts et al., 2022), with Living 
Labs, for instance (Björgvinsson et al., 2012). This has led to coining the term Community-based Par-
ticipatory Design (DiSalvo et al., 2013) and concepts such as publics (Matthews et al., 2022; Le Dan-
tec, 2016), infrastructuring (Di Salvo et al., 2013), commoning (Marttila et al., 2014; Teli et al., 2019) 
and institutioning (Huybrechts et al., 2017). Next to breaking out of the contexts and boundaries of or-
ganisations, Participatory Design during this third wave also expanded more visibly into non-Western 
contexts and parts of the world, contributing to novel perspectives, methods and epistemologies and 
conceptualisations of participation (Vines et al., 2013; Winschiers-Theophilus et al., 2010, 2019).
Finally and most recently, we see an emergence of a fourth wave in Participatory Design towards 
what we refer to as designing otherwise. In light of socio-environmental and political challenges, 
we observe an emerging interest in diverse onto-epistemologies, more-than-human stakeholders and 
ecologies (Heitlinger et al., 2018; Clarke et al., 2019; Akama et al., 2020) and the (re-)emergence 
of debates around decoloniality and pluriversality to move design theory and practices towards in-
cluding multiple epistemologies and worlds (Escobar, 2018; Smith et al., 2020; Clarke et al., 2022; 
Gaudio et al., 2020a, Arruda et al., 2020; Salazar and Huybrechts, 2020; van Amstel, 2023; Smith 
et al., 2024), as well as the ethics and politics of emerging technologies (Frauenberger, 2019), the 
long-term scaling of Participatory Design, and other core concerns represented in this book.
Grounded in these four waves that continue to form strong undercurrents for contemporary theory 
and practice, the contributions of this Handbook clearly demonstrate how the values, politics and 
ambitions of Participatory Design are reflected in the four agendas outlined in the following sections.
Agendas of Contemporary Participatory Design
This contemporary moment in Participatory Design’s evolution is characterised by ambitions, ten-
sions and critical concerns for how to practise within and respond to changing global conditions. 
In the following sections, we suggest four participatory agendas that are being shaped by, with or 
through contemporary participatory research and practice, informed by the history and pointing 
out future directions for research and development in the field. These agendas articulate central 
issues that materialise in and may be deduced from the chapter contributions and through the col-
laborative process used to develop this Handbook. Each chapter provides not only a lens to appre-
ciate and unfold the proposed agendas, but also rich landscapes and interconnections for exploring 
and engaging with contemporary Participatory Design. We describe these as participatory agendas 
to encourage and support the Participatory Design community through their engagement in con -
tingent contexts, scales and times. For the experienced researcher or practitioner of Participatory 
Design, these agendas are deeply interconnected with previous concerns, yet with novel emphasis. 
The agendas target the shaping of future alternatives for inclusive, responsible and sustainable 
futures and acknowledge increasing concerns with designing for modes of transition, disruption, 
degrowth and regeneration. 
The four participatory agendas concern:
• Politicising agendas of power, agency and participation in design and technology;
• Diversifying to embrace a multiplicity of contexts, actors, knowledges and lifeworlds;
• Relationality for interconnections of researchers, participants, actors and collectives;
• Transforming through grounding participatory practices for sustainable futures at multiple scales.

In the following sections, we unfold each of these four agendas and provide context to how they 
interconnect across this book’s chapters as well as in relation to key contemporary literature in 
Participatory Design.
Politicising Agendas of Power, Agency and Participation in Design and Technology
The politicising agenda centre-stages strong political aims of shifting power and agency in favour 
of marginalised voices through design, to include those who are affected and previously excluded 
in the design of technologies and decision-making processes
. 
Throughout this Handbook, a highly articulated call for action is the need for Participatory De-
sign to (re-)politicise its work in relation to diverse actors. Such a call asks to reconsider as well 
as emphasise the roots of Participatory Design’s political engagement in workplace contexts, ex -
tending such roots to today’s urgent need to tackle wider societal crisis through activism and im -
pact. In line with that, we have seen novel practices emerge from the shared ambition of staying 
close to Participatory Design’s political foundations. Key contributions to Participatory Design 
over the past decade have raised concerns for reimagining Participatory Design (e.g., Bannon and 
Ehn, 2013; Bannon et al., 2018), and revitalising the field for addressing the “big issues” (Bød -
ker and Kyng, 2018). They call for politicising the field toward activist stances that face larger 
societal matters of concern, and within wider global infrastructures and contexts. These concerns 
have been centrally addressed in the literature (e.g. Beck, 2002; Bødker, 2003; Bratteteig and 
Wagner, 2012; Bannon et al., 2018; Huybrechts et al., 2022; Bødker et al., 2022) and encour -
age the community to reconnect. Moreover, the themes of politics, power and democracy were 
foregrounded in consecutive editions of Participatory Design Conference (PDC) proceedings, 
including PDC 2016 in Aarhus, Denmark (Smith et al., 2017) and PDC 2018 in Hasselt, Belgium 
(Huybrechts et al., 2020). Given such calls within the current evolving challenging contexts, key 
questions still include: how can we design for social justice through Participatory Design projects 
typically involving small-scale mutual learning? And how can we empower people to become 
part of shaping their future practices within often-contested contexts of power, inequality and op-
pression? In addressing such politics, Chapter 3 for instance discusses the organisation of collec -
tives in co-steering transitions within urban, suburban and rural environments. Chapter 6 instead 
discusses the increasing concerns for how qualities of emerging technologies are configured to 
produce new and old forms of oppression and how Participatory Design needs to develop mean-
ingful and effective participation around such socio-material assemblages towards democratising 
design processes.
Diversifying to Embrace a Multiplicity of Contexts, Actors, Knowledges and Lifeworlds
The diversifying agenda engages with diverse contexts, regions, technologies, and human and 
more-than-human relations and focuses on adapting practices and methodologies to diverse 
knowledges and lifeworlds, to enable agency, self-determination and equity for diverse actors.
Participatory Design aims to pay attention to voices, agendas and knowledges that have been 
marginalised or excluded. Participatory Design has become key in addressing complex contem -
porary challenges, to diversify design processes so as to include not only diverse actors in society 
(human and more-than-human) but also diverse technologies, territories, temporalities and episte-
mologies (global North–South, East–West, etc.) (Escobar 2018; Smith et al., 2024). Contemporary 
Participatory Design practices increasingly work across technologies, societal groups, professional 

Contemporary Participatory Design
7
categories, institutions and so on, which in turn leads to new reconfigurations of participation 
(Vines et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2017; Kendall and Dearden, 2018) and raises questions about sus-
taining and future-proofing initiatives towards long-term impact beyond the specific project and 
within a wider community of practice (Iversen and Dindler, 2014; Smith and Iversen, 2018; Simone  
et al., 2022), and epistemological contexts and ecologies (Bastian et al., 2016; Heitlinger et al., 2018; 
Clarke et al., 2019; Akama et al., 2020). Key reflections on the diversification of Participatory Design 
for designing otherwise across geographies and socio-spatial and temporal framings were spurred by 
PDC 2020 in Manizales, Colombia, and the hybrid PDC 2022 in Newcastle, UK. The diversifica-
tion has led to work on new understandings of scale(s) and scaling (Chapter 2) and on navigating the 
complexities of contemporary emerging technologies and systems in their diverse manifestations and 
pervasiveness (Chapter 6), as well as to new thematic areas of decolonial movements towards pluriver-
sality (Chapter 5) and more-than-human entanglements in the context of climate and eco-sustainability 
(Chapter 4) that extend Participatory Design across diverse knowledges and lifeworlds.
Relationality for Interconnections of Researchers, Participants, Actors and Collectives
The relationality agenda acknowledges the interconnectedness and coexistence across the globe 
and between researchers, participants, collectives and other actors, focusing on calibrating partici-
pation in long-term engagements and in responsible, caring ways.
This agenda requires an acknowledgement of the diverse layers of interconnectedness that 
exist across the globe as well as in situated contexts among researchers, designers, participants 
and other actors. Contemporary participatory research and practice must pay more attention to 
relational practices, methods, tools, and languages and work across scales, cultural and politi -
cal domains, and human and more-than-human worlds. This implies a rethinking of the lan -
guages and materials that designers use and need to be fluent in as they build relationality. It 
implies readiness and relational sensitivity to responsively co-design for change in contingent 
circumstances (Akama and Light, 2018; Bardzell, 2018; Gottlieb, 2024). The movement towards 
increased relationality has been articulated in diverse ways, such as through infrastructuring, 
commoning and institutioning, concepts which are further explained in Chapters 3 and 4. The 
concept of infrastructuring, for example, known from Star and Bowker (2002), has been adopted 
and positioned within contemporary Participatory Design both as an empirical-ethnographic and 
generative-designerly resource (Simonsen et al., 2020; Pipek et al., 2017; Karasti, 2014). The 
point is to extend the focus on participation beyond social interactions or user engagement in/of 
the design process and to extend researchers’ and practitioners’ ability to continuously reposition 
through responsible, ethical and caring engagements and entanglements with diverse actors and 
communities across times and scales (Frauenberger, 2019; Choi et al., 2023; Saad-Sulonen et al., 
2018; Winschiers-Theophilus et al., 2010; Bødker et al., 2017; Brereton et al., 2014). Such rela -
tional approaches capture what is happening in the foreground but also pay attention to backstage 
labour, the political layers as well as emotional experiences associated with Participatory Design 
practice (see also Chapter 11). It extends temporal frames beyond the present and near-future 
focus of design to include long-term relations, past and contested histories as a resource in de -
signing futures. Participatory research environments demonstrate such abilities for long-term 
democratic engagements of diverse local communities through Living Labs (see Chapters 10 and 
12), while others focus on ensuring the inclusion of wider and contested historical aspects and 
politics for (re)building future memories and discourses, to enable strong relational agendas 
and knowledges (see Chapters 5 and 9).
