Transforming Through Grounding Participatory Practices for Sustainable Futures  
at Scale
Finally, the transforming agenda addresses the role of Participatory Design in generating impact 
across multiple arenas and scales, by building and grounding strong participatory practices to ac -
tively address societal challenges and shape the future of the planet.
This agenda emphasises the co-creation of sustainable and transformative futures in and 
through diverse and complex conditions. Participatory Design engagements must tackle some of 
the crucial concerns in the contemporary landscapes, at once through small acts of engagement, 
as well as at policy and governmental level and larger-scale global concerns of human exist -
ence. As Frauenberger et al. (2018) state, how do we extend the reach of Participatory Design 
without giving up on its core values? Participatory Design potentials lies in strong commitments 
(Bødker et al., 2022), grounded in values of democracy and empowerment in designing alterna-
tive technologies and futures through locally situated practices. Indeed, Participatory Design’s 
work across different contexts and domains and its embracing and connecting of participatory 
initiatives and outcomes at different scales are only powerful through its strong situatedness 
and grounding (rather than generalisation). To achieve this, we need not only to move towards 
empirically grounded, deeply situated socio-material practices (Blomberg and Karasti, 2013) 
but also to develop our understandings of scoping and scaling possible outcomes and impacts of 
Participatory Design efforts for particular contexts and (future) communities of practice (Bossen 
et al., 2016; Bratteteig and Wagner, 2016; Smith and Iversen, 2018; Winschiers-Theophilus et al., 
2019). This also demands research and development of ways to ensure, transfer and teach Par -
ticipatory Design practice to extend its reach and empower coming generations in a digitalised 
society (e.g. D’Andrea et al., 2010; DiSalvo et al., 2017; Christiansson et al., 2018; Schaper 
et al., 2023, Chapter 13). This entails designing for contingent transformation in circumstances 
of uncertainty for both tangible and intangible outcomes, understandings and knowledges 
(thus not only for artefacts, systems and services or technology designs), in order to shape 
social-political, technological and ecological alternatives (Chapters 3 and 9). Robust participa -
tory practices, based on strong theoretical and methodological explorations, have always been 
core to Participatory Design (Simonsen and Robertson, 2013; Luck, 2018; Bødker et al., 2022). 
Their ongoing renewal will be essential in contemporary landscapes for building sustainable and 
transformative futures, inspired by material and decolonial practices (Chapter 7) and through 
engaging with design and technological innovation across academic, industry, governmental 
and public contexts (see Chapters 6 and 8). 
Together, these four agendas advocate the continued dynamic development of strong theoreti-
cal, methodological and practical approaches for contemporary Participatory Design.
Defining Contemporary Participatory Design
Early Participatory Design conferences (PDC) introduced Participatory Design as “a set of diverse 
ways of thinking, planning, and acting through which people make their work, technologies, and 
social institutions more responsive to human needs” (e.g. the call for PDC 1998, accessible on 
pdcproceedings.org). In later conferences, this introduction was elaborated as follows:
Participatory Design is about the direct involvement of people in the codesign of the tech -
nologies they use. Its central concern is how collaborative design processes can be driven 
by the participation of the people affected by the technologies designed. Participatory 

Contemporary Participatory Design
9
Design embraces a diverse collection of principles and practices aimed at making tech -
nologies, tools, environments, business and social institutions more responsive to human 
needs.
(cf. Simonsen and Robertson, 2013, p. xix)
A further developed definition of Participatory Design as collaborative processes of interaction 
and design was given in the 2013 handbook by Simonsen and Robertson (2013). They defined 
Participatory Design as follows:
a process of investigating, understanding, reflecting upon, establishing, developing, and 
supporting mutual learning between multiple participants in collective ‘reflection-in-action’ 
[Schön, 1983]. The participants typically undertake the two principal roles of users and 
designers where the designers strive to learn the realities of the users’ situation while the 
users strive to articulate their desired aims and learn appropriate technological means to 
obtain them.
(2013, p. 2)
While this definition continues to be fundamental, we observe that its focus on participation and 
users in the design process no longer suffices given the shifts we currently face in socio-technical 
developments and how participation and contexts are conceptualised due to the diverse design 
knowledges and responsibilities discussed above. The diffusion and diversification of Participatory 
Design with varying practices and research directions motivated Bødker et al. (2022) to emphasise 
what (historically) grounds and connects Participatory Design to its contemporary practices. The 
authors formulate four strong commitments crucially focused on democracy at the workplace and 
beyond; empowerment of people through the process of design; emancipatory practices rooted in 
mutual learning between designers and people, and seeing human beings as skilful and resourceful 
in the development of their future practices (2022, pp. 115–116).
Bødker et al. integrate important foundational layers into their definition of the field to char -
acterise Participatory Design as a set of emancipatory practices whereby human beings engage, 
within their current practices, to define and shape shared goals and future alternatives in critical 
and inclusive ways (Bødker et al., 2022, p.  3). Core commitments to politics and politicising 
are clearly foregrounded, as are unequal power relations of mutual learning in collaborative de-
velopment activities for technological alternatives. In addition, and in alignment with the afore-
mentioned agendas, the authors refer to the past decade as an era of reconnecting the political 
responsibilities of and in design to mobilise local and global actors to work towards scaling and 
sustaining Participatory Design initiatives at local, national and international levels.
While definitions of Participatory Design are deeply rooted in Scandinavian and Western 
modes of knowledge, the demand to make space for alternative ways of knowing, thinking 
and being has become increasingly apparent as contemporary Participatory Design diversifies 
across different contexts, institutions and scales. This implies that both research and practice 
need to be leveraged to work with hyper-connected technologies, systems and environments 
and entanglements between humans, species and ecologies. The new interconnected environ -
ments vastly extend the focus on participation, users and engagement in the design process and 
enhance the need for Participatory Design to play a key role in supporting societal changes at 
multiple levels.
The changing circumstances also call for expanding, or even diversifying, how we conceptual-
ise Participatory Design across a plurality of contexts, epistemologies and worlds. While remaining 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
10
truthful to its core values and principles of mutual learning and emancipation of unheard voices, 
contemporary Participatory Design is moving towards redefining some of these core values to 
embrace new actionable agendas for the future. With our four participatory agendas in mind we 
characterise and propose the following definition for contemporary Participatory Design:
Participatory Design is a dynamic practice concerned with principles of equity, aiming at en-
suring openness, inclusion and agency in decision-making processes. By actively engaging 
marginalised voices as well as human and more-than-human actors, Participatory Design 
collaboratively shapes everyday environments and technologies through an exploration of 
alternative futures. Leveraging a range of methods, tools and techniques to support engage-
ment across diverse contexts, experiences and knowledges, Participatory Design engages 
diverse actors in collective reflective practice, situated interventions and inquiries to ulti -
mately work towards sustainable local and global transformations.
This definition seeks to include fundamental concerns of the field and calls for action at the basis 
of current complex societal and planetary conditions. If we incorporate and foreground the four 
agendas described earlier, we can elaborate the definition further as follows:
Participatory Design embraces concerns of power inequalities through collaboration with 
affected actors, as well as those excluded by design processes and technologies. By doing 
so, Participatory Design fosters equity, agency and self-determination in decision-making 
(politicising). Working across contexts, regions as well as human and more-than-human 
actors, technologies and domains, Participatory Design adapts practices and methodolo -
gies to diverse knowledges and lifeworlds ( diversifying). Participatory Design articulates 
participation through the interconnectedness and coexistence across the globe among 
researchers, participants and other actors, through relational and caring approaches ( re-
lationality). Participatory Design addresses shifting societal challenges and aims for 
impact across multiple arenas and scales through strong participatory practices that sup-
port the ambitions, needs and sustainable futures of collectives, societies and the planet 
(transforming).
The agendas included in the previous definition, we argue, articulate core concerns of contempo-
rary Participatory Design that are addressed in rich and inspiring ways throughout this book. The 
authors explore such concerns while articulating contemporary themes and trajectories for Partici-
patory Design in the context of their chapters.
Contemporary Themes and Trajectories
The chapters in this handbook review and reflect on key themes of contemporary Participatory De-
sign practice that have emerged globally in the past decade alongside the discourse on the nature of 
participatory practice. These themes connect to and across other fields, from human–computer in-
teraction to interaction design, design research, informatics, design anthropology, architecture and 
beyond. The chapters offer comprehensive literature reviews of relevant contributions published 
in the past decade from the biennial Participatory Design proceedings (PDC 2012–PDC 2022) as 
well as international journals and ACM proceedings from the conferences on Human Factors in 
Computing Systems, Computer Supported Cooperative Work, Interaction Design and Children, 
Design Research Society, Designing Interactive Systems, and Communities and Technologies, to 

Contemporary Participatory Design
11
name but a few. Additionally, literature reviews include recent volumes, special issues and journal 
and conference papers addressing specific Participatory Design issues (see complete list in the 
section ‘Further Reading’). In two main sections, the 13 chapters offer state-of-the-art surveys of 
particular themes and strands within Participatory Design. In this regard, they serve as starting 
points for engaging further with the field.
Section I: Contemporary Participatory Design
Section I articulates the past ten years of Participatory Design research through the lens of key 
themes and through the voices of Participatory Design researchers and practitioners working at the 
core of this development and evolution across a wide and diverse range of organisations and aca-
demic institutions. Each chapter is dedicated to one key theme and provides an academic review of 
the state-of-the-art in contemporary Participatory Design, framed within the perspectives of core 
researchers in the field: scaling (Chapter 2); collectives (Chapter 3); sustainability (Chapter 4); 
decolonisation (Chapter 5); emerging technologies (Chapter 6); new approaches (Chapter 7); and 
beyond academia (Chapter 8). Each of the chapters includes examples of contemporary research 
and demonstrates how new and ongoing themes, connected to core aspects of Participatory De -
sign, are being translated into novel approaches, methods and tools that are part of advancing 
participatory research and practice.
Chapter 2, Scaling Participatory Design, explores the challenges and experiences of scaling 
Participatory Design. The authors overview and reflect on four case studies and offer a conceptual 
framework for how to approach scaling in Participatory Design. Specifically, two key framings 
are discussed – socio-spatial and temporal – alongside key reflections on how the diversification 
of Participatory Design across geographies complicates the socio-spatial and temporal framings of 
both scale and scaling. The authors also discuss how the challenges of scaling are a matter of in -
creasing complexity in Participatory Design research and practice. Countering the general notion 
that ‘most Participatory Design projects are small scale’, this chapter highlights how scaling has 
been explored within Participatory Design from its inception. Moreover, the authors demonstrate 
the need for diverse forms, nuanced concepts and frameworks of scaling, as participatory design-
ers contend with the complexities of the world and diverse forms of scaling become intertwined. 
Readers are encouraged to draw inspiration from the cases presented and consider issues of scale 
in their own engagements with Participatory Design.
In Chapter 3, Collectives and Participatory Design, the authors explore how Participatory De-
sign has supported the formation and organisation of collectives, with an emphasis on urban, 
suburban and rural environments and close attention to their politics. The term ‘collectives’ is here 
used to underline the complexity of human and more-than-human actors (i.e. parts of lifeworlds, 
such as trees, birds, technologies or buildings). Building on previous work in community-based 
Participatory Design, the authors discuss how moving outside organisational settings can affect 
concepts such as collectives, infrastructuring, commoning and institutioning – and their many 
ramifications. Participatory Design’s general interest in the formation and organisation of collec -
tives can be traced to its engagements with complex realities in urban, suburban and rural environ-
ments. In these contexts, Participatory Design processes are dealing with contested issues such 
as mobility or migration, which calls for solidarity and for collective understanding and actions. 
Participatory Design researchers have therefore strengthened their capabilities to experiment and 
work with the diverse experiences and worldviews of collectives on key matters in urban, sub -
urban and rural contexts, while building upon Participatory Design’s political ethos informed by 
discourses in agonism.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
12
Chapter 4, More-Than-Human Participatory Design , explores the different philosophical 
and political underpinnings of Participatory Design to rethink relations and be more mindful 
of material consumption, given that life on the earth will continue to be greatly impacted by the 
decisions we make now about technologies and design. The authors unpack the intellectual tradi -
tions of Participatory Design work with an emphasis on sustainability, from the perspective of 
the innately interdependent and entangled nature of the world we live in. The chapter discusses 
how, for all their focus on inclusivity and democratic practice, Participatory Design practition -
ers too are challenged by rapid transformations and increasing uncertainty For instance, while 
technological progress is predicated on the availability of carbon-neutral energy, renewables cur -
rently depend on mining of not readily available minerals, causing perils (e.g. pollution, habitat 
loss, modern-day slavery
1) that destabilise the environment further. The reader is challenged to 
question whether continuing to focus on immediate problems is the way forward or whether we 
should instead acknowledge a radically changed landscape and shift design theories and practice 
to be fit for a changed purpose.
Chapter 5, Decolonisation and Participatory Design, presents contributions from Participa -
tory Design and decolonial movements, categorised into four strands: anticolonial, postcolonial, 
decolonial and pluriversal. The authors demonstrate how designers and researchers in diverse 
global contexts are working with and adapting modes, concepts, methodologies, and sensibilities 
into Participatory Design practices. A number of exemplary cases are reviewed to demonstrate, 
at different levels of practice, how new methodological and theoretical contributions to the field 
of Participatory Design can be developed. The authors argue that understanding decoloniality and 
Participatory Design requires extended temporal and spatial frames and offer researchers a lens 
to engage with possible pasts/presents/futures of such concerns, in support of sovereignty and 
self-determination of future making. The chapter encourages the Participatory Design commu -
nity to continue following a relational decolonisation agenda in which introspection, challenging 
hegemonies and taking responsibilities in situated actions become part of a wider decolonisation 
movement.
In Chapter 6, Emerging Technologies and Alternative Futures, the authors provide a review of 
contemporary discourses between Participatory Design and current emerging technologies (e.g. 
artificial intelligence, large-language models, immersive media). They investigate the qualities 
of such technologies and how they are configured to produce systems of old and new forms of 
oppression. The authors argue that in the context of destabilised democracies, increasing social in-
justice, an out-of-bounds surveillance capitalism and the climate emergency, Participatory Design 
needs to develop meaningful and effective participation around these socio-material assemblages 
so as to offer alternatives. Through a review and analysis of contemporary Participatory Design’s 
engagement with such systems and technologies, the chapter covers ongoing themes of platforms, 
civic technologies, and democratic engagements with communities, as well as recent work on 
artificial intelligence and automation. Finally, the authors contribute four trajectories for future 
Participatory Design research and practice. These target novel methodologies that can engage 
with pervasive systems of scale, with the ultimate objective of rekindling Participatory Design’s 
commitment to be involved in the creation of emerging technologies and configurations of just 
and sustainable futures.
Chapter 7, New Approaches, Methods and Techniques, describes new trends and develop -
ments as well as more specific methods and techniques that can support the practice of Partici -
patory Design. The literature review exposes three overall trends: first, a shift from a focus on 
initial design and development processes to including the appropriation and reconfiguration of 

Contemporary Participatory Design
13
technologies and use practices that follow after the initial implementation; second, an expansion 
of Participatory Design approaches to adjacent research areas and communities, influencing the 
development of new approaches, methods and techniques; and third, internationalisation beyond 
Western and modernist traditions, enriching the field through new and contrasting approaches 
for decolonial Participatory Design practice and research. The chapter concludes by summaris -
ing the opportunities and challenges that the trends identified open up to inspire future research. 
This, in conjunction with two other chapters from the 2013 Participatory Design Handbook (on 
methods as well as on techniques and tools), provides an authoritative overview for the reader 
of approaches, methods and techniques used in the field since the Participatory Design research 
area was established.
Chapter 8, Participatory Design Beyond Academia , focuses on participatory practice 
in non-academic contexts.The chapter discusses three themes central to the past decade of 
non-academic Participatory Design practice. First is the critical impact of context  on prac -
titioners’ ability to fully apply Participatory Design; second is key aspects surrounding the 
work itself (methods, strategy, tactics and logistics); and third is the implications of Par -
ticipatory Design as a Western practice seen alongside emerging work at the intersection of 
Indigenous and Participatory Design practices. In overviewing the historical tensions that 
exist between academic and industry Participatory Design , the authors suggest that owing to 
terminology divergence and the academisation of Participatory Design, deeply participatory 
practices and work have been largely excluded from academic-led communities. Additionally, 
they suggest that new ways are urgently needed to describe the plethora of non-academic 
participatory practices that have emerged over the past decade. The chapter proposes that 
new metrics would provide opportunities to recognise and invite in a broader set of practices, 
one that would provide legitimacy to under-recognised non-academic Participatory Design 
approaches.
Section II: Exemplary Participatory Design
Section II introduces exemplary Participatory Design initiatives that demonstrate and unpack the 
various ways in which contemporary trajectories and practices have developed in academic as well 
as industrial and public/private contexts. These chapters highlight work that demonstrates practi -
cal, large-scale applications of Participatory Design awarded with the Artful Integrators Award 
(see http://pdcproceedings.org) at the Participatory Design Conferences over the past decade. This 
award is given to projects and initiatives nominated and recognised by the community as outstand-
ing achievements in exceptionally creative co-designing of new configurations of technologies 
and practices. Chapters in Section II include cases on dementia cultures (Chapter 9), living labs 
(Chapters 10 and 12), reconciliation (Chapter 11) and teaching (Chapter 13) that demonstrate how 
Participatory Design is configured and practised across situated contexts and scales. In what fol -
lows, we provide an overview of all the chapters and how they connect across themes, challenges 
and trajectories for contemporary Participatory Design.
Opening the second section of the handbook, in Chapter 9, Co-Designing Dementia Culture(s), 
the authors share two case studies on design with dementia in two different cultural contexts 
of Belgium and Hong Kong. They raise fundamental questions about target groups and how to 
engage them and about how to highlight key aspects of designing participatory experiences, in -
cluding the challenges of ensuring full participation. Authors advocate the integration of lived 
experiences into the design for co-creating dementia-friendly cultures. The Belgian case describes 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
14
a shift from focusing on participation to prioritising relationship-building and human connec -
tions, discussing four key aspects: long-term embedded work, prioritising human connection 
over design identity, viewing participation as a process, and adapting to specific situations. The 
Hong Kong case defines three stages: design by people living with dementia that can leverage 
insights from direct experiences, co-design with service providers and students to create innova -
tive services and public-focused design to raise awareness. Spanning social activism and academic 
application – both these cases aim to influence the lives of those affected by dementia and their 
loved ones’ supporters, impacting various stages from societal debate to redefining participation 
in social innovation and higher education.
Chapter 10, Collective Capabilities in Living Labs, focuses on a living lab in Genk, Belgium, 
created after the shutdown of its mining and manufacturing industries, to explore alternative ap -
proaches for the city to transition its urban landscape. Founded with the goal of re-politicising the 
conversation on this evolving work landscape, the project started with a series of soft interventions 
to understand the local context and actors and create awareness of the researchers and their agenda. 
The authors discuss their work mapping the capabilities of the people of Genk to shift the focus 
from the loss of jobs to highlighting how existing capabilities could support collective transition 
in the socio-environmental landscape. The chapter shows how such techniques helped reach a 
better understanding of the rich and complex interdependencies between human capabilities and 
more-than-human actors in shaping past, current and future landscapes. The authors discuss their 
work shaping and using such interdependencies into collective capabilities to articulate and pro -
totype alternative work and living spaces in Genk – and how the approach was extended to other 
urban, suburban and rural contexts.
Chapter 11, Reconciliation Through Digital Textiles , provides a critical reflection on the 
geopolitics of knowledge mobilisation. The interdisciplinary research project presented was 
carried out by a consortium of researchers from Colombia and the United Kingdom working 
with women’s textile collectives in four different rural areas of Colombia. The project aimed to 
generate connections among the collectives and to understand their use of textiles as a language 
of memory and care for life in wartime. The authors describe their participatory techniques 
and discuss how the use of digital technologies to engage participants in unusual material dia -
logues triggered challenging conversations from new perspectives about armed conflict, peace 
and reconciliation. They discuss how awareness of the politics of knowledge production and 
mobilisation within Global North–Global South research collaborations brings a set of criti -
cal challenges that, while not necessarily new, reconfigures what counts as participation, who 
participates and how.
Chapter 12, Living Labs for Open-Ended Participatory Design , focuses on the experiences 
of living labs in Malmö, Sweden, exploring how processes of change and collaborative work -
ing relations in the city of Malmö could be further democratised. Inspired by Umberto Eco’s 
metaphor of the forest as a narrative place of potential transformation, through a series of 
‘Wanderings’ as a community of remembrance, the authors recall and revitalise memories of 
engagements and experiments not previously told, making a big imprint on all the Participatory 
Design researchers involved. Intersecting with these reflective stories, the authors also revisit 
core living lab characteristics, as well as concepts of labour, infrastructuring and heterogene -
ity that can provide sensitive encouragement through artful practices in long-term open-ended 
Participatory Design.
The final chapter, Chapter 13, Teaching Participatory Design, is written for scholars who may 
be teaching Participatory Design for the first time but have an understanding of, and possibly 
concrete experiences in, Participatory Design work. The authors place a strong emphasis on the 

Contemporary Participatory Design
15
need to base the teaching of Participatory Design on the continuous combination of practice and 
reflection. They argue that students can and should engage in ‘real’ Participatory Design processes 
outside the classroom. The chapter contributes to the development of a pedagogical framework for 
teaching Participatory Design. The authors centre teaching practice on two pedagogical modes: 
mutual learning and reflection-in-action. They highlight three main aspects central to teaching 
Participatory Design: (1) support students’ awareness of the relevance of the social dimension 
and engage them in reflection on related issues while promoting critical thinking; (2) provide 
guidelines for considering materiality aspects in the facilitation of workshops, as well as providing 
opportunities to practise and combine practice with reflection; and (3) guide students in analysing 
Participatory Design outputs, a complex, frequently overlooked critical practice. The chapter ends 
with an annex that provides nine case examples of teaching Participatory Design to bachelors, 
masters and PhD students as well as to practitioners engaged in NGOs and living labs.
Taken together, the 13 chapters of this handbook provide an extensive overview of the diverse 
engagements, challenges and trajectories of contemporary Participatory Design. They demonstrate 
richly how the field is engaging with dynamic and complex challenges across multiple disciplines, 
contexts, technologies and scales.
Audience
This handbook is intended for anyone who is active as a researcher, practitioner, or educational 
professional in the field of Participatory Design and wants to dive deeper into the histories, cur -
rent practices and potential futures of emerging themes in the past decade. At the same time, it 
is intended for anyone who is not currently familiar with the field but is interested to know more 
about the field of Participatory Design and how this field has developed recently. This focus aligns 
with the first handbook yet does so from a perspective on contemporary Participatory Design. It 
is specifically aimed at:
• Young researchers looking for a scholarly handbook on contemporary Participatory Design. 
The chapters in Section I describe and review the most important themes of Participatory De -
sign of the past decade. Each chapter is concluded by an outline of current challenges and 
opportunities as an inspiration for further research. Section II presents multiple Participatory 
Design projects from the past decade – all of which were awarded the Artful Integrators Award 
as representing outstanding exemplary research initiatives.
• Senior researchers interested in an updated reference handbook that supplements the 2013 
Handbook, by reviewing the Participatory Design literature along the themes that have un -
folded during the past decade. The book is designed to make this contemporary literature 
available for teaching advanced bachelors, graduate, or doctoral courses. Section II includes a 
chapter focusing on teaching Participatory Design.
• Practitioners who use, or aim to use, participatory approaches in their design practice. The 
book presents an updated overview of theoretical, methodological and technical trends. This 
includes theoretical issues related to sustainability (Chapter 4), new methodological approaches 
(Chapter 7) and emerging technologies (Chapter 6). Chapter 8 is written specifically for and 
by practitioners with a dedicated focus on how participatory practices unfold in non-academic 
contexts.
In the following, we provide resources for engaging further with the field, history and global com-
munity of Participatory Design. We hope they inspire you to participate.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
16
Further Reading
Participatory Design is a well-established, widespread and inclusive area of research and practice. 
The Participatory Design research community has, ever since the 1990s, met at the biennial in-
ternational PDCs. Participatory Design is also represented in many other local and international 
conferences, as well as in a number of books and special journal issues. For those who wish to 
know more about Participatory Design, we have provided a list of further reading, as well as a full 
list of the Participatory Design conferences (and their themes) from 1990 up to 2024. All confer -
ence proceedings from 1990 are accessible from pdcproceedings.org. That website also contains 
an updated list of other Participatory Design literature, links to PhD courses and information from 
the PDC Advisory Board.
