SECTION I
Contemporary Participatory Design 



   
2
SCALING PARTICIPATORY 
DESIGN
Claus Bossen, Reem Talhouk and John Vines 
This chapter explores the challenges and experiences of scaling Participatory Design. The chapter first 
discusses the notion of “scaling” and what that might mean for Participatory Design by presenting 
how different researchers have explicitly conceptualised “scale” in their work. There are very diverse 
understandings of what “scaling” may mean, and though it is often expressed as an important concern, 
definitions of scaling are often missing and only occasionally go beyond a “small and simple” and 
“large and complex” dichotomy. The chapter presents four contributions that more extensively deal 
with scaling and propose conceptual frameworks for how to approach scaling in Participatory Design. 
Subsequently, two dominant framings of scaling Participatory Design: Socio-spatial and temporal are 
presented. This is then followed by a discussion of the ways through which the diversification of 
Participatory Design across geographies – termed as onto-epistemological scaling – complicates the 
socio-spatial and temporal framings of scale and scaling. Finally, the chapter discusses how the chal-
lenges of scaling are a matter of increasing complexities in Participatory Design research and practice.
Overall, the chapter shows that scaling has been explored within Participatory Design from its 
inception in many publications thus countering the notion that “most Participatory Design projects are 
small scale”. We demonstrate how each form of scaling intertwines with one another as Participatory 
Design contends with the complexity of our world(s). In doing so we highlight the need to develop 
nuanced concepts and frameworks of scaling to consolidate the present somewhat dispersed contribu-
tions to this topic.
Readers will learn about different meanings and framings of scaling, including socio-spatial and 
temporal ones, and how this is complicated by onto-epistemological scaling. Further, readers will learn 
about conceptual frameworks for understanding scaling and a variety of cases from which inspiration 
and experiences can be gathered for considering issues of scale in their own engagements with scaling 
of Participatory Design projects.
  DOI: 10.4324/9781003334330-3

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
28
Introduction
Over the last decade, there has been a growing recognition that Participatory Design methods and 
practices are being widely adopted. However, alongside this proliferation questions have been raised 
regarding the scaling of Participatory Design. It is often suggested that Participatory Design projects 
engage at small scales, in local contexts, and that the research and practice community lacks exam-
ples of large-scale Participatory Design work. Why Participatory Design continues to be labelled as 
primarily “small scale” is an open question. It could be related to “large-scale” studies being scat-
tered across various publication venues and a lack of comprehensive overviews. However, it could 
also be related to the multiplicity of how scale is understood and framed within Participatory Design.
This chapter speaks to the latter as it attempts to frame “scale” and “scaling” within Participa-
tory Design. We set out to highlight that, despite the age-old impression that Participatory Design 
is primarily for small-scale, localised, highly time-bound and context-specific projects, there is 
a growing body of work that is moving the field beyond this and in doing so responding to the 
complexities of our world(s).
We start the chapter by discussing how different researchers in the Participatory Design com -
munity have explicitly conceptualised “scale” in their work. We note that there are very diverse 
understandings of what “scaling” may mean within Participatory Design and how, outside of a 
small number of more seminal works, “scale” is often expressed as an important concern but one 
that is also often lacking definition and has multiple framings. Following this initial overview of 
scaling, we discuss the more dominant understandings of scale that are appearing in the literature, 
and which shaped each of our understandings of scale as we started to write this chapter.
First, we explore examples of socio-spatial scaling, where scale is understood as moving beyond 
initial projects groups and where the practices, outcomes and results transfer to new communities, 
organisations and places. With this, scale involves increasing the complicities of engagement, 
participation and cooperation across more settings, stakeholders and technologies.
Second, we go through examples of temporal scaling, where Participatory Design is concep -
tualised as evolving over timescales between interconnected activities and initiatives. Viewing 
Participatory Design as an ongoing and durational practice highlights how knowledge from Par -
ticipatory Design projects diffuses to other projects over time, and how long-term engagements 
involve working with different participants and stakeholders through a variety of activities.
Third, we bring attention to how onto-epistemological scaling through the diversification of 
Participatory Design, and specifically the Participatory Design community of researchers and 
practitioners, across various geographies and the coexistance of multiple worlds complicate the 
socio-spatial and temporal framings of scale.
Finally, we conclude the chapter by discussing how notions of scale in general can be seen as 
instances of how Participatory Design pursues complexity.
Scaling Participatory Design
From the beginning, Participatory Design dealt with scaling, both in the sense of building a re -
search community (e.g. the first Participatory Design Conference (PDC) in 1980 bringing together 
researchers from Europe and the USA) as well as integrating Participatory Design in “large-scale” 
projects and organisations (e.g. Grudin, 1990; Bødker, 1996). More recently, Roland and Sanner 
(2017) argue that in a context fraught with large-scale information technology systems, the condi-
tions for small-scale prototype-based approaches are increasingly difficult. They conclude that 
“To remain relevant, Participatory Design needs to find ways to accommodate more distributed 

Scaling Participatory Design
29
development settings . . . and interplay with complex and evolving ecosystems of ICT capabilities” 
(Roland and Sanner, 2017, p. 4) (for a similar argument, see Bødker and Kyng, 2018).
The scaling of Participatory Design has been addressed by many papers, yet, as this chapter 
will show, the discussion still has to stabilise around a framework or set of core concepts. A central 
challenge is that scaling has different forms and meanings depending on what we think of as the 
ingredients of Participatory Design. Often, scaling Participatory Design implies a concern for how 
to involve persons beyond the initial project group where typically people meet face-to-face and 
engage in mutual learning and co-design. For example, how can mutual learning and providing 
users with competencies to make active choices with respect to technology and new work practices 
be scaled beyond workshops and the groups most actively involved in a project? Or, how can new 
technologies and practices developed in small project groups be transferred into the larger organi-
sation or even other organisations?
Already in 1990, Grudin (1990) pointed out the difficulties of diffusing Participatory Design in 
large software development organisations; software developers were structurally separated from 
end-users who were the responsibility of other divisions such as sales, marketing and customer 
support. Grudin was optimistic though, because “the forces in development companies that work 
systematically against user involvement undermine product optimization and success” (Grudin, 1990, 
p. 20). Similarly, Bødker (1996) pointed out the necessity to “spread the collective experiences of 
participation beyond those directly involved in the project” (p.  233) to spur individual as well as 
collective learning. Bødker also pointed to the challenge of handling different interests in organi -
sations, for example between management and employees. A different kind of early scaling was 
seen in the DUE
1 project (1977–1980) where courses for up to 500 union members were offered 
every year for over 10 years (Bødker, 1996).
Thus, scaling has been understood in different ways with Participatory Design: Spreading a de-
signed artefact and accompanying work practices from a small project group to the larger organi-
sation or to other organisations, settings and geographical places; extending mutual learning and 
involving a larger group of people; addressing and attending to different interests and values; and 
spreading knowledge and competences with others. Additionally, scaling can concern sustaining 
Participatory Design results and aims beyond project time (Simone et al., 2022). If we include the 
proliferation of Participatory Design results through, for example, the spread and implementation 
of technologies that increase people’s ability to act (Bratteteig and Wagner, 2016), then yet another 
aspect of scaling is added.
Many Participatory Design publications apply a distinction between small- and large-scale  
without exact definition but implicitly point to a difference between projects that are relatively 
“simple” and involve “fewer” people, stakeholders and technologies than more “complex” ones 
(e.g. Clement and Van den Besselaar, 1993; Oostveen and van den Besselaar, 2004). Here scaling 
seems to be a question of numbers of people as well as increasing social and technological complex-
ity. Other papers make more explicit distinctions. For example, a distinction between geographical 
scaling – pointing to the extension of projects organisationally and geographically – and temporal 
scaling – where projects are extended in time (Blomberg and Karasti, 2013). Other distinctions have 
been made between: maintaining – carrying on initiatives beyond project time; scaling-up – con-
cerns the small- to large-scale distinction; replication – where initiatives are replicated in new set-
tings; and evolving – the continuous development beyond project time (Iversen and Dindler, 2014). 
Maintaining and evolving point attention to the temporal scaling of Participatory Design and at -
tentiveness to processes beyond “project time”, which is the subject of the section “Socio-Spatial 
Scaling”. Addressing scale in the related field of human–computer interaction, Brown et al. (2017) 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
30
distinguish between the number of users, the different contexts of use and the multitude of systems 
and technologies. Criticising the association of scale with size, growth, numbers and the logic of 
business, Larsen-Ledet et al. (2022) argue for “un-scaling computing”. Instead, they propose differ-
ent concepts: Proliferation stresses how ideas and designs travel through learning and collaboration 
between communities or locations; scalar trajectories point to how designs travel across locations 
through creative sharing; and meshing directs attention to how relations and locality may evolve 
to go together to become a whole more than its parts. Instead of size and numbers, they argue for a 
focus on the processes of learning, sharing and community building. Finally, Zahlsen et al. (2022a) 
propose that large-scale information technology projects should include at least one of five features: 
“Distribution across heterogeneous settings, a variety of stakeholders involved (e.g. multiple user 
groups), multiple stakeholder organizations, and different uses of a software product over time. 
Large-scale projects typically have a duration of several years” (Zahlsen et al., 2022a, p. 144).
Overall, then, there are a number of partially overlapping and orthogonal ways in which to con-
ceptualise what it means for Participatory Design to scale. However, research publications are rarely 
explicit about what aspects of a Participatory Design initiative are being scaled. To cut through the 
various ways in which to think of scale and avoid long conceptual and theoretical dissections, we 
have honed in on two understandings of scale: socio-spatial and temporal. However, before moving 
into these, we present four of the few works that go into more detailed conceptualisations of scaling 
(namely: Gärtner and Wagner, 1996; Roland et al., 2017; Simone et al., 2022; Zahlsen et al., 2022a).
Conceptualisations of Scaling
Gärtner and Wagner (1996) combine actor-network theory and symbolic interactionism and aim to un-
derstand the different organisational and political contexts in which design and participation take place. 
Both approaches reject a notion of micro- and macro sociology and hence the notion of small- and 
large scale. Instead, they focus on networks that may have different reaches and are constituted by and 
through relations between technologies, artefacts and human actors. To ground systems design in space 
and time, Gärtner and Wagner introduce the notion of a social arena to designate a place where “actors 
meet to discuss shared or overlapping projects and concerns” (Gärtner and Wagner, 1996, p. 192) and 
which can exist within or across organisations. Arena A is where specific designs are developed, arena 
B is where agreements around productivity and labour conditions are negotiated and arena C is where 
legal and political issues are negotiated. Scaling in this approach is hence about networks and their 
extension and about how different design issues are discussed in different arenas. The approach enables 
both analyses of how participatory structures differ between and are interlinked with other social are-
nas, and it is suggested as a tool through which actors can position themselves and craft future actions 
(Gärtner and Wagner, 1996, p. 209). The main message is that “taking politics seriously in systems 
design requires designers not only to analyse existing actor networks but ultimately to redesign them in 
ways that help establish and maintain participatory structures” (Gärtner and Wagner, 1996, p. 212). A 
conclusion that resonates with Bødker et al. (2017)’s more recent notion of “knotworking”, establishing 
and maintaining relationships within and without projects (Bødker et al., 2017).
More recently, Roland et al. (2017) develop a four-fold typology to analyse their Health In -
formation Systems Project that started out as a custom-made desktop application in one setting 
and over 20 years developed to become a modular web-based platform used globally in more 
than 50 countries. Singular Participatory Design  is a small development project with close in -
teraction between users and developers. Serial is a process of interactions between local innova-
tions in local settings and the continuous development of standards. Parallel is characterised by 
the development in parallel of designs in multiple projects leading to the formation of generic 

Scaling Participatory Design
31
structures. Finally, Community designates projects where a community negotiates design through 
power users and domain experts at workshops and meetings (Roland et al., 2017, p. 9). For each 
of the four types they describe (1) the typical “politics of design” of how users are empow -
ered; (2) the “nature of participation” of how users–developer interaction is facilitated and how 
user interests can be accommodated; and (3) the “Participatory Design techniques” that facilitate 
participant-led design. They distinguish between design flexibility  and use flexibility  referring, 
respectively, to the ability to incorporate new designs in the future and redesign a system locally. 
Web-based platforms are scalable and layered software architectures that enable both forms of 
flexibility and are hence an opportune way to pursue large-scale Participatory Design, they argue. 
The challenges are diverse: the logistics of enabling meetings between distributed users, develop-
ers and stakeholders; catering to new users and allowing them to adapt software in unforeseen 
ways; incorporating yet new users into an existing system; and the technical challenge of pro -
viding user and design flexibility. Whereas Gärtner and Wagner (1996) point to heterogeneous 
networks, Roland et al. (2017) point to different processual models and different kinds of means 
to facilitate participation.
Zahlsen et al. (2022a) recently conducted a systematic literature review of scaling in Partici-
patory Design and included 17 papers from which they derived seven categories of challenges: 
“(1) Involving users, (2) Ensuring continuous user engagement, (3) Handling user heterogeneity, 
(4) Capturing and utilizing insights, (5) Applying participatory methods, (6) Acquiring appropriate 
project conditions for Participatory Design, and (7) Maintaining democratic control” (Zahlsen et al.,  
2022a, p. 146). They define six guiding principles of Participatory Design: equalising power rela-
tions, democratic practices, situation-based actions, mutual learning, developing tools and tech -
niques and promoting alternative visions about technology. These six principles are then used as 
lenses through which to discuss the challenges of scaling in Participatory Design. They see the six 
guiding principles as interlinked and conclude somewhat pessimistically that the challenges “raises 
serious concerns about PD’s ability to scale and remain true to its heritage . . . there is a consider-
able risk of watering down the principles while scaling up to a point where the Participatory Design 
ideology in a project is no longer recognizable” (Zahlsen et al., 2022a, p. 151).
Finally, an elaborate engagement with scaling is presented in Simone et al. (2022)’s book on 
“Future-Proofing”. in which they propose a comprehensive framework for achieving sustainabil -
ity of design solutions. To Iversen et al.’s (2012) categories of maintaining, scaling, replicating, 
and evolving they add two additional categories; “discontinued” and “(Still) open”. Discontinued 
means that an initiative even though promising did not go on for some reason, while “(Still) 
open” indicates that an initiative’s sustainability is uncertain and may require more cycles of 
development. Further, they suggest a framework for how to work with sustainability in which 
important elements to take into consideration are the type of innovation (social innovation, in -
novation of practices, large technical innovations); the often-invisible work of creating alliances 
with various stakeholders and taking the context of the project into consideration; and ensuring 
continuous financial funding. Further, for a design solution to be sustained it must be appropri -
ated, which entails that capacity building and learning processes for use and maintenance of the 
solution must be in place. The technological solution itself must have qualities of robustness, 
malleability, tailorability and ongoing ownership to be sustainable. Roland et al. (2017) and Si -
mone et al. (2022) are presently the most elaborate and recent frameworks for scaling.
Overall, the literature on scaling is still relatively new and often not organised around specific 
frameworks or concepts. To navigate through this literature, we will focus on the two overriding 
ways of framing scale in the Participatory Design literature in the following sections: socio-spatial 
scaling and temporal scaling.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
32
Socio-Spatial Scaling
In the following, we discuss scaling as a matter of extending, moving between or establishing 
social networks which most often entails matters of space, since social actors can be distributed 
closely or widely across space. We have organised this into five themes that we present as we go 
through them.
Extending a Project to an Organisation at Large
This theme concerns how to spread Participatory Design from a temporary, stable small part of 
an already organised social network (e.g. a project group) to a network at large (e.g. an organisa -
tion). Bødker (1996) addressed this challenge by offering learning workshops available to all in 
the organisation, easy access to prototypes, a newsletter, allocating resources to employees outside 
of the project and handling conflicts. Closely related, Iversen and Dindler (2014) describe their 
experiences from a project at a primary school where they started out working with sixth graders 
but aimed to involve the whole school from first to ninth grade (Iversen and Dindler, 2014). They 
identify four main concerns: (1) engaging key stakeholders; (2) creating visibility and accessibility 
of Participatory Design activities at the school level; (3) supporting the fertilisation of Participa-
tory Design outcomes; and (4) opening up for general critique (Iversen and Dindler, 2014, p. 162). 
The means for achieving this was the creation of a core group of teachers that could pioneer the 
Participatory Design initiative to colleagues and pupils, and conducting workshops visibly in com-
mon areas of the school and thus opening up for teachers and pupils in general to interact with and 
comment upon the activities.
Working Within Large Organisations
In an almost inverse of the previous scenario, conducting Participatory Design in large-scale or -
ganisations is about how to facilitate engagement with an extensive, organised network through 
temporary events. This has been explored especially in the context of public organisations and 
healthcare. One interesting case is that of a public library in a city in Denmark (Dalsgaard, 2010). 
The library was developed over a long period from 2005 to 2015 and the researchers became in -
volved when the issue of how to integrate interactive technologies in the building emerged. This 
led to a series of “participatory events involving citizens, experts, cooperation partners, networks, 
employees and other interested parties” (Dalsgaard, 2010, p.  24). The challenges the researchers 
met were summarised as managing a heterogeneous group of stakeholders and end-users, inform-
ing stakeholders, establishing participation as a relevant activity, developing new techniques and 
technologies to scaffold participation and the interplay between iterative development and insti -
tutional transformation (Dalsgaard, 2010). From the perspective of the managers involved, the 
challenges were listed as time and resources; developing the techniques and skills for facilitating 
participation; understanding decision-making processes and analysing input from participatory 
events (Dalsgaard and Eriksson, 2013). The library staff found the process of participation moti -
vating and they learned about and practised design thinking, but some were so frustrated by the 
openness of the process and the vagueness of goals that they opted out of the project (Dindler 
et al., 2016) (for another library case, see Hyysalo and Hyysalo, 2018).
Within healthcare, Simonsen and Hertzum (2012) worked with a regional healthcare organi -
sation and an electronic health record (EHR) vendor to evaluate the implementation of an EHR 
module at a stroke unit. The researchers facilitated collaboration, developed and refined the Par -
ticipatory Design approach and investigated the early use of the EHR module. Based on their 

Scaling Participatory Design
33
experiences, they characterise the challenges as revolving around: (1) establishing conditions for 
doing Participatory Design such as a mutual understanding, (2) managing stakeholder interests, 
(3) handling an iterative implementation process, and finally (4) conducting realistic Participatory 
Design experiments that fed into further development. They suggest that to go large-scale Partici-
patory Design needs to go beyond traditional prototyping and instead evaluate systems exposed 
to real work practices and engage in improvisational change management and stepwise imple -
mentations constituting overall technology-driven organisational change. Also, in the context of 
large-scale EHR implementation, Zahlsen et al. (2022b) point to how a project’s structure shapes 
the conditions for user involvement. In their case, users shifted from being user representatives 
to becoming participants-as-technocrats – that is, technical experts, in this case within medical 
specialties – supporting the progression of system development (Zahlsen et al., 2022b).
Finally, the work of Pilemalm and Timpka (2008) should be mentioned. Based on a large-scale 
project to develop an information system to augment peer-to-peer empowerment for the Swedish 
labour union and its 175,000 local representatives, they suggest a three-phased model for what 
they refer to as “third generation Participatory Design” based on action research and Participatory 
Design. Their three-phased model includes pre-design, Participatory Design and post-design and 
details specific activities for each phase (Pilemalm and Timpka, 2008) (reflecting a “phasic” Par-
ticipatory Design conceptualisation; see the section “Temporal Scaling”).
Community Participatory Design
Whereas the former two themes concern Participatory Design within stable, organised social net-
works, the subfield of community Participatory Design, deals with more fluid social networks 
that present different challenges to scaling than have been detailed above. Not all communities 
are stably organised with clear spokespersons and members, and often they are loosely organised 
regarding membership, leadership, hierarchies, division of work and decision-making. Addition-
ally, their resources are often scarce with regard to money, places to meet and time (see, e.g., 
Carroll and Rosson, 2007). Since communities are diverse and can be based on location, shared 
identity or interests, community Participatory Design may take many forms (DiSalvo et al., 2013). 
A core learning in community Participatory Design is that it is a central and continuous process 
to establish and maintain relationships, negotiate roles, discuss ethics and aims, acquire resources 
and sustain results. Challenges that are much less in established organisations (for reviews of com-
munity Participatory Design, see (Klerks et al., 2020) and (Cooper et al., 2022).
Another learning is that conventional methods in Europe and North America such as work-
shops, interviews and cultural probes may not be adequate or work in other settings and might 
rather undermine and exclude, rather than empower, participants who are historically and pres -
ently marginalised and silenced (e.g. Harrington et al., 2019). Yet, some scholars in the community 
Participatory Design field argue for the potential of democratic change beyond local communities, 
as in the “democratic design experiments” of Binder et al. (2015) and in DiSalvo’s “design experi-
ments in civics” (DiSalvo, 2022).
Distributed Participatory Design
Whereas community Participatory Design has to work with fluid social relations, distributed Par-
ticipatory Design works with vastly distributed participants, who primarily relate to each other 
through online platforms. This creates a challenge of how to achieve aims like mutual learning, 
co-creation and co-determination (Gumm et al., 2006).

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
34
Obendorf et al. (2009) report their experiences with user involvement in a long-time open-source 
development project working with a vastly distributed set of users. They focus on the challenge of 
building inter-contextual Participatory Design where participants are members of different com-
munities of practice. Hence, a “community of interest” had to be created to empower users to 
assess their own practices and technology use, which was done through yearly face-to-face work-
shops where participants from various locations met, and through online commenting on case 
studies that users could share (Obendorf et al., 2009).
Whereas online and face-to-face interaction is combined in some projects, other ones move 
cooperation entirely online. Hess and Pipek (2012) suggest the concept of “Community-Driven 
Development” to characterise how design with users could be conducted via online communities. 
In their case, a company wanted to develop new media centre software with the help of an existing 
online community. The community was organised into a “user parliament” consisting of users and 
user representatives that provided input to the “central committee” consisting of user representa -
tives and company representatives. Through distributed interactions, the project generated learn -
ing for both users and developers, according to Hess and Pipek. The organisation into a parliament 
and the central committee worked with some quirks, and the motivation from users was generally 
high (Hess and Pipek, 2012).
Since Hess and Pipek’s work, several projects have pursued opportunities for scaling through 
distributed forms of Participatory Design online, especially in the context of Covid-19 (For an 
overview, see Slingerland et al., 2022). Slingerland et al. (2022) supported Irish teenagers during 
COVID-19 to build relationships with each other and the community during a two-week online 
summer school. They list the do’s and don’ts of online distributed Participatory Design as the fol-
lowing: Provide strong facilitation to keep participants involved and build trust, and monitor what 
is going on; do not assume that going online requires less preparation and involvement by the 
researcher, and don’t use a platform that limits interaction (Slingerland et al., 2022, pp. 675–6; 
see also Dalsgaard et al., 2022; Gumm et al., 2006; Kautz et al., 2018; Korte et al., 2021).
Nation-Wide Initiatives
Nation-wide initiatives lie at a cross-section of the aforementioned themes: They can be seen as 
a particular instance of distributed Participatory Design as participants will be vastly distributed, 
possibly share a sense of common identity like community Participatory Design and have a range 
of established and stable resource ready through an administrative and political apparatus like 
Participatory Design in organisations.
One instance is from Canada and concerns the development of a system for documenting Ad -
verse Drug Events (ADE) and disseminating that information to local pharmacies nation-wide 
conducted by Balka and colleagues. This Participatory Design project first did a comprehensive 
survey of existing ADE reporting systems, while at the same time conducting qualitative studies 
of clinicians’ work and reporting practices. Over three funding cycles and three funding schemes, 
the project developed from prototyping on an iPad in one hospital to become connected with a 
state-wide database owned by a private company which linked that information to local pharma-
cies (still ongoing in 2022) (Simone et al., 2022, pp. 122–135). Amongst the challenges were those 
of negotiating new contracts, ownership of data, removing bureaucratic barriers, achieving actual 
rather than stated cooperation, changing stakeholders and handling new outcome requirements.
Another nation-wide project is described in a series of papers based on the FabLab@School 
project that developed an approach to teaching primary school pupils how to engage with the design 
of digital technologies (Iversen et al., 2018). The project subsequently became part of the Danish 

Scaling Participatory Design
35
Education Ministry’s trial initiative to implement a course on “Technology Comprehension” within 
43 primary schools. Aiming at providing pupils with competences within digital empowerment, de-
sign processes, computational thinking and technological skills and knowledge, the course had a 
clear Participatory Design element. Hence, in this case scaling Participatory Design was achieved 
by Participatory Design being taught in courses (see Bødker, 1996) and becoming ministerial 
policy (Smith et al., 2020). This tying-in of Participatory Design into policy aligns with the efforts 
to develop technology agreements between unions and employers’ associations (e.g. Bansler, 1989)
Summary: Many Studies on Socio-Spatial Scaling Exist
One takeaway from the previous discussion should be that the statement that “Participatory De-
sign has most often been conducted in small-scale projects” – repeated multiple times since the 
early 1990s in Participatory Design literature (see a summary in Dalsgaard et al., 2022) – needs 
to be supplemented with “and many studies of large-scale projects have been conducted as well”. 
Scaling here implies an increasing complexity socially and spatially, since an increasingly heter -
ogenous number of participants, research, management and other stakeholders have to be brought 
together without necessarily being able to rely on existing relations, structures or resources. 
Hence, building trust, establishing communication channels, managing stakeholders, handling 
multiple interests, while at the same time ensuring empowerment and mutual learning are among 
the many challenges. Approaches to resolving these challenges range from adaptations made to 
traditional workshops, increasing communication and relationship development, making activi -
ties and designs public, creating new project structures and processes and disseminating learning 
modules and courses. It has been suggested that when scaling with a socio-spatial understanding, 
Participatory Design projects should be viewed as organisational change (Pilemalm and Timpka, 
2008; Simone et al., 2022; Simonsen and Hertzum, 2012).
Temporal Scaling
As noted earlier, temporal scaling is one of the more prominent perspectives on scaling up Partici-
patory Design. Participatory Design projects have for a long time distinguished between different 
“times” within projects. This includes “before project time” (establishing the foci of a project, 
building relationships, defining shared agendas), “project time” (focused on workshops and col-
laborative prototyping) and “use time” (when a new system designed from the project is in use 
by participants and other users). Some researchers have pointed out the problems of distinguish -
ing between times in projects where things are designed and when things are used. Storni (2013) 
highlights how the simplistic characterisation of design time and use time reinforces a separation 
between design and use and, thus, designers and users. Storni’s work goes on to highlight a myriad 
of examples of where design happens through use and also how in the practice of much Participa-
tory Design work there is a messier relationship between “designing” and “using”. Echoing these 
concerns, others have highlighted the inevitable blurring of the boundaries between “times” like 
these in Participatory Design projects – for example, the idea of “use before use” or “design in 
use” or even “design after design” (Redström, 2008).
The previous discussion highlights that time and Participatory Design go together in some 
form – Participatory Design projects take time to do, and at different times in a Participatory De -
sign project different types of activities may need to be conducted.
However, time (and by association Participatory Design over timescales) has only started to 
come to more prominent attention over the years since the publication of the 2013 Participatory 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
36
Design Handbook. For instance, Vines et al. (2015), called for the Participatory Design commu-
nity to bring more attention to the “beginnings, middles and endings” of participatory processes. 
They set out to explore how Participatory Design might be “understood as a durational practice 
guided by a particular commitment and way of working over time” (Vines et al., 2015), inviting 
practitioners and researchers to reflect on projects across their lifespans. Subsequent research has 
highlighted the importance of understanding the role of relational work in developing Participa -
tory Design projects (Dindler and Iversen, 2014), the “back-stage” activities that make the “front 
stage” Participatory Design work (like workshops, prototyping) happen over time (Bødker et al., 
2017) and how to sustain Participatory Design initiatives beyond “project time” (Iversen and Din-
dler, 2014). It has also led to recognition of the important work and decision making that goes into 
imagining protagonist users and “figuring out” how people will participate in Participatory Design 
initiatives before even start (Smith and Iversen, 2018).
In 2018, Saad-Sulonen et al. (2018a) called for further attention to how participatory processes 
are “unfolding over time”. Following this, Saad-Sulonen et al. (2018b) examined in greater de -
tail the ways in which Participatory Design researchers have engaged with temporalities in their 
published research. They describe two temporalities that are “deeply entrenched” in the history of 
Participatory Design: the future-oriented temporality and the project-based temporality.
The future-oriented temporality emphasises how Participatory Design is always looking for -
ward, to establish new practices, systems and things that have a positive effect on people. This 
was highlighted strongly in the 2013 handbook, with Robertson and Simonsen (2013) noting how 
Participatory Design has been “defined by a perspective that always looks forward to the shaping 
of future situations”. The field of Participatory Design is rich of examples of techniques, methods 
and approaches that exist primarily to support designers and participants to explore futures to-
gether – such as futures workshops and more recent work that bridged Participatory Design with 
approaches that utilise fiction and speculation (Lyckvi et al., 2018).
The project-based temporality  recognises that the vast majority of Participatory Design 
research – at least that which gets published – are supported by grants and funding aligned to spe-
cific projects. One consequence of this is that such projects are highly time-bound – with activities 
occurring while the project is funded, with little space to engage beyond this timescale. Halskov 
and Hansen (2015) and Saad-Sulonen et al. (2018b) observe that this means published research 
tends to report on the tangible aspects of the work conducted – the workshops, the prototyping, 
the methods developed – rather than aspects that may have occurred prior to the project or follow-
ing it. Saad-Sulonen et al. (2018b) also note that while participatory projects might be viewed as 
short-term endeavours, they are often also connected to broader programmes of work and projects 
that occur over extended periods of time. As observed by Halskov and Hansen (2015), there is 
“untapped” potential for researchers and practitioners to report on these broader programmes of 
work and the relations between activities that might, when published, appear as disconnected to 
each other. Furthermore, at the time Saad-Sulonen et al.’s work was published in (2018a), they rec-
ognised there was a quickly growing body of work drawing on the concept of infrastructuring in 
Participatory Design; this collection of work signals a shift from tightly bound, isolated, Participa-
tory Design projects to more relational, emergent and “in the making” perspectives on designing 
over extended periods of time. We will return to this in the following text.
In their paper examining how Participatory Design researchers have engaged with temporality 
in their work, Saad-Sulonen et al. (2018b) also define five temporal “lenses”. These lenses can be 
used to further understand the temporal scaling of Participatory Design activities and used as an 
analytical tool to highlight how participation changes and unfolds over time. They also help elabo-
rate on how temporal scaling may work in practice – rather than thinking of scaling Participatory 

Scaling Participatory Design
37
Design in terms of the numbers of groups, the size of organisations, or the number of sites that are 
engaged in a project, we instead look at how Participatory Design extends over periods of time 
where different activities, with different participants, are connected to one another. We discuss 
each of these in the following.
Retrospective Lens: Looking Back at Long-Term Projects
Perhaps the most common way that Participatory Design researchers have engaged in exploring 
long-term projects has been through retrospective accounts. Here, researchers look back at projects 
to understand the dynamics of participation and how they changed over time. The retrospective 
lens also recognises that, in many instances, it is very hard to fully comprehend or to understand 
the dynamics of complex projects as they are unfolding in situ and in real time, and therefore it 
is useful to step back once a project is completed and retrospectively review how Participatory 
Design has worked over the duration of a long-term set of connected activities.
There are multiple examples of papers that have provided a retrospective account of Participa-
tory Design over time – including examples from earlier Participatory Design papers (e.g. Clement 
and Van den Besselaar, 1993). More recent examples include Poderi et al. (2018), who reflect on 
how different groups of stakeholders and users came together to influence design and implemen -
tation decisions in a three-year project developing energy demand management infrastructures 
in Italy. They focus on “interaction spaces” – periods of activity where different constellations 
of users and decision-makers come together at different points of time to influence design and 
implementation decisions. However, these interaction spaces were obscured in the practice of the 
project itself, which involved orchestrating a multiplicity of participants and voices – and were 
only identified through a process of tracing where eventual design features and decisions were 
grounded in specific stages of the project.
Kapuire et al. (2015) similarly reflect on a long-term community-based Participatory Design 
project in rural Namibia, focusing on the “participant gains” reported by community members and 
observed by the native researcher throughout the course of their work. They highlight qualities of 
their then six-year long engagement that indicate the success of their project in terms of develop -
ing sustained engagement of their community and adoption of the storytelling systems they were 
designing with them. This includes drawing on community-level communal values rather than 
just the values of individuals and focusing on “local workability” where language, methods of 
engagement and the practices of communication and facilitation are continuously reflected upon 
and revised.
Perhaps in contrast to Kapuire et al. (2015) and their points around “local workability”, Hyysalo 
and Hyysalo (2018) look back over a three-year period of a large-scale Participatory Design project 
that involved hundreds of participants scoping and development of the Helsinki Central Library. 
Through their retrospective analysis, they highlighted the significance of the interaction between 
“mundane work” (e.g. booking different types of spaces for activities) and “strategic work” (e.g. 
relating the project to policy and political mandates) in the practical conduct of a long-term and 
large-scale project – both of which fundamental to successful Participatory Design engagements.
Phasic Lens: Conceptualising Activities Across Project Phases
Saad-Sulonen et al. (2018b) describe the phasic lens as where researcher characterise their Par -
ticipatory Design projects as occurring over distinct phases or cycles of activities over time. The 
aforementioned characterisations of Participatory Design occurring across “project time”, “design 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
38
time” and “use time” relate to this phasic lens. Often phases, or stages, are used as a way to or -
ganise the reporting of a Participatory Design project in a structured, chronological format – for 
example, from building relationships to fieldwork, co-ideation, prototyping and co-realisation.
A phasic view also poses some problems. By invoking the different notions of “times”, they 
are open to similar critiques as per Storni (2013). They can also be interpreted as a linear process 
where the completion of one phase smoothly moves into the next. Botero and Hyysalo’s (2013) 
work on extended Participatory Design presents a complementary perspective here where Partici-
patory Design occurs over a portfolio of activities which happen alongside an enquiry into partici-
pants’ social practices and the socio-technical infrastructures that support their everyday activities. 
They note that project initiation activities are always needed at the start – for example, building a 
constituency of participants, exploring that constituency and starting off with small well-bounded 
design projects. However, beyond this there is a plethora of design strategies to draw upon that are 
pervasive across the life of a project and cannot be conducted in an easily defined chronological 
order.
Emergent Lens: Participatory Design as Unfolding Activity Involving  
Reflection and Reflexivity
In contrast to the previously discussed lenses, the emergent lens highlights that Participatory De-
sign is a “continuous and unfolding phenomenon” in practice. The focus on emergence somewhat 
eschews that Participatory Design can be thought of in phasic terms, or as stages and cycles, and 
that methods can be formalised or abstracted.
Instead, framing the temporal dynamics of Participatory Design as emergent brings into focus 
the moment-to-moment interactions and actions of the designer and how these are contingent on 
the dynamics of specific settings. Thus, core to this lens is the reflexivity of the designer-researcher 
and the role of facilitation in activities where outcomes and directions are uncertain. For example, 
Light and Akama (2012) draw attention to the “microdynamics of participation” and bring to the 
fore the specificities of a Participatory Design researcher’s practice as it evolves in the conduct 
of activities with participants in situ and in relation to a designers particular “way of working”. 
Subsequent work has provided reflexive accounts highlighting the importance of “readiness” in 
Participatory Design activities and working in a state of openness that is responsive to the contin-
gencies of specific engagements with participants and the topics under exploration (Akama and 
Light, 2018). Others have characterised this emergent quality as “wandering” (Van Reusel, 2016) 
without a set outcome in mind. It also comes with a greater appreciation of the “informal” engage-
ments that happen with participants (Mosleh and Larsen, 2021).
It has also been noted how navigating such emergent and wandering processes can be highly 
complex and challenging, especially when there is a multiplicity of voices involved and a range of 
factors influencing decision-making and the direction of projects. Building on this, recent Partici-
patory Design work has started to explore supplementary practices that support periods of pausing 
and reflection amongst complex Participatory Design processes (e.g. Agid and Akama’s, 2020). 
Similarly, Frauenberger et al. (2015) developed a “tool to think with” for Participatory Design re-
searchers to use as part of both planning and ongoing reflection during the conduct of their work. 
Their tool brings attempts to “unearth [.  . .] mostly tacit aspects” of Participatory Design work 
through the lenses of epistemology, values, outcomes and stakeholders. A particularly valuable 
aspect of this tool is that it enables researchers to understand potential dichotomies or dissonances 
in their projects between these different lenses and the projects’ overall coherence – for example, 
where the “values” of the project conflict with the intended outcome.

Scaling Participatory Design
39
To a degree, the emergent lens appears to eschew the notion of long-term engagements, and 
its focus is more on emergent and unfolding activities. However, typically work that focuses on 
these unfolding qualities of Participatory Design is embedded within long-term, or interconnected, 
projects and activities. They also emphasise the situatedness of knowledge, which poses some ten-
sions with the ideas presented on scaling up Participatory Design.
Long-Term Lens: Stretched and Extended Over Time
Saad-Sulonen et al. (2018b) define the long-term lens as a “stretched view” of participation, 
where a long-term perspective on the work being conducted is a “foundational design concern” 
and is “continuously attended to as a part and parcel of the ongoing, everyday work” of a pro -
ject. This would work that frames Participatory Design as a form of “design in use” (Henderson 
and Kyng, 1992) or “co-realisation” (Hartswood et al., 2008). More recent examples of this are 
Roland and Sanner’s (2017) work and Botero and Hyysalo’s (2013) conceptualisation of evolu -
tionary Participatory Design. In the latter, from the outset, the intention is to collaborate with a 
community of participants over an extended period of time and to ensure Participatory Design 
activities work alongside and build on participants’ own projects, practices and infrastructures. 
Participatory Design approaches that draw from the concept of infrastructuring also tend to be 
characterised by such a long-term lens – with a focus on harnessing existing socio-technical 
practices and establishing new ones to support sustained engagement with new systems cre -
ated through participatory activities. Karasti and Syrjänen (2004) explicitly invoke the inher -
ently temporal qualities of infrastructuring in collaborative design practices, as an ongoing 
negotiation of short-term, more immediate requirements, with longer-term anticipated needs. 
More latterly Karasti et al. (2010) have distinguished between project time and infrastructuring 
time – the latter emphasising a form of “continuing design” which, like notions of “design in 
use” and “evolutionary” Participatory Design, emphasises long-term design work in partnership 
with participants.
As literature at the intersection of infrastructuring and temporality has matured, researchers 
have started to articulate specific qualities of Participatory Design that extend over long peri-
ods of time that need to be considered by practitioners. Schepers et al. (2018) viewed long-term 
Participatory Design from an infrastructuring perspective in their collective work on designing 
technologies with children – noting the need to configure the different types of roles and respon-
sibilities of participants as designers throughout the process – with participants acting as match -
makers and process designers at the start of a project, to shifting to roles as users, design partners, 
protagonists in design workshops, to mediators and process designers (again) between sessions. 
Bødker et al. (2017) build on Karasti’s (2014) work to elaborate on the notion of participatory 
infrastructuring – “infrastructuring activities that engage users in processes of design and use” and 
which extend in time. As we’ve noted in this chapter already, the back-stage work that is critical 
to sustaining complex participatory infrastructuring activities over time is rarely reported on: the 
“preparations, negotiations, and political work that fundamentally shapes the set-up and outcomes 
of the entire process” (Bødker et al., 2017). Bødker et al. (2017), building on Dindler and Iversen 
(2014), further invoke Engestrom’s notion of “knotworks”, which in participatory infrastructur -
ing refer to “the fluid, yet momentarily stable, constellations that emerge among participants with 
different backgrounds, perspectives, and agendas as they come together in matters of common 
concern”. A key element of sustaining long-term and ongoing infrastructuring projects is the for -
mation and maintenance of such networks – again, a point that often gets missed when publica -
tions focus on reporting the tidier “front stage” (e.g. workshop) activities.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
40
Prospective Lens: Engaging With Sustaining Outcomes
Finally, the prospective lens relates to the future-oriented focus on Participatory Design but is 
more immediately focused on how activities and outcomes may be sustained beyond the formal 
end of a specific project. The aforementioned work of Iversen and Dindler (2014) is a prominent 
example that highlights the myriad of ways that researchers may engage with sustaining work – by 
maintaining (e.g. incorporation of initiatives into existing or newly formed practices), by scaling 
(e.g. by bringing insights to bear on a wider group of people), by replicating (e.g. translating initia-
tives to other settings or organisations), or by evolving (e.g. where a project continues to transform 
or be a catalyst for new initiatives and projects).
Related to the latter point around evolving outcomes beyond the end of the project, Simon-
sen and Hertzum (2008, 2012) have coined a “sustained Participatory Design approach”, which 
focuses on how organisations can continue to experiment and learn in a participatory manner be -
yond those that are led by designers and researchers (Simonsen and Hertzum, 2008). In a similar 
vein, initiatives such as living labs and community innovation hubs provide physical spaces and 
resources to support users, participants and interested parties to maintain participatory activities 
beyond any formal engagements with researchers; although there is recognition that these still 
require careful orchestration of participatory activities and the provision of such spaces alone 
does not necessarily support long-term, ongoing, Participatory Design work (Björgvinsson et al., 
2012). Finally, Simone et al. (2022), as mentioned earlier, deal extensively with how to sustain 
Participatory Design.
Summary: Temporal Scaling Is Common yet Rarely Articulated
The temporal lenses suggested by Saad-Sulonen et al. (2018b) are useful as they draw attention 
to different qualities of time or different ways Participatory Design researchers can start to under-
stand temporal scaling in relation to their own work. As the authors note, these are not meant to 
be viewed in isolation from each other. Similarly, work that is engaged in infrastructuring has a 
tendency to both invoke an emergent “at the moment” position on participation and a long-term 
view of establishing socio-technical practices that may sustain change into the future. In a field 
where time is of such importance, yet where we rarely articulate the extended nature of much 
Participatory Design work in what we report, these lenses offer a way to stimulate new forms 
of practice and analysis. Furthermore, what the lenses highlight is that a large body of work in 
Participatory Design is already engaged with different aspects of temporal scaling – be that by 
building up projects over time through carefully orchestrated beginnings and back-stage activi -
ties, by engaging with participants and communities over extended periods of time, or by thinking 
through the long-term implications of their work. However, these attributes may get obscured in 
the day-to-day of a project, or indeed get left out of how projects, and connections between pro -
jects and activities over time are reported.
In the following, we further complicate socio-spatial and temporal aspects of scaling Partici-
patory Design, by highlighting the onto-epistemologies increasingly being used in Participatory 
Design that widen understandings of space and time.
Onto-Epistemological Scaling
So far, this chapter has primarily focused on the socio-spatial and temporal understandings of 
scale in Participatory Design. The following text will focus on the diversification, itself is a form 
of socio-spatial scaling, of the Participatory Design community. In particular it will explore the 

Scaling Participatory Design
41
ways through which the diversification of the Participatory Design community complicates the 
previously discussed socio-spatial and temporal scaling. We refer to this diversification of the Par-
ticipatory Design community as onto-epistemological scaling, where onto-epistemology is the 
intimate intertwining between ways of knowing (epistemology) and ways of being and the world 
(ontology) making them mutually constitutive. The intertwining of ontology and epistemology 
rejects Cartesian dualisms such as mind and body in favour of relationality where there is “a pro -
found awareness of the fundamental interdependence of everything that exists” (Arturo Escobar, 
2020). It is important to note that the term onto-epistemology, commonly used within decolonial/
decolonising Participatory Design, is not always clearly defined (for a deeper dive into Decoloni-
sation and Plurality in Participatory Design see Chapter 5). While some literature refers back to 
Barad’s (2007) coining of the term within Agential Realism, others point to indigenous ways of 
knowing where knowledge and reality are collapsed into one.
The notion of Participatory Design as pluriversal has gained traction within the Participatory 
Design community and is understood as a form of political action that challenges what is seen 
as the universalist knowledge structures of euro-centric design. It works with an understanding 
of the co-existence of multiple worlds and in turn that there are multiple ways of knowing, de-
signing and doing Participatory Design. Therefore, similar to Escobar’s (2018) assertion of our 
world being one made up of many worlds, the onto-epistemological scaling of Participatory De -
sign is shaping up into an ever-expanding area of research and practice in which multiple and 
diverse onto-epistemologies co-exist (i.e. onto-epistemological scaling). This will highlight 
how upon scaling across geographies and in turn onto-epistemological scaling, Participatory 
Design – as theorised and practised based on its Scandinavian roots – has encountered differ -
ent onto-epistemologies that complicate the previously presented understandings of temporal and 
socio-spatial scaling.
The Diversification and Scaling of PDCs
The onto-epistemological scaling of Participatory Design has been facilitated, and even encour -
aged, within the socio-spatial scaling of the Participatory Design community itself which is 
most evident when examining the PDC. We view the diversification approaches adopted by the 
PDC – hosting the conference in Columbia, initiating the PDC Places track and publishing online 
articles in multiple languages and not just English – to encourage the socio-spatial scaling of the 
community as playing a key role in onto-epistemologically scaling Participatory Design. This is 
not to say that the convening of Participatory Design researchers, practitioners and knowledge 
outside of the sphere of PDC has not also contributed to the move towards onto-epistemological 
scaling. However, the PDC series provides a case study through which we can observe purposeful 
efforts for diversification.
Since 2010 we have seen an increase in publications at PDC from and of the “global 
Souths”
2 – notably coming from Latin America, Africa and South Asia. This is not to say that 
Participatory Design research did not exist in the “global Souths” prior to 2010 however. On the 
contrary, as Calderón Salazar and Huybrechts (2020) and Dearden and Rizvi (2008) point out, 
the value of participation inherent to Participatory Design has long been shared with Participa-
tory Action Research, a methodology stemming from and enacted in the “global Souths”. Host -
ing PDC in Namibia in 2014, and PDC 2020 publishing articles in multiple languages, opened 
a new space for mutual learning across geographies. This further evolved to more proactively 
welcoming epistemologies of the South by PDC conferences adopting themes aligned with de-
coloniality. PDC 2020 held in Columbia (moved online due to the COVID-19 pandemic) and 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
42
PDC 2022 in the UK centred on the themes of “Participation(s) Otherwise” and “Embracing Cos-
mologies: Expanding Worlds of Participatory Design”, respectively. Furthermore, there has been 
a concerted effort to globally work with diverse geographies of Participatory Design research. In 
2022, PDC organised and facilitated the first PDC Places track, aiming to support and connect 
the coming together of Participatory Design researchers and practitioners within and across their 
own regions. As such, PDC Places ran as a decentralised constellation of 16 places in Africa, Asia, 
Australia, Aotearoa (New Zealand), South America, North America, Europe and the Middle East. 
In summary, PDC socio-spatial scaling characterised by openness to mutual learning across geog-
raphies and the political decolonising act of creating spaces for epistemological diversity enabled 
researchers from the “global Souths” to explore how Participatory Design underpinned by varying 
onto-epistemologies may be enacted (Calderón Salazar and Huybrecht, 2020), as such contribut -
ing to the onto-epistemological scaling of Participatory Design.
Among other things, the onto-epistemological scaling of Participatory Design has entailed the 
ongoing complication of the socio-spatial and temporal understandings of scale and scaling previ-
ously presented in this chapter.
Onto-Epistemological Scaling Complicating Socio-Spatial Scaling
Within literature concerned with socio-spatial scaling, the complexity of engaging with various us-
ers and stakeholders with differing agendas has been highlighted, whether it be in organisational, 
community, distributed or national scaling of Participatory Design. The onto-epistemological 
scaling of Participatory Design further nuances this complexity by highlighting how the very 
values underpinning Participatory Design are understood and practised differently when situated 
in the “global Souths”. For example, through their work with handicraft communities in Brazil, 
Noronha et al. (2020) argue that there is a tendency within Participatory Design to strive for an 
eventual consensus between Participatory Design researchers and diverse community members, 
which exclude epistemologies and ontologies “otherwise”. Rosenqvist (2020) further draws atten-
tion to differences in the ways through which Participatory Design facilitates negotiation. They 
highlight that the traditional Indonesian decision-making practices of Msuyawarah-Mufakat place 
a similar emphasis on consensus to that found in Scandinavian democratic deliberation. However, 
within Msuyawarah-Mufakat the emphasis on social harmony trumps that of agonism and there-
fore requires deliberation to take place in closed spaces, rather than public forums, prior to moving 
towards consensus. Such research draws attention to the nuanced attentiveness needed for negotia-
tion and deliberation activities when considering the socio-spatial scaling of Participatory Design 
across geographies and cultures.
Furthermore, in contexts of oppression in the “global Souths” Participatory Design researchers 
have prompted community-based Participatory Design to engage with nation-wide systems of op-
pression, thus blurring the lines between the community and national. Serpa et al. (2020) argue that 
when working with communities in Brazil Participatory Design could and indeed should take the 
form of political action using Freire’s Pedagogy of the Oppressed (Freire, 2020) thus committing 
to changing unjust realities at a national level through work at a community level.
Furthermore, indigenous understandings of the relational connectedness of humans, the earth, 
sky, waters, land, plants, animals and ancestral spirits prompt the de-centring of humans within 
Participatory Design’s understanding of participation. Such de-centring also links back to research 
on Animal-Computer Interaction (Mancini et al., 2017) and more-than-human design (Akama 
et al., 2020; Cooper, 2022; Key et al., 2022). Akama et al. (2020) do not debunk Participatory De-
sign’s human-centred focus of participation in politics, power relations and the struggles of those 

Scaling Participatory Design
43
marginalised but rather work towards complementing it through exploring different relationalities 
that embrace practices of always-participating-with-many. As such, Participatory Design should 
consider the multiplication of human and non-human stakeholders as part of socio-spatial scaling 
across geographies and the onto-epistemologies they hold.
Onto-Epistemological Scaling Complicating Temporal Scaling
Research has also complicated the temporal scaling of Participatory Design. Bringing to the fore 
non-western understandings of participation over time has introduced new dimensions to questions 
of who and what participates when and the previously discussed phasic lens of temporal scaling. In 
their work in South and sub-Saharan Africa, Winschiers-Theophilus et al. (2010) point to Ubuntu, 
as a the paradigm of “Connectedness of all” in which an individual’s existence is premised on the 
existence of others (i.e. their community) including that of ancestors. Similarly, Akama (2014) 
draws on Ma, between-ness, from Japanese philosophy where the word for “human being” is that 
of a between person. Thus, like Ubuntu, Ma positions the existence of humans to be inherently 
relational. This relational connectedness of all living and non-living beings explodes the temporal 
and socio-spatial scales of Participatory Design, because through the lens of relational connected-
ness everyone, everything and anywhere (in the past, present and future) is a stakeholder within 
a Participatory Design endeavour. Similarly, evoking elongated temporalities from a Purépecha 
worldview from Ancient Mexico, Sosa (2020) emphasises that creativity and creation does not 
exist solely within the temporalities of Participatory Design projects and “does not happen from 
scratch” but rather is opportunistic, situational and collaborative. As such creation within Partici -
patory Design is a continuous act of re-creation that cannot be contained within linear phases of 
Participatory Design projects (i.e. the beginnings, middles and ends), and therefore creativity can-
not be attributed to individuals participating in design within a single instance of time.
In relation to the future-oriented temporality Afrofuturism and Black Feminism have begun 
bringing to the fore questions regarding whose future is considered and made visible when con -
ducting speculative Participatory Design. While related to sustainability and futuring Afrofuturist 
Feminism within Participatory Design responds to the exclusion of Black diasporic communities 
from participating in the design of socio-technological futures (Bray et al., 2022). These episte -
mologies provide the basis for generating Participatory Design tools that account for the historical 
exclusion of Black diaspora communities and re-centre Black art and science fiction (Bray et al., 
2022; Bray and Harrington, 2021). Harrington et al. (2022) call for the adoption of Afrofuturist 
feminist frameworks as a means of speculating radically equitable futures and worlds in which 
“Blackness is integral to the story” (Harrington et al., 2022, pg. 4).
Summary: Complicating Scale
The previous discussion is only a brief overview of how the onto-epistemological scaling 
of Participatory Design complicates both socio-spatial and temporal scaling. It is not exhaus -
tive, however, there is no doubt that with the push for diversifying the community, multiple 
onto-epistemologies are being drawn into Participatory Design as a discipline of research and 
practice (i.e. onto-epistemological scaling). Equally as important, the literature presented high-
lights that through radical expansion and diversification the field is being continuously shaped 
through mutual learning. The onto-epistemological scaling of Participatory Design stretches the 
temporality and degrees of scale articulated previously. Living and non-living stakeholders of the 
past and present (e.g. ancestral spirits, Earth) are engaged in the present, and speculations of those 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
44
historically excluded from participation are designing for multiple and diverse futures. This is not 
to say that Participatory Design’s Scandinavian roots are being abandoned but rather that Partici -
patory Design as a disciplinary space is expanding and bringing in different approaches, values 
and principles that can co-exist in relation to one another.
Discussion: Scaling as Pursuing Complexities
In this chapter we have attempted to unpack “scale” and the “scaling” of Participatory Design through 
(1) socio-spatial and (2) temporal framing, and (3) the ways in which the onto-epistemological 
scaling of Participatory Design complicates the former two framings. We discuss how the framings 
the chapter has dealt with “scale” and how such framings – and their complications – collectively 
reflect and work in tandem with some of the complexities in which Participatory Design is situ -
ated. In significant ways, Participatory Design has embraced complexity and multiplicity and as a 
consequence engaged in various kinds of scaling.
The Complex Coming Together of Pluralistic Values, Cultures and Forms
The complexity of Participatory Design projects and initiatives increases as they move beyond one 
project, a few people, one place and a short time. This goes for engaging stakeholders, establishing 
structures and processes, ensuring resources, building capacities as well as shaping participation, 
negotiating goals and sustaining all of this over time. On all issues this makes the challenges of 
doing Participatory Design more acute. For example, in the context of the multiplication of stake-
holders, there is a need to compromise or take a position. Luckily, various researchers within Par-
ticipatory Design have addressed this. Björgvinsson et al. (2012) argue for an agonistic approach 
which supports the articulation of different interests and voices and Frauenberger et al. (2015) 
suggest a “tool to think” to reflect on the complications and contradictions of Participatory Design 
initiatives and structures. The challenges of different interests and goals are further compounded 
by a need to work with the multiple onto-epistemologies held by stakeholders as organisations 
work across borders and continents.
Another consideration is that Participatory Design often takes on a multiplicity of forms. Here, 
we encourage Participatory Design researchers to be more specific about how and why what they 
do is Participatory Design. Which particular aim of Participatory Design is pursued, through 
which activities, processes or technologies, and in which ways is scaling involved? Explicitly 
and specifically addressing this rather than referring to “large-scale” or “otherwise”, for example, 
could contribute to our understanding of what is involved. There is a need to go beyond and further 
complicate contrastive referencing and instead work towards rich and nuanced conceptualisations 
of scaling that can facilitate more focused and comprehensive research and formulations of scaling 
in all of the framings we present. We do not envision nor call for one comprehensive framework, 
but engagement with the few existing ones (e.g. Gärtner and Wagner, 1996; Roland et al., 2017; 
Dindler and Iversen, 2014; Saad-Sulonen et al., 2018b; Simone et al, 2022) or working out new 
ones could be valuable contributions.
Scaling and the Interconnectedness of Participatory Design Participants  
and Research Community
Globalisation and interconnectedness have been enabled and supported by the proliferation of 
technologies and here mutual learning, co-creation and co-determination become increasingly 

Scaling Participatory Design
45
pertinent challenges when considering scaling. Close and intensive interaction in small groups are 
well-known processes for mutual learning, whereas the results of patchy interaction with large and 
interconnected groups of people are more unknown. What do varying people and groups actually 
take away from Participatory Design? What are the lasting effects? Evaluation of whether mutual 
learning and more generally Participatory Design aims have been achieved at least to some extent 
would be informative, unless Participatory Design just wants to state its benign aims and hope for 
the best.
At the same time, our framings of scaling open up opportunities to think of new forms of mutual 
learning in the Participatory Design community. For example, the mutual learning mechanisms 
employed by the PDC over the past decade have contributed to onto-epistemological scaling of 
Participatory Design, and this may be an opportunity to understand how mutual learning is enacted 
as the community over time has scaled across interconnected locations, borders and peoples, result-
ing in multiple, yet relational, understandings of Participatory Design. The onto-epistemological 
scaling of Participatory Design also provides a new space for the complicating and re-examining 
of how we consider the temporal and socio-spatial qualities of Participatory Design as current 
understandings of other epistemologies and ontologies are further drawn into the discipline.
Scaling as Appreciating Differences Within and Through Participatory Design 
Research and Practice
The engagement of Participatory Design in the complexities of scaling is an opportunity to ex -
plore and work with differences in a manner that exceeds, for example, that of working with 
the differences held between unions and employers or Europe and North America. Bannon et al. 
(2018a) note how concerns around the “co-option” of Participatory Design permeate across a lot 
of the Participatory Design literature. Participatory Design gets dressed up as a “banal form of 
user-centered design”, where the suspicion is that much of the fundamental decision-making is 
made by the researchers and designers (Bannon et al., 2018b); while the language of Participa-
tory Design is invoked its values and ethos is not. In contrast, we view the onto-epistemological 
scaling as simultaneously invoking the language, values and ethos of Participatory Design and in 
doing so engaging with and complicating its foundations in meaningful and constructive ways. 
This involves broadening our understanding of and adding to core original aims of Participatory 
Design, revisiting old and asking new questions: Which kinds of participation, mutual learning 
and opening up of choices should be pursued in new onto-epistemological contexts? And how do 
they relate to questions on the scaling of Participatory Design?
Challenges and Opportunities
Through this chapter we highlight that “scale” can be understood through an exploration of the 
social, organisational and geographic expansion of Participatory Design projects, the stretching of 
Participatory Design projects over time as well as the engagement of Participatory Design projects 
with multiple onto-epistemologies. We argue that in important ways Participatory Design has en-
gaged in scaling and moved beyond simple initiatives and engaged in complex ones.
Our review of existing work also highlights a number of interesting challenges for future re-
searchers to examine further and treat as opportunities for new research trajectories and areas 
within Participatory Design. Clearly there is more work to be done to draw case studies of scaling 
of Participatory Design in practice within and between organisations together. We suggest that 
while more conceptual work here may be of value, so would be the creation of resources that 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
46
outline how such cases occurred in detail for greater comparison and contrast to one another. 
There are also opportunities for more practical projects that look at how researchers might antici-
pate the longer-term trajectories of their work across temporal scales, to help guide some of the 
more moment-to-moment duration aspects of Participatory Design practice. Furthermore, while 
we have positioned onto-epistemological scaling as a quality of the contemporary Participatory 
Design community more than a quality of projects per se, there are opportunities here to develop 
new projects where researchers and practitioners come together to more explicit articulate their 
different framings, assumptions and understandings of what it means to participate in design.
Finally, we see a major challenge of scaling is whether all of Participatory Design’s aims can 
be achieved at scale and, whilst the research community itself, scales; how do we handle the risk 
of “watering down the principles while scaling up”? However, achieving all aims simultaneously 
might be too ambitious, and even pursuing only a selection of aims when scaling seems to be a 
worthy ambition that could provide insights into how to scale Participatory Design. This then also 
seems like an opportunity for Participatory Design to learn more about how to do scaling by being 
specific about which kind of scaling is involved, the aim of a project, and how that aim is pursued 
by which means. In this way, future projects and research can iteratively provide valuable input to 
our understanding of scaling and how to handle its complexities.

networks regarding capital, large corporations and political alliances. Somewhat aligning with the referenced 
literature here but signalling existing differences, we will use the terms “global Souths” and “global Norths”.
