3
COLLECTIVES AND 
PARTICIPATORY DESIGN
Liesbeth Huybrechts, Maurizio Teli, Joanna Saad-Sulonen and 
Mariacristina Sciannamblo
Participatory Design’s interest in the formation and organisation of collectives can be traced to the en-
hanced field’s engagements with complex realities in urban, suburban and rural environments. Participa-
tory Design processes in these contexts deal with contested issues, such as mobility or migration, and 
there is a great need for more solidarity and collective understanding and actions around these topics. 
Participatory Design researchers have therefore strengthened their capabilities to design, experiment and 
work with the ongoing dynamics, diverse experiences and views of collectives on matters they care for. 
They build upon Participatory Design’s political ethos informed by discourses in agonism. This chapter 
focuses on the question of how Participatory Design has supported and can support the formation and 
organisation of collectives around questions that emerge in urban, suburban and rural environments with 
close attention to its politics. The term ‘collectives’ is used to underline the complexity of human and 
more-than-human actors, the latter being actors who are part of lifeworlds, such as trees, birds, tech -
nologies or buildings. In the introduction, this chapter builds further on the 2013 Participatory Design 
Handbook, which highlighted ‘Community-based Participatory Design’ outside the formal organisational 
structures where Participatory Design initially grew. Followingly, we discuss how this move outside 
organisational settings has contributed to concepts such as collectives, infrastructuring, commoning and 
institutioning and how they shape today’s research and practices. We will also engage deeper into exam-
ples of recent inquiries on Participatory Design and the formation and organisation of collectives to end 
with a discussion on Participatory Design and the formation and organisation of collectives.
  DOI: 10.4324/9781003334330-4

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
52
Introduction: A Historical Overview
Participatory Design today engages more intensely with realities outside of formal organisational 
structures, in contexts and around themes that currently cause a lot of contestation (think of, e.g. 
housing, sustainability, mobility, migration, education) and that are in need of more collective un-
derstanding and actions (Huybrechts et al., 2022). Participatory Design researchers have therefore 
strengthened their capabilities to engage with the diverse experiences and views of collectives on 
matters they care for in urban, suburban and rural contexts. To support this, Participatory Design has 
woven connections with discourses in agonism (Björgvinsson, 2012; Geppert and Forlano, 2022). In 
contrast to a representative democracy, the agonistic democratic space is constructed from a multitude 
of singular argumentation activities, expressed in various verbal and bodily ways (Gielen, 2011). The 
term ‘Community-based Participatory Design’, articulated by Di Salvo et al. (2013) in the first Hand-
book of Participatory Design (and mentioned in 2004 by Karasti and Syrjänen), has opened the way 
for a focus on designing with the politics of a broad range of social relations and the articulation of 
concepts such as ‘publics’ (Matthews et al., 2022) and ‘infrastructuring’ (Di Salvo et al., 2013), which 
have been later complemented with writings on collectives, commoning and institutioning.
It is important to note that many of the reported works in Community-based Participatory Design 
have been undertaken with urban communities (e.g. Malmö Living Labs and other cases reported in 
Di Salvo et al., 2013), bringing forward the urban context and its complex spatial, social and politi-
cal facets. This strand of Participatory Design intersects with another that emerged around the same 
period and which has explicitly explored the governance of urban spaces, namely with the role of in-
stitutional actors such as municipalities and urban planners and the growing possibilities for enabling 
people to have a say in urban planning in local urban settings, using the mediation of digital technolo-
gies (Botero and Saad-Sulonen, 2008; Nuojua et al., 2008; Redhead and Brereton, 2008; Bratteteig 
and Wagner, 2010; Nuojua et al., 2010; Saad-Sulonen, 2014). Urban Participatory Design, as it has 
been referred to in the naming of two sessions at the Participatory Design Conference of 2008, 
started with a strong focus on Participatory Design processes to design digital technologies that could 
support the complex politics of shaping the urban environment, engaging with a variety of urban 
actors. This strand of Urban Participatory Design is also closely connected with the then-emerging 
fields of urban informatics (e.g. Foth et al., 2011) and media architecture (see Brynskov et al., 2014).
Despite this initial focus on the interplay of information technology, participation and the ur -
ban context, Participatory Design scholars have also highlighted participation with collectives 
without the main focus on technology development, bringing forward similar concerns as in 
Community-based Participatory Design. Some researchers have recognised that Participatory De-
sign researchers in urban settings ‘are often collaborating with researchers from other fields as well 
as civil servants, citizens, local entrepreneurs and organisations, etc.’ (Eriksen et al., 2016). Partici-
patory Design publications have, starting the second decade of the millennium, reported on work in 
urban contexts and with varieties of urban stakeholders, without a focus on digital technologies per 
se, but rather brought forward interests such as designing analogue mapping tools for supporting 
participation (Huybrechts et al., 2012), prototyping for social innovation (Hillgren et al., 2011) or 
the co-production of public services in urban contexts (Seravalli et al., 2017). In most cases, those 
reflections were looking at the design and implementation of technologies as forms of infrastructur-
ing, that is, as ways of debating and critically intervening in the infrastructure for urban collabora-
tion (the map, the prototype, the service, the digital platform, etc.). Despite a strong interest in the 
urban, it is important to note that Participatory Design has also taken suburban and rural contexts as 
sites of inquiry and action (Dearden and Rizvi, 2008).
Challenges revealed by unsustainable modes of production and consumption in urban, subur -
ban and rural contexts triggered a rapprochement between Participatory Design’s concerns and 

Collectives and Participatory Design
53
scholarship on the commons (Marttila et al., 2014; Teli et al., 2016). From this, new potential un-
derstandings emerged regarding how to engage in collaboration – for example, as commoning – and 
how to support the shaping of commons as a way to explore more sustainable approaches of dealing 
with shared resources (Seravalli, 2018; Sharp, 2018). The focus on commons and commoning, with 
their reference not only to how technologies are built but also to how things – including technolo-
gies – are managed and nurtured, has opened up research in three directions. First, both the urban and 
rural decentralised areas have been considered as locations for commoning (Bidwell, 2020). Second, 
it has become apparent that managing resources entails a relation with institutions that govern these 
resources and has triggered reflections on the practices through which Participatory Design relates to 
existing or new institutions, verbified as ‘institutioning’ (Huybrechts et al., 2017). Finally, the emerg-
ing interest in more-than-human stakeholders in Participatory Design has also been explored with its 
implications on how to further develop inquiry and practice into being more inclusive for a diversity 
of actors, including actors such as water, trees or energy (see Chapter 4 and the work of Abram, 1997; 
Bastian et al., 2016; Heitlinger et al., 2018; Clarke et al., 2019; Akama et al., 2020).
Designing with urban, suburban and rural contexts thus highlights the politics of the very com-
plex contexts where Participatory Design is taking place, demonstrating the need for a new con-
figuration of concepts, which we will present next.
Concepts
In this section, we will explore the core terms of ‘Collectives’, ‘Infrastructuring’, ‘Commoning’ 
and ‘Institutioning’ which help organise contemporary Participatory Design practices.
Collectives
Many terms have been used to name the constellations of participants in participatory processes: 
groups, communities, publics and collectives. In this chapter, we foreground the term ‘collec -
tive’, because designing with collectives is what Ehn (2008) and other authors have articulated as 
the core of what is called Participatory Design, collective design or co-design. It underlines that 
groups of participants are made of diverse actors, both human and more-than-human: inhabitants, 
public and private organisations, technological artefacts or trees (Huybrechts et al., 2022).
As Korsgaard et al. (2022) indicate, the field of Computer Supported Collaborative Work 
(CSCW) – historically related to the Participatory Design field – discusses constellations of actors 
under the common terms of ‘group’ and ‘community’. The term ‘group’ has to do with a historical 
interest in micro-collaborations, where individuals collaborate around a specific task with a single 
groupware system. More recently, ‘community’ has become an interest in CSCW. Here, communi-
ties are mainly defined by their online existence. The challenge that these authors describe is that 
‘the group’ or ‘the community’ is mainly seen through the lens of studying, designing, developing 
and evaluating technologies, and these concepts are linked to the ‘small group’ and the ‘community 
research’ as a romantic ideal. Korsgaard et al. (2022) foreground the term ‘collectives’ to shift the 
focus in CSCW towards aspects of multiple people and multiple technologies in settings where 
‘people come and go’, and ‘the history and developments, roles, values and division of labour, ne-
gotiation and strategies, patterns of appropriation’ resonate through their artefact ecology and back’ 
(Korsgaard et al., 2022, p. 3). They build on Engeström’s work (2015) in Activity Theory where the 
units of analysis are entire work/activity systems (e.g. organisations) beyond just one actor. From this 
perspective, collectives ‘are’ not, but they ‘become’ through the contributions of actors. Building on 
these principles, Korsgaard et al. (2022) mention three elements as central qualities of collectives: (1) 
joint and distributed collective activities that mediate understandings and solidarity; (2) an identity 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
54
articulated by the collective, in relation to within-collective (internal) practices and (external) social 
influences; (3) having a history oriented towards future development (or degradation), towards ful-
filling the goals of the collective and a higher degree of interpersonal relation.
In a reflection on a series of case studies developed in the Participatory Design field, Huy -
brechts et al. (2022) add the suggestion that the term ‘collectives’ embraces both human and 
more-than-human actors. More-than-human actors are understood to include the built infrastruc -
ture, trees, animals and inhabitants (Latour, 2005). This acknowledgement of socio-ecological rela-
tions in Participatory Design builds on the rich body of scholarship developed around the concept 
of ‘pluriverse’ (Escobar, 2018) and the intersections between Indigenous/First Nations/traditional 
owner knowledge and design (Bidwell and Winschiers-Theophilus, 2015). These contributions ar-
gue for paying attention to how the history and geography of places participate in design visions and 
practices in a way that is symbolic and material at the same time. Although terms like ‘communities’ 
or ‘publics’ (Di Salvo, 2009) also take into account the more-than-human actors in collective work, 
the word ‘collectives’ more easily relates to the mixed nature of human and more-than-human as-
semblages (Tsing, 2015). The term collectives invites us to go beyond a language that labels fixed 
realities and to look at the deep relationality that develops over time between a diversity of actors. 
To work with these collectives as Participatory Design researchers, taking into account the politics 
of participatory work, also means to acknowledge that there are many ‘implicated actors’ (Clarke 
and Montini, 1993), such as trees or some inhabitants, that are silent or silenced. It means that de-
signers need to look for ways to provide these actors with a voice or at least to represent their voices 
when speaking is not possible. To summarise, we can conceptualise collectives as comprising:
• Joint and distributed collective activities mediating understandings and solidarity;
• A collectively articulated identity (made of internal and external practices);
• A history and orientation towards future development or degradation;
• The involvement of more-than-human actors (both technological and ecological); and
• The conscious articulation of implicated actors.
This definition demonstrates that there are thus various political choices involved in forming and 
organising collectives in Participatory Design processes. Within this perspective, we can articulate 
a main question for this chapter and a set of subquestions: How can Participatory Design support 
the shaping and organisation of collectives around questions that emerge in urban, suburban and 
rural contexts with close attention to its politics? Which (implicated) actors do we give a voice 
to? Who do we choose to represent? What happens when we ourselves choose to become part of 
collectives?
Infrastructuring
While thinking about the relationship between collectives and the spaces they inhabit, Participa -
tory Design scholarship has engaged and repurposed the concept of infrastructuring in relation to 
a variety of cases, from students’ engagements with the city they live in to energy management or 
various grassroots initiatives (De Angeli et al., 2014; Capaccioli et al., 2016; Chopra et al., 2022). 
The concept of ‘infrastructuring’ originated between Science and Technology Studies and Partici-
patory Design, drawing upon the seminal work done in the decade between the mid-1990s and 
the late 2000s (Star and Ruhleder, 1996; Karasti and Syrjänen, 2004; Pipek and Wulf, 2009). By 
focussing on information technologies as the infrastructure for bringing collectives together and 
the object of the practices observed, and by questioning techno-centric views of infrastructures, 

Collectives and Participatory Design
55
those contributions came to look at infrastructure as a verb, expressing the situated and relational 
characters of designing, maintaining and expanding infrastructures that can support the formation 
of collectives (Karasti and Baker, 2004; Star and Bowker, 2006; Pipek and Wulf, 2009). Since then, 
the use of the concept has flourished, with a growing number of studies relying on it as a framework 
to understand participatory and collaborative design practices (Di Salvo et al., 2013; Pipek et al., 
2017).
All contributions relying on infrastructuring as a concept share some basic elements in under -
standing how infrastructure plays out in the formation and organisation of collectives. Those ele -
ments have been refined over time, but they were always close to core arguments developed in the 
period in which infrastructuring established itself as a meaningful framework in Participatory De-
sign. Karasti (2014) sketched out those elements stressing how the origin of infrastructuring as a 
concept puts emphasis on ongoing activities of collectives unfolding during an extended period of 
time. The ongoing and temporally expanded characteristics of infrastructuring activities have been 
one of the ways through which political conflicts have become visible again in Participatory De -
sign’s understanding of the shaping of collectives. As Karasti puts it, ‘Finally, infrastructuring has 
been taken up as an opportunity to reintroduce politics into Participatory Design’ (2014, p.  146). 
Conceptually, what has allowed infrastructuring to be taken up as a way of re-politicising Partici-
patory Design were elements already present in Star’s work on infrastructures (Neumann and Star, 
1996; Star and Ruhleder, 1996) and in Karasti’s elaboration of them in the light of Participatory 
Design practices (Karasti and Baker, 2004; Karasti and Syrjänen, 2004; Karasti, 2014). First, the 
fact that infrastructures are simultaneously technical (by having a specific materiality that needs 
to be understood), semantic (by assuming different meanings for various social groups over time) 
and generative (by allowing people to build and create new semantic content, material elements 
or collaborative practices) allows for relational tensions to arise and for design researchers to map 
and situate themselves in the field created by those tensions. Second, as infrastructures can be seen 
as relations between different ways of doing things, some questions become immediately relevant 
and almost unavoidable. When decisions that consolidate those relations are taken, which kind of 
practices are sustained the most by the shape of the infrastructure at a certain moment? Which are 
the social groups benefiting the most from it?
Another element has contributed to the success of infrastructuring as a concept to understand 
the unfolding and design of infrastructures as relational artefacts: the idea of a ‘point of infrastruc-
ture’, ‘the moment when an infrastructure becomes visible to its users’ (Pipek and Wulf, 2009). 
Methodologically speaking, the articulation of a point of infrastructure as either a breakdown or a 
form of use innovation (Pipek and Wulf, 2009) allows Participatory Design researchers to retrace 
those moments with various methodological tools, being interviews, ethnography or workshops. 
For instance, such a point of infrastructure can be revealed when a web platform starts to integrate 
video logs to diversify the actors it can give a voice to. As shown recently, focussing on points 
of infrastructure can allow design researchers to reconstruct the biography of projects over time, 
showing when crucial decisions were taken, how and why (Bødker et al., 2016; Lyle et al., 2018).
Finally, when Participatory Design takes place, there is an orientation to the future. It questions 
who could be the users of a future infrastructure and who should be involved in the participatory 
process of designing the infrastructure itself. This reveals that an infrastructure is also an intel -
lectual space, which is inherently political. For instance, how does the infrastructure facilitate the 
sustainable transformation of housing, energy use or education, and for whom? Ethnography and 
design processes can help Participatory Design researchers to orient themselves in the domain they 
are working in, but deliberately need to be complemented by foregrounding questions on whose 
and which interests are advanced by the way the participatory process is methodologically shaped.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
56
Commoning
The reflection around infrastructuring among heterogeneous collectives in Participatory Design 
has brought to the fore the issue of governance as a way to foster participation and to produce 
modes of social (re)production alternative to the capitalist one in the contexts of urban, suburban 
and rural contexts (Sciannamblo et al., 2021). An important strand of research relates to the shared 
production and maintenance of common resources between human and more-than-human actors, 
such as gardens or energy, variously understood as ‘the commons’, ‘the common’ and ‘common-
ing’ (Bresnihan, 2015; Gibson-Graham et al., 2016). These different labels refer to similar ways of 
understanding and practising the common development and management of resources. All these 
terms have been employed in Participatory Design (Marttila et al., 2014; Teli et al., 2016; Serav -
alli, 2018; Teli et al., 2018; Teli et al., 2022) to stress the increasing engagement of co-designers 
with collective action related to commons and to reinvigorate the political orientation of Par -
ticipatory Design towards ‘structuring future social relations’ (Light and Akama, 2014). Broadly 
speaking, commons refers to a particular way to manage property and access to resources, which 
is an alternative to the private and the public model (Ostrom, 1990). The collective management 
of resources is based on collaborative arrangements through which participants elaborate actions 
and decisions concerning shared resources.
Marttila et al. (2014) identify three main approaches through which the issue can be addressed.
The first one concerns the role of institutional arrangements in supporting the management of 
shared natural resources and focuses on the collective development of patterns and practices of 
collective action beyond the market and the state (Ostrom, 1990).
A second strand of research concerns the emergence of the new commons in the mid-1990s con-
nected to the rise of the network society and the widespread circulation of knowledge/information 
goods (Hess, 2008). Unlike traditional commons, new commons are intangible resources which 
are not subject to depletion due to competition or overconsumption. It is a research trajectory 
informed by discussions concerning copyright and the legal aspects of digital resources (Lessig, 
2001), examining the emergence of new forms of enclosure in the digital domain (e.g. digital 
rights management, copyright protection and licensing strategies) and the formation of ‘open ac -
cess commons’ characterised by a symmetric use of privileges for the general public and commu-
nity governance (Benkler, 2006). This body of knowledge shows how digital infrastructures can 
be designed to favour access to open commons or to create new enclosures.
A third and more recent line of research is inspired by critical theory and Autonomous Marxism 
which elaborates reflections about ‘the common’ and ‘commonwealth’ (Hardt and Negri, 2009), 
seen as both the product of labour and also the basis for struggles to create democratic forms of 
management of social production to construct alternatives to contemporary capitalism. This line of 
thinking resonates with feminist scholarship on ‘commoning’ (Federici, 2019), understood as ‘the 
production of ourselves as a common subject [. . .] as a quality of relations, a principle of coopera-
tion and of responsibility to each other and to the earth, the forests, the seas, the animals’. Such 
an understanding of common resources in relation to Participatory Design practices emphasise a 
number of relevant issues. First, it points to the nature of collectives gathering around commons, 
which are characterised by clear political stances concerning the unsustainable conditions of the 
current economic model as well as by more-than-human relationships that challenge dominant 
extractivist models of contemporary capitalism. Second, it also uncovers and values the amount 
of invisible work necessary to initiate and maintain processes of infrastructuring and to manage 
negotiations among the members of the collective (Sciannamblo et al., 2021). Thirdly, it points 
to the process of institutioning (Teli et al., 2018), which refers to the increasing commitment to 

Collectives and Participatory Design
57
commoning-engaged Participatory Design in institutional contexts and the related management 
of collaboration, tensions and conflicts, as well as to the creation of new institutions (Fumagalli, 
Giuliani, et al., 2019), which we now explore further.
Institutioning
Infrastructuring, as we have seen, involves design activities that engage participants in collective 
processes of design and use (Bødker et al., 2017, p. 246) when addressing questions that emerge in 
urban, suburban and rural contexts. These include design practices of commoning and institution-
ing (Teli et al., 2020). While commoning has been explained as Participatory Design work aiming 
to design from the perspective of and with collectives questioning the current economic model 
and thus is deeply rooted in everyday life (Foth and Turner, 2019; Teli et al., 2020), institutioning 
has been described as doing design work with an attention to institutional dynamics (Lodato and 
DiSalvo, 2018; Cibin et al., 2019; Teli et al., 2018).
Huybrechts et al. (2017) have stressed the importance of Participatory Design not only to en -
gage with the micro-political scale of fieldwork with communities but also in regard to their inter-
activity with institutional framing processes. Their study introduced the notion of ‘institutioning’, 
which highlights the move in participatory processes to engage with existing and creating new institu-
tions. Institutioning was defined as a strategy that encourages collectives of institutions, human and 
more-than-human actors on the ground to carefully acknowledge and give form to their mutual rela-
tions when designing for and with (sub)urban and rural contexts. The concept of institutioning was in-
troduced to enhance the potential of Participatory Design processes for effecting political change, not 
solely as an analytical framework, but as a verb or practice which highlights work that often remains in 
the backstage when participation on the ground is privileged. Institutioning is a process of articulation 
of and reflection on these processes and their dependencies on various institutional frames, which can, 
conversely, directly and/or indirectly lead to changes in institutional frames themselves.
Institutioning draws attention to the institutional character of Participatory Design processes, 
stressing that: (1) they cannot be understood exclusively as projects on a micro-scale, but are de -
pendent on and informed by institutions at larger scales; (2) they have the capacity to effect direct 
and indirect institutional change; (3) their institutional dependencies and potentials are multi-scalar 
and multi-directional, as is navigation through them; and (4) although they operate primarily on 
a micro-scale, Participatory Design processes generate many direct and indirect effects on other 
institutional frames through relations that are consolidative, challenging and/or formative. Moreo-
ver, institutioning’s expanded recognition of potential political capacity alters our understanding 
of what participation is. Institutioning involves an articulation and reflection on the ways in which 
various public and private institutions explicitly or implicitly ‘participate’ in Participatory Design 
processes and vice versa. Institutioning can thus be seen as participation in an expanded sense: 
potentially including not only persons or groups but also local and regional or even national and 
transnational organisations and institutions. In this notion of participation, researchers do not only 
engage with institutions as external actors but are already a part of institutional framing processes 
in their capacity as researchers.
When starting to map the radical interdependencies in collectives, it becomes more evident 
for designers that they need to interweave the aforementioned Participatory Design approaches 
of infrastructuring, commoning and institutioning (referred to as ‘ontologising’ infrastructuring 
by Huybrechts et al., 2022). There have been recent efforts to conceptualise this interrelation. For 
example, Teli et al. (2020) have identified four different kinds of processes of institutioning and 
commoning – intermediation, co-optation, entanglement and public formation – that differ among 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
58
each other depending on the more strategic or tactical set of actions that is available for design 
researchers, institutional actors or grassroots collectives.
Case Studies
In the following case studies, we can see how the diverse interrelations turned out in practice. The 
case studies will unravel the multiple answers to our questions. Particular attention in the analysis 
of the cases will be paid to how collectives are shaped and organised based on the discussed charac-
teristics, namely joint and distributed collective activities mediating understandings and solidarity; 
a collectively articulated identity; a history and orientation towards future development or degrada-
tion; the involvement of more-than-human actors, consciously involved or implicated actors.
In selecting the case studies, we decided to work with projects that we were part of our -
selves to be able to discuss their politics in more embodied and nuanced ways. A result of this 
approach is that all cases are European. This does of course not mean that these questions 
are not dealt with in non-European cases. Interesting references are for instance the work of 
Winschiers-Theophilus et al. (2010); Winschiers-Theophilus and Bidwell (2013); Pérez-Bustos 
and Franco-Avellaneda (2014); Sacks et al. (2022). To dive deeper into the non-European 
cases, we refer to chapter 5.
Commonfare 2016–2019 Case 3.1
The first case we discuss is Commonfare, a project that has produced a digital platform commonfare.
net, an association committed to the maintenance of the platform, and a few novel socio-technical 
features rooted in the practices and aspirations of the people involved. It was funded by the European 
Commission as part of the ‘Collective Awareness Platforms for Sustainability and Social Innovation’ 
topic in the ICT domain. Commonfare has been seen as a key project in recent Participatory Design 
scholarship, highlighted for example by Bødker et al. (2021), for the specific way the project articu-
lated its own practices and politics. Commonfare worked with grassroots initiatives involved in social 
cooperation from a caring perspective and, in this way, constituting social practices supplementing 
existing welfare systems and/or their failures (Bassetti et al., 2019).
From the point of view of this chapter, Commonfare is particularly relevant as design researchers 
engaged – with various fortunes – in what was defined as the entanglement of design research with 
the political practices (Teli et al., 2020) and theoretical perspectives (Sciannamblo et al., 2018) 
characterising already existing collectives. In particular, Commonfare included in its partnership 
with local associations, such as the Basic Income Network Italy and the Croatian Center for Peace 
Studies, and it engaged in forms of Participatory Design with collectives that had been questioning 
the current economic model on the basis of the financial distress put on the members of the collective. 
The social groups involved were deeply investigated, with a specific deliverable devoted to it that 
was questioning the economic development model of the countries involved (Croatia, Italy and 
the Netherlands) while identifying ‘good practices’ that collectives develop to challenge the model 
of economic development through bottom-up collaboration (Fumagalli et al., 2017). Among those 
good practices, it was possible to find, for example, cultural centres in occupied buildings, repur -
posed factories or community centres. The study of the selected good practices constituted the basis 

Collectives and Participatory Design
59
for the design researchers’ understanding of ‘joint and distributed collective activities mediating 
understandings and solidarity’. The overall project was aiming indeed at supporting ongoing collec -
tive activities based on solidarity.
During the project, it was clear that the Participatory Design researchers needed to engage with 
existing funding contracts (Lyle et al., 2018), ongoing political struggles (Fumagalli, Gobetti, et al., 
2019) and previous collective experimentations with specific technologies (Wilson et al., 2019). Al -
though these situated constraints existed, Commonfare achieved both technological and theoretical 
results, while trying to align the values of design researchers and activists (Bassetti et al., 2019). 
Technologically, the project has innovated on (1) representing the supposed trustworthiness of par -
ticipating individuals (Rough et al., 2023), (2) visualising the dynamic growth of the group of people 
engaging with commonfare.net (Rough et al., 2019) and (3) the possibility of supporting the creation 
of group-managed currencies (Teli et al., 2018; Wilson et al., 2019).
In the case of representing trustworthiness, the technological innovation started with questioning 
through interviews and workshops the basic assumptions of one of the topics the call for application 
was stressing, reputation systems. Fieldwork had suggested that the way the most well-known reputa-
tion systems work, subordinating the supposed trustworthiness of individuals to constant subjective 
judgement by others (as in online reviews on eBay, Amazon or Airbnb, just to mention a few), was 
highly unpleasant for interviewees that felt constantly judged when, for example, applying for wel-
fare benefit (Wilson and De Paoli, 2019). They prompted a rethinking of how such a system could 
work and novel algorithms and visualisations centred on the actual contribution of people to the life 
of commonfare.net, the digital platform that was the main output of the project. Such conceptualisa -
tion focussed mostly on network analysis of the different kinds of contributions people would bring, 
measured through indicators pointing to the robustness of the whole network more than on the evalu -
ation of the single action (Rough et al., 2023). The basic technological components that allowed for 
the elaboration of new concepts on representing trustworthiness were then employed, showing their 
malleability and agency, to monitor the overall status of the network of uses of commonfare.net, both 
in a public dashboard and an administration interface (Rough et al., 2019).
A different set of technologies was mobilised to provide participants to rethink currencies and how 
a digital platform like commonfare.net could support the creation of group-based currencies, a feature 
successfully deployed in two relatively big festivals, one of which hosted the overall project’s final 
event (Figure 3.1). These festivals were co-organised by adopting some ‘good practices’ mentioned 
earlier and identified through empirical work in the early stages of the project. There the effort was to 
find ways of granting the project a future beyond the duration of the European grant, exploring the pos-
sibilities of future development (Fumagalli, Gobetti, et al., 2019). Along this line, it should be stressed 
how the model adopted to achieve sustainability beyond the grant has not been successful. The intui-
tion of aligning different professional figures in a non-profit cultural association, constituted close to 
the end of the EU grant to maintain commonfare.net, while trying to obtain more grants has made the 
path to development difficult, and the role of the digital currency functionalities has been extremely 
limited from this perspective.
To summarise, the forms of technological innovation brought forward by Commonfare have helped 
in redefining the collective identity of the project, platform and cultural association which, especially 
in Italy, have been recognised as relevant actors by networks promoting forms of economic solidarity 
(e.g. the platform has been used in different ‘schools of political activation’ in different regions, and 
the association has become a member of the ‘Rete Italiana di Economia Solidale’ – ‘Italian Network 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
60
of Solidarity Economy’). The work on supporting such collective activities has, nevertheless, not been 
sufficient to guarantee a path towards the future development of the materialised outputs of the project, 
the platform and the cultural association.
Theoretically, the conversation on development and degradation that we can have is different when 
considering the academic outputs and the actual maintenance of the digital output. Although the main-
tenance of the digital output has appeared to be difficult, the research done in Commonfare has opened 
up – through the direct entanglement with the activists’ theoretical framework – the academic space 
for (1) explicitly including feminist social reproduction theory in the design of digital technologies 
(Sciannamblo et al., 2021); (2) re-engaging with critical theory with an understanding of the political 
economy of technologies design and potential use (Fumagalli, Giuliani, et al., 2019); and (3) strength-
ening the understanding of Participatory Design processes as including processes of institutioning 
(Teli et al., 2018) and of the position of design researchers as in-between grassroots initiatives and 
existing institutions (Teli et al., 2020).

building system (right). Pictures taken from Fumagalli, Gobetti et al. (2019).
Grassroot Wavelengths, 2017–2020 Case 3.2
A second case study significant for this chapter concerns Grassroot Wavelengths (henceforth GW), a 
European project funded between 2017 and 2020 and aimed at supporting the creation of low-budget 
and low-power FM radio stations in so-called remote European areas such as the Danube Delta in 
Romania, small islands off the southwestern coast of County Cork in Ireland and the island of Madeira 
in Portugal. The project employed a Participatory Design approach to support community deliberation 
and media pluralism and was characterised by the involvement of local communities in the setup and 
management of the radio stations built through a free/open hardware and software platform called 
RootIO (Cibin et al., 2020). The participation of local inhabitants of the islands thus not only entailed 

Collectives and Participatory Design
61
the collective learning of technical skills necessary to run the platform but also concerned editorial 
choices regarding programmes and show schedules.
The case of GW is relevant to highlight and problematise a number of issues deriving from the 
conceptual apparatus we have outlined in this chapter. In the first place, because GW was situated in 
remote locations (mostly islands and provinces) across Europe, the project entailed interesting insights 
concerning how the formation of collectives through Participatory Design is practised in rural settings 
(Hartley et al., 2003). The implementation of project activities has been in fact fully undertaken by lo-
cal universities, research centres, local organisations and population to deploy micro-radio stations for 
enabling effective messaging in the language(s) spoken in the target regions and offering community 
members a means of accessing and creating radio content. Since the very start of the project, the par -
ticipants showed a rather peculiar composition, characterised by both local volunteers and former local 
residents living abroad as part of the diaspora. The latter were included in radio activities since the be-
ginning of the project through the regular broadcast of specific shows such as the local mass and other 
community events particularly important for community members (Figure 3.2.). The diverse composi-
tion of GW’s participants resonates with the discussion about the term ‘collectives’ insofar as partici-
pants manifest as a stratified body of people that ‘come and go’ with different roles, unfolding their 
own strategies and patterns of appropriation. The relevant participation of diaspora confirmed initial 
expectations regarding the opportunities connected to the development of community radio stations 
such as the creation of bridges between permanent residents and people emigrated (Cibin et al., 2020). 
The radio stations thus worked as mediators among different spaces, allowing those living abroad to 
‘return’ and ‘be present’ in their native communities while being physically located elsewhere.
Reading the case of GW through the lens of collectives also emphasises the kind of socio-ecological 
relations that Participatory Design can entail. The attempt to install and maintain the radio antenna in 
the island settings happened to be quite challenging due to harsh weather conditions (such as storms) 
that caused the antenna to break and the radio broadcast to be disrupted. The entanglement between 
human conditions and environmental phenomena became even clearer with the spread of coronavirus 
SARS-CoV-2 and the consequent outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic. The restrictions on people’s 
movement significantly impacted the development of the project: radio programmes and schedules 
significantly changed to meet local needs. The Sunday mass started to be broadcast on the radio due 
to the impossibility of taking place in the church; the radio stations were also useful for broadcasting 
school assemblies, keeping regular encounters between teachers, students and families up.
The outbreak of the pandemic also impacted the licences as initially they were not set up to enable 
daily FM broadcasts. In a context clearly altered by the pandemic, local radio volunteers decided to 
extend and upgrade their licence to communicate in different languages with fishermen stranded in the 
bay because of travel restrictions. Similar events resulted in tensions among local residents and design-
ers concerning the reliability and durability of the technical and material apparatus, also shedding light 
on the agency of natural elements that take part in design endeavours (Cibin et al., 2021).
Being radio regulated by licences, the lens of institutioning becomes useful to illuminate a number 
of issues concerning the setup of radio stations from an institutional point of view. Compliance with 
regulatory frameworks became quite an obstacle to achieving the main objective of the project, that 
is, building small community radio stations through the participation and engagement of local vol-
unteers. These challenges respond to a number of issues imposed by institutional frames, such as the 
expectation of a certain degree of professionalism, the promotion of a particular division of labour as 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
62
Figure 3.2  Mass in Castletownbere, which was broadcast on community radio.

Collectives and Participatory Design
63
well as the need to have a physical place (Bidwell et al., 2021). The involvement of volunteers with 
expertise on spectrum and transmission equipment reproduced an expert-layperson divide within the 
group of volunteers, which, in turn, negatively affected the project goal of fostering diversity in design. 
The location of the installed antenna and the licence’s obligation to limit access to the transmitter and 
technical equipment only to those skilled in radio frequency engineering determined a gendered divi -
sion of responsibilities, with men installing the antenna and women undertaking administrative work. 
This configuration of roles and responsibilities uncovers the reproduction of traditional power asym -
metries, which characterise also grassroots and activist collectives pursuing practices of commoning. 
The implementation of licensing processes required indeed a clear technical and legal expertise needed 
to identify, for example, the details of studio equipment, to develop an editorial strategy and to comply 
with regulatory decisions. These constraints inevitably ended up in inclusive and exclusive processes 
and in the reproduction of gender-based hierarchies of labour. The need for technical and legal exper-
tise re-enacted the expert/layperson divide in design, with a few people taking major decisions con -
cerning the station governance and management as well as programme creation and broadcast before 
licences were granted. These vignettes are enlightening about the kind of tensions that can occur when 
Participatory Design supporting commoning practices is involved in institutioning processes. The (re)
production of traditional divides based on gender identities, age and skills is indeed typical of not only 
institutional and corporate settings but also of activist circles (Dunbar-Hester, 2008).
De Andere Markt, 2015– Case 3.3
The case study of the Living Lab De Andere Markt started in 2015 by UHasselt research line Spatial 
Capacity Building (ArcK) and LUCA School of Arts (KULeuven), as further explored in Chapter 10. 
In Participatory Design, Living Labs are shaped as open innovation milieus where groups, issues and 
ideas emerge from bottom-up, long-term collaborations between diverse actors (Björgvinsson et al., 
2012, p. 41; Dezuanni et al., 2018). In the case description here, we focus on the ways of working in 
more recent years of the Living Lab, in the Waterrijk Waterschei project. The work of the Living Lab in 
this context was challenged with a shift that needed to be made in the neighbourhood from mainly being 
a place for people (that in the past often implied paving the streets) towards making a place for water 
(which requires depaving) and thus also implied taking away that what people have built and cared for.
The case looked at joint and distributed collective activities mediating understandings and solidar-
ity around this shift. These collective activities were focussed on jointly critically questioning how 
design researchers are often invested in the ‘materiality’ of design (buildings, streets, bricks, maps, 
technologies) and how now, in times of immense socio-environmental challenges, such as the water 
challenge, designers are increasingly confronted with polarisation, such as a daily need for home and 
shelter versus an ecological need to build less and give room for water. In the Waterrijk Waterschei, 
the focus was on how to design for alternative types of ‘careful’ relations between actors who’s worlds, 
projects – and thus also how they consider the things designed – seem opposed to each other. Water -
rijk Waterschei was shaped as a Participatory Design process of ‘valuing in practice’, negotiating 
various world-making projects and ways of valuing the world and reconnecting these in new patch -
works. This case study description zooms into some collective design capabilities that were built to 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
64
form and organise collectives around such an approach of designing beyond oppositions for complex 
socio-environmental challenges: ‘being’, ‘knowing’, ‘doing’ and ‘relating’ together.
To get to know the living environment of the neighbourhood in a caring way and build up a collectively 
articulated identity around water, Waterrijk Waterschei has been conceived as a Living Lab. This Living 
Lab approach means that the project focussed on building collective capabilities with inhabitants, designers 
and policymakers in observing or – as what Mol would call – ‘being with’ the everyday inhabitants to gain 
deep insights into how different people and groups are concerned about caring for water. At the same time, 
also being with institutional actors was foregrounded, to understand how they care for water. We combine 
and confront the design, daily and the institutional knowledge about caring for water, to work towards a 
concrete and ambitious shift to making space for water. This is a build-up to a water campaign that aims to 
be carried out in the district in 2024 to move inhabitants and policy to water-friendly design interventions.
The project has a history and orientation towards future development and more particularly re- or 
de-development, focussing on undoing the overly built infrastructure focussed on humans and design 
space for water. The process wanted to build capabilities in connecting knowledge from the field, from 
different actors and bring this together through the creation of an Atlas, which started to develop in 
November 2021. This connecting of knowledge from different worlds, is what Mol calls ‘knowing with 
or together’ with others and was initiated at three different scales: the mapping of the waterways (hy-
drospatial scale), a more personal mapping (participatory research in the neighbourhood) and an institu-
tional mapping (networks of water-related actors). These three trajectories were supported by historical 
research on the development of the neighbourhood in Waterschei and previous activities linked to the 
water event in the district, as well as broader activities related to the environment and our surroundings.
The historical research was aimed at understanding neighbourhood dynamics and climate-related 
interests. In the water mapping section, the water landscape was read: a physical lecture and insights 
from the desktop research into the interaction between the natural water system, the human infrastruc-
tural water landscape and the role that institutional water stakeholders play in the water system. We 
learned that the latter organise the water system in the public domain and make tentative attempts to 
also support measures in the private domain (for example, by a subsidy for a rainwater cistern or green 
roof). We also observed that design interventions that reorganise and manage the public domain also 
determine developments in the private domain. For instance, replacing parking spaces with greenery, 
can unintentionally simulate private paving in (front) gardens and moving parked cars. Therefore, de-
sign interventions need to take into account developments both in the public domain and in the private 
space, to make a shift possible in the water system.
To start designing futures with more-than-human actors (both technological and ecological, in 
this case water and technical water infrastructure), the project quickly moved to building capabili -
ties of ‘doing together’ across public and private actors. The capability of ‘connecting’ the different 
ways of doing and caring for water publicly and privately was consciously designed. For example, 
together with the neighbourhood an unused basketball court was addressed to soften and green it 
with diverse actors: inhabitants, people from the municipality and from the water company and 
the neighbourhood manager. The concrete pavers were removed and room was made for a flower 
meadow, a herb garden and a berry forest around the pergola against which grapevines grow. Dif -
ferent practices regarding water, softening, collecting rainwater and conscious planting were made 
publicly visible and brought together, and actors collectively learned about these practices during 
‘doing together’ (Figure 3.3.).

Collectives and Participatory Design
65
Figure 3.3  Images by @Constructlab and @Waterland.


Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
66
In what was learned from making water practices visible and connecting them, prototypes for 
the future were distilled, thanks to the ‘imagining’ capability. This relates back to the idea of a point 
of infrastructure, the moment when an infrastructure – in this case, water infrastructure – becomes 
visible to its users (Pipek and Wulf, 2009). This is the case in the practice of daylighting that diverts 
an open-air watercourse below ground back into an above-ground channel (Lee et al., 2020), a prac -
tice that is also known as deculverting (Wild et al., 2011). For example, we learned from this doing 
together that designing a sustainable neighbourhood needs to deal more consciously with the tension 
between what is considered dirty and where people simultaneously derive an identity from, being 
proud of water in Waterschei. It turned out that many residents regard a paved surface as clean to 
invite friends and family. This invites us to think further about garden surfaces that are perceived as 
both ‘clean’ and water-permeable and can therefore also make people proud of how they deal with 
water.
Finally, there was great attention paid to nurturing all actors’ capabilities to ‘relate’: to institution 
that which is being visualised together in the community and to common and exchange in the com -
munity what is being crafted on an institutional level, thus making it relevant across different scales, 
communities and institutions and to make it guiding and challenging for planning and policy. This 
capability of relating makes it possible to be conscious about involved and implicated actors and 
include these where and when possible and – when they are excluded – at least to be conscious about 
that. The water case study showed that water companies often view water issues and transformations 
from a technical point of view, but that many social concerns, such as receiving family on clean 
surfaces in the garden, play a role and can help inspire the designs. In addition, many people are 
inclined to treat water more carefully but find the technical issues surrounding new installations too 
complex or the maintenance of softened areas too intensive. They often do not have the resources 
to carry out certain interventions. These insights can inspire policy on both measures that unburden 
(e.g. a number of maintenance tasks are taken over) and that free up resources for stimulating private 
initiatives.
This and similar cases of the Living Lab lead to an ongoing reflection on which capabilities as 
designers we need to form and organise collectives in Participatory Design with attention to its politics 
and the dynamics between commoning and institutioning practices (Huybrechts et al., 2018; Dreessen 
et al., 2021; Huybrechts et al., 2022).
Kallio Urban Gardens, 2014– Case 3.4
The three cases presented earlier are all part of funded research projects, in the form of one project, 
as with the Commonfare and Grassroot Wavelengths projects, or several projects that the research -
ers and other stakeholders have tried to build to have continuity. The fourth case we present is not 
related to any specific funded project. Rather, it is a grassroots urban gardening initiative – the 
Kallio Urban Gardens (KUG) – with which several Participatory Design researchers living in the 
Kallio neighbourhood of Helsinki became engaged (Figure 3.4.). The researchers have been vol -
unteer members of the initiative and have studied it using a Participatory Design lens (Marttila 

Collectives and Participatory Design
67
Figure 3.4  Two of the KUG urban gardens in the Kallio neighbourhood.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
68
and Botero, 2016; Botero and Saad-Sulonen, 2019), but there were no funded research projects 
put in place to specifically support their work, nor the initiative itself. As such, this case brings 
forward reflections on the role of Participatory Design researchers and practitioners in relation to 
the infrastructuring, commoning and institutioning work being carried out by collectives that are 
non-professionally defined, without the framing of a funded Participatory Design project per se. 
In this case, we notice the importance of the Participatory Design researcher being a member of 
the collective (Botero and Saad-Sulonen, 2019). KUG is an initiative that was started in 2014, by 
members of the Kallio-movement – an initially informal movement that emerged in 2011 to main -
tain the attention to the diversity of the Kallio neighbourhood of Helsinki and protect the food help 
for the needy that took place there (Marttila and Botero, 2016; Botero and Saad-Sulonen, 2019). 
During the time of the Participatory Design researchers’ initial engagement with KUG (some of 
them joined the initiative in 2014, others in 2016), KUG included around 85 gardeners and around 
60 planter boxes in three public parks. These three areas had been designated as suitable for urban 
gardening by the City of Helsinki, in their first inventory of such spaces other than the traditional 
allotment gardens (Marttila and Botero, 2016).
The case of the urban gardening initiative in Helsinki highlights the formation of a collective of hu-
man and more-than-human actors around the shaping, maintenance and nurturing of urban commons. 
In referring to this case, Marttila and Botero (2016) explain the infrastructuring processes that unfolded 
through the self-organisation of the members, their coordination through a closed Facebook group, and 
the workarounds they came up with to have access to water or resorting to a third party association of 
one of the members to have a representative legal entity for renting the plot of land from the city. Mart-
tila and Botero (2016) further refer to ‘strategising’ combined with ‘patchworking’ when relating how 
KUG members had made use of many available resources, combining those shared by not-for-profit 
organisations that have paved the way for urban agriculture and gardening in Helsinki, while at the same 
time following the emergence of new official guidelines being set up by the municipal authorities. What 
is reported is an entanglement of continuous infrastructuring and institutioning efforts that unfold and 
shape the becoming of the KUG as a functioning collective. Commoning activities are also identifiable 
in the interest that the KUG had – although not all members necessarily deliberately had – in shaping 
urban commons (Marttila and Botero, 2016). Botero and Saad-Sulonen (2019) also highlight the poten-
tial of addressing documentation – a needed yet challenging practice in self-organised collectives – as 
knowledge commons (Lyle et al., 2015). This reflection also triggers the authors to question their dual 
role as Participatory Design researchers and designers and as members of the KUG: interventions within 
a membership model may have different rhythms than in projects. As such, infrastructuring may also 
include the Participatory Design researchers’ navigation across their engagements with the collectives, 
combining their roles as members as well as those of designers/researchers. As Winschiers-Theophilus 
et al. (2010) discussed, Participatory Design is also about ‘being participated’ in a dual role of designer/
researcher and member of a community and navigating these different contexts.
Discussion: Shaping and Organising Collectives
In this chapter, we have asked: How can Participatory Design support the shaping and or -
ganisation of collectives around questions that emerge in urban, suburban and rural contexts 
with close attention to its politics? Which (implicated) actors do we give a voice to? Who 

Collectives and Participatory Design
69
do we choose to represent? When and how do we choose to become ourselves – design 
researchers – part of collectives? In addressing these questions via the aforementioned lit -
erature and case studies, it becomes apparent that there are many challenges in making the 
contribution of collectives matter in addressing large societal issues. The previous cases have 
shown that there are various forms of political choices involved in forming and organising 
collectives, which are relevant for better understanding Participatory Design processes now 
and in the future. Ambitious participatory transition processes of our daily life environ -
ments (e.g. from paved environments into open space) are most often driven by institutions, 
because there is little experience with and perhaps trust in how the dynamics of collectives 
can assure the transitions to actually take place. The aforementioned Participatory Design 
literature and cases have described the need to problematise dichotomies (e.g. centre/pe -
riphery, expert/lay, researcher/participant, human/nonhuman) and move in the direction of 
understanding participation as contributing to the shaping of collectives, made of varying 
everyday life and institutional actors, as drivers of participatory processes. This has implica-
tions that need further discussion.
First, we need to enhance our understanding of the organisational dynamics of collectives: 
they are shaped and reshaped in the form of changing networks, co-operations and more or 
less temporary organisational synergies (Boonstra and Boelens, 2011), which nurture and 
oppose institutional and community dynamics. When collectives drive Participatory Design 
processes, there is not one steering actor who can oversee everything and thus steer a process 
in one direction. This challenges traditional roles of facilitation found in Participatory Design. 
Such a shift toward a more dynamic definition of Participatory Design uncovers the need for 
continuous care for and understanding of how collectives work and how they can be supported 
to connect to each other and to everyday life and institutional frameworks that can co-steer 
transitions. This understanding can prevent instrumental (e.g. a Living Lab on the water 
should fix the water problem) or romantic perceptions and involvement of these collectives 
(e.g. a Living Lab on the future of water will organically create new water solutions) and can 
support the organisational dynamics with which these collectives can collaboratively shape 
socio-ecological transitions. Hence, Participatory Design practices and politics can openly 
confront risks of co-optation and the reproduction of countervailing power (Teli et al., 2020) 
that inevitably characterise any attempt at collaboration between grassroots collectives and 
institutions. To deepen our knowledge of how such processes can shape (sub)urban and rural 
contexts, we identify the need for further research into how collectives work and how they 
work together (their radical interdependencies) in-between everyday life and institutions and 
the key challenges they face. There is also more knowledge to be collected on how multiple 
types of participatory practices can be visible and can work together. Finally, more careful 
attention can be paid to politics in participatory set-ups: representing the trustworthiness of 
participating individuals, the dynamic growth of the group of people and the possibility of 
negotiating a position as design researchers in-between collectives in everyday life and exist-
ing institutions.
Secondly, the cases have shown that in Participatory Design a lot of experimentation has been 
done and still needs to be done with designing in-between infrastructures (Botero and Saad-Sulonen, 
2010) that facilitate these formation activities with collectives: in-between infrastructures have 
and can be designed to mediate how different spatial and timescales can be crossed (e.g. Grassroot 
Wavelengths); how groups can be organised or exchanges can take place (e.g. Commonfare); how 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
70
actors come together, separate and build relations (e.g. maps, atlas, online platforms in De Andere 
Markt); and how different participations work together, including designers and researchers as 
participants (e.g. KUG).
Third, the literature we have discussed shows that the evolving discourse on the shaping and 
organisation of ‘collectives’ has sharpened the attention to its relational politics. The coining of 
the term ‘infrastructuring’ has refined the debate, but later also terms such as ‘commoning’ and 
‘institutioning’ have enabled a more nuanced and politically sensitive understanding and shaping 
of collectives. From the case studies, we can see that there are roughly four ways of reading and 
framing these infrastructuring processes: commoning, institutioning, their intertwinement and the 
careful formation of the collectives in these processes.
In commoning processes, building relations with and for groups in daily life is central. These 
processes can involve (1) the relations with and between actors in daily life (the case study Kallio 
urban garden was a good example), (2) the relations of institutions with actors in daily life (e.g. 
the case of De Andere Markt) or (3) the relations between roles, genders and knowledges and the 
related issues of labour distribution that may be sources of power asymmetries (e.g. the case of 
Grassroot Wavelenghts).
In institutioning processes, building relations with and for institutions is central. These relations 
can take shape (4) between institutions mutually (Commonfare deals with how institutions, like 
academia, social organisations, community organisations, can relate in a transformative trajec -
tory) and regularly, not only within the range of funded projects but also can involve (5) relations 
between actors in daily life and institutions (in the Grassroots Wavelengths project, community 
initiatives are negotiated with institutional frameworks).
It is clear from the case descriptions that the commoning and institutioning processes inter -
twine in intense ways. Moreover, bringing a Participatory Design lens to cases like the KUG pre-
supposes an expanded understanding of design, in general, and Participatory Design, in particular, 
as taking place outside the confines of design or research projects (Botero, 2013; Botero and 
Hyysalo, 2013), with references to concepts that have influenced the emergence of scholarship 
on infrastructuring, commoning and institutioning, such as design-in-use (Henderson and Kyng, 
1992; Botero and Saad-Sulonen, 2010, Saad-Sulonen, 2014), design after design (Ehn, 2008; 
Björgvinsson et al., 2010), expanding design as unfolding over time (Saad-Sulonen et  al., 2018) 
and across diverse scalar trajectories (Botero and Saad-Sulonen, 2022). Most of the cases indeed 
worked with non-professionally organised collectives (see, for example, most of the practices in 
Commonfare) or extended beyond the confines of the professionally organised project. In many 
cases the Participatory Design researcher was or became an active part of the non-professional 
collective, something also apparent in earlier works on infrastructuring or Community-based 
Participatory Design (Karasti and Syrjänen, 2004; Winschiers-Theophilus et  al., 2010).
Finally, the different approaches to infrastructuring described also lead to a clearer articulation 
of the different characteristics of the shaping and organisation of collectives and their politics.
In what concerns the joint and distributed collective activities mediating understandings and 
solidarity, all cases addressed shaping solidarity around matters of care, be it water or work or 
gardening or community media. For instance, De Andere Markt uses a Living Lab approach to 
trace the different relations people have with water, to shape solidarity around this matter of care. 
The cases also uncovered how unanticipated matters of care may arise through the articulation of 
design activities. For example, access to the radio transmitter was limited only to those equipped 
with technical expertise within the Grassroot Wavelenghts project reproduced a traditional gen -
dered division of roles, with men taking major decisions concerning the station governance and 

Collectives and Participatory Design
71
management and women performing clerical and care labour. How can we pay attention to the 
unanticipated matters of care that may arise through making Participatory Design with collectives 
and institutions?
In what concerns a collectively articulated identity De Andere Markt engages in a strategy of 
‘being with’ people and water in the neighbourhood to understand how people identify with water. 
In the gardening case, the researchers were even actively part of the studied collective. This raises 
questions: How do we share ‘being’ as Participatory Design researchers, more than just distantly 
observing the contexts we study? How do we embed ourselves in other ways of being that make 
up collectives? How to share ‘our being’ with each other?
In relation to history and orientation towards future development or degradation, De Andere 
Markt uses an atlas to go back into the histories of how people live with water in the urban context, 
how it has evolved over time and how it can further develop into possible futures (see also further 
discussions on memory, recuperation and reviving stories entangled with the design settings but 
neglected by prevailing design narratives; e.g. in Rosner, 2018). How can we embrace knowing 
of collectives that evolves? Designs often ask for a moment where we freeze things and propose 
a ‘solution’. Or how do we design infrastructures (for communities, water, gardening, .  . .) that 
enable this evolving? From our cases, we learn that this idea of evolving infrastructures frequently 
conflicts with the time and confidence institutions have in investing in designed things that do not 
have a fixed form.
All projects actively involve more-than-human actors in the collective formation process, where 
challenges are encountered in how, for instance, water, wind or a digital currency can become an 
actor with equal agency in the debates on sustainable futures. As designers, we design and inter -
act with material things and technologies which are in themselves more-than-human actors with 
roles to play in the collectives. In recent years, ecological actors as more-than-human actors have 
become more and more important in Participatory Design practices, posing additional challenges 
on how to frame the relations between all the components of a collective. Paraphrasing Eduardo 
Kohn (2013), how can we imagine Participatory Design ‘beyond the human’ and interact with the 
many creatures that inhabit global ecosystems?
In designing with urban, suburban and rural contexts, there are many implicated and silent 
actors who are challenging to involve. This means that what can be reached might not neces -
sarily be deemed ‘good enough’ for all those involved. How can we design for (sub)urban and 
rural contexts, embracing continuous change while at the same time sometimes accepting the 
good enough? What is good enough? Can this be evaluated? For instance, should we involve 
inhabitants in accepting the ‘as good as it gets’ situation in relation to water infrastructure?
To conclude, all discussed projects are modest attempts to form, alter, organise or support 
collectives. Because these attempts can never be complete or completely satisfactory for every -
one, there is a strong need for memory-making on how collectives have formed in various urban, 
suburban and rural contexts, which can enable collective learning on collective-making. This 
memory-making can be considered an important challenge for the field of Participatory Design 
in the future not only to document methodologies and tools but also particularities of cases and 
contexts (Zuljevic and Huybrechts, 2021). The described cases already attempt to shape the 
memory of Participatory Design approaches that have tried to work consciously with the organi -
sation and formation of collectives on societal challenges in urban, suburban and rural contexts 
(Teli et al., 2018). We detected a relational approach to Participatory Design when working with 
these collectives: the Participatory Design processes were not focussed on working with a fixed 
concept of a collective but worked towards an understanding of a Participatory Design process 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
72
as a continuously shifting collective of collectives. However, this requires ongoing research 
into and care for where, how, when and with whom relations are built with, within and outside 
collectives.
Summary of Challenges and Opportunities
Participatory transition processes of our daily life environments are often driven by established 
organisations like public institutions or companies. However, they have little experience with and 
trust in how the dynamics of collectives can support the transitions they aim for. Therefore, the 
future of Participatory Design research should engage with the growing need to move in the direc-
tion of understanding participation as contributing to the shaping of collectives, made of varying 
everyday life and institutional actors.
Going more in detail, we need, first, to enhance our understanding of the organisational dynam-
ics of collectives: they are shaped and reshaped in the form of changing networks, co-operations 
and more or less temporary organisational synergies, which nurture, strengthen and oppose con -
servative or transformative dynamics.
• We detected the need for more insights into how collectives work and how they work together 
with each other in-between everyday life and institutions and the key challenges they face.
• There is also more knowledge to be collected on how multiple types of participatory practices 
can be visible and can work together.
• More careful attention can be paid to politics in participatory set-ups: representing the trustwor-
thiness of participating individuals, the dynamic growth of the group of people and the possibil-
ity of negotiating a position as design researchers in-between collectives in everyday life and 
existing institutions.
Second, the literature we have discussed shows that the evolving discourse on the shaping and 
organisation of collectives around questions that emerge in urban, suburban and rural contexts, has 
sharpened the attention to its relational politics in roughly four ways.
• In commoning processes, building relations with and for groups in daily life is central: (1) the 
relations with and between actors in daily life, (2) the relations of institutions with these daily 
life actors or (3) the relations between roles, genders and knowledges and the related issues of 
labour distribution that may be sources of power asymmetries.
• In institutioning processes, building relations with and for institutions is central: (4) between 
institutions and (5) between actors in daily life and institutions.
• It is clear from the case descriptions that the commoning and institutioning processes intertwine 
in intense ways and that they present an expanded understanding of Participatory Design, as 
taking place outside the confines of design or research projects.
Finally, the different approaches to infrastructuring described earlier, also lead to a clearer articula-
tion of the different characteristics of the shaping and organisation of collectives and their politics.
• All cases addressed are conceptualising solidarity around matters of care. The cases also uncov-
ered how unanticipated matters of care may arise through the articulation of design activities.
• All cases worked on a collectively articulated identity, reflectin g on how to embed ourselves in 
a diversity of ways of being.

Collectives and Participatory Design
73
• The cases focussed both on specific histories and included an orientation towards future devel-
opment, while questioning how to design infrastructures that enable the evolving of Participa-
tory Design processes.
• All projects actively involved more-than-human actors in the collective formation process, 
where challenges were encountered in how water, wind or a digital currency can become an 
actor with equal agency in the debates on sustainable futures, posing additional challenges on 
how to frame the relations between all the components of a collective.
• In designing with urban, suburban and rural contexts, there are many implicated and silent actors 
that are challenging to be involved. This means that what can be reached might not necessarily 
be deemed ‘good enough’ for all those involved, which raises questions on how to design for 
(sub)urban and rural contexts, while at the same time evaluating what we accept as good enough.
In general, we detected a strong need for memory-making on how collectives have formed in vari-
ous urban, suburban and rural contexts, which can enable collective learning on collective-making 
and that opens up a stronger connection between Participatory Design research and history-  
making.

4
MORE-THAN-HUMAN 
PARTICIPATORY DESIGN
Sara Heitlinger, Ann Light, Yoko Akama,  
Kristina Lindström and Åsa Ståhl
  DOI: 10.4324/9781003334330-5
The ecological crises we face are fed by a disconnect from interspecies interdependencies and mis -
guided human-exceptionalism (the belief we are somehow distinct from nature). Given that design 
may contribute to our worsening socio-ecological conditions, this is seen as a pivotal moment to ques-
tion and expand Participatory Design’s traditional tenets, such as those grounded in democracy, rights, 
fairness, inclusion and empowerment, to consider what a different philosophical starting point and 
commitment to more-than-human Participatory Design might bring.
This chapter explores the different traditions underpinning existing Participatory Design work ori-
ented towards sustainability. We show the beginnings of a Participatory Design drawn from an apprecia-
tion of the innately interdependent and entangled nature of the world, called here the more-than-human. 
Two lineages of Participatory Design scholarship are traced: Sustainability (with branches in Modernist 
and rights-based thinking) and Entanglement (with branches in care-based and co-ontological being). 
The chapter presents three cases to ground our explorations and bring to light how human-nature separa-
tions in systems, structures, values and mindsets inadvertently condition our practice. Our cases ground 
the theories and paradigms identified in the four branches and show how commitments play out and 
evolve through practice. This allows us to critically examine existing tenets of Participatory Design and 
reinterpret the visions that these hold to explore what more-than-human relationality might entail. Our 
discussion reveals the tensions, politics, paradoxes and difficulties in turning towards more-than-human 
relationalities and in working across and between worldviews. The chapter closes with the questions 
that the ambitions of more-than-human Participatory Design pose for our practice. At best, we hope they 
present a means to tread more gently and responsibly on the earth we share.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
80
Introduction
Life on Earth will continue to be impacted by decisions we make now about technologies and 
design long after our current choices and justifications look obsolete. Even in Participatory De-
sign, where we strive to be inclusive and democratic in our practices, we can expect rapid trans-
formations and increasing uncertainty to undermine our capacity for good long-term choices. For 
instance, much technology development is predicated on reliable sources of carbon-neutral energy 
becoming available, but present renewables depend on the mining of minerals that are scarce, 
causing different perils, such as pollution, habitat loss, Indigenous land dispossession (Ninomiya 
et al., 2023) and modern-day slavery.
1 All this contributes to worsening socio-ecological condi-
tions. Knowing this, we have another decision to make. We need to tackle immediate problems 
but also take the wider context into consideration and ask how design theories and practice must 
change to be fit for purpose as we recognise the damage that industrial priorities have caused.
In this chapter, we explore the different intellectual, philosophical and political traditions un-
derpinning existing Participatory Design work, especially those oriented towards sustainability,
