and consider the beginnings of a Participatory Design drawn from an appreciation of the innately 
interdependent and entangled nature of the worlds through which we move. In doing so, we ac -
knowledge that, while this thinking may bring a fresh perspective to Participatory Design, it ech -
oes worldviews that go back in time and across the planet to cultures and people who better 
recognise the need for ecological balance and respect.
We write in the context of mass species loss, rising forever pollution and extreme weather events with 
impacts experienced unequally across the globe. The ecological crises that we face are fed by misguided 
human-exceptionalism (the belief that we are somehow distinct from nature) and a disconnect from 
interspecies interdependencies. We see this as a pivotal moment to question and expand Participatory 
Design’s traditional tenets, grounded in democracy, rights, fairness, inclusion and empowerment, which 
emerged from a commitment to support people to self-determine their own wellbeing (Greenbaum, 
1993). In considering the future of Participatory Design, we are alive to several tensions, not least that 
human flourishing depends on all flourishing and that this matter is remote from Participatory Design’s 
historic domain: coming together to make better technology to foster democracy in workplaces and 
solidarity in communities. But we remain in the terrain of considering design processes for the better-
ment of conditions and worlds – a form of ethics that is familiar, if differently expressed, for most people 
working in Participatory Design and which has been argued to unite the field (Iversen et al., 2010).
Approaches which question the basis of current resource management have been called strong sus-
tainability, with a commitment to system change beyond tweaking current behaviours and consumption 
patterns. Though we address sustainability in Participatory Design in this chapter, we can draw on a 
far wider range of Participatory Design concerns, such as building solidarity, and be more radical in 
our commitments, such as embracing entanglement theories, if we reframe our commitments to look at 
relations as the fundamental focus of our work. Again, this will be familiar to Participatory Design prac-
titioners and we stress this through-line even as we explore the key tensions and inspirations of commit-
ting to more-than-human relationships. We introduce three cases to ground our explorations in practice.
“More-than-human
” is a term used here to acknowledge that all life and non-living entities 
are interdependent.2 Not everyone shares a definition of “more-than-human”. We are not seeking 
a consensus here either. Our literature review shows this variety. We offer our position: that the 
more-than-human points to the fundamental relational condition of our ontological co-existence. 
This orientation is characterised by a movement towards a deeper ecological embrace, one which 
recognises interdependence and care as the fundamental relations that pertain to all beings and 
non-beings on Earth. Because it is an ontological position, we think it changes why, what and how 
we do things in Participatory Design. To clarify, “more-than-human” is not a category that others 

More-Than-Human Participatory Design
81
non-human species; rather, it is an ethics of committing to relationality. For our discussion here, 
we use non-humans as a noun to indicate individual actors, entities, species and such like.
To explain the difference between our broadly aligned position and other philosophical tradi -
tions, we trace two lineages of Participatory Design scholarship, each with two branches. We are 
calling these lineages (1) sustainability (with branches in Modernist and rights-based thinking) and 
(2) entanglement (with branches in care-based and co-ontological being) (see Figure 4.1).
Figure 4.1  Top: sustainability lineage. Bottom: entanglement lineage (image credit: Yoko Akama, with 
permission)


Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
82
We arrived at these lineages and their branches by analysing Participatory Design Conference 
(PDC) proceedings, adjacent discourses and other works since 2012 (when the 2013 Participa -
tory Design Handbook was published) and endeavouring to make sense of the differences in 
focus we were seeing. Distinguishing these trajectories helps clarify the politics when the term 
more-than-human and similar ideas appear. For instance, in the cognate field of human-computer 
interaction, the term more-than-human is used to describe quite varied relations (e.g. Yoo et al., 
2023), such as between humans and other species, between humans and machines, in rethinking 
agencies (e.g. Wakkary, 2021) and remaking interspecies relations. Work that is not related to eco-
logical concerns is not in our review.
Sustainability and Entanglement
The two lineages we trace in recent Participatory Design work on addressing climate care and 
environmental crises concern what we are calling here sustainability and entanglement.
The sustainability lineage in Participatory Design builds on design’s tradition of working tech-
nically to improve products with a focus on outcomes. We show how sustainability approaches 
are based on paradigms of productivity and development, involving linear thinking from defining 
problems to moving towards solutions. This includes delivering behaviour change and better re-
source management, linked to broader sustainability work in science and positivist social science. 
Aligning with mainstream narratives of modern “advancement”, initiatives based on these tradi-
tions are powerful in developing and scaling up sustainable interventions to meet the challenges of 
climate catastrophe. This is urgent to protect biospheres or ensure the livelihoods of marginalised 
communities but does not change the underlying relations that pose the threat.
What distinguishes these logics from the entanglement tradition is the binary at the centre, 
where ambiguities and paradoxes are eliminated in the pursuit of Enlightenment clarity. As such, 
a separation of self-other, human-nature, brain-body and so on proliferates.
The lineage of entanglement and relationality draws on a different philosophical tradition with 
roots in the environmental humanities, feminist STS, New Materialism and theoretical critiques of 
positivism. This lineage stems from ontological practices that include ancestral wisdoms acknowl-
edging interdependencies as part of different and pluriversal roots. Work influenced by these posi-
tions tends not to pursue the linear, logical or outcome-led results of the sustainability lineage. For 
those schooled in traditions of (post)industrial Modern thought, it may, consequently, be harder 
to recognise the priorities and achievements of what the entanglement branch offers and how it 
might support design. Reading our cases may help the reader understand its potential in practice.
In presenting these roots (and branches), we know that our review is not exhaustive; many valu-
able papers are missing. Our aim is not for comprehensiveness, but, rather, we have selected those 
materials best able to help us articulate the politics of these areas of concern. For instance, we 
regret that groups with entangled ancestral wisdoms and expanded notions of “participation” have 
often felt excluded by the Anglophonic, Global North and Euro-US leaning academic conven -
tions of Participatory Design and adjacent fields and we have chosen some texts to refer to these 
excluded traditions. It is important to acknowledge First Nations’ practices, onto-epistemologies 
and ancestral wisdoms that have always premised relational interdependence and which Western/
Modern thought has eroded and disconnected.
The plurality that underlies such relational starting points is important to recognise and respect. 
The five authors have differing worldviews and intersectional experiences, which then shape our 
politics, positions and, thus, how we practice Participatory Design. These differences inflect the 
authors’ cases. The authors are part of various prior assemblages that have fostered long friendships 

More-Than-Human Participatory Design
83
or fresh collaborations with one another. We are academics working within well-resourced West-
ern institutions (Sweden, the UK and on lands now called “Australia”) that afford us certain privi-
leges. As such, regardless of individual or collective positionality, our work acknowledges how 
we are part of global asymmetries in which power has been accumulated and distributed unevenly.
We hope, through the cases presented here and reviewed in the discussion, we bring to light 
how human-nature separations in systems, structures, values and mindsets inadvertently condition 
our practice. In our commitment to a fuller embrace of the more-than-human, we have begun to 
recognise the inconsistencies and tensions that working across and between world(view)s bring. In 
choosing to reveal these tensions, we accentuate the politics, paradoxes and difficulties of turning 
towards more-than-human relationalities.
Our cases ground the theories and paradigms we identify in the four branches as they evolve 
through our practices. This allows us to critically examine tenets of Participatory Design such as 
democracy, rights, fairness, inclusion and empowerment and reinterpret them for more-than-human 
relationalities at their fullest. Trying these new positions does not negate older practices; our tradi-
tions are the context against which we evaluate and reflect. We close the chapter with a discussion 
of how the ambitions of more-than-human Participatory Design pose questions for our practice and 
offer a different lens. At best, we hope they present a means to tread more gently and responsibly.
A Review of Two Lineages and Four Branches
Sustainability: Modernist Branch
Sustainability and design are well-paired because design has long been an agent in the unsus-
tainability of industrial processes. Mindful of this, approaches to change this relationship have 
included “green design” in the 80s, “eco-design” in the 90s and “sustainable design” or “design 
for sustainability” in the 2000s (Walker and Giard, 2013). These movements all aimed to reduce 
environmental impact through efficient use of resources, materials and energy, minimising waste 
and making advancements with technology and innovation. But, while advocating for a change 
from business-as-usual, nothing much was changing (Fry, 2009). The solutions being offered re -
mained in the paradigm of the problems they were solving; that is, they were tethered to a Modern 
tradition that sees development, growth and productivity as essentials. This tension is caught in 
the idea of the Triple Bottom Line, popular in the 90s, where evaluating people, profit and planet 
aimed to shift commercial and consumer imperatives. Yet design was reluctant to let go of produc-
tion and consumption cycles (Manzini, 2006). Much early work in sustainable interaction design 
focused on the individual, with limited behaviour change models and conceptions of agency (DiS-
alvo et al., 2010). It was felt this work did not go far enough, only minorly mitigating the worst of 
industrial practices. Individualist and Modern approaches to strengthening environmental aware-
ness have been dismissed by many (Brynjarsdottir et al., 2012; DiSalvo et al., 2010; Dourish, 
2010; Strengers, 2014). The absence of spiritual dimensions has also been addressed (Inayatullah, 
2005; Walker, 2013). Fry (1999, 2009) has been a prominent critic of design, noting its apolitical 
disposition and lack of response to the crises of our time.
Within Participatory Design, there is no strong tradition of prioritising ecological concerns; 
instead, the focus has been on social viability. This is confirmed by Poderi and Dittrich (2018) who 
found Participatory Design has had a nebulous and tentative relationship with sustainability. They 
identified 21 out of 693 articles using the term “sustain” over 28 years of PDC history. When it ap-
peared, the term was mostly used to refer to project longevity and duration beyond external inter-
ventions, owing more to criteria for evaluating development projects than to sustainability science.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
84
There are examples of participatory processes being used to develop tools for matters of eco -
logical concern, such as monitoring water use (e.g. Carroll et al., 2019). But, largely, the presence 
of time-old Participatory Design values (rights, fairness, inclusion, democracy, empowerment) 
continues to throw a focus on the human. We see, for example, ways to foster awareness, solidar-
ity, community and relationships to shift behaviours towards socially just and ecological transi -
tions (Dick et al., 2012). Building neighbourhoods may be a practice that creates conditions in 
which sustainable futures can be explored and established (Huybrechts et al., 2017). There are 
considerations of scale, where climate change and other environmental crises require people to 
think and act more consciously with larger systems and structures for global impact. For instance, 
citizen participation in ICT infrastructuring for community energy management is helping people 
imagine futures beyond the limitations of capitalism (Capaccioli et al., 2016). We find discussions 
around sustainable smart cities at these scales (Chopra et al., 2022; Heitlinger, et al., 2018), while 
a strength of Participatory Design work is that, even when issues scale, there is an attempt to keep 
in sight the local and the marginalised.
Sustainability: Rights-Based Branch
Participatory Design has a long history of considering human rights. Human rights are intended 
to provide a universal commitment to protect people and give them due as equal subjects of the 
world. Rights (as a political entity) come into their own with the Enlightenment, when human 
life and learning became an end in itself. But rights are structured in an extension of self-other, 
human-nature separation and closely follow old religious hierarchies. Principal among these is the 
command in the Bible, informing all Judeo-Christian faiths, that man should hold dominion over 
all creatures of the earth and waters, which has structured living relations in much of the world 
(e.g. Lent, 2017). For many centuries, women, animals and plants were deemed to have no soul or 
reason and the legacy of that thinking – and what counts as sentience – is only now being evalu-
ated. Rights are adjusted as such beliefs change. When we see transposition of rights to non-human 
entities like animals and rivers for their protection, they may be granted “legal personhood”. This 
relies on a human to represent and speak on their behalf and downplays other lifeforms and Indig-
enous cosmologies that relate and exist differently (Salmond, 2014).
A vein through many Participatory Design works is the exclusion and inclusion of “voices”, 
their representation directly or via a proxy and the agency they are afforded in shaping the de -
sign process. While voice is an important, continued marker of inclusion, it is curious how a 
rights-based notion is applied literally to non-humans: “Ecosystems cannot voice their opinion on 
their own, and it is up to their codesigners to find ways of inviting them” (Pettersen et al., 2018). 
Relatedly, digital technologies like algorithms, sensors and data are seen as actors that “influ -
ence who counts as a ‘user’: .  . . they often provide us with the (only) means to include nature 
as a participant, at least as a matter of concern to be considered here and now” (Parmiggiani and 
Karasti, 2018). Intermediaries and forms of representation have been a long-standing concern for 
Participatory Design, now raised to ask how these can mute or skew non-human presence. If we 
consider ecology, rather than species or individual entities, rights become tenuous. Bastian et al. 
(2016), who ask how to participate with water and bees, point out (with feminist and critical race 
scholars, e.g. Ahmed (2012)) that merely increasing the kind and quantity of representation can 
mask deeper structures of power and causes of exclusion and oppression.
Research in most Western contexts arises out of Enlightenment traditions, supporting a sep-
aration between ontology, epistemology, axiology (values) and methodology (Wilson, 2008). 
When humans and non-humans are accounted for, it is very often in such a way that follows the 

More-Than-Human Participatory Design
85
conventions of scientific research. But, just because barnacles, humidity and rocks have been 
named and measured by humans does not mean that they exist in that way. Increasingly, scientists 
are recognising that the scientific method creates results rather than discovering them (Barad, 
2007). The act of measuring is becoming regarded as a creative act of interpretation, rather than 
only of explanation. If Participatory Design follows this line of reasoning, we can see how it might 
turn towards the more-than-human to trace a different paradigm, commitment and politics, while 
holding true to its interest in wellbeing and inclusion.
Entanglement: The Relational Turn
If we attempt to articulate the emerging turn to the more-than-human as a philosophical, ontologi-
cal and practical commitment (Light et al 2024a), we must do so provisionally, noting that this is a 
field of inquiry that is rapidly expanding. For some time, without using the term more-than-human, 
scholars in Participatory Design, including the authors of this chapter, have grappled with the 
challenges of the Anthropocene and working with non-humans to find new meanings in, for and 
through design. Lindström and Ståhl (2016) explore composting plastics with common meal -
worms to politicise everyday material participation (Marres, 2015) and argue for “respons-able 
stakeholders”, sensitised to entanglements and obligation. Similarly, an explicit focus on care and 
relationality acts as a harbinger in Light and Akama’s work (e.g. 2014), who build on Puig de la 
Bellacasa’s thinking with care (Puig de la Bellacasa, 2011, 2012). Ludic encounters for multispe-
cies care and cohabitation through Participatory Design with marginalised urban farming commu-
nities are the focus of Heitlinger et al. (2014; Heitlinger, 2016). Creative practice for decentring 
the human and approaching ecological concerns is explored in DiSalvo et al. (2009) and DiSalvo 
and Lukens (2011).
Further, Participatory Design in these branches is necessarily pluralistic. Some concepts and 
articulations are in formation now and others arise from practices millennia old, etching a path 
that fundamentally questions the human-world relations that have dominated in philosophy and in 
how the majority lives. Inspiration is not from one distinct ontological position, but comes from a 
range of associated theorists, stressing different parts of the evolving relational sensibility. These 
cluster around various themes: feminist technoscience; entanglement; relational ontologies. There 
are also powerful wisdoms and axiologies shared by Indigenous scholars and communities that 
continue to teach and inspire, such as those we cite (Kimmerer, 2013; Moran et al., 2018). The 
turn to plural onto-epistemes, philosophies and belief systems, such as Buddhism and Indigenous 
cosmologies, is becoming a significant movement. For this reason, it is particularly important that 
debts are paid: many scholars and practitioners on the margins have been thinking relationally, 
while much Western/Modern thinking continues to be mired in positivism.
Entanglement: Care-Based Branch
This branch has a theoretical lineage that comes from several scholarly fields anchored in cri -
tiques of positivism and Modernist thinking (i.e. they question or reject the dualism, categorisation 
and hierarchies of self-other, mind-body, human-nature, etc., forged in the Enlightenment). Criti-
cal discourses for decentring human-exceptionalism or radical re-distributions of agency across 
humans and non-humans have emerged from STS as actor-network theory (e.g. Latour, 1999; 
Law, 2004; Mol, 2002), Feminist Techno-science (e.g. (Barad, 2007; Haraway, 2016; Tsing et al., 
2017) and object-oriented theory captured in concepts like the “hyper object” (Morton, 2013). 
Other literature has taken a more applied focus, drawing on burgeoning research on alternative 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
86
infrastructuring, such as Gibson-Graham’s alternative economies (2006). Taken together, they 
challenge technological reductionism, asserting all things on the earth are beings in kinship rela -
tionships and refusing their reduction to subjects of or vehicles for exploitation, extraction and de-
pletion. The more-than-human becomes a powerful rhetorical device for considering how power, 
agency and values are distributed across actors and emerge through unfolding relations (Akama 
et al., 2020; Heitlinger et al., 2021) and resituating care as a foundational quality of interdependent 
life (Puig de la Bellacasa, 2011, 2012, 2017).
The explicit use of the term more-than-human becomes pronounced in Participatory Design 
after 2018. The year leading up to that edition of PDC was marked by a turning point, when the en-
vironmental crisis was growing in the public consciousness. For many researchers, it marked a pe-
riod of re-evaluation (Light et al., 2017). PDC’18 came on the heels of key feminist publications, 
including Haraway’s Staying with the Trouble, Tsing’s The Mushroom at the End of the World; 
Puig de la Bellacasa’s Matters of Care; and the edited collection, Arts of Living on a Damaged 
Planet. The 2018 PDC invited us to amplify the politics of democracy in addressing urgent global 
challenges (Huybrechts et al., 2018). We can see this as a critical moment in opening Participatory 
Design concerns beyond the pursuit of well-made products and systems (Kyng, 2010). Research -
ers took up this invitation in a workshop on more-than-human Participatory Design (Heitlinger, 
et al., 2018) and with a speculative walk to imagine cohabitation in urban spaces (Clarke et al., 
2018). These experiments attempted to recognise urban spaces for more-than-human flourishing. 
Important themes emerged: decentring human agency, critiquing human-exceptionalism; explor -
ing temporalities, recognising tensions between climate urgency and longer timescales like geo-
logical deep-time; incorporating other wisdoms, learning from Indigenous onto-epistemes; and 
introducing expertise from distant disciplines and a non-Western canon, including folklore (Clarke 
et al., 2019). These themes drew inspiration from feminist technoscience in their exploration of 
agency, power and values.
As Chapter 5 reports, running alongside this concern has been another decolonising current. 
PDC’20 went to the Global South,
3 and its chairs’ theme-setting helped onto-epistemes from the 
Global South make inroads into the narrowness of participation defined by Euro-US worldviews 
(Del Gaudio et al., 2020). The conference provided an opportunity to learn with and from genera-
tions that have taught wisdoms through stories and practices. We witnessed the focus shifting from 
methods, projects, theories, methodology and epistemologies towards embodiment of “sentipen -
sar” (Borda, 1979), bringing a feeling-thinking dimension (Salazar et al., 2020). Then, at PDC’22 
(Vlachokyriakos et al., 2022), we observed a pronounced self-reflexive stance in experimenting 
with data, methods, multispecies communing (Haldrup et al., 2022) and creative practices to en-
gage more critically, creatively and deeply in more-than-human relations (Cooper, 2022; Dole -
jsova et al., 2022; Szaniecki, 2022; Westerlaken et al., 2022). There, “Reworlding” was a term 
offered for self-critique (Huybrechts et al., 2022): to develop capabilities needed in Participatory 
Design to articulate radical interdependence.
Entanglement: Co-Ontological Branch
Sitting alongside these theoretical critiques and new experimentations are practices from age-old 
living, making and being. We use the term “ancestral wisdoms” in this chapter to allude to all 
the practices and stories we encounter that have been passed through generations and which are 
related to, but may not have the status of, the onto-epistemes, worldviews and cosmologies of 
those that politically identify as Indigenous or First Nation members. These include recipes for 
fermenting, know-how for sourcing food and practices for saving seeds. Speaking of ancestral 

More-Than-Human Participatory Design
87
wisdom allows us to address the vernacular teachings and practices that continue to live and be 
embroidered through many hands, families and cultures everywhere. This body of work appearing 
in Participatory Design is still nascent, so all analysis must be tentative and possibly premature, 
but, by widening our understanding of such expertise, we draw attention to and reposition the 
heritage upon which much-revitalised thinking sits. In this branch of entanglement, we see both 
implicit and explicit evocation of different knowledge traditions that do not fetishise separation 
and categorisation.
In this vein, commitment to empowering those who are structurally marginalised from domi -
nant constructs of “participation”, such as tribal groups and First Nations peoples living in 
Africa and Australia (see Bidwell and Browning, 2010; Rodil et al., 2020) are important early 
precedents. More recently, we see onto-epistemes from the Global South (Loh Chee Wyai et al., 
2022) and Traditional Ecological Knowledge (Lujan Escalante and Mortimer, 2022) making 
impact.
Commons-like initiatives for managing shared natural resources (Heitlinger et al., 2019; Mart-
tila et al., 2014) nod to ways people have always governed and managed in agriculture, forestries, 
fisheries and more, preceding and/or beyond the state, institutions or market-based interventions. 
While work on commoning (Teli et al., 2018) and infrastructuring (Chopra et al., 2022; Vlachokyr-
iakos et al., 2018) may not identify specifically with sustainability or the more-than-human, it 
points to engagement with alternative, solidarity and pluralist cultures and belief systems neces-
sary for system change. In other words, traditional Participatory Design strengths accompany dis-
courses that critically examine the who and expand these beyond humans and, with this expanded 
inclusion of other-than-human lifeforms, reconfigure power and political agendas with the same 
critical, reflexive enquiry.
There are important precedents when Participatory Design foregrounds peoples’ ecological 
kinships with animals, ancestors and spiritual entities. Guidance from First Nation scholars and 
creative practitioners has been significant, reminding us as to what may have been eroded from 
Western mindsets through modern living and working.
4 Indigenous Elders teach us to see how de-
signing is already embedded and enacted between all living beings as co-operating and co-creating 
and not contained within a human-only frame. We quote the wisdoms shared by Bundjalung and 
Wiradjuri Elders from Aboriginal Australia to inspire reflection:
Design is how all living beings co-operate to co-create .  . . (p. 93) . . . .Living in intel -
ligent environments, it is obvious that things of all kinds have always gathered, shared, 
and decided their best way to be and to do things. These gatherings continue regardless of 
human beings. We respect this already existent design where knowledge lives in a peopled 
landscape.
(Moran et al., 2018, p. 96)
Other species and non-beings are also teachers. There are hierarchies, but not Western/Modern 
ones. Potawatomi Nation artist, writer and scientist Robin Wall Kimmerer explains:
in Native ways of knowing, human people are often referred to as “the younger brothers of 
Creation”. We say that humans have the least experience with how to live and thus the most 
to learn – we must look to our teachers among the other species for guidance. Their wisdom 
is apparent in the way that they live. They teach us by example. They’ve been on the earth 
far longer than we have been, and have had time to figure things out.
(Kimmerer, 2013, p. 9)

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
88
Knowledge, place and relations are inseparable, tethered to time, bodies, stories, species and 
ecologies in ways that must be respected to be considered as teaching, as wisdom. This resonates 
with existing discourses in Participatory Design that see all knowledge as situated (Suchman, 
1987) yet goes further. In contrast to feminist technoscience, this situatedness is understood to 
be ontologically entangled with being and becoming of everything spanning geological time and 
planets.
Participation, then, takes on a new dimension when we reflect on these wisdoms. In Participa-
tory Design, Akama and colleagues (2020) wrestle with the implications of putting an unusual 
emphasis on ontology rather than methodology. By learning from those who understand sentience 
differently – where rocks are living and growing in Japan and rivers are in kinship relations to Māori 
peoples in Aotearoa – they conclude that “participation” can no longer be addressed only by ex -
panding categories of stakeholders. More-than-human relationships have always involved partici-
patory practices, such as listening to ancestral “voices” of people, lands, waters and tremors when 
making decisions about co-existence and passing this to future generations. These cosmological 
rhythms speak to “co-ontology where being and becoming are always-participating-with-many” 
(Akama et al., 2020).
Examples in Action
In this section, we see how different commitments are addressed in three cases. These are offered 
to make visible how the different lineage, branches and commitments can play out in practice. 
Each study is written in the first person (as individuals or pairs). The cases vary from a small 
project across three workshops to a fleeting encounter, to a 3-year platform/project. This variety 
captures the different timescales in the way we work and the need for problematising “projects”, 
with their finite offer of care.
Algorithmic Food Justice Case 4.1
I, Sara, present a pilot research project, called Algorithmic Food Justice, exploring more-than-human 
values in food systems. Through this project I examine democracy, inclusion, justice and giving a 
voice to the voiceless, discussing how these are enacted and troubled in more-than-human Participa-
tory Design. I show how the project links to the first lineage of sustainability by proposing to design 
new blockchain-based prototypes for fairer and more ecologically nourishing food systems, thus sug-
gesting a Modernist techno-fix. It also draws on rights-based approaches within Participatory Design 
to explore ways to bestow rights and privileges to non-human actors, particularly within accounting 
systems. At the same time, I show how the project connects to the second lineage through care and the 
commons, as well as links to ancestral wisdoms.
My collaborators (academics Lara Houston and Alex Taylor and artist-curator Ruth Catlow, from 
the arts organisation Furtherfield) and I were interested in how we might transition from an unjust 
food system that focuses on human benefits alone, towards alternative food futures where benefits 
are distributed more fairly across the food web, and in ways that are more nourishing to the earth. 
We were motivated to re-design away from unsustainable inequalities, injustices and monopolies that 
prioritise profit, towards a multispecies food commons – with the help of blockchain technology.

More-Than-Human Participatory Design
89
The project ran for three months and involved three workshops at Spitalfields City Farm, an urban 
farm in East London characterised by high socioeconomic deprivation and cultural diversity. It grew 
out of ten years of prior collaborative research with the farm (Nichols and Heitlinger, 2022) that began 
with my PhD, which looked at Participatory Design of urban encounters for interspecies care and co -
habitation. This prior research worked to surface the expertise of migrant communities typically elided 
in industrial food production (Heitlinger, 2016; Heitlinger et al., 2019). It taught me much about the 
interrelations between humans and non-humans such as microbes, plants, seeds, animals, water and 
climate, as well as sensors, batteries and data, in urban food systems, and the rich ancestral wisdom 
of the farm community, especially around growing, sharing, preserving and eating food from different 
places and heritages.
The Algorithmic Food Justice project was funded with UK research money distributed by a 
platform dedicated to social justice and digital technology. It asked if blockchain might help us 
think differently about the urban food web and move beyond extractive relationships towards fair 
and nourishing ones where the benefits are distributed more evenly across species. One way we 
thought blockchain might help us was by making visible and accounting for the contributions of 
diverse multispecies actors who otherwise remain invisible in the global industrial food system. 
Doing so might allow us to imagine alternative food systems that prioritise healthier ecosystems 
and increased biodiversity. We used creative speculation and co-design of blockchain conceptual 
prototypes to reflect on the current inequalities in urban food systems and flesh out ideas for a mul -
tispecies food commons.
As described previously in (Heitlinger et al., 2021, 2022; Houston et al., 2023), we resisted a 
techno-optimistic approach to a “blockchain solution”. Rather, we approached the technology as de-
sign material; a tool with which to critically engage and think creatively about value systems and 
ethics. Simultaneously, we hoped to reveal some of the risks this technology might pose. Approaching 
it in this way opened up conversations about values, governance and democracy within the context of 
more-than-human politics and helped reveal some tensions and limitations of doing more-than-human 
Participatory Design.
In the first workshop, we mapped human and non-human stakeholders in the city farm into 
the future. These activities privileged the perspectives of urban growers, drawing on their expert 
knowledge of regenerative agricultural techniques and thereby bringing attention to the many in -
terspecies interdependencies in the urban food web. It highlighted the contributions, needs and 
resource flows between the different human and non-human stakeholders of the farm now and to 
come. Participants were prompted to think about resources beyond the human, material and fi -
nancial, which revealed examples such as volunteer labour, oxygen, time and care, all of which 
are invisible in the global industrial food systems. This mode of knowledge production, grounded 
in the perspectives of community growers and organisers, formed the basis for the scenarios we 
developed in the second workshop.
In the second workshop, the research team facilitated a speculative participatory activity in the 
form of a multispecies live-action role-play (LARP), where human actors took on both human and 
non-human roles in a future deliberative decision-making forum (see Figure 4.2). The role-play 
was set 15 years in the future, following a fictional food crisis, when London is turned into an 
urban farm and decisions must be made about how to organise it as a multispecies food commons. 
Drawing on the list of stakeholders generated in the first workshop, the human characters held 
representative roles on committees including Coordination, Health, Agriculture, Security, Culture, 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
90
Justice, Resources and Waste Management, Education, Energy, Infrastructure and Liaison, while 
non-human characters included birds, insects, farm animals, honey bees, soil, plants, trees, sensors, 
water, air and weather.
We worked through dilemmas and conflict in considering governance for sustaining our fic -
tional commons, adhering to the values of inclusion, democracy and rights, and following an 
agenda informed by Ostrom’s (2015) design principles for the commons. Role-play and ritual was 
used as a way to embody/enter the spirit of, and speak as, non-humans and attempt to represent 
their interests in decision-making. Players’ actions were informed by scenarios based on what we 
learnt about “matters of care” (Puig de la Bellacasa, 2011) from the first workshop, as well as 
real-world events, and current facts about food and environmental injustices. We tried to establish 
new decision-making systems and urban infrastructures and to stress-test them to find out what 
might go wrong. Player-participants were able to draw on their experiences and knowledge of being 
community gardeners and activists who had intimate knowledge of mutually-beneficial multispecies 
relationships within the food web.
To illustrate with an example, in workshop 1, we discussed ways to support pollinating insect com-
munities (arising from concerns about their population decline) through the creation of new habitats 
and the ban on pesticides. This “matter of care” was included in the role-play script as an agenda item 
in the LARP introduced by the assembly Chair: “An issue that’s come up recently in the sharing policy: 
so the bees, as you know . . . have been on strike now for six months. They’ve stopped working”. The 
Chair continued: “How was the Justice Committee proposing to resolve the dispute between the bees 
and the gardeners?”
Figure 4.2
  LARPing in the multispecies decision-making forum at Spitalfields City Farm (photo 
credit: Lorenzo Strappelli, with permission).


More-Than-Human Participatory Design
91
The character playing the representative from the justice committee then replied (unscripted), 
“We are piloting various multispecies assemblies, which have representatives of all sorts of actors 
on the farm, to give equal voice to them all. But also working closely with infrastructure to meet 
the bees’ demands. Which on the whole don’t seem too wild and quite fair”. Other members from 
other committees then contributed to the discussion, representing both the interests of their human 
and non-human characters. These scenarios helped us to imagine our emerging food commons 
and work out a system of governance that would produce and distribute food for the benefit of all 
species.
In the final workshop, participants developed blockchain-based conceptual prototypes for gov-
erning a more-than-human food commons. Together we used these to consider the implications for 
algorithmic food justice. How could we use blockchain, sensors and artificial intelligence to co-design 
food governance systems that consider multispecies justice? What risks and challenges would these 
designs pose? We explored these questions through conceptual prototypes of speculative future 
socio-technical systems that foregrounded thriving multispecies relations, more-than-human values 
and fairer distribution of resources.
To give a flavour of the outcomes, DAO’n-to-Earth was to be a London-wide currency exchange 
for community currencies – to federate and help manage smaller community currencies and scale 
sustainable interventions to meet environmental challenges. The exchange rate is set automatically 
according to the soil health data of each community, as measured by networked sensors and AI, and 
calibrated over time. The better the quality of the soil, the higher the value of that local currency. As 
a participant explained, “The aim of the DAO
5 platform was to create a common incentive for people 
to create healthy soil and transmute that into a positive market value for their community”. This fits 
within what we have been calling the “sustainability” lineage, in problem-solving, but conversations 
were wider ranging.
One of the richest discussions took place in LARPing about the problem of vegetable theft (a real 
problem for the farm). As described in Houston et al. (2023), the discussion circled around punishment, 
education and rehabilitation of offenders, before reaching the limits of more-than-human justice. The 
Resources representative asked: “Is justice an anthropocentric concept though? You couldn’t expect a 
carnivorous animal to be just to its prey”. The Energy representative drew hard limits: “Driving other 
species into extinction is a no-no”. The Coordination representative’s answer prioritises the overall 
balance of the ecosystem over relations between individual subjects: “Mostly, if you create the right 
conditions and the structure is right then most organisms will exchange fairly and that usually works. 
And there are a few that will take and not give back, but still, overall, the system works”. In this kind of 
exchange, we see both rights-based and care-based approaches emerging in a reckoning with ecological 
entanglement.
As well as considering justice, the project invoked core Participatory Design values of democ -
racy and sharing of power. For example, growers brought up power imbalances and the potential 
for blockchain-based systems to intensify inequalities depending on whose stories were told. In the 
DAO’n-to-Earth prototype, currencies are affected by soil health determined by sensors. But such an 
intervention surfaces inclusion and power imbalances, as one grower highlighted: “If you’re focusing 
on PH or the chemistry of the soil, then that’s telling us a story about the soil. A chemical story rather 
than a microbiological one”. Does the proxy of chemical balance adequately reflect the creatures and 
plants of that land? Whose stories are technologies telling and who benefits? As a participant said, dif-
ferent stories around data “produce different types of truth” and “could be corrupted in lots of different 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
92
ways”. Intensifying the capability of these technologies could prioritise some narratives over others, 
benefiting some interests over others. A chemical story might support an extractive and profit-driven 
food system, benefiting humans alone over a regenerative and fairer one that considers interspecies 
interrelations in a living soil community. Without an examination of these power dynamics, new de-
signs may accelerate inequalities. In looking through both sustainability and entanglement lenses, the 
project was able to consider critical questions of power and democracy provoked by acknowledging 
more-than-human relations.
HYBRID MATTERs: Plastic Imaginaries Case 4.2
In the year of 2015, we (Åsa and Kristina) were part of a project called HYBRID MATTERs, inves -
tigating hybrid ecologies and the transformation of our planet through human activity. At the time we 
had just finished our collaborative PhD where we combined feminist technoscience and Participatory 
Design to explore designerly public engagement in issues around living with technologies. In line with 
a lot of Participatory Design work at the time, ours was grounded in an understanding of distributed 
agency between human and non-human actors.   It was also part of a move within the Participatory 
Design community that had started to expand its commitments from participation in the workplace 
into broader societal issues and emerging publics (Binder et al., 2015; Ehn et al., 2014; Lindström and 
Ståhl, 2014).
The themes addressed in HYBRID MATTERs were somewhat new to us as they involved a shift 
from primarily working with social implications of living with (digital) technologies to engaging 
with long-term socio-ecological implications of design. Put in a slightly different way, we worked 
with hybrid matters that had come into being in the aftermath of what had previously been made. 
Within the Participatory Design community the term “non-human actor” was at the time primarily 
used to acknowledge agency of technological devices and systems. For us, the term and framework 
of hybrid matters and ecologies became an invitation to expand our understanding and use of the 
term non-human actors not only to include technologies but also other species and entities such as 
stones, oceans and fire. This move made us attend to participatory processes as material configura -
tions over long timescales as something that is not only about future-making, which tends to be 
design’s usual focus, but also taking into account how pasts, presents and futures are intricately 
intertwined.
Our part of HYBRID MATTERs puts focus on plastics – fossil-fuel-based materials with long 
histories – and how they come to matter in strange, unexpected and often undesired ways. Plastic is a 
material that has been central in design in enacting Modernist imaginaries of human mastery over na-
ture in several ways. Plastics have been understood as a passive and malleable material for designers to 
shape according to their wishes. It has been praised for its durability and its capability to resist decay. 
It is different from many other materials in that it has come out of scientific laboratories and is named 
after its characteristic plasticity. More recently, imaginaries of malleability and control associated with 
plastics have been brought into question. Plastics are ubiquitous and now appear in unintentional con-
stellations and interact with other materials and actors in unanticipated ways – in oceans, polar areas 
and species of all kinds.

More-Than-Human Participatory Design
93
To further engage with shifting materialities and imaginaries of plastics, we invited different 
groups to engage with two findings related to plastics that, at the time, had generated both curiosity and 
worry. The first finding was a new geological entity called plastiglomerates (Corcoran et al., 2014), 
fused from plastic and stone. It comes into being through burning plastic and inadvertent littering, 
lack of recycling and bonfires. This appeared in dystopian narratives pointing towards the severity of 
the problem of plastic waste. The second discovery showed that common mealworms can biodegrade 
styrofoam (Yang et al., 2015), a particular form of plastic. The media portrayed this story as a potential 
solution with optimism.
To move beyond these polarising media responses oversimplifying “bad” and “good” futures and 
to further explore what we could learn from these matters, we brought them into everyday situations, 
where participants could make them tangible and negotiable. We hosted walks along beaches in Ice -
land where we went looking for plastiglomerates. In a separate event, we invited people in the Öresund 
region, mainly Malmö and Copenhagen, to try out composting their own plastic waste in collaboration 
with common mealworms.
We focus on the plastiglomerate walks here (for work with mealworms, see Lindström and 
Ståhl, 2016, 2020). Departing from normative expectations for design to solve issues around 
plastic waste, we invited participants to explore how these plastiglomerates come into being, 
like the practices that have generated this hybrid matter, how we can understand them, to whom 
and how they might be a concern or a potential resource and what it might entail to continue 
living with these. The walks were attended by locals, families, tourists, artists, geologists and 
those who enjoyed outdoor activities. To some people’s relief and to others’ disappointment, we 
did not find any plastiglomerates. Still the event allowed us to engage with our questions since 
the walks were designed to encounter not only plastiglomerates but also the different kinds of 
matters (such as plastics and lava stone), practices (such as having bonfires) and forces (such 
as currents and waves) that participate in plastiglomerates coming into being. For example, we 
encountered a lot of plastic waste that potentially could become plastiglomerates in the future. 
We collected a Christmas tree, a cassette tape, a container for oil, threads from fishing nets, 
the canvas from a tent, as well as plastic pieces that were hard to identify (Figure 4.3). Some 
were later taken to a recycling station to yet again become part of plastic products, rather than 
plastiglomerates.
Following what we have called the sustainability lineage, plastiglomerates were here ap -
proached as a problem to be solved by removing plastic waste from the beach. For some, this 
felt “good” as a responsible visitor concerned with environmental sustainability. However, we re-
flected that this way of intervening in the becoming of plastiglomerates also has limitations. What 
would those recycled plastics become, and would they end up on these shores or elsewhere, again? 
How do we live within the aftermath of design driven by Modern imaginaries of human mastery 
over nature?
In contrast to the dominant agendas in Participatory Design that seek to empower margin -
alised groups through an increased agency like voice and visibility, this event became an ex -
ercise of rethinking agency. For us, it revealed distributed agencies and responsibilities within 
entanglements that stretch far in time and space. We figured that these plastics arrived on these 
shores from distant locations and practices, maybe from other parts of the world too. Directing 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
94
our shared attention towards the multiplicity of activities and lives they are part of, such as cel-
ebrating Christmas, listening to music, fishing and going hiking, further emphasised the multiple 
ways in which we are all, already, entangled in plastics. In other words, rather than considering 
the ways in which the event enabled the empowerment of marginalised groups, the event had a 
focus on fostering response-ability amongst a group of more or less privileged actors. We use 
response-ability here with reference to Haraway (2016), to emphasise the practice of learning to 
act in emerging, uncertain and entangled relationships and to do so responsibly. This compelled 
us to recognise the distributed character and lack of control in how plastic comes to be and comes 
to matter in hybrid ecologies. There are no easy fixes, but rather something we will have to live 
with for a long time to come. There is no pristine past to return to and no clean cuts between 
nature and culture.
In other words, recognising the distributed character and lack of control of how plastic 
comes to matter in hybrid ecologies, in this and other locations, could potentially result in a 
Figure 4.3  Top: Findings during a plastiglomerate walk: Bottom: pieces of tent canvas, a container 
for oil and part of a Christmas tree (photo credit: Kristina Lindström, with permission).


More-Than-Human Participatory Design
95
sense of hopelessness or disempowerment, as it does not lend itself to easy solutions. How -
ever, recognising entanglements and lack of human control does not mean letting go of a desire 
to do something. Rather, the act of troubling anthropocentric imaginaries of human mastery 
of nature entails a shift from seeking empowerment to attending to emerging commitments, 
obligations and responsibilities (Lindström and Ståhl, 2016), within existing entanglements 
with plastics. It also means revisiting and learning from commitments that are, or were once, 
part of our families, ancestries, cultures and communities, to re-ignite the resilient wisdoms 
we have inherited (Akama, 2021). Emerging commitments in this case involved taking care 
of waste that we were not directly responsible for, while at the same time recognising our 
entanglements in plastics.
The event further provoked a range of responses that suggest different ways of attending to, 
as well as intervening into, the becoming of hybrid matters and ecologies that we are already part 
of. Some participants, tongue-in-cheek, started to make compositions of findings into a kind of 
speculative material sketches of plastiglomerates or other forms of hybrid matters (Figure 4.4). 
One participant stuck a piece of gum to a seaweed. Another participant pressed small stones into 
a foam-like material. Others made small installations of collected materials along the walk that 
were captured in photographs. Yet another hesitated to pick up the pieces of plastic that were 
stuck underneath a stone in a small waterfall where moss had started to grow on top of the bits of 
plastic. Some of us gathered around this piece of hybrid matter and sat there for a while with the 
dilemma of deciding whether to pull it out or leave it (Figure 4.5). Taking away and carrying it 
to a recycling station did not seem like the easy choice when there was new life growing. Taken 
together these responses could be seen as attempts to confront or envision ongoing and continued 
living within entangled hybrid matters.
Figure 4.4  Compositions during a plastiglomerate walk as expressions of curiosity about how to 
live with hybrid ecologies and hybrid matters (photo credit: Kristina Lindström, with 
permission).


Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
96
While there are limitations to all of these responses, they point towards an important challenge 
when it comes to Participatory Design practices. While early Participatory Design was committed 
to democratising the development of emerging technologies, Participatory Design is now faced 
with how to collectively respond to and care for the aftermath of design and technologies devel -
oped to solve immediate problems and desires (Lindström and Ståhl, 2020). Much like a game 
of cat’s cradle (Haraway, 1994) and located accountabilities, we might not be fully responsible 
for the patterns we have in our hands, but we need to cultivate our ability to respond, and to do 
so with consideration for the patterns we participate in making and handing over to generations 
to come. In other words, living responsibly with hybrid matters in the aftermath of design driven 
by imaginaries of human mastery over nature implies that we cultivate the ability to respond to 
matters that one is implicated in but not fully responsible for. This also requires responses beyond, 
but not excluding, those available in the sustainability lineage.
Figure 4.5
  A sheet of partly melted plastic that has started to become overgrown and fully entangled 
in its new environment (photo credit: Kristina Lindström, with permission).


More-Than-Human Participatory Design
97
CreaTures Case 4.3
CreaTures (a European-Union-funded project on Creative Practices for Transformative Futures: 
creatures-eu.org; creaturesframework.org) was unusual in applying entanglement logics to both its 
research design and its analysis of others’ designing, thereby tackling some of the issues raised in 
moving “beyond sustainability” head on. It set out to resist not just business-as-usual in what it pro -
duced, but also the accepted norms of research and the underlying Modern productivist philosophy 
behind them. The project was devised by more than 30 participatory researchers and practitioners 
to ask how creative practice could change cultures towards more liveable futures, based on a dif -
ferent understanding of relationality that embraced interdependence at its core and attempted to act 
on that acknowledgement. We wrote it to incorporate an entangled understanding of relations and to 
see how these might be generative of new relations within and between the projects and people who 
participated or came into contact with the researchers involved (see Light et al., 2024). In doing that, 
we considered all life forms but focused most on relations as they might manifest between people 
changed by encounters with a different way of thinking (see Light, 2023), to look towards the human 
in the more-than-human and a concern for our reflexivities and what it is possible for us to imagine.
I, Ann, helped construct the proposal, introducing the overall theme from earlier work (Light, 2011; Light 
et al., 2018), and led one of the CreaTures work packages. The whole project involved 11 partners and many 
productions over three years (see Dolejšová et al., 2021; Light et al., 2024), but I focus on two aspects chosen 
for their relvenance to more-than-human entanglement to ask what we learnt through our research about:
• Considering the human in the more-than-human;
• How trying to enact entanglement puts people and projects in tension with everything around them 
in practical terms.
CreaTures was an action research project based upon a rhetoric of care, a resistance to abstraction 
for the sake of it and a refusal of extractive practices. Involving an ambitious plan for recognising 
the whole person as researcher and learner (with no expectation for emotional objectivity to accom -
pany professional analytic objectivity) as a microcosm of changed human-world relations, it sought to 
produce analyses that are deeply situated and contextualised. It started from a premise that, although 
more-than-human futures concern (and show concern for) all living beings, how humans make mean-
ing from relations and what surrounds us, affects all life. Humans are the only species that, collectively, 
may have the agency to halt or slow the systems that are destroying life across the planet and to pre -
vent the worst of climate change and biodiversity loss (which is not to say that all humans have equal 
agency). So, a tenet of CreaTures was the decentring of humanity and replacing a hierarchical view of 
life (where humans dominate) with one that explores interdependencies. In slowing down and working 
on self-other relations, we anticipated the change we want to see happening more broadly around us: a 
cultural shift towards responsiveness and a new gentleness towards the damaged planet.
We embraced and enacted this ethos for two reasons: first, it enabled us to be the change 
we wanted to see and attempt to bring this into the world; second, this approach is (perhaps the 
only one) congruent with understandings of agency that acknowledge interdependencies and 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
98
entanglements, so this complemented more traditional forms of trying to exert influence. In this, 
we heeded a sense that “we do not need to attune ourselves to the entanglements and encounters 
of being-with, becoming-with, and living-with; these relations pre-exist us. We need to attune our 
judgement to experience these relations fully and allow (endlessly) different potential to emerge” 
(Light, 2019).
The theme of the project was that creative practices (broadly understood as work by design -
ers, artists, cultural workers and citizen-led collectives) can mediate complex issues of climate 
change and social inequalities. These practices include a wide range of aesthetic, affect-driven, 
reflective and participatory approaches designed in different ways to enact societal change, 
though often poorly resourced and badly understood in their goals and achievements (Light  
et al., 2018).
Of particular significance, some artist work addressed (inter)species relations, hoping to impact 
how people understand themselves as part of the world, relate to other species, embrace the need 
for greater social and environmental justice and protect biodiversity (see Light et al., 2024b). Some 
processes included quite specific more-than-human elements – we were invited to centre ourselves 
in the relations of another type of being as part of the play. Furtherfield presented The Treaty of 
Finsbury Park, where more-than-human negotiations are in play as humans take on the roles of 
other species to consider a future for the open spaces of London (Light et al., 2024b). Superflux 
staged Invocation for Hope, where the burned forest gives way to a flourishing clearing in which 
we see ourselves alongside neighbouring species. By contrast, some projects proposed different 
care relations and enacted them through new social structures or encounters with others (Dolejšová 
et al., 2021). Cassie Thornton’s The Hologram continues to offer a (sub)version of healthcare 
where emotional, social, and physical support comes in an ever-reproducing viral triangle of 
friends (Thornton et al., 2020). There were at least 17 more sponsored works, designed and iterated 
to affect people’s sense of themselves. Some targeted global systems of oppression using creative 
means and some focused on local action. While these were more human-focused, they upheld the 
values of relating differently and with more alignment to other creatures and all made moments of 
reflection possible, more or less explicitly articulating the changes they intended to make as part 
of making them. Further, most brought individuals or small groups to consider existential issues 
through affective interventions designed to help people see themselves and their worlds differently. 
So, we might see a third commitment – to reflexivity – as part of the overall project thinking about 
more-than-human concerns. This might be understood as a way of getting to a more-than-human 
approach in Participatory Design, starting with the entangled researcher-practitioner-self.
Instead of focusing on the problems of climate emergency and other crises, a common interest was col-
lectively creating desirable paths away from existing values and finding new possibilities in the journey, 
impacting people’s sense of meaning. This was performed by helping people to encounter themselves as 
one living being among many types and to reflect on how that position relates to connection and belong-
ing. It proposes an intrinsically entangled way of coming at the world: linking local actions to the wider 
movements of the planet and its politics so that interdependencies become more tangible. We hoped for 
care, rather than success, growth or independence, to operate as a core value. CreaTures concerned itself 
with transformation, not just once, but in an acknowledgement of the intrinsic flow of the world around us. 
But this emphasis also accepted that the relative certainties of much Western future(s) planning give way 
to a situation where there are no future states to propose, but only a period of flux to embrace.

More-Than-Human Participatory Design
99
This is caught in what is (as close as we got to) a CreaTures manifesto: a definition of the term that 
we began to use for articulating our vision, CreaTurely:
“Being creaturely incorporates our understanding of eco-social change: it is post-capitalist, play -
ful, more-than-human and fundamentally relational . . .
“CreaTures transformative practices encourage this creaturely-ness . . . . Creaturely ways of doing 
aim at capturing the paradoxical connectedness and separateness of being alive. Given the struggle 
for language that talks of changing/changed ways of being, we offer creaturely as a placeholder for 
gentler, connected, pluralist and life-focused ways of doing, being and making. The term is an adverb, 
not a noun – it points to a way, not a state” (creaturesframework.org).
Multiple intellectual strands were woven together in the concept of creaturely, though the 
more-than-human is evidently a guiding factor. As an overall way of working, the project was charac-
terised by a strong commitment to plurality. Practitioners’ productions were designed to support trans-
formation in multitudinous ways – the research team did not produce an a-priori definition of what 
transformation should be but used the work being observed to understand what creative practitioners 
were trying to achieve and how. While some artists involved were more oriented towards rights for all, 
eco-social justice and what that meant at meeting points between lifeforms, most were oriented towards 
care for all or simply making visible other worlds, and these nuances were a subject of discussion for our 
understanding of more-than-human relations. This range in itself became a research finding.
Despite the scale of activity, we formed the project to be intimate, entangled and involved in peo-
ple’s lives. The many studies we made became part of a whole that also had these values. This raised 
tensions between a rationalist model of activity (linear, objective, categorised, segmented) and a pull 
towards mutual trust and creative emergence. In upholding entanglement from philosophy to project 
design, the work was explicitly engaging with “alternative” onto-epistemes which value interdepend-
ence, but also looking for something positive and even joyful in the possibilities ahead of us. In this, 
it deliberately contrasted itself with the norms of European funding, evaluation and production, with 
their ethos of problem-solving at a time of great risk and focus on accountability. However, we had 
to follow EU rules of reporting and commissioning in making creative work, which created tension 
throughout. Research into the productions further exemplified these tensions: on the one hand, we 
sought to capture, break down and analyse creative partners’ practices, strategies and ambitions and, on 
the other, to respect the complexities that come with working across systems and focusing on complex 
societal-ecological relations. This incommensurability followed us about, caught in encounters with our 
project assessors who held conflicting values to ours, yet became a proxy for the funders to judge the 
significance of the work. The same incongruity ran between the formal project structure of work pack-
ages and the actual activities. At any time, most people were working across these structures as well as 
within them. Regular, frequent meetings in different groupings within the project team produced col-
laborative knowledge, culminating in investigating the project itself as a form of Participatory Design.
However, this was clearly not a conventional Participatory Design project, despite being par -
ticipatory in its preparation and execution. The experimental productions were not the end point 
and the artefacts being created by them were not products or systems as such. The outcomes 
were intended to be changed participants, holding new understandings or an increased sense 
of agency, and it was mostly open to participants to decide what this might mean. Further, the 
partners had no intention of scaling their processes in traditional ways but instead were inclined 
to operate outside, or in challenge to, capitalist paradigms and avoid contributions to growth.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
100
CreaTures was necessarily unlike more traditional sustainability-focused design activities. 
We realised it might be possible to make the project itself a practical contribution to interpret -
ing the difference in philosophy that we wanted to make as participatory designers. In this, as in 
the opportunity to see ourselves as other forms of life and discover our connections, we played 
up more-than-human relationalities to make them legible and open to interrogation, so, in our 
writings, we stress plurality, co-authorship, the paradoxes we face, the tension between different 
forms of knowledge and, perhaps above all, reflexivity as people bridging incompatible worlds. 
We might expect similar organisational and methodological faultlines to run through all work that 
seeks a different relationality. It will be counter-cultural and, if it eschews current forms of cat -
egorisation, segmentation and evaluation, it needs to be very clear about what it offers instead. For 
us, this was captured in a framework for designing and evaluating experiential projects, offering 
dimensions for attending to affective and prefigurative change and challenging current modes of 
evaluation (https://creaturesframework.org).
Discussion
The cases we describe earlier help illuminate the distinctions of lineage but also problematise 
them. Sara’s case may be most familiar for Participatory Design: it intervenes in injustices experi-
enced by marginalised members of a community and seeks to design new prototypes and methods 
for more-than-human food futures. Åsa and Kristina’s case explores being-with plastics, once ma-
nipulated and highly valued, then reviled when they find a home inside our bodies or on seashores. 
Ann’s CreaTures case is a study of how transformation might be attempted within (a recognition 
of) entangled relations.
These contrasting explorations suggest that lineages and branches are never clean separations, 
even if they are presented that way in an academic book. In showing the branches connected to 
tree trunks and roots, we hope to underscore that theories and practices are already entangled at 
the base (Figure 4.6). Nothing, including knowledge, is ever isolated. Knowledges are ontological 
instruments that make worlds, so those wielding research, analysis, thinking and writing must take 
care of what they propose.
The cases are not aligned in their understandings of what change is to be made or what meth -
odologies are needed: they demonstrate that our relationships to many worlds can always be 
different, in different ways. Each makes an offer as to how. Multi-epistemic collaborations are 
fundamental to revaluing human-nature relationalities and attempting to move away from separa-
tion towards entanglement. Underscoring this is another point: that self-awareness is a constant 
necessity since we are part of making worlds. This includes interrogating values and worldviews 
sometimes taken for granted, including the tenets of Participatory Design. The cases invite us to 
sharpen our understanding of ourselves and more-than-human relationships. They suggest ways in 
which we might revisit the ethics of our relationships, rediscover relationships and revalue them. 
Such acts are needed in systems change, not to mitigate the crisis and abuse of present regimes, 
but to appeal to regimes of care and fulfilment.
We have been deliberately provocative by selecting familiar Participatory Design prin -
ciples, such as rights, fairness, democracy, inclusion and empowerment, to explore – to re -
veal there is no easy transposition when entangling with more-than-human relationalities. 
However, this does not mean abandoning Participatory Design tenets. In fact, the cases con -
firm how these are critical in combating human-made structures and processes that harm 
ecosystems.

More-Than-Human Participatory Design
101
Figure 4.6  Entangled theoretical roots (image credit: Yoko Akama, with permission).
From Rights to Relationalities
A more-than-human agenda may not sit comfortably for Participatory Design practitioners be -
cause the prevailing value system in Participatory Design is based on social justice relating to 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
102
human rights. Forlano (2017) warns that posthuman and more-than-human perspectives may make 
room for multiple subjectivities, but may not serve those who have historically been considered 
“less-than-human” and excluded from society, based on intersectional categories such as gender, 
race, religion, class, sexuality, belief systems and geographies. While Forlano argues for taking this 
critique seriously, she also suggests that works intending to decentre the human share this politics, 
“in that they aim not to essentialise distinct categories, but rather to complicate them and illustrate 
the ways the human and nonhuman, nature and culture are mutually co-constitutive” (Forlano, 
2017, p. 29). Much more-than-human work starts by rejecting all discrimination and domination, 
revealing the same abusive powers at work across disadvantaged humans and non-humans and 
arguing for fundamental change. If we abandon vertical power structures, we also abandon dif -
ference as the basis for structural exclusion (while remembering to stay mindful of the effects of 
current regimes).
Concern regarding a narrow and literal framing of “voice” and expanding “stakeholders” trou-
bles the rights-based lineage of the sustainability branch. Those drawn to Participatory Design 
commit to the ethics of listening to those who are experts in their own lives, yet often excluded. 
Some rights-based literature extends this to non-humans. Can we engage non-human actors di -
rectly as participants? Do we need human intermediaries to speak as, or on behalf of, non-humans? 
Sara’s case shows how these questions can arise and examines them. The team used role-play to 
embody and enter the spirit of a non-human like a bird, farm animal or honeybee, and to speak for 
their interests, that is, species were individualised through a human-individual. While informa-
tive in context, this cannot be undertaken naively. Sara’s study sought to sensitise participants to 
issues in this way, ready for a design workshop. Yet, individualising a creature still separates out 
the creature from its entanglement with species and ecologies (Anzaldúa, 2007). Problems with 
human-individual mindsets are revealed starkly when one group of stakeholders is potentially the 
meal of another. What “co-existence” can the role-playing human negotiate? Species eat other 
species to live and for ecological cycles to continue. As shown in Sara’s example, this upsets no -
tions of justice or inclusion. The rights-based framework of the sustainability lineage is not based 
on relationalities within ecosystems. The insights from Sara’s case help us see how tricky it is to 
overcome human-nature separations, including in how we design our methods and technologies.
Nonetheless, the cases affirm that Participatory Design principles are vital in working with 
and listening to those with specific expertise and enduring relationships with non-humans. Sara’s 
project involved community growers with ancestral wisdoms such as how to grow crops not typi-
cally grown in a UK climate. These communities have intimate knowledge of interspecies rela -
tionships supporting regenerative agricultural techniques. By recognising people holding long, 
close relationships with specific non-human species and places – now and in the past – we learn 
how we may continue contributing knowledge and experiences to collaborative design situations. 
Knowledgeable, concerned humans must continue to represent non-humans and voice their stake 
and value in redesigning exploitative and harmful systems. There is no easy transition to a new 
system, but finding multiple ways of encountering being-with-relationalities may begin to deal 
with the complexity (and complicity).
Power, Structure and Democracy
Reflecting on rights leads us to ask what happens to Participatory Design’s democratic commit-
ments when we broaden concern to non-humans. Farmers with hands deep in rich ecology under-
stand soil liveliness (Puig de la Bellacasa, 2015), but are not powerful enough for their voices to 
be heard. In Sara’s example we learnt how Artificial Intelligence and big data selectively “listens” 

More-Than-Human Participatory Design
103
to a “chemical” story rather than a “microbiological” version, exposing how the entire game is 
rigged – and riddled with human-nature divisions. What gets “counted” is atomised and lifeless, 
used to extract value and enrich shareholders rather than promote a dynamic web of relations 
within a living soil community. There are hierarchies: Artificial Intelligence and big data in agri-
culture have more power than experimental farmers, let alone the microbes-of-soil. Democracy for 
non-humans is mired in the same limitations as the rights-based framework because individualism 
is carried into democracy by the way it counts representatives in decision-making processes. Ar -
guably, microbes should have the deciding power if this system is taken to its logical conclusion. 
While this illustrates the limits of transposing democratic values to more-than-human ecologies, 
it also shows the importance of Participatory Design tenets that we work for and with minorities 
to keep addressing power-asymmetries between actors, such as farmers versus large agribusiness.
Important in this is how both Ann’s project, as an overview, and Sara’s project, in its detail, 
demonstrate the relevance of playful, speculative, embodied approaches for more-than-human 
Participatory Design practice. They provide important avenues to pay attention differently to 
entangled relationships that elicit profound experiences in some participants. Sara and her col -
laborators suggest that the LARP was “ultimately an exercise in failing at more-than-human de -
sign” (Houston et al., 2023). However, in recognising the anthropomorphic irony of speculating 
how bees could go on strike so that humans would reasonably support their demands, they crea -
tively deconstruct human governance structures. The improvisational qualities of gameplay allow 
lively spaces, entertain “absurd” scenarios and invite shared, emotional experiences to foreground 
co-existences. What we might learn from this is the importance of not knowing, but experiencing, 
relating and being-with. Arguably, this is not a failure but the promise of what creative approaches 
to research can always offer (DiSalvo et al., 2009).
Kristina and Åsa’s Plastic Imaginaries example shows a way of governing without steering 
towards parliaments of voices. Rather, practising agency by approaching and taking action on that 
which is speculative, curious and repulsive is a way of not letting others decide how to interpret 
new emerging relationships and entities. It is a way of understanding democracy as something we 
do everyday with one’s own body and presence on location.
The theme of Ann’s CreaTures project – how creative practice can be transformative and in -
spire cultural change – takes up these questions. As part of the work, the team developed an 
evaluation strategy stressing the creative act of evaluating. This was undertaken to help redress the 
balance between artist-activists, who anticipate new worlds, and the constraints of funders, whose 
priorities are based in present worlds where values of efficiency prevail. The nine categories of 
design/engagement/impact stress the embodied, affective and inspirational. Divided into three 
clusters, they propose to change meaning (embodying, learning, imagining), connection (caring, 
organising, inspiring) and power (co-creating, empowering, subverting). An activist approach to 
evaluation was understood to be a core part of helping accountability cultures to transform into 
more compassionate spaces. While evaluation itself prioritises accountability, by simultaneously 
criticising it and making a radical version core to its activity, CreaTures has hoped to question 
these aspects. It is notable that the Participatory Design ethic of co-creation is one of the nine 
dimensions stressed as foundational to rethinking dynamics.
CreaTures can be seen as a bridging project, working in hybrid ways to include different world-
views, stretching from artists interested in overthrowing the injustices of capitalism to those antici-
pating new forms of engagement based in care. Its mission was, in part, to create dialogue between 
different philosophical orientations and show how to stay faithful to them. In this exploration of power 
structures and imbalances, CreaTures’ outputs were oriented to the difficulties of translating concepts
