such as democracy into worlds informed by entanglement.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
104
Not More Stakeholders, but Deepening the Engagement
If plurality is intrinsic to more-than-human relationships, the concern becomes less about the 
inclusion of different non-human “participants” and diversifying representatives and more about 
deepening relationships. In two of the cases we use, the authors are not concerned with a tan -
gible outcome, such as a better product: relationships are the focus. Åsa and Kristina’s project 
invites intense engagements with non-humans deemed value-less as waste and, further, harmful 
as polluters. Through their work, we are invited to find footholds to renew our relationships 
with plastics, acknowledging that, despite best efforts to recycle, these materials are likely to 
be turned into further plastic objects only to be carried along currents to end up on further 
shores. This throws up sharp tensions in “sustainability”, revealing the delusion of productivity 
in re-processing waste. Plastiglomerate is a fusion where process and outcome can no longer be 
separated, used to show the web of production and reproduction at its starkest. Their explora -
tion and eye-witnessing of everyday objects found on Icelandic beaches take us into this web, 
in which we are all implicated and show it afresh. They invite us to step in and “stay with the 
trouble” (Haraway, 2016), showing care and compassion in living with such open wounds. The 
focus is less on inclusion and empowerment and more on cultivating response-abilities in mat-
ters we are already implicated in. This might mean taking care of the consequences of that which 
one has not individually contributed to, but still share, in a culture of interdependencies.
This fundamentally questions the borders of “participation”, with its implicit statement of se -
lectivity and the (sometimes arbitrary) way that this manifests. Just as Participatory Design prac -
titioners wield power in choosing particular human stakeholders (Light and Anderson, 2009), so 
issues of inclusion and choice continue into more-than-human politics. For instance, it is easy to 
choose species or features of a landscape that are charismatic, preferred and uncontroversial, like 
dolphins, forests or waterways and there may be reasons to do so; we might need persuasion before 
focusing on mayfly, nematodes or bacteria. Åsa and Kristina’s example is interesting for engag -
ing with waste, commonly discarded as distasteful. It asks about the designer’s intrinsic hubris in 
choosing cases, creatures or species.
Ann’s case puts human experiences in the context of the more-than-human, asking if we can 
abandon human-exceptionalism. The project examines possibilities for different ways of feeling 
and meaning-making in a world where all of us are already entangled in the systems and structures 
that perpetuate harm and maintain human-nature divisions. Acknowledging that we may all be 
“victims”, yet complicit in such violations, asks us to be reflexive of our privilege, power and poli-
tics. So, while CreaTures may not, in its aggregated whole, seek to work with other species, it is 
profoundly concerned with how we relate to them and what needs to change in our encounters, de-
spite journeying into unknown territories. Reflecting – and applying a reflexive process through-
out engagements – is fundamental to achieving new relations, allowing new alliances to develop.
In finding alternatives to relentless “solutioneering”, we may hear, see and feel differently and 
find new ways to work. We live with a paradox, that to transform even to the extent of abandoning 
a rush to progress is a design challenge, but one that cannot be solved; it is a predicament to be 
managed. In redesigning Participatory Design to take on board these different, more entangled, 
traditions of thought, we may be able to reshape our trajectories through our challenges, but the 
outcomes may feel and look wholly unfamiliar.
Conclusion
The 2013 handbook (Simonsen and Robertson, 2013) captured an important moment in Partici -
patory Design that recognised the shifting frame of reference and locus of ethics and politics in 

More-Than-Human Participatory Design
105
expanding beyond ICT and the workplace. In honouring that precedent, this chapter has examined 
shifts in ethics and politics in expanding Participatory Design to accommodate a fuller embrace 
of more-than-human relationalities. We honour another precedent in Participatory Design too: 
that we respond to change in the sites of design, technology and systems by continuing to broaden 
and attend to the new relationships created and the politics that come with them. This includes 
extending our commitments beyond the immediate implications of new designs and technologies 
to collectively care for long-term implications. To do so allows us to consider how designs have 
mattered and will continue to matter in more-than-human relationalities. Such accountability 
asks us to regard history and learn theories of agency and the potential of our own contributions.
We have shown that embracing more-than-human relationalities is neither merely including 
non-humans in Participatory Design processes nor finding methods for their “participation”, but 
instead a philosophical undertaking. We have shown how entanglement necessarily goes deep 
to questions of worldview, values, of being and becoming-with and how human/nature lines are 
drawn or erased. When we regard ontological co-existence, we generate possibilities for change 
in why, what and how we practice Participatory Design. It has been with this end in mind that 
we have juxtaposed different philosophical lineages (sustainability vs entanglement) alongside the 
different types of practices that ensue. Our goal has been to offer insight into why these differences 
are significant and what informs them.
In closing this chapter, we offer some questions about our designing for the Participatory De -
sign community and those considering more-than-human Participatory Design:
• How are we attending to the presence (or absence) of non-humans?
• Where do our theories, methodologies, mindsets and worldviews come from? How might we 
trace their lineage to understand the cause and symptoms of perceived human-nature separation 
in Participatory Design work?
• What means might strengthen reflexivity and confront the values, assumptions and worldviews 
that we take for granted and that perpetuate damaging binary thinking?
• Which systems, structures, principles and procedures are eroding care-based interdependen -
cies? What Participatory Design actions are critical to addressing this erosion?

5
DECOLONISATION AND 
PARTICIPATORY DESIGN
Heike Winschiers-Theophilus, Rachel Charlotte Smith,  
Frederick M. C. van Amstel and Andrea Botero 
DOI: 10.4324/9781003334330-6
Decolonisation is increasingly a matter of concern in global design and technology research and prac-
tice. Decolonising discourses address the ongoing societal challenges of political, economic and racial 
justice rooted in coloniality and perpetuated within global Eurocentric structures and worldviews. In 
attempts to counter systemic biases, design and research communities call for diversity, equity and 
inclusion of the marginalised in collaborative design processes.
This chapter presents contributions from Participatory Design and decolonising movements and 
how they engage across four core strands: the anticolonial, postcolonial, decolonial and the pluriversal. 
Each of the strands addresses attempts to reconcile different worlds, knowledges and epistemologies 
that can contribute towards new framings and directions for (de)colonialites in Participatory Design. 
Based on our survey of literature and research cases on Participatory Design and decoloniality, we 
demonstrate how researchers, designers and users in diverse contexts across the globe are working 
with and adapting modes, concepts and methodologies. They provide significant contributions at dif-
ferent levels of theory or practice and generate new trajectories for diverse and inclusive forms of 
knowledge production. The final section discusses the challenges and potentials raised by and across 
the strands and appeals for a relational agenda in Participatory Design.
Contemporary debates on decolonisation in Participatory Design need to be understood within 
their past interrelations grounded in anticolonial movements and how historical and geopolitical is-
sues continue to shape the conditions for design and knowledge creation. The chapter provides a 
lens that enables Participatory Design researchers to position themselves and engage with the pos-
sible pasts-presents-futures of these concerns, in support of sovereignty and self-determination of 
future-making. It provides a starting point for participatory researchers to engage with a relational 
agenda in which introspection, challenging epistemological hegemonies and responsibilities in situ-
ated actions are central to the wider decolonisation movements.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
112
Lo “decolonial” es una moda
lo poscolonial es un deseo
y lo anticolonial es una lucha.
1
Silvia Rivera Cusicanqui, as quoted in Makaran and  
Gaussens (2020).
Introducing Strands of Decoloniality
Contemporary socio-economic challenges rooted in coloniality, such as digital exclusion, land dis-
possessions, resource exploitation and racial discrimination are continuously perpetuated within 
an imminent unjust system. Recognising the responsibility of designers, academics and technol -
ogy developers in propagating Eurocentric worldviews and fostering systemic bias and injustices 
across all spheres of life, the urgency to decolonise design and education has been put forward by 
a rising number of concerned and marginalised peoples.
Although Participatory Design has a long history of addressing concerns of power relations 
through democratic deliberation and mutual learning (Bødker et al., 2022; Bannon et al., 2018a), 
its theories, concepts, empirical methods and approaches have not directly addressed the impli -
cations of colonial legacies and several forms of coloniality that are implicated in their histories 
(Smith et al., 2020, 2021). Bødker and Kyng (2018) have strongly advocated for Participatory 
Design to reinvigorate its political and democratic ideals, in ways that the field becomes relevant 
to contexts outside of Scandinavia and Western societies and to tackle global matters of concern, 
such as systemic injustices rooted in coloniality.
Attempts to affiliate with discourses of anti-, post- and de-coloniality in Participatory Design in 
recent years have unravelled a number of issues, contradictions and confusions within its research 
and practices (Clarke et al., 2022). These have led to questioning its underlying values and biases, 
ways of creating and sharing knowledge and situated actions, accountabilities and responsibilities 
entangled in the spread of Eurocentric research, technology and design practices. Concerns about 
a lack of engagement with alternative ways of knowledge production (Winschiers-Theophilus 
and Bidwell, 2013), misrepresentation of indigenous societies (Stichel et al., 2019), appropriation 
and commercialisation of indigenous knowledge and unfitting research design have been calling 
for serious methodological revisions to be made (Bossavit and Parsons, 2016). However, only in 
recent years, as decolonisation movements have emerged in academic spheres as calls for decolo-
nising design (Escobar, 2018; Mignolo and Walsh, 2018) and ongoing student and staff strikes for 
decolonising (higher) education in general (e.g. the “Rhodes must fall” movement in South Africa 
in 2015), did concerns of (de)coloniality per se have received attention among Participatory De -
sign researchers.
Within the context of current debates over the role and position of Participatory Design in rela-
tion to decolonisation discourses and movements, this chapter recovers colonial histories that have 
been downplayed, or even systematically erased, with the implication that important connections 
have been lost or overlooked in Participatory Design and nearby fields. As the field continues to 
expand, increasing research projects are developing participatory approaches in support of sov-
ereignty and self-determination in future-making around the globe. Anchored in their own locali-
ties, researchers provide significant theoretical and practical contributions, thereby generating new 
trajectories for diverse and inclusive forms of knowledge production in addressing contemporary 
global challenges. In this chapter, we present a survey of contributions from Participatory Design 
categorised into four strands. We distinguish between anticolonial, postcolonial and decolonial 
approaches, as identified by Davis and Walsh (2020), and add a fourth strand of pluriversality, as 

Decolonisation and Participatory Design
113
represented in more recent attempts to reconcile different worlds. With that, we believe to accom-
modate the multiple ways researchers and practitioners are finding their critical position within 
Participatory Design to represent their geographical regions, local and indigenous communities 
and collaborations.
When debating decoloniality, it is clear that historicity becomes key to understanding contem-
porary discourses. Thus, each strand presented in the chapter is situated within the wider historical 
contexts of (de)coloniality, followed by Participatory Design’s engagement with these move -
ments. The aim of contextualising each strand is not to separate concerns but to provide some 
clarity to how discourses of research and knowledge production have been used and shaped within 
and across wider historical and geopolitical processes. As such, the chapter provides a unique 
overview and contribution to untangling and (re)connecting decolonisation movements and their 
connections to Participatory Design research within such wider frames, which are often forgotten 
in design-oriented discourses on decolonising design. Before moving deeper into each strand, we 
provide a brief overview of the four strands and how they are situated within early and contempo-
rary Participatory Design.
The first strand is related to the influence of anticolonial work in the foundational years of 
Participatory Design in Scandinavia and beyond. Anticolonial movements originated during colo-
nial times, when indigenous populations actively went against the colonial regime and any of its 
remaining legacies (Choudry et al., 2013). Later, intellectuals, from former colonies, developed 
a rich economic, political and cultural criticism of colonialism (Fanon, 2004; Nkrumah, 1971; 
Freire, 1985), laying the foundations for empirical and theoretical work in human sciences. The 
literature found here spans many venues and little has been done so far to consolidate the contribu-
tions or the concepts and practices that originated in the Global South
2 (Cusicanqui, 2012). This 
fragmentation has resulted in historical erasure, and the relations and connections of anticolonial 
discourses and Participatory Design have escaped the attention of the research that consolidated 
the foundations of the field.
The second strand, identified from 2010 onwards, brings forth postcolonial issues like 
critical positionality, voice suppression, geopolitical power and cultural differences. The post -
colonial strand emphasises the unsettling or rupture with new forms of colonialism, such as 
long-standing theoretical discourses of postcoloniality and challenges of “modernity” and 
development aid coming from former metropolises, in favour of local initiatives based on 
situated knowledge(s). Particular examples from the Participatory Design Conference (PDC 
2014) in Windhoek, Namibia, are brought into discussion for their knowledge and epistemolo -
gies from the Global South, mainly from the African continent. The conference played a large 
role in extending Participatory Design practices and approaches into non-Western contexts 
and communities.
The third decolonial strand is based on calls for Participatory Design and human–computer 
interaction (HCI) research to engage more deeply with onto-epistemologies and knowledge 
constructions, in local sites and regions and across the Global South-North divide and through 
South-South cooperations, to develop more inclusive, diverse, equitable practices and research 
approaches. The decolonial strand emphasises the ongoing subtle forms of colonialities that 
cannot be easily displaced or unsettled. Based on prevailing struggles between natives and set -
tlers about identities, power and cultural practices, contributions to decoloniality engage with 
the challenges of conviviality and hybridisms in contemporary research. The virtual edition 
of PDC 2020 hosted in Manizales, Colombia, spurred such perspectives and debates further 
by connecting and integrating Latin American research communities, politics and concerns of 
designing otherwise.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
114
Though partially overlapping with the decolonial strand, the fourth pluriversal strand pursues 
divergent interests and utopias, which are highly relevant for and within Participatory Design for 
reinvigorating some of the more loosely coupled (geo)political agendas and social movement val-
ues of the anticolonial strand. Under this extensive umbrella, Participatory Design researchers are 
trying to address issues such as environmental crisis, indigenous peoples’ existential conditions 
and rights of the land, global power struggles, oppressions and wars. The hybrid PDC 2022 confer-
ence in Newcastle, UK, advanced these themes a step further through a focus on more-than-human 
participations and onto-epistemic-cosmologies. A number of contributions directly addressed as-
pects of pluriversal design, connecting to participatory approaches increasingly endorsed by con -
ferences in areas beyond computing, such as the Design Research Society Pluriversal Special 
Interest Group (DRS Pluriversal SIG) and its online conference PIVOT 2020 and 2021 (Leitão 
and Noel, 2022).
Addressing issues of coloniality across the four strands, the chapter invigorates the debates 
and practices in Participatory Design. Based on our survey of literature and research cases on 
Participatory Design and decoloniality, we demonstrate how researchers, designers and users in 
diverse contexts across the globe are working with and adapting new modes, concepts, methodolo-
gies and advancing theoretical contributions to the field. The chapter ends with an appeal to the 
Participatory Design community to follow a relational agenda in which introspection, challenging 
epistemological hegemonies and responsibilities in situated actions become part of wider decolo-
nisation movements.
Anticolonial – Fighting for National Liberation
Participatory Design is historically circumscribed to the Scandinavian worker self-determination 
movement, which was linked to larger international movements on workers’ resistance to automa-
tion. Participatory Design’s initiation in the 1970s was motivated by the accelerated introduction 
of information technology in the workplace and sought to empower workers and managers at the 
risk of being replaced by automated processes (Nygaard and Terje Bergo, 1975; Bødker et al., 
2022). This wave of automation was pushed in part also by the rearrangement of production forces 
provoked by liberation wars in former colonies in Africa, Asia, Latin America and Oceania (Vieira 
Pinto, 2005). As capital could no longer be easily transferred from colonies to metropolises, the 
Global North had to extract more surplus value from their own workers, through new management 
styles and computer-based automation (Harvey, 2011).
The historical links between the Global North worker self-determination movement and Global 
South decolonisation movements extend into contemporary Participatory Design, manifested 
through the influential work of anticolonial intellectuals from former colonies, such as Paulo 
Freire. The anticolonial criticism revealed the exclusionary characteristic of Western humanism, 
whereby people in new worlds were considered less-than-humans or even non-humans due to 
their body features and/or culture and, therefore, in need of support, guidance and subjugation 
(Freire, 1985). Instead of rejecting Western humanism and its modern ways of humanising, anti -
colonial intellectuals fought to revise the programme and include the historically excluded through 
popular democratic governance, such as the Andean mingas (Testori and D’Auria, 2018). Within 
this context, critical pedagogy (Freire, 1985) and participatory action research (Fals-Borda, 2013) 
emerged. Drawing on Paulo Freire’s anticolonial critical pedagogy (and other authors from the 
Global North), Participatory Design researchers (Carlsson et al., 1978; Ehn, 2017) linked par -
ticipation to learning and research, thus bypassing the anti-dialogical divide between theory and 
practice that characterises the colonial situation. The emphasis on developing new theories of 

Decolonisation and Participatory Design
115
HCI alongside new technological systems enabled Scandinavian software developers to resist the 
US information technology development model (Asaro, 2000), which a few decades later grew 
to become what is now known as digital colonialism: the global concentration of essential digital 
infrastructures in the hands of a few data-extractivist companies (Faustino and Lippold, 2023; 
Kwet, 2019).
Despite providing a key contribution to the field in its infancy, the contributions of Paulo Freire 
and other anticolonial thinkers and ideas remain to be properly recognised in Participatory Design. 
In PDC 2020, Serpa and colleagues (2020) presented a first step in that direction by summarising 
Freire’s basic tenets of Participatory Design, whereas Lucia Garcés (2020) presented a stunning 
case of Freirean popular education and game design with X Yatil’s Maya people. Another founda-
tional contribution worthy of mention is the contribution of Homi Bhabha (1994) and his concept 
of third space used to grasp cultural hybridisms between colonisers and colonised. This concept 
has been applied to enable dialogue between the critics of the predominant software development 
model in the US and Scandinavian researchers who presented an alternative that could not be 
directly applied in the US (Muller, 2007). While the concept has been widely used and devel-
oped (see the following postcolonial strands), the wider geopolitical narratives of the anticolonial 
strands were not made explicit in the history of Participatory Design, nor were similar develop-
ments of participatory approaches from outside of Scandinavia mentioned.
While Scandinavian projects in the 1970s involved cooperation with trade unions, in 
well-known projects (e.g. Demos, DUE, UTOPIA) (Bødker et al., 2022), similar revolutionary 
projects endorsed participatory approaches in Latin America. A project that deserves mention -
ing is Cybersyn, a national information system developed by the Chilean government between 
1971 and 1973 to resist US anti-communism international sanctions (Medina, 2006). Aiming 
at supporting a different kind of socialism, less planned and more emergent, the system was 
designed to connect worker-controlled factories (many of them just nationalised) to organise 
production, distribution and consumption of goods in real-time. The project was one of a series 
of Chilean revolutionary projects developed with the participation of worker representatives, 
similar to the early Scandinavian projects, and an early example of a design for autonomy (Cal -
derón Salazar et al., 2018) or what Arturo Escobar (2018) calls autonomous design. Although 
there is no documented direct connection between the Chilean and the Scandinavian experi -
ences, three Cybersyn participants had indirect connections: Stafford Beer, Fernando Flores 
and Gui Bonsiepe. Beer, the cybernetic theoretician who devised the system architecture, re -
turned to the UK and consolidated his Viable System Model, an approach often used in combi -
nation with soft-systems methodologies (Checkland, 1984), a similar approach to organisation 
problem solving that laid the foundations of early Scandinavian Participatory Design. As for 
Fernando Flores, who after the Chilean coup fled to the US, he later collaborated with Terry 
Winograd to develop a new foundation to design (Winograd and Flores, 1986), a phenomeno-
logical theory that supported the communicative and collaborative interests of Scandinavians. 
Gui Bonsiepe is perhaps the least known of the three, possibly because he remained in other 
Latin American countries for a while after the coup. Bonsiepe developed an explicit anticolo -
nial criticism of Industrial Design founded in Marxist dependence theory, with touches of phe -
nomenology and cybernetics (Bonsiepe, 2022). His theoretical work followed his practice as 
an industrial designer and design educator. He was one of the first to raise the anticolonial flag 
against the colonialist dependence bias of early humanitarian social design (Bonsiepe, 1983). 
He demonstrated, by example, that it was more ethical to send people (and not just products) 
to the periphery and to design with the locals. Design in partnership, an approach that grew out 
of the Brazilian readings of social design, might be considered a response to Bonsiepe’s call. 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
116
This approach was presented by some of their proponents at PDC 2022, in the Portuguese track 
(Araujo et al., 2020).
Another piece of history to consider are the various attempts to articulate Free Software 
and Participatory Design together in Brazil. Luiz Inácio Lula, in his first presidential term 
(2003–2007), took the bold action of nationalising public software by terminating contracts with 
multinational companies and signing new contracts with local companies and cooperatives that 
offered similar solutions based on open-source software. Influenced by the Brazilian Free Soft -
ware movement – which deliberately did not adopt the open source terminology due to its depo -
liticising content – and the early Scandinavian Participatory Design experience, Faber-Ludens 
Interaction Design Institute developed the Design Livre ideology to stimulate design students 
and young designers to take a political stance in their profession (Instituto Faber-Ludens, 2012). 
Different from the Open Design approach that emerged about the same time in Europe (Van Abel, 
2011), Design Livre emphasised sharing the design process in addition to the source code (Van 
Amstel and Gonzatto, 2016). To support the realisation of this ideology, Faber-Ludens developed 
the Corais Platform in 2011, a digital infrastructure built on free software that hosted collabora -
tive projects of any kind. The initial aim was to offer an alternative to Google Drive and other 
imperialist cloud services to participatory designers, yet the Brazilian design community did not 
make wide use of it. Instead, cultural producers, popular educators, indigenous people and activ -
ists populated the platform with collaborative projects such as hackerspaces, traditional culture 
preservation projects, online courses and so on (Van Amstel and Gonzatto, 2016). The platform 
pioneered the use of digital money to mitigate the budget cuts in government funding which 
severely affected the Digital Culture movement in Brazil (Gonzatto et al., 2021), in a move that 
can be considered a popular form of service design (De Siqueira and Van Amstel, 2023). The 
platform was designed and maintained by its users through its metadesign project. A couple of 
studies analysing design participation in the Corais metadesign project have been presented at the 
Brazilian information design and Computer-Supported Cooperative Work conferences (Pelanda 
and Van Amstel, 2019a, 2019b).
Long after Faber-Ludens closed its doors and Corais drowned in inactivity, the Design Livre 
ideology continued to remain current. This ideology motivated the development of a critical peda-
gogy for interaction design (Van Amstel and Gonzatto, 2020), a monster aesthetics for collective 
design bodies (Angelon and van Amstel, 2021), a historical account of the user oppression in HCI 
(Gonzatto and van Amstel, 2022) and two special issues of Diseña (a Chilean journal) on the role 
of design in the liberation from oppression (Van Amstel et al., 2022, 2023). The surge of the De -
sign & Oppression Network at the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 reinvigorated the 
anticolonial strand by promoting several public debates on what constitutes an oppressive and a 
liberating design (Van Amstel et al., 2021). While looking at its Critical Design Education activity, 
the network found itself crafting six relational qualities: freedom, criticality, solidarity, autonomy, 
dialogicity and monstrosity (Mazzarotto et al., 2023). These qualities may work as a provisional 
agenda for anticolonial strands in Participatory Design.
As evident, the anticolonial strand is characterised by strong past and present engagements 
with social movements fighting for emancipation, national liberation, information technology 
sovereignty, workplace rights and peer-to-peer commoning. Connecting these disparate nar -
ratives, which has not been done in the literature on decoloniality and Participatory Design, 
makes clear how early movements in Participatory Design are interconnected with discourses 
on (de)coloniality and technology design across different continents. Future research that pri -
oritises this agenda may prefer to adopt the anticolonial label over labels from other strands.

Decolonisation and Participatory Design
117
Postcolonial – Unsettling Colonial Legacies
As post-war liberation processes spread through Asia, Africa and Oceania, the anticolonial lit -
erature was read and reconsidered in different contexts. In South Asia, for instance, a group 
of scholars founded subaltern studies by the end of the 1970s (Guha, 1982), later expanded 
by researchers in the Middle East (Said, 1978) to what is now known as postcolonial studies 
(Schwarz and Ray, 2000). This is a variegated group of scholars who raised their voices against 
prevailing colonial relationships in academia and in societies that had gone through recent in -
dependence processes. The term postcolonial tried to capture this condition of being politically 
independent while culturally and/or economically dependent. Postcolonial intellectuals were 
sceptical that the assisted development proposed or imposed by former metropolises could lead 
to authentic independence, in part, because it did not address the cultural issue (Said, 1978).
Postcolonial intellectuals were located or had strong ties to universities located at the centre of 
the largest former colonial empire, the UK and the current top military and cultural power, the US. 
To speak and be heard there (Spivak, 1988), they had to develop an intellectual profile that focused 
on theory and somehow detached them from the practice of decolonisation in the former colonies. 
Looking critically at the not-always-successful outcomes of the liberation wars in African na -
tions, they criticised anticolonial scholars for being too simplistic, idealistic and dichotomic. In 
their attempt to engage with post-structuralist debates in Europe, they focused much on analysing 
language, meaning, power and semiotic issues (Mbembe, 2001). This engagement resulted in a 
fruitful analysis of hybrid languages, spaces and modes of being human, where the colonisers and 
the colonised could be kept apart from each other (Bhabha, 1994). Since then, multiculturalism 
theories could no longer rely on the traditional dichotomies between universalism and relativism.
Anthropology was one of the first fields to welcome the uneasy discussion proposed by post -
colonial thinkers. Disciplines of cultural anthropology that were born out of the colonial era, have 
continuously struggled to overcome the relational aspects of time and “othering”, between “us” 
and “them”, through which anthropology has made its object and continued its Western domina -
tion (Fabian, 1991; Said, 1978). Fabian’s (1991) criticism of “allochronism”, which places the 
“other” culture in another time, is a constitutive element of othering and the structural denial of 
“coevalness”. It became a cornerstone in debates over representations and knowledge produc-
tion in the field (Clifford and Marcus., 1986). Fabian’s theories supported the development of a 
more performative engagement with the aim of creating coeval relations between researchers and 
their interlocutors through dialogues in the present – or speaking subjects in dialogue with each 
other – based on their diverse (inter)subjectivities, imaginations and experiences, which are still 
highly relevant in the decolonial discourses. An example of that is the ongoing dialogue between 
designers and anthropologists in the hybrid field of Design Anthropology, which Dori Tunstall 
(2013, p. 239) defines as such: “Design anthropology draws from core sets of theoretical perspec-
tives – the critical anthropology of Third World peoples and their allies, indigenous and Scandina-
vian traditions of cooperative/Participatory Design, and indigenous, critical, feminist, ontological, 
and phenomenological knowledge traditions”. Building on that definition, she offers seven princi-
ples for approaching value systems, social, ethical and cultural issues, towards self-determination 
and constructive change, as well as recentring of design theory and practice from within indig -
enous cultures and histories towards larger cultural justice in design and technology development 
(Tunstall, 2023). As an example of that, Noronha and colleagues (2020) developed anthropologi-
cal knowledge on thinging and correspondence by designing with craftswomen in Northern Brazil.
In parallel to Design Anthropology, researchers in HCI engaged with postcolonial authors to 
add cross-cultural sensitivities and problematising power relations with users from colonised 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
118
backgrounds. Irani and colleagues (2010) introduced the concept of postcolonial computing, fo-
cusing on a generative view of culture, enacted in everyday life (Philip et al., 2012). The con -
cept was crafted on the general postcolonial literature, yet without much acknowledgement of the 
nuances and tensions that postcolonial authors found in their condition. As such, these tensions 
continue to be re-enacted in technology adoption and deployment initiatives, such as Human–
Computer Interaction for Development (HCI4D). Participatory Design has been defined as the 
key approach for postcolonial computing, even if some scholars in this field were critical of this 
way of “doing good” through computing (Bødker et al., 2022). People from the former colonies’ 
participation in the design of information technology for development was seen as a way of re -
alising that discourse. Scandinavian Participatory Design was summoned as an allied approach, 
although interpreted mostly through the US understanding of participation as the third space of 
HCI (Muller, 2007).
The concept of third space was drawn from Homi Bhabha’s (1994) assertion that cultural iden-
tity is formed in the ambivalent cultures and in-between spaces of the colonisers and the colonised. 
Based on such theories, Muller and Druin (2012) defined the third space as the space where con -
structive discussions, dialogue, negotiations and mutual learning between the designers and the 
users can take place. Cultural hybridity becomes a challenge for the colonial opposition between 
self and other, Western and non-Western or designer and user (Merritt and Stolterman, 2012). Out-
side of the US but still in America (the continent that is often reduced to a single-nation territory 
in imperialist discourses), De los Reyes and Botero (2012) found that hybridism can be explored 
by designers to identify with the community they are working with.
Cultural differences between designers and users have been the focus of attention of much 
Participatory Design research, yet only those who have engaged with postcolonial literature have 
acknowledged the colonial basis of such differences. Nevertheless, this colonial basis is some -
times interpreted as a metaphor, analogy or a weak association to other challenges faced in Partici-
patory Design. A case in point is the postcolonial reformulation of design/use time: “knowledge 
and categories fixed in a design and circulated through scripts can act as colonising forces that, by 
affording certain behaviour, actually limit the possibility to appreciate what was not known at the 
time of design but became relevant at the time of use” (Storni, 2013, p. 51).
In attempts to contribute to overcoming this divide, the Participatory Design research commu-
nity engaged in the debate cautiously. PDC 2014, besides integrating the global research community 
into the local NGOs, artistic, educational and political communities, was the first occasion for 
collective reflections on global (North–South) aspects of Participatory Design research. Building 
directly on postcolonial studies, Mainsah and Morrison (2014) called for a theoretical focus on 
postcolonial theory and its apparent applicability to Participatory Design practices. On that same 
occasion, Hakken and Maté (2014, p. 89) warned that: “Participatory Design will never be able to 
deal satisfactorily with culture if it continues to treat culture as an actual, empirical phenomenon, 
something with a real ontological status and thus to be apprehended directly, irrespective of the 
number or fixity of its channels”. They suggested that Participatory Design practitioners should 
therefore first narrow down their focus to single aspects of culture, deemed relevant, then attend to 
other aspects and finally merge the foci into a cohesive narrative of the situated cultural context.
A major criticism of postcolonial computing has been the lack of including marginalised and 
indigenous perspectives, thereby still manifesting a Eurocentric perspective (Ali, 2014). While 
framing their work in postcolonial computing, Taylor and colleagues (2018) have collaborated 
closely with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in Australia. They recognise that technol-
ogy design is always culturally situated and socially constructed. Expanding on this notion, they 
“advocate for a vision of digitising culture in which technology supports people to enact culture in 

Decolonisation and Participatory Design
119
the digital age, and people are equipped with both cultural knowledge and the skills to perform it” 
(Taylor et al., 2018). Thus, within their project Digital Community Board, they used a participa-
tory approach to learn about diverse cultural practices, such as storytelling and timing, and how 
best to translate these into a digital process. They found out that in such a cross-cultural design 
context, some cultural values can be explicitly or implicitly encoded in the technology designed.
Despite the recent efforts to ensure the involvement of indigenous communities, the concep-
tualisations and practices of Participatory Design still struggle with the legacy of Western and 
Eurocentric perspectives ingrained in the design methods, tools and measurements themselves 
(Barcham, 2023; Winschiers-Theophilus and Bidwell, 2013). The ongoing appropriation of Par -
ticipatory Design outside of Scandinavia, in particular to the Global South, has prompted concerns 
about the applicability of the Scandinavian alternative model to the rest of the world (Bødker and 
Kyng, 2018), which is now finding points of integration and conflict through cross-engagements 
(Calderón Salazar and Huybrechts, 2020; Smith et al., 2020).
Hence postcolonial approaches to design research and practice, even though well intended, 
inherently still often promote a neocolonial design (Smith et al., 2021). Smith and authors (2020) 
stress that Participatory Design given its political nature and motivation must keep challenging 
existing power structures through bottom-up engagements and embrace participation by those 
historically excluded through colonising processes. This demands more focus on developing de-
colonial practices of Participatory Design, which is a central challenge of the general decolonising 
design discourse.
Decolonial – Research and Design Otherwise
In Participatory Design, the term postcolonial is increasingly being replaced by the term decolo-
nial, as if they were interchangeable. A distinction based on its historical origins might clear up 
this confusion. Since the 1990s, postcolonial studies have been reviewed by a new generation of 
mostly Latin American and Caribbean authors: the modernity/coloniality group (Escobar, 2007). 
This group emerged from the dissidents of the earlier Latin American branch of subaltern studies 
who wanted to break free from European academic canons and their modern way of developing 
knowledge (Grosfoguel, 2011).
The modernity/coloniality group has been responsible for demonstrating the necessary link be-
tween the modernity project and the colonial project in producing a culturally homogenous world 
(Quijano, 2000, 2007). These projects generated certain relational qualities that got ingrained in 
political, economic and cultural practices of both metropolises and colonies. They named these 
the colonialities (Wynter, 2003) or forms of coloniality, but they also recognised the opposite 
qualities crafted by anti-modern and anticolonial projects: decolonialities (Mignolo, 2020). From 
that distinction came the adjective decolonial, which emphasises the active stance against colonial 
qualities through the “de” suffix. With this suffix choice, they also wanted to draw a distinction to 
the postcolonial approach, which admits the possibility of overcoming colonisation (Walsh, 2010). 
Decolonial approaches assume that colonialities are historical and structural products of colonial 
societies that will probably never go away, hence the need to keep a constant production of deco-
lonialities. Instead of favouring a rupture with the colonial ways as earlier anticolonial intellectuals 
fought for, decolonial intellectuals are more interested in problematising the uneasy conviviality of 
indigenous, colonisers, forced immigrants and settlers in former colonies and metropolises.
At once, a decolonial perspective points out that design practices are based on Western epistemol-
ogies and are nevertheless deployed in non-Western contexts without consideration of local knowl-
edge systems (Escobar, 2015, 2018; Lazem et al., 2022; Tunstall, 2013; Winschiers-Theophilus 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
120
and Bidwell, 2013; Smith et al., 2024). The denial of coevalness was demonstrated in a design re-
search conference, where a generation of PhD students who came from the Global South to study 
design in Europe, wrote a provocative article on decolonising design initially disregarded from the 
debate (Schultz et al., 2018) later becoming influential in several fields, including Participatory 
Design. These authors suggest that we can only break out of one’s “colonised mind” through the 
inclusion of marginalised perspectives, such as the previously colonised, indigenous communities 
and the socio-economic disenfranchised.
Inspired by this and others’ contributions, Alvarado Garcia and colleagues (2021) criticise a 
“fixed view of truth and knowledge” in HCI, which “shapes every aspect of our knowledge pro -
duction practice, from over-trusting the capabilities of digital technologies, to dismissing diverse 
perspectives for informing their design”. Western ways of knowing are still deeply embedded in 
current design thinking and acting (Ambole, 2020), which constrains researchers in future-making 
and methodological reflection. In common with other authors, they argue that the task of decolonis-
ing design discourse is ontological in nature and that the radical transformation of design requires 
both transdisciplinary and transcultural approaches (Smith et al., 2020; 2021). Again the emphasis 
on “delinking” (Mignolo, 2007) and finding alternative ways of producing knowledge to move 
forward is emphasised.
However, over time, decolonisation movements have been dominated by Kantian and utili-
tarian thinking, which is typically “individualist”, as opposed to relational and immaterial no-
tions brought forward for example in African philosophies, such as Ubuntu (Tavernaro-Haidarian, 
2019). A fundamental distinction is a focus on the “we” rather than the “I”. In this light, Van 
Stam (2021) emphasises that a decolonial turn will require a paradigm switch from “an oriental 
projected self, linked with universalism, to be replaced by a locally-grounded African authentic 
self, linked with diversity [.  . .] based on value epistemologies like ubuntu or ifa”. Grounding 
the decolonisation strategies in the moral values of Ubuntu as normative mutualism allows to 
reimagine the way forward as an integrative and participatory process of “collective maturation” 
(Tavernaro-Haidarian, 2019).
In this sense, Kambunga and coauthors (2020) report from a case study in Namibia, a collabora-
tion with Danish and Namibian researchers, in which the topic of postcoloniality and decoloniality 
was explored with local Namibian youth, students and stakeholders and also brought forward new 
aspects advancing Participatory Design. The Memory Making with Namibian Born Free project 
(2018–2022)
3 addressed the everyday experiences of postcolonialism of youth, the Born Free, 
in contemporary Namibia, and the dilemmas they face being born after independence in 1990, 
while struggling to envision and take control of futures that radically differ from their predeces -
sors (Oyedemi, 2021b). The case demonstrated how Participatory Design research addressed the 
topic of decolonisation in a highly political and fraught postcolonial context, integrating local 
youth communities to explore memories and possible futures in which their voices and ambi -
tions were integrated into the mainstream historical narrative of the liberation struggle (Smith 
et al., 2020). Digital technologies were used to co-create and probe new decolonising dialogues 
through curatorial processes and physical and virtual exhibitions. The research integrated ap -
proaches from community-based Participatory Design and Design Anthropology, through design 
interventions, dialogic curation, prototyping and co-design, using the various positionings of the 
researchers within, between and beyond, to create reflective practices of what and how historical 
and socio-political issues and memories where entangled in contemporary everyday life and op-
portunities for alternative collective future-making.
A central outcome of the research was the development of the concept of the “safe space” in 
design interventions: a socially developed environment for thoughts, actions and mutual learning 

Decolonisation and Participatory Design
121
in political and contested contexts (Kambunga et al., 2023). The “safe space” was introduced as a 
decolonial design practice that enables researchers and participants to engage more freely in col -
laborative research and design activities relating to decoloniality. Based on ideas of social construc-
tions of spaces (Lefebvre, 1991) and discourses of decoloniality, the authors define the safe space as 
a consciously developed social environment for thoughts, situated actions and mutual learning that 
allows participants both to engage in dialogues about their everyday experiences, tensions and con-
tested pasts and consequently to imagine and co-create alternative and plural futures. Through pro-
cesses of critically exploring contemporary experiences of past-present-future (de)colonisation, 
such participatory practice can allow researchers to develop new ways of knowing, being and doing 
(Mignolo and Walsh, 2018; Kambunga et al., 2024) that reduce possible fears of repercussions or 
judgement by other community members in the society or the decision-making authorities. The safe 
space also prompts researchers engaged in such projects to be critical of their own positionalities 
within the socio-cultural and historical research context, as well as of their own particular adapta-
tions of dominant design methods and approaches. Designing and using safe spaces as a decolonial 
approach to design enables working with multiple temporalities and epistemologies – especially 
in contested hybrid cultural contexts where modern coloniality (Quijano, 2007) and postcolonial 
struggles (Mbembe, 2001) continue to shape people’s everyday realities and futures.
This temporal extension of Participatory Design includes the past as a flexible resource and 
material that is highly relevant to balance the, often, over-emphasised future-orientation in Partici-
patory Design research practice. According to decolonial research in this regard, the past is “far 
from static, monolithic, immutable, and is rather subjective, fluid, and constantly renegotiated” 
(Soro et al., 2019; Kambunga et al., 2024). Huybrechts and Hendriks (2016) have contributed with 
different approaches to include the past as a resource in imaginative future scenarios. Such percep-
tions of the past emphasise the continuous entanglements of different pasts, presents and futures. 
Because the past is continuously shaped as a part of the emergent present and future (Smith and 
Otto, 2016), it can also be used to open up space for legacies and memories of colonialism, con -
temporary everyday experiences of the decolonial, as well as to refer to plural future imaginations.
Such approaches can support the situated adaptations of participatory research in diverse con -
texts, to enhance agencies and coevalness in our dialogues between researchers and communities.
For instance, local research communities in Namibia have demanded researchers “being par -
ticipated” before they actually participate (Winschiers-Theophilus et al., 2010). Participatory 
drawing, for instance, has enabled designers to understand how they can meaningfully become a 
participant in Afro-Brazilian decolonial rituals (Paterman Brasil, 2020). Instead of inviting people 
to participate in an outsider design project, Participatory Design can respond to an insider’s invi -
tation like the mega-mingas public meetings of the Andinan people (Testori and D’Auria, 2018) 
or the musyawarah-mufakat gatherings of the Pacific Island nations (Rosenqvist, 2020). By par -
ticipating in community-initiated projects rather than imposing their own projects, participatory 
designers may contribute to decolonise their own field. From another perspective:
It can also be regarded as a generative means of understanding and reporting of ourselves 
and others, either through the decolonisation of well-known methods or through unfamiliar 
one’s that can be generated in our embodied actions and activities as creators and organisers 
of our social world.
(Adamu, 2020)
Many contemporary Participatory Design practitioners have been searching for new tools to 
help them navigate the complexities of the decolonial agenda, keeping the “constant production of 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
122
decolonialities” alive in their work. In her analysis of the collective participatory work of a group 
of neighbours in Rio de Janeiro devising ways to confront the violence of their neighbourhood, 
Ibarra (2020) uses the Latin American notion of sentipensar – feeling/thinking (Fals-Borda, 2013) 
to illustrate a set of Participatory Design commitments that can speak to an alternative set of values 
connecting feeling and thought. These values recognise the inevitability of working with everyday 
struggles and concerns and the necessity of being attentive and embracing the emotional aspects 
of even the more rational forms of action. Especially for projects where the participatory designer 
is part of the collective that designs (Bittencourt and Freire, 2022). Thinking about these kinds of 
projects, Albarrán González (2022) develops the concept of corazonar, taken from Mayan views 
of the heart. Using onto-epistemologies from the Global South, she discusses the relevance of a 
holistic integration of the body, mind, heart and life-force (spirit) where corazonar, or the act of 
reasoning with the heart in collectivity, allows going beyond analytic reasoning towards decolo -
nial actions. She calls for Participatory Design practitioners and researchers to interweave culture, 
creativity, cycles, connection, community, care and courage as guiding principles, at the heart of 
Participatory Design research in collaboration with communities. Corazonar has also been an il -
luminating concept to enable designers to design games and books that share and document the 
Kichwas indigenous knowledge in Amazonia (Garcés, 2021).
Drawing on other indigenous concepts, Sosa (2020) explores Purepecha myths of creation to 
contest and expand Western notions of creativity and world-making that inform (explicitly and 
implicitly) much of the work on Participatory Design methods and approaches so far. In Mesoa -
merican worldviews, Sosa explains, creation has never been a matter of well-defined and orderly 
sequence of incremental steps or stages (like in the biblical genesis or indeed design thinking 
methods); it is instead an opportunistic, situational and cyclical process. One that is more accu -
rately viewed as re-creation, where even deities need each other and often work with, for example, 
the help of animals. The author invites participatory designers to practise more inclusive and richer 
versions of creativity that embrace – and problematise – some of its basic tenets. Besides creativ-
ity, other central tenets of design craft have also been scrutinised with a decolonial attitude. For 
example, seemingly bureaucratic practices like that of ensuring consent have been turned towards 
a more radically co-constitution, drawing from experiences of a Participatory Design education 
programme in Western Arrarnta Country in Australia (St John, 2022). Informed and respectful of 
ilkwatharra, or a “good feeling” indigenous conceptions, consent is understood here as an ethi -
cal practice which unsettles dominant consent requirements while presenting a respectful way of 
entering into collaborative work.
Talhouk and Armouch (2022) likewise use decolonial approaches to address their own research 
practices based on the Lebanese national-wide protests in the fall of 17th October 2019, which 
ignited a revolution condemning the political elite and the dire socio-economic conditions that 
people engendered. The events prompted not only local people to (re)imagine their lifeworlds, 
but also the authors, as Lebanese design researchers to (re)imagine Participatory Design within a 
decolonial and decolonising narrative. The authors’ approach to (re)imagining through this revolu-
tionary perspective, includes dialogues held among themselves, with Lebanese public health prac-
titioners/activists and with decolonial literature. An example of this (self-)reflexive representation 
and dialogue is presented here (Talhouk and Armouch, 2022: 54):
Nonetheless, this brings us to another issue that made us pause. In our efforts to design with 
the revolution, are we potentially excluding or disregarding those resisting from within the 
system to create decolonial cracks? Walsh (Mignolo and Walsh, 2018) posited that rather 
than viewing decolonial efforts as existing outside the matrix of modern/colonial power 

Decolonisation and Participatory Design
123
(Quijano, 2000) we should acknowledge and work within decolonial cracks. Through our 
dialogue, we acknowledge that practitioners and public health workers within the Lebanese 
healthcare system are themselves positioned to be the upholders of political sectarianism 
and its corruption by the design of the system and their own experiences of oppression. 
However, this does not necessitate that they do not practise resistance by creating and work-
ing within decolonial cracks. Therefore, rather than viewing them as accomplices, should we 
not explore the less visible decolonial cracks that they may be working within and consider 
how we may think/do with them? Is it possible that those that work within such cracks are 
forming a communal that resists sectarian divides maintained by the political elite?
(Talhouk and Armouch, 2022, p. 54, emphasis in original)
Following the broad literature influenced by the modernity/coloniality group, Participatory Design 
is going beyond the opposition between coloniality and decoloniality, towards the possibility of 
uneasy conviviality of modern and anti-modern ways of being and living together. Among the 
many forms of colonialities, the coloniality of knowledge (Quijano, 2007) has been prioritised 
in this field so far, in part due to Participatory Design’s tradition of democratic knowledge for -
malisation. Sousa Santos (Santos, 2018) denounced the epistemic injustice of disregarding knowl-
edge produced in the peripheries of the world and proposed, instead, to put into the spotlight the 
epistemologies of the South developed by social movements in the Global South. Following this 
proposal, authors in the Global North incorporated indigenous knowledge, many at times without 
providing due credit or proper attention to what indigenous people wanted to do with their words 
(Makaran and Gaussens, 2020; Cusicanqui, 2012). Despite connecting Latin-American with Eu -
ropean in some way, some might argue that Sousa Santos did not pay the same level of attention 
to the coloniality of power and the coloniality of gender
4 equally emphasised by other modernity/
coloniality authors (Quijano, 2000; Lugones 2013).
The concept of decoloniality and its derived adjective decolonial have been overused in many 
research fields, in shallow attempts to engage with decolonisation movements but without paying 
respect to its history and agenda (Makaran and Gaussens, 2020). While observing opportunistic 
situations like these, many authors in Participatory Design and nearby fields have started to adopt 
the pluriversal instead, in search of alternative paths for designing otherwise. A better understand-
ing of its historical context might clear up further confusion and show how notions of pluriversal-
ity might open up constructive ways ahead.
Pluriversal – A Universe of Many Universes
Colonialism has often been framed as political and economic dependence justified on cultural or 
bodily differences (Fanon, 2004). However, anticolonial, postcolonial and decolonial literature 
denounced the ontological differences manufactured by colonialism, which produced the colo -
niality of being (Maldonado-Torres, 2007; Wynter, 2003), White supremacy and the hierarchisa -
tion of worlds, for instance, into the First, Second, and Third worlds (Santos, 2017). Indigenous, 
communalist, socialist and quilombola social movements in Latin America targeted this onto -
logical inequality for the last 40 years. They have claimed to exist in a different world from that 
one of the former colonisers and, as such, demand they should be allowed to keep that difference 
while joining globalisation dynamics. The World Social Forum, which started to gather social 
movements first in Latin America and later from other geographical areas, probably best repre -
sents the alternative globalisation project pushed by the decolonisation movement (Fisher and 
Ponniah, 2003). The presentation of research stemming from the Global South in Global North 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
124
venues, be that from Latin American living in the diaspora (Pinto et al., 2022; Reynolds-Cuéllar 
et al., 2023) or from those who publish in English not to perish in their countries of origin for 
the lack of citational justice (Ogan et al., 2023), is a strong evidence of this alternative globali -
sation project.
When making sense of this insurge to create commonality in global differences, decolonial 
scholars began using the concept of pluriverse, originally coined in the context of the pluralistic 
democracy programme envisioned by early 20th-century US pragmatism (James and Callaway, 
2008). However, instead of pointing towards the melting pot of US pluralistic democracy, for 
decolonial scholars, the concept was initially used to mean the opposite of the universe (Mignolo, 
2011). They rejected the colonialist imposition of a single universe because their worlds would be 
included in a universe that does not welcome their differences. World differences in the Eurocen-
tric universe are measured by criteria that always favours the colonial powers like, for example, 
the Human Development Index. Joining the universe, for Latin American and Caribbean worlds, 
means becoming less developed, subaltern or not even worlds in themselves in relation to Euro-
pean worlds. Instead, joining the pluriverse, as implied by the often quoted Zapatista motto “a 
world where many worlds fit” (Marcos, 2002, p. 197) means recognising that world differences 
could be generative, even if not easily comparable (Escobar, 2018).
Questions such as land ownership, border politics, official idioms, resource management, mil-
itary sovereignty and democratic governance come to the fore and present strong contradictions 
that the pluriverse needs to harbour (Escobar, 2020b). World differences go way beyond cul -
tural differences and require more than multiculturalism (García Canclini, 2001). Pluriversality 
is increasingly becoming a new paradigm for inter-world and inter-being relations, condensing 
(and, eventually, homogenising) all of the decoloniality qualities. In this light, Escobar (2018) 
advocates striving for a design which embraces “a world where many worlds fit”, allowing for a 
pluriversality of voices, knowledges and epistemologies to be incorporated into creating social 
transformation. Pluriversality is used here and in relation to ontological and religious plurality, 
as an undeniable phenomenon of the human condition, that we take active or passive part in – a 
condition however, that humans often fail to recognise and lead to conflict, oppression and war 
(Rahman and Setia, 2021). The pluriverse concept insists on the democratic coexistence of on -
tological differences even at the cost of eventual friction and conflicts (Van Amstel, 2023; Smith 
et al., 2024).
Such calls have shown themselves in participatory research and cases that advance transdiscipli-
nary and transcultural approaches to engaging with communities and stakeholders in diverse cultural 
contexts. Based on more than a decade of collaborative technology design projects with indigenous 
communities in Namibia, Winschiers-Theophilus et al. (2019) have established a community-based 
co-design approach, rooted in practices of Participatory Design yet anchored in principles of Ubuntu 
and Afrocentricity. This approach has provided a foundation for indigenisation of Participatory De-
sign methods and has offered new perspectives on Participatory Design principles and values. Along 
these lines, Winschiers-Theophilus et al. (2019) have proposed a transcultural approach to technol-
ogy design, which looks beyond traditional individual cultures and focuses on transcultural technol-
ogy design methods that adopt, support and continuously create new meanings from diverse settings. 
Thus, a transcultural approach focuses on being culturally aware when designing with culturally 
diverse communities and groups, embracing pluralistic social practices and increased awareness 
(Winschiers-Theophilus et al., 2019).
In an attempt to go beyond localised engagements and with the global pandemic preventing 
research on the ground in many places, a virtual collaboration explored potentials for extending 
the safe space, and various exhibition spaces, into pluriversality across global contexts (Kambunga 

Decolonisation and Participatory Design
125
et al., 2021). The result was a virtual Pluriversal Design Exhibition, engaging audiences in virtual 
environments as alternative spaces to decolonise design practice and shared knowledge produc -
tion. The collaborative exhibition brought together design research and exhibition projects from 
Australia, Denmark, Ecuador, Finland, Ghana, Greenland, Italy, Malaysia and Namibia. For each 
exhibition space, the question was: How can we create virtual spaces for pluriversal dialogue 
and engagement? What can a virtual exhibition on decoloniality teach us about designing for the 
pluriverse? They answered these questions by appropriating Mozilla Hubs platform, which of 
course presented new challenges of access and virtual engagement (Kambunga et al., 2021). The 
exhibition successfully demonstrated how diverse projects addressing of decoloniality could coex-
ist to promote voices of otherwise unheard communities.
The large push for practice and new practices of Participatory Design has forged contributions 
around methods and techniques for decolonisation and towards the pluriverse (Smith et al. 2024; 
see also Chapter 7). These are also largely integrated earlier with approaches to sentipensar and 
safe spaces, yet we highlight a few contributions here that speak to other concepts. Lujan Escalante 
and Mortimer (2022) present research notes used to devise the Participatory Design method they 
propose as “Pluriversal Transition Value Mapping”. This is a reflection on three exercises carried 
out in three countries of the “Pacific Ring of Fire”, a label that describes the Southeast Asian 
regional disposition to intensifying disasters of epic proportions. They maintain that Traditional 
Ecological Knowledges are of utmost significance in risk management and describe the ethics and 
facilitation of a transdisciplinary approach. Similarly Muashekele et al. (2023) infused futuring 
techniques in established community-based co-design with indigenous communities in Namibia, 
thereby deviating from a linear need-based approach towards exposing alternative futures merging 
modernity with futures of the past, which were lost due to colonisation. Following this approach, 
community members reflected on the lost futures of the past and evaluated their validity and desir-
ability alongside other futures.
Aiming to foster epistemological pluriversality in HCI, Alvarado Garcia et al. (2021) present 
an actionable decolonial pathway based on a co-constructed shared positionality of diverse au -
thors, encouraging others to reflect on their own positionality within their diverse contexts. Their 
manifesto questions the why, the what, the how, the with whom and the what for when practising 
decoloniality. Alvarado Garcia et al. (2021) suggest that the colonial legacies ingrained in insti -
tutional, cultural and disciplinary engagements, which directly affects established and accepted 
tools, methods and approaches in HCI, should be acknowledged and publicised, as also proposed 
by Barcham (2023) and Smith et al. (2021). They appeal to explicitly expose tenets and practices 
constraining diverse and unequal knowledge productions. Furthermore, Alvarado Garcia et al. 
(2021) suggest shifting the focus from academic to community validation and impact, with a focus 
on mutual learning throughout community engagements. Lastly, the authors request that the ques-
tion of power and consequent injustice is addressed heads on.
Baroncelli Torreta and colleagues (2023) also found that reflecting critically on positionality is 
crucial for doing Participatory Design in the pluriverse. Their empirical basis is the River Project, 
a participatory space for decolonising design created for designers and practitioners to reflect on 
power, privilege, politics and access in relation to design. According to their findings, pluriversal 
participation emerges when participants participate in their own way, stemming from their posi-
tionality, rather than from a universal methodological standpoint.
After summarising part of the literature mentioned in this section, Calderón Salazar and Huy -
brechts (2020) went as far as to state that Participatory Design “otherwise will be pluriversal (or 
it won’t be)”. They envision Participatory Design building knowledge and designing otherwise, 
that is, based on inclusive epistemologies (Santos, 2018), participatory research methodologies 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
126
(Fals-Borda, 2013) and southern theories (Calderón Salazar and Gutiérrez Borrero, 2017), praxes 
that converge under the banner of the pluriverse. As much as we recognise the power of this single 
all-encompassing concept to unite the decolonisation efforts, we have chosen here not to subsume 
the postcolonial and the decolonial under the pluriversal. After going through all of the literature 
here mentioned, we think that it is possible to do Participatory Design otherwise in the other 
strands and through different approaches that may emerge in the future.
Towards A Relational Agenda in Participatory Design
Participatory Design initiatives conducted in contentious cultural and geopolitical contexts have 
shown the need to revisit established paradigms, values and biases, thus we call for both individual 
and collective introspections. Besides, considering established forms of knowledge production 
and dissemination, participatory designers have an obligation to abolish inherent systemic injus-
tices which directly influence design paradigms and practices responsible for perpetuating coloni-
ality. Failure to do so will lead to dilemmas and contradictions that threaten the very fundamentals 
of Participatory Design, being mutual learning and the combat against power inequity.
Arturo Escobar, in his PDC 2020’s keynote (Escobar, 2020a), called for a relational approach 
to Participatory Design based on the radical interdependence of beings of all kinds, not just human 
beings. In similar vein, Victor Udoewa (2022) suggested that relationality is the next frontier for 
radical forms of Participatory Design. Responding to these calls, our relational agenda comprises 
three topics of concern. Firstly, the need for introspection and understanding of inherent biases and 
values propagated through mainstream Participatory Design; this includes recognising Eurocentric 
frames. Secondly, recognising and eliminating systemic biases reinforced through established and 
formalised knowledge creation and sharing processes, thereby embracing different epistemolo-
gies. And lastly, closing the gap between theory and practice (Smith et al., 2020), as we consider 
Participatory Design within situated actions, and understanding roles, accountabilities and respon-
sibilities of the involved.
These concerns resonate with Clarke et al. (2022) framework for Participatory Design decolo-
nial action that includes three movements: decolonising in design by recognising frames of refer-
ence that can remain prevalent in Participatory Design practice; decolonising by design where 
collaboration becomes a catalyst for challenging institutional perspectives that foreground alter -
native epistemologies and ontologies; and lastly with a movement towards decolonising through 
design, which implies mobilising cracks to effect change, going beyond research to work with au-
tonomous and communal forms of action and sociability. While our appeal to relationality could fit 
in Clarke et al. (2022) “decolonising through design” concept, our aim here is broader: to position 
Participatory Design within the larger decolonising processes. These processes surely go through 
methodological challenges – for example, how to include people from diverse cultures – and also 
epistemological questions – for example, what to learn from them – however, the common ground 
amongst these movements is ontology (in its original philosophical sense of the word), regarding 
the quantum of being human that colonisation prevented from being more (Fanon, 2004; Freire, 
1985). In the following sections we detail three main trajectories for a relational decolonisation 
agenda in Participatory Design research and practices.
Revisiting Participatory Design Paradigms, Values and Biases
In an attempt to move beyond mere theoretical deliberations, we start the section with a very real 
tension and uneasy conviviality expressed by one of the chapter reviewers, Professor Pelle Ehn, 

Decolonisation and Participatory Design
127
famous for his contributions to the field of Participatory Design and who – according to us – was 
historically engaged with the anticolonial strand. Pelle Ehn agreed that we share an extract from 
his review to illustrate the positionality and conundrum of Global North researchers dealing with 
this topic:
In fact, inspired by reading Hannah Arendt and especially Simone Weil I have been directed 
towards the prime narratives of western culture and the epic richness of the Iliad and the Odys-
sey. Hence, being forced to rediscover and rethink taking for granted concepts like war, power, 
force, violence and love. All central to Participatory Design and I guess also to decolonisation 
and pluriversality. So you see, I do not know how to escape this Eurocentric prison. Not even 
if I want to. Even if you try to rescue me. Under what conditions could or should someone like 
me be invited to the “safe space” where the future of Participatory Design could be collabora-
tively explored across modernity and coloniality and different ontologies, as you so promisingly 
write, “towards the possibility of uneasy conviviality of modern and anti-modern ways of being 
and living together”. Is there in this space also room for and a potential contribution from also 
rethinking the ancient western heritage and not only the colonial atrocities? For example with 
Arendt to rethink design as stories of heroic political action linked to plurality and the possibil-
ity of forgiveness? Or with Weil to rethink narratives of design as the grace of affirmatively 
leaving be, of becoming host rather than parasite. And are there, or should there be, similar ways 
of trying to reimagine narratives from other ontologies and open them up for rethinking design?
(Professor emeritus Pelle Ehn,  
personal communication, October 1, 2023)
Indeed, numerous authors have recognised that Participatory Design still maintains legacies of 
Western and Eurocentric perspectives ingrained in the design methods, tools and measurements 
themselves (Barcham, 2023; Winschiers-Theophilus and Bidwell, 2013). For example, Akama and 
colleagues (2022) have written: “Reflexively exposing and leaning into our complicities, no mat-
ter how awkward, helps to be vigilant of such conciliatory desires, because we cannot step ‘out -
side’ of what global histories have implicated us in already”. However, a major dilemma persists, 
namely that the point of reference seems to remain the “Scandinavian Participatory Design”. The 
suggestion that it simply needs to be adjusted and appropriated in a new and local context does not 
seem to hold true (Krüger et al., 2019). As long as the point of reference does not shift, all efforts 
remain anchored in Eurocentrism. 
The emphasis on values systems and cultures highlights how these are dynamic, mutually bor-
rowed and exchanged, and co-produced over time, into new forms of cultural production and 
change, is central to expanding decolonising Participatory Design practices (Gunn et al., 2013). In 
line with that, Akama et al. (2019) suggest reciprocal, respectful and relational approaches to col-
laboration, which require sensitivity to precarious asymmetries and cultural values among others. 
Bourgeois et al. (2022), grounding decolonisation in humility, uncertainty and plurality, propose 
five design principles, namely “transdisciplinarity, cooperative design, contextualised learning for 
being, locally led initiation of the inquiry together with the empowerment of local actors.”
Combating Systemic Injustice in Knowledge Production and Dissemination
Participatory Design’s overreliance on the prevailing knowledge production structures keeps aca-
demics and social movement agents apart and keeps Global North institutions as publication gate-
keepers. Due to that separation, research and practice develop disjointly, thereby creating cultural, 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
128
theoretical and methodological gaps (Loi et al., 2018; Schultz et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2020; 
Tlostanova, 2017). These gaps create practices and structures that do not challenge the status 
quo, such as universal design methods that are exported from the Global North to the Global 
South (Ansari, 2016), Eurocentric design education (Angelon and Van Amstel, 2021), assisted 
development strategies (Escobar, 2012) and global market distributions such as one-size-fits-all 
tech applications to the “Next Billion Users” that do not yet have access to an internet connection 
(Oyedemi, 2021a). These solutions create dependencies and inequalities between the periphery 
and the centre, with incentives for the marginalised to design solutions in the periphery, from one 
periphery to another (Batista e Silva, 2023; Marques and Mass, 2020). This status is further mani-
fested through Global North institutes as gatekeepers of knowledge production and dissemination 
thereby claiming ownership of the only rightful solutions to local and global challenges. An at -
tempt to formulate strategies of inclusion and diversity in prominent HCI communities has yielded 
tokenisation at best, without addressing the systemic marginalisation of knowledge production and 
practices (Dankwa and Draude, 2021).
Bidwell (2016) points out that a colonised technology design space has been established by an 
academic community guilty of continuously undermining African and other researchers pushed to 
the margin. Non-Western researchers’ methods and knowledges are questioned and the credibility 
of their work is judged within biased review systems (Lazem et al., 2022). Reviewers, who lack 
sufficient understanding of local contexts and other ways of knowing, reject valuable research 
papers (Smith et al., 2021), and authors from the Global South (Reynolds-Cuéllar et al., 2022). 
Akama et al. (2022) see potential in open review processes as blinded reviews allow reviewers not 
to be held accountable towards their feedback provided to authors, reinforcing power imbalances. 
Moreover, skewed citation patterns further foster unequal knowledge dissemination, discriminat -
ing against the spread of knowledge created in the Global South. For example, in September 2023, 
Nordichi 2018 proceedings recorded 640 citations while Africhi 2018 proceedings recorded 224 
citations in the ACM Digital library. In Participatory Design, like in any other Western knowledge 
field, new research findings need to be positioned in relation to previously published research,
