thereby creating a vicious circle of enforcing citing the already established rather than the ones at 
the margin (Akama et al., 2022).
Akama and colleagues (2022) further point out the complicities of perpetuating dominant de-
sign through venues, such as conferences. The PDC 2022 conference organisers attempted to lev-
erage the organising mechanisms in academic conferences to surface implicit agendas, normalised 
approaches and confront tensions and paradoxes of decolonising own practices. Questions around 
labour, privilege and ethics of being present and situated during sharing and coming together on 
unceded indigenous land, and proposed methodologies and alternative conference engagements 
came to the fore in organising meetings. The authors argue for sharing endeavours through prac -
tice and ontologies of our feeling-thinking (sentipensar), responding to the question posed by an 
Indigenous Elder to them: “Why are you here and what is your purpose?”. In response, the PDC 
2024 has involved local stakeholders and indigenous community members in the planning of the 
conference and activities. Generally, concerned with the lack of participation of indigenous com-
munities in conferences and academic dialogues, Winschiers-Theophilus and colleagues (2022) 
put forward the concept of a knowledge fair as a pluralistic approach to knowledge creation and 
sharing. Based on years of experience from a bi-annual indigenous knowledge fair held in Sarawak 
(Harris, 2017), the concept was further explored in Namibia, having hosted 100 participants with 
the majority being indigenous community members who were involved in the Participatory De-
sign of conservation technologies. The programme consisted of diverse sessions ranging from 
ethnobotanical tech demo walks, to intestine reading and reflections, and community focus group 

Decolonisation and Participatory Design
129
meetings, accounting for the different knowledge-sharing paradigms. A similar request for alter -
native ways of sharing research beyond written articles was put forward by Bossavit and Parsons 
(2016). The authors suggest “incorporating traditional practices into meetings and workshops, 
conducting face-to-face meetings in sites that hold meaning or significance to indigenous partners, 
active listening as oral histories are shared”.
Staying in the Path of Praxis
As much as we can tell from this survey, Participatory Design has not yet fully engaged with 
the large-scale design of everyday life performed through radical (and) emerging technologies 
(Greenfield, 2017). Global platforms, artificial intelligence, machine learning, data-driven soci -
eties and extended realities have not been properly addressed by Participatory Design and are 
often at odds with the smaller-scale democratic praxis and methods of participation (Murphy and 
Largacha-Martínez, 2022; see also Chapter 6 for a comprehensive outline). Nevertheless, govern-
ments all over the world struggle to regulate digital work platforms, social media and blockchain 
applications that reproduce the old divide between a powerful centre that extracts resources in the 
periphery – in this case data – and sell it back to the periphery as business intelligence services or 
the likes (Couldry and Mejias, 2019). More often than expected, these platforms are also under 
scrutiny for political actions, hijacked by spies and hackers, in geopolitical moves, similar to how 
former colonial trade routes were used for cultural impositions and war (O’Neil, 2016). Research-
ers in other fields have already suggested that participation in design can indeed localise such 
collective resources, thus contributing to counter the digital form of colonialism (Faustino and 
Lippold, 2023; Kwet, 2019; Oyedemi, 2021a), but Participatory Design has not fully embraced the 
challenge yet. Design Beku is one of the first documented efforts into that: a Participatory Design 
studio that trains critical technological citizens in India (Ray Murray et al., 2021). Its decolonising 
motivation is similar to the anthropophagic studio in Brazil (Van Amstel and Gonzatto, 2020), yet 
more focused on training communities rather than training students.
The decolonising movement has brought attention to new issues in Participatory Design – like 
epistemological plurality, citational justice and historical repairs – but also recovered old issues 
that have not been discussed much in past decades, such as technology development geopolitics, 
cultural differences beyond Scandinavia versus the US, tokenistic participation and decentralised 
power structures. The contribution of this movement to Participatory Design in its early years, 
mainly through the work of Paulo Freire, has kept an open door for further dialogue, an opportu -
nity explored in depth only in recent years (Serpa et al., 2020). Like in any dialogue, both sides are 
expected to contribute to each other and make something together.
To avoid the anti-dialogical praxis (Freire, 1985), or extractivism, the contributions of anticolo-
nial, postcolonial, decolonial and pluriversal Participatory Design should also aim at contributing 
to the decolonisation movements they originate from, otherwise, Participatory Design becomes 
a (colonialist) end in itself. Other authors have also made similar points regarding other social 
movements (Bannon et al., 2018b). Thus rather than just incorporating new theories and practices 
stemming from the Global South, Participatory Design has to find its political place in the decolo-
nising movement and, from that position, act meaningfully for the emancipation, liberation and 
independence of the oppressed people.
Among the many positions suggested in this chapter, we would like to draw attention to the 
position against digital colonialism (Barendregt et al., 2021; Faustino and Lippold, 2023; Kwet, 
2019), which we think Participatory Design can have a strong impact on. Against this form of 
colonialism, people from the Global North and the Global South should join forces, as the process 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
130
does not follow the traditional North-to-South route. Digital colonialism supports new forms of 
imperialism, such as the US’s influence over Europe and China’s influence over Africa, for ex -
ample. The Scandinavian workers and citizens of today are also prone to these new forms of 
colonialism, which would require organised forms of resistance across countries and regions to 
be operationalised. The decolonisation movement today should be betting on collective, inclusive 
and democratic participation to counter digital colonialism and similar geopolitical menaces. This 
won’t be achieved through a design by the oppressors, for the oppressed, but through a design by 
the oppressed, for the oppressed – as the Design & Oppression Network likes to put it (van Amstel 
et al., 2023).
Concluding Remarks
As we stated in the introduction, our ambition in the chapter is not to cover all grounds in re-
lation to the diversified theoretical discourses, research and practices of decolonisation. More 
broadly speaking, the literature on anticolonial, postcolonial, decolonial and pluriversal is greatly 
divergent and often tied to geographically and culturally situated understandings of decolonisa -
tion rather than following coherent theoretical strands (Davis and Walsh, 2020). At once, there are 
many contributions written based on geographical regions, reporting on research projects, but who 
tend to take the political, theoretical and historical background for granted and thus only engage 
superficially with the challenges of decolonisation. Hence, this chapter is by no means exhaustive 
and does not aim to reduce the entanglement and complexity of the concepts, methods and theories 
involved but rather to take a Participatory Design stance on these for the matter of this book and 
for future research.
Looking at past and contemporary Participatory Design decolonisation initiatives, it is evident 
that these efforts have remained isolated, often disjointed from and unaware of actual decolo-
nisation movements and consequently with limited impact on the ground. Weaving alliances, 
partnerships and coalitions is fundamental to position the field within the wider decolonisation 
movements but also to ground their responsibilities and accountabilities on very specific lo -
calities and lifeworlds. We believe that, through the dialogues here united, we positioned and 
repositioned ourselves as self and other, unsettling entanglements and raising contradictions and 
questions lingering in the Participatory Design field, potentially contributing to making worlds 
otherwise.
Notes
1 “The ‘decolonial’ is a trend, the postcolonial is a desire, and the anticolonial is a struggle”.
2 We prefer to use the non-geographical distinction between Global North and Global South to capture the 
manifestation of the colonial difference across the globe (Mignolo, 1999), in alignment with contemporary 
social movements and the decolonial and postcolonial strands that are introduced later in the chapter. An-
ticolonial strands typically used metropolis/colonies, developed/underdeveloped nations and First/Third 
Worlds to outline a different difference. Postcolonial strands have not emphasised these dialectics and, 
instead, try to emphasise their synthesis in hybrids and other forms (Bhabha, 1994).

to 2019 (see the official report on https://www.ces.uc.pt/ficheiros2/files/Final%20Report%20-%20CI_
en.pdf). The Independent Commission was appointed to investigate complaints about moral and sexual 
harassment practices and concluded that the hierarchical structure, and lack of precise instruments and

guidelines may have led to asymmetries of power in which for example students and researchers from

6
EMERGING TECHNOLOGIES 
AND ALTERNATIVE FUTURES
Christopher Frauenberger, Rachel Charlotte Smith,  
Daria Loi, Laura Forlano and Ole Sejer Iversen
Participatory Design’s core ambition is to democratise technological innovation to bring about al-
ternative futures, underpinned by its strong value propositions of empowerment, social justice, and 
socio-ecological sustainability. As such, Participatory Design has always sought to engage with novel 
and emerging technologies within shifting societal challenges, continuously evolving its theory and 
practice to have an impact to this effect. This chapter provides a review of contemporary discourses 
between Participatory Design and current emerging technologies and develops stepping stones for 
future research and practice in the field.
The chapter investigates the qualities of emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence 
(AI), large-language models, and immersive media and how these are configured in ways that 
produce systems of old and new forms of oppression. The qualities identified relate to their scale, 
hyper-connectedness, and pervasiveness but also their increasing agential capabilities. Configured 
within the conditions of destabilised democracies, increasing social injustice, an out-of-bounds sur -
veillance capitalism, and the climate emergency, we argue that Participatory Design needs to develop 
meaningful and effective participation around these socio-material assemblages to offer alternatives.
The chapter surveys examples of Participatory Design’s engagement with such systems and tech -
nologies over the past decade, covering themes of platforms, civic technologies, and democratic en -
gagements with communities, as well as more specific work on AI and automation in the field. Finally, 
we develop four stepping stones as trajectories for future Participatory Design research and practice:
• Developing novel methodologies to engage pervasive systems of scale;
• Re-conceptualising material participation in design in response to the increasing agential capabili-
ties of emerging technologies;
• Fostering ambitions to shape technological innovation landscapes for sustainable futures; and
• Working across diverse political arenas towards democratising technology.
This chapter aims to rekindle Participatory Design’s commitment to be involved in the creation of 
emerging technologies as they are key actors in configuring just and sustainable futures.
DOI: 10.4324/9781003334330-7

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
140
Shifting Socio-Technical Realities
Emerging digital technologies, such as artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, or extended reality 
(XR), are deeply implicated in large-scale change that impacts individuals as well as communities 
and global societies. They often manifest themselves as data-intensive, hyper-connected, algorith-
mic systems that operate as ubiquitous infrastructures and become instrumental for hegemonic 
power structures that enable new and old forms of oppression.
Putting forward strong value propositions of empowerment, emancipation, and democracy, 
Participatory Design has, arguably, engaged with emerging digital technology since its 1970s in -
ception when computing was introduced into the labour market (Nygaard and Terje Bergo, 1975). 
Contemporary emerging technologies and their social configurations have created new and unique 
complexities and challenges, shaping the world at scale through increasingly pervasive, auto-
mated, and agential technologies, calling for Participatory Design to evolve its theory and practice 
to engage with such socio-technical systems.
By tracing contemporary research that seeks to tackle these challenges within and beyond the 
field of Participatory Design, this chapter offers stepping stones for future Participatory Design 
trajectories to advance research, practice, and design of emerging technologies. As argued, this 
evolutionary process is not new to Participatory Design: digital technology was always emerging, 
and Participatory Design has always engaged with this emergence. However, the role of digital 
technology in society has shifted along contemporary challenges, requiring Participatory Design 
to create new ways in which participation is configured around their design. Similarly, we argue, 
this is the challenge for contemporary Participatory Design.
The chapter is outlined as follows: first, we make the case for evolving the theory and practice 
of participation in design, before conceptualising what is meant by emerging technology and in 
which ways this matters for the field. We then review contemporary Participatory Design work 
to exemplify how the field has engaged with different forms of emerging technologies. While a 
full and systematic review is out of scope for this chapter, we aim to offer a purposefully selected 
overview alongside three cases to acknowledge the wide range of work being done. Finally, in the 
last part of the chapter, we build upon our argument and the review to develop four stepping stones 
to highlight trajectories for Participatory Design to evolve.
Evolving Participatory Design
We identify three main sources of change that, in their interplay, drive the need for contemporary 
Participatory Design to evolve its theory and practices in the face of emerging technologies and 
digital transformations of society.
The first source of change relates to the qualities of technology as a relational actor. It is well 
established in Participatory Design that materials and artefacts are never neutral, merely opera-
tionalised, or moulded by human intentionality. Historically, Participatory Design was early to 
embrace a perspective of socio-technical systems to acknowledge the situated and interlinked 
character of technology and social practices (e.g. Suchman, 1987). However, while technologies 
always actively participated in that sense, we argue that the type, intensity, and significance of 
agential capabilities of emerging technologies – that is, the capacity to act in and shape the world 
in increasingly autonomous ways that are remote to or even outside of human control – has given 
this notion a new quality (Frauenberger, 2019). The active participation of emerging technology in 
producing reality makes a re-evaluation of our understanding of what it is we co-design, or even 

Emerging Technologies and Alternative Futures
141
co-design with, inevitable. Thus, regarding technology as a relational actor requires new perspec-
tives on its participation in design that neither unduly anthropomorphises its qualities, nor ignores 
its active, non-neutral and mediating role (e.g. see Suchman, 2023a, for a discussion about the 
ontological status of AI).
Second, emerging technologies are not only powerful relational actors but also political 
agents. Their ubiquitous and increasingly insidious nature impacts everyday life at all levels, 
shaping humans and society through their pervasive, systematic , and political influence. De -
signing these systems then becomes not only a wicked problem in the classical sense, but a 
deeply political endeavour at a human and societal level, fundamentally requiring a renegotia -
tion of all aspects of the human condition. Examples include fundamental questions over what 
is authenticity, creativity, truth, free will, fairness, or legitimate participation but also more 
practical questions around systemic manipulation, regulation, policy-making, or ethical inno -
vation milieus. In other words, similar to the beginnings of Participatory Design in the labour 
movement or in early systems design (e.g. Ehn, 1988), big political matters must be engaged 
through the creation of strong value propositions, to ultimately enable the configuration of 
socio-technical systems that can lead us to desirable, technological alternatives that are politi -
cally legitimised.
Finally, humanity faces multiple, unprecedented crises in which these emerging technolo -
gies are deeply implicated. First and foremost, this concerns the climate emergency, where 
digital technology takes on both, a key role in enabling the efficient use of natural resources 
(e.g. big data systems in agriculture or energy efficiency in smart homes) and being a ma-
jor source of emissions itself (e.g. cryptocurrencies or intensive training of large-language 
models (LLMs)). The role of emerging technology in modern warfare and human conflict 
more generally is another major contemporary concern, be it directly in the form of weap -
ons, or more indirectly in facilitating hybrid-warfare or manipulating public opinion in con -
flicts. Moreover, societal crises are thriving or forged by emerging technologies in relation 
to data-driven health care, increased social isolation, loss of privacy, economic and social 
inequality, polarisation, radicalisation, misinformation, cyber-terrorism, exploitation of mar -
ginalised communities, disengagement from one’s own corporeality, and the amplification 
of systemic injustices (e.g. racism, sexual oppression, xenophobia) – to name a few. Hence, 
Participatory Design does not merely need to respond to new configurations of emerging 
technologies, but engage with novel socio-ecological challenges that these technologies are 
implicated in bringing about.
Designing Alternative Futures
Participatory Design’s ambition to democratise technological innovation within the context 
of these multiple crises needs to strive for the development of alternative just and sustainable 
futures. At its core, this is a challenge that needs to stay clear of the two extreme positions: a 
backwards-looking techno-phobia that seeks to untangle humans from their unruly tools on the 
one end, and the grand promises of technologies and the techno-solutionism that drives much in-
novation on the other. Neither of these two positions, we argue, offers a productive way to engage 
with emerging technology in response to these multiple crises. Instead, we propose a different 
approach that takes humans and technologies as already mutually entangled in situated relation-
ships across a wide variety of domains (Barad, 2007; Suchman, 1988). And it is precisely here that 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
142
Participatory Design has an essential role to play as it can build on theory, methods, and practices 
that allow negotiating alternative futures through the ongoing engagement of the politics of tech -
nology at various levels and arenas.
This chapter, then, echoes the calls for Participatory Design to have technological ambition and 
to create the systems that matter for bringing about alternative futures (Bødker, 2003; Korsgaard 
et al., 2016), addressing contemporary complex societal challenges (Bødker et al., 2022; Bødker 
and Kyng, 2018). This, we argue, requires Participatory Design to engage with diverse but inter -
connected arenas, like those identified by Gärtner and Wagner in a more work-oriented context 
(Gärtner and Wagner, 1996; see also Chapter 2). These arenas span from the specific and local 
contexts in which Participatory Design has proven to be so effective, to larger communities and 
sectors, and to the arena of big politics where matters of societal concern need to be negotiated 
and translated back for designing the socio-material conditions that may enable desired realities. 
Developing this understanding for design and participation in the context of contemporary chal-
lenges relating to emerging technologies is what this chapter aims to bring on its way.
Conceptualising Emergence
Historically, Participatory Design engaged with fault lines, shifts, and disruptions enabled by new 
digital or emerging technologies, to create alternatives with strong value propositions based on 
empowerment and democratisation. Many researchers have defined emerging technologies (Cor -
rocher et al., 2003; Cozzens et al., 2010; Srinivasan, 2008; Stahl, 2011) with a focus on their 
transformative nature and impact on the economy and society, their origins in radical innovation 
and/or technology convergence (Day and Schoemaker, 2000), to create, transform or disrupt new 
or existing industries (Boon and Moors, 2008).
Rotolo et al. (2015) foreground five characteristics of emerging technologies: radical nov -
elty; relatively fast growth; a degree of coherence and momentum; prominent impact on specific 
domains or on society more broadly; and uncertainty and ambiguity  about possible outcomes 
and areas of use. The authors discuss fast growth and radical novelty when proposing that 
emerging technologies are characterised by a degree of persistent coherence and the ability 
to exert a considerable, multi-layered impact on the socioeconomic domain, and, crucially, on 
the future, even if the “emergence phase is still somewhat uncertain and ambiguous” (cf. van 
Mechelen et al., 2022, p.  4).
Such definitions are rather techno-deterministic, and it is important to acknowledge that the 
technologies and futures they suggest are as much defined by their characteristics, uses, and im -
pacts as they are by their origins within very specific, historically situated milieus.1 Daub (2020), 
for example, critically reviews the innovation landscape in Silicon Valley, pointing out their cul -
tural and intellectual roots: individualism, the relentless call for disruption and the primacy of 
the medium (aka platform) over the message (aka content). Equally, Zuboff (2019) points out the 
links between what she calls surveillance capitalism and concepts of radical behaviourism (e.g. 
as advocated by Skinner, 1985). Similarly, Rosner (2018) argues human-centred design’s focus on 
individualism, solutionism, universalism, and objectivism and suggests alternatives that engage 
feminist scholarship. Recent books such as Data Feminism (D’Ignazio and Klein, 2020), Design 
Justice (Costanza-Chock, 2020), and Designs for the Pluriverse (Escobar, 2018) highlight alterna-
tives that build on Black feminism as well as South American and decolonial scholarship (see also 
Chapter 5).
To characterise emerging technologies, it is thus key to look at what historical pathways led us 
to current innovation landscapes and suggest what may be next. Here, we discuss some of such 

Emerging Technologies and Alternative Futures
143
pathways and their interactions with society to ground the review of contemporary Participatory 
Design research on emerging technologies that follow.
Pervasive computing and persuasive design, driven by intellectual roots such as objectivism 
and behaviourism, successfully made headway by embedding computation in a wide variety of 
things while making them more dynamic, agential, and responsive. While pervasive and ubiqui-
tous computing focuses on embedding tiny computers into bodies, homes, workplaces, and cit -
ies (Weiser, 1999), persuasive design is specifically intended to influence human behaviour. Not 
only are computers increasingly embedded in a wide range of things, they are also increasingly 
designed to influence people.
Besides objectivism and behaviourism, a particular and functional conception of human cogni-
tion in early cognitive sciences informed the field of machine learning (ML), leading to what today 
makes headlines under the term AI. Algorithmic systems trained on large datasets through super -
vised and unsupervised learning result in highly complex models that are highly efficient in iden-
tifying and reproducing patterns of human behaviour to mimic plausible output. OpenAI’s GPT 
(Generative Pre-trained Transformer) chatbots (and similar systems by Google, Meta, or others) 
are an example of how such emergent technologies are marketed and talked about in human-like 
terms. Bender et al. (2021) remind us, however, of the dangers of such “stochastic parrots”, which 
base responses on statistical relationships between terms and phrases, but do not understand or 
care about what speech they produce, nor are able to assess or validate their outputs as true or 
correct.
LLMs like the GPT series illustrate very well the challenging qualities of emerging technolo -
gies (V ogels and Anderson, 2020). While their fundamental principles are not novel, their creation 
at a large scale (many billions of parameters) coupled with training on large data sets, generated 
the conditions for these systems to produce seemingly natural responses to a very wide range of 
inputs. Additionally, and importantly, ChatGPT, made publicly available in late 2022, shifted the 
perception of the possibilities of LLMs. While Natural Language Processing (NLP) as a whole has 
therefore some coherence as rooted in the historical trajectories of ML and its idea of cognition, it 
is also radically new in how applications manifest themselves and interact in society. An example 
of such tension in society, universities globally are currently evaluating ChatGPT’s positive us-
ages in higher education as well as how to prevent less desirable uses. While ML already attracted 
significant financial momentum and had impact on the innovation landscape, it is important to 
recognise its ambiguous and ill-defined nature and our limited knowledge of its possible conse -
quences from a societal perspective. Currently, to design more ethical and responsible systems, a 
new framing of human-centred AI attempts to connect these technologies with human needs (Ab-
dul et al., 2018) without, for example, changing the business and economic models that ground the 
design of emerging technologies.
A further hallmark of these large ML systems is their discriminatory nature. While their ability 
to discriminate input along useful categories (pattern finding) is a powerful function, it comes 
with unwanted biases, opaque in the system yet leading to real-world injustices. Many offered 
critiques to raise awareness around emerging technologies’ challenges. O’Neil (2016) for instance 
demonstrates how algorithms powered by big data can exploit humans and distort reality, with 
relentless pervasiveness in regulating everyday life and ongoing reinforcement of pre-existing 
inequalities. Advocating for closer scrutiny and regulation of search engines, Noble (2018) dis-
cusses the role of algorithms in creating, maintaining, and disseminating racism and how search 
engines, even in the absence of bad actors, are easily manipulated to perpetuate discriminatory 
practices and racist stereotypes. Benjamin (2019), arguing that emerging technologies reinforce 
white supremacy while deepening social inequity, points out their ability to do so while appearing 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
144
benevolent or neutral. Focusing on gender bias, Criado-Perez (2020) points at dangerous pat -
terns in big data’s systematic impact on women’s lives – patterns originating from approaches 
where men are the default. Eubanks (2017), investigating the impact of data mining, predictive 
risk models, and policy algorithms on poor and working-class people in America, discusses how 
the speed and scale of such tools intensify structural inequities even when they are not explicitly 
designed with that aim.
Another prominent historical trajectory to consider is transhumanism, focused on augment -
ing and extending humans through technology, to enhance capabilities and overcome perceived 
limitations of our species. The many, diverse utopias attached to this trajectory (e.g. exoskel -
etons, memory aids, or biotechnologies) are mirrored by a similar number of ethical and moral 
concerns, including relationship to eugenics. Another area linked to this trajectory is immer -
sive media that, by leveraging varying degrees of immersiveness and multisensorial techniques, 
generate alternative realities. While Virtual Reality (VR) and Augmented Reality (AR) started 
in the 1980s as concepts and experimentation arenas, the progression of Moore’s Law
2 accel-
erated the development of key capabilities, making them cheaper and more marketable. Such 
advancements created the conditions for concepts such as XR (basically a combination of VR 
and AR) first, and the Metaverse more recently. While in all these cases, a headset (or glasses) is 
the key technological component providing full immersion, recent advancements extended the 
notion of immersion by leveraging data from on-body sensors (e.g. physiological data through 
smart gloves) as well as contextual data, historical data, and the integration of data aggregates 
from diverse datasets. An example for where these technologies may be headed is offered by 
Meta’s vision of the Metaverse, where the company’s headset (codenamed Project Cambria) 
is equipped with multi-sensory immersiveness and control – from high-resolution, full-colour 
video pass-through (enabling a mix of physical and digital worlds) to the ability to capture the 
wearer’s facial expressions and a wrist-worn neural interface  that “uses differential electro -
myography, or EMG, to measure electrical pulses in the arm’s neurons, essentially creating the 
effect of a phantom limb the wearer can use to interact with the glasses” resulting in the wearer’s 
ability to “think to type or control a virtual interface” (Heath, 2022; Velazco, 2021). Advanced 
immersive media technologies pose numerous social and ethical challenges, from health con -
cerns to biometric data privacy, identity and IP protection, bias and discrimination, high carbon 
footprint of algorithms, and increased inequalities and polarisation, to name a few (Benjamins 
et al., 2022; Thomason, 2022).
The aforementioned examples characterise what we mean by emerging technology by con -
necting their historical and intellectual roots with computational features and their social 
and cultural entanglements. To avoid techno-deterministic narratives and predictions about 
future emerging technologies, we acknowledge that the offered range is not conclusive and 
constantly evolving. That said, it offers a backdrop for the kinds of socio-technical systems 
and dilemmas that Participatory Design urgently and increasingly needs to engage with. In 
what follows, we survey where this has happened in the past decade to inform a new genera -
tion of Participatory Design theory, methods, and practices dedicated to creating sustainable 
digital futures.
A Survey of Emerging Technologies in Participatory Design
In the following sections, we survey relevant literature from the past decade concerning themes 
of emerging technologies in Participatory Design. We centre the survey around the research on 
emerging technology that has been published within the core academic venues of Participatory 

Emerging Technologies and Alternative Futures
145
Design such as the proceedings of the Participatory Design Conference, the Design Research Soci-
ety, Interaction Design and Children (IDC), and the International Journal of CoCreation in Design 
and the Arts (Codesign). Relevant work beyond these venues, for example, in venues related to the 
technologies themselves or more broadly in Human–Computer Interaction (HCI) and Computer 
Science are integrated through each section. Due to the relative nascent theme in the context of 
Participatory Design research and the scattered contributions across fields, what is presented is 
less a systematic or complete literature review, rather it is a purposefully selective survey, intended 
to illustrate and contextualise the range of Participatory Design practice and research that is rele-
vant to the contemporary landscapes of emerging technologies. We provide examples of cases and 
research projects to demonstrate how Participatory Design is engaging in and across these fields, 
for academic, industry, and non-governmental organisations. Each subsection takes stock of some 
main themes, concerns, or potentials between Participatory Design and emerging technologies that 
have previously been, or still are, emphasised in the field. The learnings we identify from these 
themes are summarised at the end of this section and lay the grounds for building stepping stones 
and future trajectories in the chapter’s final section.
Platforms, Civic Technologies, and Democracy
Research fields around computing are rapidly embracing the rise and potential of emerging tech-
nologies in all sectors of our society. The Participatory Design community, however, has been 
more reluctant to take up this focus as a cornerstone of the field, despite its core historical en-
gagement with these evolving technological processes. In the past decade(s) much research has 
been done in areas of community, urban, and civic technologies, leading to increasing research 
on automated platforms and infrastructures. For example, in urban planning, architecture, and 
related fields of urban informatics, early publications on “smart cities”, civic media, and situated 
technologies raised essential questions about participation in shaping these systems for the public 
good including the role of “civic hacking” as well as resistance to dominant logics of surveillance, 
control, optimisation, and efficiency (Foth et al., 2011; Gordon and Mihailidis, 2016; Greenfield, 
2013; Halegoua, 2020; Powell, 2021; Townsend, 2013). Rather than small, in-person participatory 
workshops or engagements with communities or organisations, some of these early efforts used 
crowdsourcing, mapping, data visualisation, and participatory platforms to gather data about cities 
and citizens (Kurgan, 2013; Shepard, 2011; Williams, 2022). Through examples from art, critical 
design, and activism, scholars argued for alternative modes of imagining the social life of cities 
along with emerging technologies.
The past decade has seen a rise in contributions that highlight the deeply embedded tensions of 
power and democracy of the capitalist platform economy. Discussions on commoning in Partici -
patory Design have advocated for a shift from a “sharing” to “caring” economy (Teli, 2015; see 
Chapter 3 for extended descriptions on commoning and institutioning) with calls for the demo -
cratic design of open platforms, data, and systems. Botero et al. (2020) advocate for the notion of 
commons as an objective and commoning as a way of critically protecting and supporting sustain-
able futures through activist practices in Participatory Design. In a CoDesign special issue, Avram 
et al. (2019) invited wide participation around the themes of digital social innovation, design for 
change, environmental sustainability, as well as platform cooperativism. The contributions ad -
dress how new digital platforms are transforming communities (of interest, place, practice, and 
circumstance) to establish new forms of connection, welfare, labour, and service. They highlight 
the power, inequalities, and uneven access to resources that the platforms exacerbate (van Doorn, 
2017), and show the potential for the platforms to shape and be part of a diffused caring economy.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
146
Edward (2020) addresses the power of tech giants such as Uber, Amazon, and Apple, which 
drive new business models and work orders through “algorithmic control” where workers are 
managed and outputs are measured through online platforms. Based on a literature survey 
of global resistance to this model, Edward argues for new regulatory practices that combine 
top-down regulations of the companies with collective workforce initiatives, through deeper un -
derstandings of ownership in the platform economy. In another study, Huttunen and Joutsenvirta 
(2019) show how collaborative design makes it possible to create complementary currencies 
with particularist and inclusive approaches. They argue that new technologies offer opportunities 
for rethinking money and designing new economic structures that support a fair and sustainable 
sharing economy.
Such contributions, critiquing the tensions of power and democracy of the capitalist platform 
economy, also highlight the potential for designing platforms based on alternatives, of commons and 
care, which are viable and sustainable, and respond to diverse needs and desires of individuals and 
collectives. Based on a survey study Silva and Baek (2022) address what they term “the major issues 
in digital democracy platforms” and how Participatory Design can contribute to generating more 
effective digital public participation and digital democracy. Building on approaches to design as 
democracy, project-centred democracy (Manzini, 2019), an agonistic Participatory Design (DiSalvo, 
2012), the authors identify challenges for participation in digital democracy platforms relating to, 
for example, the lack of shared skills, hegemony, and unequal power between different demographic 
groups and literacies. Additional barriers of political bias and mistrust, as well the lack of common 
agreement on the condition of digital democracy, are identified to online engagement, such as demo-
cratic debates and government elections. Based on six solutions they develop a Participatory Design 
guide for digital democracy, including methods that can be applied when designing digital participa-
tion platforms. Several solutions highlight how designers develop their “participatory ambiences” 
with a focus on delivering mechanisms for individuals to expose and oppose social hegemonies. 
For example, “Challenging Hegemony in the Platform Core” and “Agreement-driven design before 
Design” that enable renegotiation of power relations and establish an agonistic arena before core de-
cisions are made. Other solutions focus on the organisation of the participatory processes themselves, 
and how the technologies are “implanted” – assisted by humans and nonhumans to add essential 
practices and tools to the platform network – to have positive impacts on allowing participants to 
join, not just as opinion-makers, but as genuine co-creators of the platforms (Zhang et al., 2022).
What becomes clear from the different contributions is how platforms and increasingly auto-
mated decision-making processes are entangled across corporate, public, and private domains in 
ways that challenge our fundamental democratic values through top-down implementations. At 
once, Participatory Design’s potential role in creating alternative models and spaces for dialogue, 
mutual learning, and engagement around the platform technologies in their everyday lives be -
comes clearly evident.
A focus on sustainability, urban engagement, and cultural preservation can be seen in a range 
of small-scale community-based Participatory Design projects. Here researchers and practition -
ers focus on the bottom-up codesign with citizen groups and communities, to develop situated 
technologies and solutions that are based on everyday experiences and lifeworlds. Participatory 
Design’s long history of community-based engagement with diverse groups from local organisa -
tions, indigenous communities, to urban innovation and living labs, makes it extremely relevant 
in shaping emerging technologies according to social constructs, relations, and knowledges to 
benefit specific groups. As DiSalvo et al. (2012) argued a decade ago, community-based Partici -
patory Design “promises to grow in the light of the continuing expansion of digital networking in 

Emerging Technologies and Alternative Futures
147
the context of prevailing neo-liberal market globalisation forces and the publics organised against 
those forces”.
Such small-scale initiatives are often long-term citizen-driven community initiatives in which 
emerging technologies at local and global scales play a central role. Two exemplary projects worth 
mentioning are the Agbogbloshie Makerspace Platform (AMP) in Ghana and Te Hiku Media in 
New Zealand. AMP is a participatory project focused on shaping the future of the Agbogbloshie 
e-waste scrap yard in Accra, Ghana (Osseo-Asare and Abbas, 2019). Agbogbloshie is portrayed in 
the global media as “the world’s largest e-waste dump” and an example of Western consumer cul-
ture’s sustained impact on the African continent. Initiated in 2012 by local artists, the AMP maker 
collective has engaged youth from East Africa, Europe, and the United States, local scrap dealers 
and makers, and young entrepreneurs, in reimagining the electronic landscapes and waste-streams 
into co-developing manuals for e-waste handling, mobile phone app for grassroots maker eco-
systems and makerspace “spacecraft” prototypes. Building on top of local recycling practices, 
AMP honed those existing capabilities by creating opportunities for new skills and knowledge (in 
design, material science, and construction) to emerge and be co-created by leveraging makerspace 
tools and techniques (Nolan, 2018). By focusing on the materiality of waste, rather than pollution, 
the project has managed to work with transforming forms and perceptions of industrial waste.
Te Hiku Media, a New Zealand radio station that broadcasts in the Māori language, used 
open-source technologies to train its own speech recognition model “to listen to its archive and 
produce transcriptions” (Brible, 2023). By inviting Māori community groups to participate by 
recording themselves while reading pre-written statements, a corpus of annotated speech was 
generated to train the model that within a matter of weeks reached 86% accuracy. As reported 
by Brible (2023), this is a great example of AI “being used to benefit specific communities by 
Co-Designing Indigenous Community-Based Gesture-Controlled VR Case 6.1
Under the umbrella of an ongoing long-term Participatory Design and research collaboration be -
tween a Namibian Ju\’hoansi San community settled in Donkerbos, and the Namibia University 
of Science and Technology, in partnership with Aalborg University, emerging technologies are 
explored and leveraged to (1) safeguard cultural heritage practices, (2) amplify indigenous voices, 
and (3) instigate the creation of alternative futures encompassing the lost futures of the past. Re-
cent developments in VR applications, such as hand gesture tracking, provide new opportunities 
to create embodied cultural user experiences. After exploring and evaluating VR technologies, 
the Donkerbos community decided to engage in a Participatory Design endeavour of a traditional 
hunting story as a VR application. First, the story was told by a village elder to the entire com -
munity in the native language. It was then translated for non-native researchers. Gestures were 
collectively identified through a demonstration of a simulated hunt in the bush. In dedicated 
design sessions with groups of community members, they demonstrated hunting equipment and 
gestures used for non-verbal, human–human interaction, as well as the different scenes were de-
signed including activities and 3D models to be inserted. The hunting story was then implemented 
with hand gestures and narrative elements from the traditional hunting story as a VR prototype 
based on situated knowledge from the San community. To validate the implementation within 
the community, different members played the hunting VR and participated in post-experience 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
148
interviews and adjustments, confirming that an authentic experience was created (Arendttorp 
et al., 2023; Johansen et al., 2022). The community expressed the desire to share their cultural 
heritage widely, thus the VR application has been showcased at many national and international 
venues as a demonstration of cultural heritage preservation with emerging technologies. Besides 
providing visitors with a memorable embodied traditional hunting experience, the VR application 
reinvigorated debates about the San tribes’ hunting rights in contemporary Namibia as a recogni -
tion of indigenous cultural practices. Meanwhile, the VR application is also used in community 
project activities inspiring the creation of alternative futures, encompassing emerging technolo -
gies and lost futures of the past, while reflecting on new participatory approaches to futuring 
(Muashekele et al., 2023).
bypassing the entrenched power of corporations”. Both AMP and Te Hiku Media are two powerful 
examples of participatory community initiatives where emerging technologies are adapted into 
existing cultural ecosystems. A third example can be found in an ongoing research collaboration 
between indigenous San communities and Namibian as well as Danish researchers working with 
the digitalisation of intangible cultural heritage using VR through iterative cycles of development, 
implementation, and evaluation (Rodil et al., 2020).
Several interesting examples of VR technologies and methods that were explored in collabo -
ration with target participants are emerging from diverse domains. These include Baker et al. 
(2019) who report on participatory workshops with older adults to understand their views on 
social VR experiences. Flobak et al. (2019) discuss a participatory approach for prototyping VR 
scenarios and Matsangidou et al. (2022) worked with dementia patients as well as medical and 
paramedical personnel to co-design an intelligent and personalised VR system meant to enhance 
symptom management of dementia patients in long-term care, that they saw as being of value to 
older adults. The examples demonstrate how VR and other emerging technologies are becoming 
situated in particular everyday practices alongside more well-known participatory community 
engagements.
The focus on sustainability and environmentalism, also seen in the previous cases, has been 
consistently involved in many exploratory small-scale urban engagements over the past decade(s). 
DiSalvo and Jenkins (2017) and DiSalvo et al. (2016) explore the use of Internet of Things (IoT) 
technologies, specifically environmental sensing, to support urban foraging. Based on research 
through design inquiries and interventions into local farming communities in the US, the research-
ers co-design a simple proof-of-concept sensing platform to monitor the ripeness of a fruit in 
trees and reflect upon its potentials for urban foraging. The authors address the use of drones and 
presumed “smart” technologies of IoT systems and highlight issues in designing to support diverse 
community economies. In a related series of urban explorations, Marttila and Botero (2016) use 
concepts of infrastructuring, patchworking, and commoning to discuss potentials of public engage-
ment and civics, in two citizen-driven initiatives around urban gardening and public DroneArt in 
the city of Helsinki, Finland. Drones were used to capture images of public statues, collaboratively 
transformed into 3D models, and projected as matters of concern in public engagement activities. 
The authors argue for seeing the “participatory strategising approach that these citizen-driven 
initiatives exercise offers flexible agency and alternative ways to take part in societal debates 
through everyday action” (Marttila and Botero, 2016: p85), and how such cultures of common -
ing – through ongoing strategies, practices, and city-making experiences – can be translated into 
design language.

Emerging Technologies and Alternative Futures
149
Various sense-making projects have explored data and platforms for creating more sustainable 
smart cities. One example is using “participatory sensing” through flexible platforms for partici -
pants to get involved in collecting and visualising data (Tangmunarunkit et al., 2015). Here a par-
ticipatory process was used to design the platform that was scaled to 20 projects. Matos-Castaño 
et al. (2020) also use participatory approaches to support sense-making while anticipating techno-
logical effects in the smart city. Visualising technological impacts “makes things public” reveal -
ing existing perspectives and fostering new ones. Rather than treating smart cities as technical 
problems, the authors argue that reframing technological impact enhances empathy for diverse 
interests, and imagining supports understanding the connections between technology and society 
to anticipate impacts. Also, Heitlinger, Foth, et al. (2018) interrogate how more-than-human per -
spectives can shape Participatory Design practices and policies towards cohabitation in the context 
of sustainable smart cities, urban informatics, IoT, and design (see also Chapter 4). Additional ex-
amples from the same authors focus on Participatory Design in the context of IoT and sustainable 
food practices in urban areas (Heitlinger, Bryan-Kinns, et al., 2018; Heitlinger et al., 2019). While 
there are many small-scale research projects, larger-scale civic tech projects also exist that build 
on similar values of inclusion and access to public services.
Another exciting intersection between Participatory Design and emerging technologies on a 
larger scale is civic technology (civic tech). Some of the recent predecessors to civic tech include 
Free Libre and open-source software, community, and municipal wireless networking, open geo -
graphic information systems, and digital government. For example, in the early 2000s, technolo -
gists in cities around the world such as Montreal, Berlin, Athens, and New York as well as in 
more rural areas built their own wireless networks to provide free, public access to the Internet 
(Forlano and Powell, 2011). While primarily driven by technologists exploring the affordances of 
emerging technologies such as laptops and wireless routers, these networks engaged communi -
ties in the design and use of the networks as part of a focus on the “digital divide”. While many 
of these groups became less active as the cost of broadband access became less expensive and 
mobile phone access expanded, at the same time, their efforts carry on today through a mix of 
government, corporate, and citizen-led initiatives, linked to democratising platforms and com -
moning described earlier.
More recently, organisations such as Code for America have focused on designing applications 
and websites to simplify and make government data, services, and systems more accessible. As 
a human-centred design, user experience and interaction design have expanded beyond corporate 
clients, designing with government stakeholders becomes a new opportunity. Another example 
of the expansion of civic tech is in universities. Specifically, the Public Interest Technology Uni-
versity Network is a network funded by a group of foundations in the United States including 
the Ford Foundation and run by the New America Foundation, which currently includes over 40 
universities in the US as well as several international partners. The purpose of the network is to 
fund projects around public interest technology and open up career paths for students working on 
public issues.
In sum, emphasis on platforms and civic and community technologies in Participatory Design 
is often placed on small-scale engagements across public, private, and corporate domains that 
demonstrate how more inclusive or sustainable alternatives might be forged. The research tends 
to draw out learnings focusing on aspects of participation and democracy and less on the techni-
cal and agential capabilities of technologies, code, and materials themselves. It is evident also 
that long-term research engagements in these local sites and communities enable researchers and 
practitioners to more easily integrate emerging technologies with issues and concerns that are rel-
evant to specific people and contexts. In the following section, we look more closely at the recent 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
150
developments around AI and automation in Participatory Design and related fields, which have 
seen increased interest in recent years.
AI, Automation, and Participation
Authors addressing the role of AI and automation for Participatory Design have focused on pos -
sible ways to tackle the challenges that these present both theoretically and methodologically. 
Bratteteig and Verne (2018) addressed these challenges, asking bluntly: “Does AI make Participa-
tory Design  Obsolete?” The authors use basic Participatory Design principles to analyse the char-
acteristics of AI and ML and discuss the extent to which users can participate in design decisions, 
when technology that involves AI is designed. Their main findings point to mainly one central 
challenge of emerging technologies: their unpredictability  in terms of how they will change and 
evolve over time due to the complexity of their underlying learning mechanisms (self-learning). 
While explainable AI makes efforts to mitigate such unpredictability, in most cases these technolo-
gies remain unknowable as a design material, challenging both the power and responsibility of the 
designer, as well as users in making informed decisions in the design process.
In a similar vein, Choi et al. (2020) discuss the dilemma of participation in the face of auto -
mation. Introducing the notion of situated automation, they explore how emerging technologies 
of automation become actors in shaping the public and private lives of citizens, of AI, ML, and 
algorithms to everyday life. Examples are provided of practices and projects that address the 
paradoxes of automation and participation, as a site where the different actors collide and form 
what they describe as “algorithmic creatures”. They map different modes of reflection about 
automated technologies to argue for Participatory Design with algorithmic creatures that are 
based on values of pluralism, justice, equity, and care, rather than existing computational, or 
principled values. The authors problematise the notion of algorithmic actors in more-than-human 
assemblages and how they can be understood as agential participants alongside stakeholders in 
Participatory Design.
Another perspective on participation in the development of AI systems focuses on human-centred 
AI and the ways in which people, their labour, and their data are currently being used in such sys-
tems (Sloane et al., 2020). In this sub-field, computer scientists seek to counteract the technologi-
cal focus and address concerns about ethics by increasing the degree to which human needs and 
values are considered. However, Sloane et al. caution against the logic that increased participation 
itself will solve the ethical problems posed by these systems, especially as they are predicated on 
the logics of extraction. They propose three modes of thinking about participation in the context of 
AI systems: participation as work; participation as consultation and participation as justice.
Participatory Design’s historical attendance to workplace technologies has always played a 
large role in the literature; however, only a few recent examples specifically address the integra -
tion of AI, automated decision-making, and other emerging technologies into workplace contexts. 
Wolf and Blomberg (2020) for instance reflect on how practices of care configure workplace Par-
ticipatory Design efforts in the context of designing and implementing an ML system to support IT 
architects in a large global company. Norberg-Schultz Hagen et al. (2020) report on developing big 
data-driven systems in the context of automated curation of front pages of a large newspaper, and 
Gyldenkæne and authors report on the push for healthcare AI in the context of electronic health 
records (EHRs) (Gyldenkaerne et al., 2020). The authors call for Participatory Design approaches 
to understand and reconfigure the socio-technical setup in healthcare, especially where AI is 
being used on EHR data that are manually being submitted by healthcare personnel. Loi et al. 
(2018) question and explore participatory approaches, tools, and guidelines to tackle the cultural, 

Emerging Technologies and Alternative Futures
151
ethical, political, and social implications surrounding the design, development, and deployment 
of intelligent systems for diverse domains (e.g. healthcare, manufacturing, transportation, finance, 
and agriculture). The authors suggest that while AI systems are already impacting everyday life 
“through scripted automation and transactions, such as factory automation or heath/financial trans-
actions”, newer assistive systems frequently “rely on unscripted, autonomous transactions, and 
play active roles in a person’s life”, hence posing serious “challenges that increase even further 
when such systems include affective or human-like attributes (e.g. digital assistants) and when 
they become integral part of the environments we inhabit daily” (Loi et al., 2018).
Based on the use of predictive technologies and algorithms to optimise efficiencies in services 
and government processes Kariotis and Mir (2020) argue for fighting back against “algocracy”. 
The authors focus on the need for Participatory Design approaches to technology assessment in 
city, municipal, and government use of algorithmic solutions, where automated services are in -
creasingly applied to optimise public services. The authors argue that under the pursuits of ef -
ficiency, openness, transparency, public accountability, and community-based deliberation, key 
pillars of democracy come under threat when decision-making is black-boxed in an algorithm. 
Relating to such concerns, many Participatory Design researchers address data commons and the 
design of open platforms to support democracy and empowerment in a data-driven society.
In a report for Deloitte, Pobiner and Murphy (2018) argue that designing large-scale AI prod-
ucts in complex settings requires bringing more stakeholders into the design process to better 
understand the problem, build trust, and aligning outcomes to the long-term needs of communi -
ties. They acknowledge that participation comes with additional costs in the process but argue that 
this could be offset by better products and more acceptance when deployed. It is noteworthy that 
such arguments can be made as a business case. However, Sloane et al. (2020) also caution us to 
think carefully about participation in designing AI systems, as this may well exacerbate extractive 
practices. They point to the many ways in which ML is already dependent on human labour and 
that such participation in designing algorithmic systems is merely exploitative, not empowering.
This concern is also reflected in one of the nine principles developed by (Caselli et al., 2021) for 
incorporating Participatory Design in the development of NLP systems: “Community involvement 
is not scraping”. The case of AI in natural language systems such as LLMs discussed earlier (e.g. 
OpenAIs GPT series) is a prime example for the tensions in configuring participation around their 
development. Teaching an LLM appropriate and non-abusive responses could be seen as genuine 
participation in its design, but it is mostly configured as cheap human labour labelling data. Two 
other principles developed by Caselli et al. (2021) are relevant here. First, the principle that “Data 
and communities are not separate things” speaks to the reductive commodification of language as 
data without meaning in AI practices. Second, “Never stop designing” engages with the fact that 
most NLP systems develop in use and therefore continue to be shaped in their behaviour after their 
initial development or training. For both of these challenges, Participatory Designers may not have 
immediate answers, but is a viable starting point for collaborative meaning making and “staying 
with the trouble” (Haraway, 2016) when technology is folded into real-world contexts.
Within closer proximity of mainstream Participatory Design research, Birhane and colleagues 
(2022a, 2022b) report that AI has taken a “participatory turn”, with the reasoning that participa -
tion provides a means to incorporate wider publics into the development and deployment of AI 
systems. With an outset in general “participation” research they suggest that participation can open 
the gateway to an inclusive, equitable, robust, responsible, and trustworthy design and use of AI. 
This approach to participatory AI is also found in Inie et al. (2023) interview study with design -
ers and “creative professionals on the potentialities of participatory AI”. The authors extract four 
pathways for a more inclusive design process to understand, cope with, adapt to, as well as exploit 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
152
AI. The perspectives of including end-user perspectives in AI development for understanding, cop-
ing, adapting to, and exploiting AI seems promising although more studies are needed to provide 
understanding of how, when, and where to  participatory AI is enacted in AI design processes. 
Further, it will be important to avoid seeing Participatory Design as a vehicle for user acceptance, 
but as a means of opening a space for negotiating which technologies are designed and how.
Within the realm of social robotics Lee et al. (2017) have employed Participatory Design to 
counter the predominant technologically driven development process with a “socially robust and 
responsible approach to robot design”. Within the context of older adults diagnosed with depres -
sion, they particularly highlight the core concept of mutual learning that allows them to better 
understand the complex and interwoven socio-material relations that expand beyond the target 
group to therapists and other actors in the context. They highlight the direct benefits for partici -
pants who were a particularly vulnerable group whose voices were heard and listened to in the 
design process. Thus, they argue that Participatory Design is effectively mitigating the tendency in 
Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) to embed “stereotyped images of older adults into assistive robot 
design, which prompted older adults to reject the robots despite their perceived potential useful -
ness”. They also explicitly reflect on the wider power structures in which much robotic develop -
ment is taking place, for example, organising care for the elderly, and that Participatory Design 
may be a means to start negotiating desirable roles of technologies.
A different form of participation in designing social robotics is presented by Winkle et al. 
(2021). They propose a process in which domain experts are directly involved in designing the 
behaviour of social robots, by allowing them to teach the robot in situ, leading to an autonomous 
system that can even operate in ill-defined and sensitive environments. In two case studies they 
offer first insights into how such “end-to-end Participatory Design” can be implemented. The 
authors reflect on the mutual shaping of users, teachers, and robots when they identify and de -
velop their relationships during this process. This highlights how emerging technologies such as 
autonomous, robotic systems are qualitatively different in design than the computing systems that 
Participatory Design was traditionally concerned with. Robots as learners have become more akin 
to active actors in the design process rather than a passive object to design.
Weiss and Spiel (2022) use two case studies to identify three main challenges in Participatory 
Design of social robotics: the first is how robotics is strongly shaped by a cultural framing. Pro-
duced by popular media (e.g. science fiction) as well as the promises of innovation, the “narrative 
of service robots comes with a lot of baggage” that complicates involving participants in designing 
a robotic system. Second, prototyping robots is still not very accessible for participatory methods 
and many key design decisions are already made when resorting to off-the-shelf robotic platforms. 
And finally, most robots are autonomous, self-learning systems that limit human control at the 
time of design. Participatory Design then stretches all the way towards teaching a robot during use. 
The authors call for a new culture of participation in HRI that takes these challenges to heart and 
investigates designing robots as co-shaping of socio-technical networks.
The HCI community has seen a wealth of contributions, around the potential of efficient and 
advanced machines, and more recently urgent calls and research agendas for responsible, ethical, 
transparent, and accountable  technologies (Abdul et al., 2018) and AI for Good (Floridi et al., 
2018b, 2018a). A survey of contributions from the first four conferences of F AccT – Fairness, 
Accountability, and Transparency, reveals an extension of these HCI concerns, around ethics and 
accountability, fairness and ML, explainability, bias, privacy, and security (Laufer et al., 2022). 
The authors identify gaps in the themes of the contributions, calling for more empirical work that 
supports the move beyond principles and values towards practical implementation, as well as the 

Emerging Technologies and Alternative Futures
153
need to centrally tackle issues of power, politics, values, education, and non-western perspectives, 
to mention a few that Participatory Design is excellently positioned to address, but have not yet 
done. One obvious reason for this is the dilemma with scale, and the challenge that AI produces 
“scale” both in data and impact, that Participatory Design struggles to engage with through small 
scale(s) of participation (Frauenberger et al., 2018).
Kun et al. (2022) discuss that while many HCI practitioners have embraced participatory ap-
proaches, these methods are often not valued in the community. Authors suggest that they should, 
however, play a key role, because “using these approaches will allow the HCI community to bet -
ter tackle our grand societal challenges such as racism, sexual oppression, xenophobia, and other 
systemic injustices”. The article also claims that “we have to think about ways in which systems 
in our field, such as reviewing expectations and researcher evaluations, pose systemic barriers to 
utilising such [participatory] methods”.
There are only a few larger-scale design research projects that address the fundamental chal -
lenges of emerging technologies of AI, ML, and data for a digital society. The DCODE project 
(Case 6.2) is an example of a pan-European (MSCA-2020) network and research project bringing 
together diverse disciplines and stakeholders to address the challenges of increasingly data-driven 
societies and open pathways towards inclusive, sustainable digital futures.
Design Fundamentals for Our Digital Futures (DCODE)3 Case 6.2
This research project addresses five big challenges to bridge the gap between people, technology, and 
society, based on the potential implications of AI, ML, and data-driven technologies for future society. 
Examples are:
• Inclusive Digital Futures  to develop new human–computer relations built on human values and 
interdisciplinary collaborations at the front end of innovation;
• Trusted Interactions addressing the hegemony of anticipatory and decentralised systems through 
new co-performance interactions; and finally,
• Sustainable Socioeconomic Models promote alternative values and inclusive business models 
against skewed data-driven technologies and economies.
Based on design research and more-than-human design, the project addresses and rethinks the role 
of AI, algorithms, and interfaces in HCI, shifting towards equitable, ethical, and human-centred ap -
proaches, across anthropology, engineering, and design in collaboration with industry, government, 
and public institutions. As a central innovation of this project, “ prototeams” deploy researchers 
from diverse disciplines in real-world, cross-sector contexts to experiment collaboratively around 
specific issues. The objective of the prototeams is to develop and prototype future professional 
design roles and practices, including the scientific knowledge needed to support them. While PhD 
projects have individual research focuses, the prototeams integrate high-level learnings from these 
via a structured exchange of experiences and results during summer and winter schools. This re -
flexive practice across disciplinary divisions is challenging but can lead research and education 
beyond state-of-the-art knowledge and training. The cross-fertilisation of ideas and emerging best 
practices is likely to pave the road to new ethical standards for digital design practice. In addition, 
the project is developing approaches, methods, and solutions in and across key sectors that address 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
154
major societal challenges in Europe and beyond. One example is a framework for inclusive digi -
tal futures that challenges the one-dimensional, interaction-based understanding of algorithms that 
pervades HCI research and shifts levels of abstraction across times and scales (from microethics to 
cultural niche constructions). Insights are being translated into practical engineering implications 
that have the potential to guide regulatory efforts (i.e. EU AI Act). Another example is a framework 
for decentralised interactions between human and non-human performers that shifts the idea of 
human-machine interface from a control surface to a relational site for the orchestration of multiple 
effects. Such insights can lead to novel approaches for designing interactions that move past princi -
ples of user-centred design and seamless experience to open up to conflicting interests, worldviews, 
and notions of futurity. Finally, ongoing work addresses understanding of ethics in practice, and 
developing methods to identify potential ethical issues and value tensions as something core to the 
design process.
It is clear that both Participatory Design and the broader research fields around emerging technolo-
gies are also themselves “emerging” and finding ways to engage across disparate disciplines, inter-
ests, and domains. The urgency for cross-disciplinary engagements, with a focus on human values 
and democracy, between computational, human, and engineering sciences are highly needed for 
shaping sustainable digital futures. Until now, participatory research in areas of automation, algo-
rithms, and complex systems still faces challenges of how the fundamental Participatory Design 
concerns of participation, values, politics, and democracy can engage in the critical processes of 
designing alternative futures for emerging technologies.
In recent years, Participatory Design scholars also engaged with emerging technologies in edu-
cation. With the rapid influx of advanced technologies in children’s everyday lives, new educa -
tional initiatives (classroom experiments to government policy) have emerged to help increase 
computational skills, competences, and literacies for current and the next generation of children. 
Iversen et al. (2018) urged Participatory Designers to help shift such an agenda from computational 
thinking, as globally widespread in K–12 technology education, to computational empowerment. 
Children are computationally empowered when they develop the skills, insights, and reflexivity 
needed to understand technology and its many impacts and learn how to engage critically, curi-
ously, and constructively with the construction and deconstruction of technology – as individuals 
and in groups (Iversen et al., 2018; Schaper et al., 2023).
A few researchers, in collaboration with AI experts and teachers, have developed guidelines to 
learn about AI in K–12 (Touretzky et al., 2019) and, through co-design workshops with teachers, 
identified opportunities for integrating AI education into the curricula (Lin and van Brummelen, 
2021). Sosa et al. (2022) studied creative technology approaches to youth participation by bringing 
students and teachers into a makerspace to discuss computation and automation while preparing 
and sharing food. Based on their research, the authors suggest that generative activities that use 
food as design material can benefit innovation in curricular, pedagogical, and educational policy 
strategies.
Researchers from Participatory Design and IDC communities called for more participatory 
and holistic approaches to emerging technologies (van Mechelen et al., 2022; Schaper et al., 
2023) and contributed to participatory research agendas and trajectories for sustainable educa -
tional practices at scale (Smith et al., 2023). For example, researchers investigated how children’s 

Emerging Technologies and Alternative Futures
155
agency could be supported in the process of designing technology for others through the lens of 
bullying issues in Finnish schools, hereby creating engagement in wider societal issues (Iivari 
et al., 2023), while researchers in Namibia and Finland engaged students and teachers in use 
case design workshops to determine desirable affordances for mixed reality devices, such as the 
hololens, deriving future development agendas of emerging and educational technologies (Hahta 
et al., 2023). Despite IDC’s thriving contributions to Participatory Design research, examples of 
larger or longer-term projects to advance formal educational agendas for emerging technologies 
are limited. A well-documented example of sustained initiative comes from Aarhus University, 
Denmark. Based on long-term Participatory Design research into digital fabrication technolo -
gies for education (Smith and Iversen, 2018), approaches for design-based learning (“coding”) 
and digital technology comprehension and analysis (“decoding”) (Dindler et al., 2020), authors 
have explored emerging technologies from a computational empowerment lens with students and 
teachers in the Danish school system.
Computational Empowerment for Emerging Technology Education Case 6.3
A research project focused on computational empowerment, digital literacy, and emerging technolo -
gies is Computational Empowerment for Emerging Technologies in Education at Aarhus University 
(2020–2024). The project addressed the urgent gaps in research relating to educational practices and 
visions for teaching emerging technology in K–12 education. Building on core Participatory Design 
values and approaches, the project shifts the current focus on Computational Thinking in STEM 
education towards computational empowerment as a concern for how children are empowered to 
make critical and informed decisions about the role of technology in their lives (Iversen et al., 2018). 
That is, the capacity to understand, reflect upon, and engage critically in the construction and decon -
struction of technologies that impact our present and future. Through long-term collaborations with 
stakeholders; teachers, students, policy makers, and research fields; humanities, computer science, 
and engineering, the project explored and co-designed digital tools, learning practices, and educa -
tional principles for teaching children and teenagers about AI, ML, IoT, AR, and VR. The research 
focused on bringing the complex and evolving technologies close to the children’s everyday lives, 
expanding societal implications and themes of diversity, bias, privacy, and ethics, as well as toolkits 
and digital technologies to support their understanding of, for example, ML mechanisms through 
hands-on exploration. Outcomes and best practices from the research are scaled through various 
channels: as foundations for future Participatory Design research agendas for emerging technologies 
education in HCI and IDC (van Mechelen et al., 2022; Smith et al., 2023), design principles and learn-
ing strategies for educational professionals and communities (Schaper et al., 2022) as best practices 
for evolving aspects of computational empowerment in the new national curricula on Technology 
Comprehension in Danish schools (Smith et al., 2020), and as digital tools and platforms distributed 
through industry collaborations such as the global Micro:bit Educational Foundation
4 and the Danish 
National Broadcasting Corporation (Bilstrup et al., 2022). The project demonstrates how Participa -
tory Design results are obtained through long-term participatory engagements and how ambitions for 
social sustainability and computational empowerment for the coming generations are embedded as 
foundational premises in the framing of such initiatives.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
156
Stepping Stones and Trajectories for Participatory Design
Reading across the surveyed literature and cases, it becomes evident that there are many good rea-
sons why more participation is highly needed in the research and design of contemporary and fu-
ture emerging technologies to counter the technology-driven agendas of disruption, efficiency, and 
quantification. The reach of these technologies into individual lifeworlds and their structural power 
to mutually shape societies as part of complex socio-technical systems demand democratic forms 
of involvement and control to bring about alternative technological futures – which is why Partici-
patory Design as a field needs to continue to put a focus on engaging with emergent technologies.
It also becomes clear, that participation in designing emerging technologies now is of a dif -
ferent nature than traditional Participatory Design methods and techniques: from citizen science 
approaches with sensor networks, to labelling data for algorithmic systems, to teaching desired 
behaviours to social robots – new formats of participation are emerging that need to be config -
ured to negotiate expertise, decision power, and impact at multiple scales. The previous literature 
offers many valuable starting points for developing such methods, approaches, and best practices, 
but also reveals key tensions that Participatory Design as a field needs to engage with. Against
