this background, this section offers four stepping stones for a Participatory Design agenda that 
poses interwoven challenges and questions to both the practice and theory of participation.
Methodologies for Scale and Impact
Emerging technologies present themselves as systems of scale. Unsurprisingly, with computing 
power, storage, networking capacity, or number of sensors growing exponentially, the systems 
that Participatory Design needs to engage with are increasingly unwieldy, dynamic, complex, 
and hardly delimitable. As we have seen in the aforementioned examples, they are also pervasive 
in diverse everyday contexts, as well as deeply and powerfully integrated into the socio-material 
practices that make up our world. Because of their technical intricacies, black-box nature, and 
large dataset-centric capabilities, such systems are hard to bring into typical Participatory Design 
environments (e.g. workshops) and are difficult to design conceptually with low-fidelity materials. 
Thus, Participatory Design requires methodological innovation to configure participation around 
systems of scale, with toolkits that can handle not only complexity but also contexts where change 
is frequent and technological developments occur within increasingly accelerated timelines. As a 
case in point, a recent study by Hartmann and Henkel (2020) has shown that much high-impact 
research in AI is now being conducted in corporations, because public and academic institutions 
lack access to the large amounts of data that are used in this kind of research. In such conditions 
of centralised power structures, Participatory Design researchers also need to develop methods 
that allow for a decolonising of technology futures in opposition to ongoing Westernised innova -
tion and design (see also Chapter 5). Key questions for future Participatory Design research and 
practice therefore include:
• How can participatory methods and techniques engage with complex and dynamic systems of 
scale that have no clear boundaries?
• How much do modes of participation themselves need to be scaled to engage such sys -
tems and along which dimensions? (e.g. social, organisational, geographical, temporal, and 
onto-epistemological scaling; see Chapter 5)
• How can situated, small-scale, and localised Participatory Design efforts strategically engage 
with openings in systems of scale to trigger larger processes of change?

Emerging Technologies and Alternative Futures
157
Material Participation
The nature of intelligent systems poses another challenge to Participatory Design, requiring us to 
rethink the role of material in design (Holmquist, 2017; Lloyd, 2022). Participatory Design has 
proven to be highly innovative in configuring participation around materials that every stakeholder 
has access to, not only physically but also conceptually. It has been argued that by using craft -
ing and prototyping materials, for example, design processes can become more accessible to and 
inclusive of non-experts, giving them a medium for creative expression. Material participation 
allows people to tap into latent knowledge that they are not able to articulate verbally (Sanders 
and Stappers, 2008).
In this sense, materials have always participated in Participatory Design, non-neutrally mediat-
ing access, and means of expression. However, the increasing agential capabilities of emerging 
technologies are shifting this notion to novel distributed domains at different levels and scales. 
Differently from the past, technology is now playing a more active role in design. This implies 
that the materials we design and design with, are and will increasingly be much more akin to ac -
tors, maybe even stakeholders, in the Participatory Design process. While these actors may not be 
intentional in the same sense as humans, the boundaries between human and non-human actors 
become increasingly unstable and fluid. Think for instance of the developments stemming from 
the broad usage of generative AIs in creative processes. Agencies and intentionalities become 
distributed in hybrid assemblages that fluidly form around a matter of concern (Wakkary, 2021; 
Latour, 2004).
This also calls for the need to engage with design in the particular sites where technology is 
used. Just as companies are marketing technologies that will dynamically evolve as AI and ML al-
gorithms learn from new datasets, Participatory Design must seek out opportunities to understand 
and engage in these contingent contexts and processes to inform and influence future designs, 
business models, and policies that are shaping these technologies. A key focus of future Participa-
tory Design practice should be configuring the right kinds of hybrid assemblages around particu -
lar and relevant matters of concern, facilitating politically negotiated change towards alternative, 
technological futures.
Thus, key questions for Participatory Design include:
• How can Participatory Design conceptualise the active role of emerging technologies in partici-
patory practices as hybrid assemblages?
• How can materiality and temporality be put into conversation with more long-standing con -
cerns about power in Participatory Design?
• How can these shifting conceptualisations of hybrid assemblages effectively be translated into 
methodology?
Politics and Democracy
The pervasive scale, entangled nature, and agential capacities of emerging technologies bring to 
the forefront a number of questions and challenges related to their moral status and impact on hu-
man activity. In Moralising Technology, Verbeek (2011) argues that technologies not only mediate 
and are deeply implicated in moral practices but also re-frame normative ethics as a whole, that is, 
the very basis upon which we judge and guide actions and construct responsibilities within socie-
ties. The examples discussed earlier illustrate how emerging technologies are prominently impli-
cated in these processes and highlight the political dimension of their design and use. Pervasive 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
158
systems of scale have come to matter in ordering our societies in unprecedented ways, but their 
design is far beyond the reach of democratic participation or even control. As Suchman (2023b) 
argues, in a critical reading of the current revival of AI and the discourse of automated military 
intelligence (e.g. the cybernetic model of situational awareness in the US military): “As the ex -
cess of data now threatens to destabilise the technopolitical imaginary of just-in-time information, 
artificial intelligence (AI) is advanced as the promissory solution to automating data analysis and 
reclosing the world” (Suchman, 2023b: 1).
Participatory Design has a long tradition of engaging with the human values and politics of 
technology (Bødker et al., 2022) and we argue here that this ambition requires focused updating in 
relation to the shifting nature of technology, and its impacts and implications for human existence. 
In line with multiple calls such as Bødker et al. (2022), Bannon et al. (2018), and Korsgaard et al. 
(2016), we call for Participatory Design to have strong human, political, and democratic ambitions 
in relation to these technologies and ambitions to create and drive technological alternatives. His-
torical examples such as the CPSRC (Computer Professionals for Social Responsibilities) or the 
early role of Kristen Nygaard as a computer scientist and politician serve as inspiration as much as 
many contemporary examples in Tech Activism, such as the work of Joy Buolamwini as founder 
of the Algorithmic Justice League,
5 the Tech Workers Coalition6 or groups like Turkopticon7 that 
advocate for the rights of platform workers. Key questions for the political role of future Participa-
tory Design include:
• How can Participatory Design develop its role in modern political landscapes and thus increase 
its impact on policy-making, agenda-setting, and critical public discourse?
• How can Participatory Design nurture strong and mutually informing alliances with various 
forms of tech activism?
• In what ways can Participatory Design researchers and practitioners connect scales of 
bottom-up and top-down socio-political processes to address urgent societal concerns towards 
social change?
Responsible Innovation to Drive Sustainable Futures
While a socio-material and political view on emerging technologies is essential, it is key to bring 
such perspectives to where these technologies are actually developed. Contemporary innovation 
landscapes have dramatically changed from early computing in terms of pace and disruption. The 
most powerful companies in the economy are no longer trading in oil but creating digital tech -
nology for a globalised market with unprecedented reach as near-monopolies. Similar to private 
institutions in the financial sector, some may be considered “too big to fail”. The development of 
emerging technologies and the economic interests at its basis have also created fertile conditions for 
many tech superpowers to play a key role in hybrid-warfare, for example through misinformation 
and cybercrime. The role of companies like Meta (formerly Facebook) and X (formerly Twitter) 
in the misinformation cycle spearheaded by Cambridge Analytica during the 2016 US Presidential 
Elections (Wylie, 2019) is a prime example of this trend. At the other end of the spectrum, the fi-
nancial rationale behind venture capital and start-up investments has enabled and continues to push 
for a hyper-competitive start-up culture, where many innovators are pressed to relentlessly push for 
(revenue-generating) disruption within extremely compressed innovation cycles.
These innovation milieus created a sterile environment for Participatory Design to bring impact 
for different reasons (see Chapter 8). There are a number of factors at play for this situation, from 
timelines
6 to budget decisions, organisational culture and alignment, and workforce distribution, 

Emerging Technologies and Alternative Futures
159
to name a few. We argue that Participatory Design researchers and practitioners need to respond 
to these shifting innovation landscapes and offer novel ways to engage them if they wish to bring 
their participatory practice to the forefront of future technology innovation. Key questions for 
future Participatory Design research and practice include:
• How can Participatory Design engage with and help change the radicalised innovation land -
scapes in which emerging technologies are developed?
• How can Participatory Design offer alternatives that are seen as both commercially viable and 
socio-politically desirable?
• What might be alternative approaches to computational innovation based on the values and 
politics that are rooted in Participatory Design?
