7
NEW APPROACHES, METHODS 
AND TECHNIQUES
Jesper Simonsen, Christian Dindler and Chiara Del Gaudio
  DOI: 10.4324/9781003334330-8
This chapter explores how ways of conducting Participatory Design have evolved based on a literature 
review of Participatory Design research published during the past decade. We describe new develop-
ments and trends in general approaches, as well as more specific methods and techniques used to sup-
port the practice of Participatory Design.
The literature review exposes three overall trends: (1) A move in the application area addressed 
by Participatory Design approaches embracing evaluation, sustainability and infrastructuring. This 
trend is characterised by a shift from a focus on initial design and development processes to include 
the appropriation and re-configuration of technologies and use practices that follow after the initial 
implementation. (2) Transferring Participatory Design approaches to other research areas and com-
munities. Participatory Design inspires other adjacent research domains and these domains influence 
the development of new approaches, methods and techniques. The chapter highlights one of these 
intersections by reviewing how this has evolved within the Interaction Design and Children research 
community. (3) Internationalisation beyond Western and modernist traditions characterised by North 
European and North American research. During the past decade, the Participatory Design community 
and conferences have made systematic attempts to include and interact with researchers from and in 
the Souths. This enlarges the field through interesting and contrasting approaches for decolonial Par -
ticipatory Design practice and research.
This chapter is structured as follows: A condensed introduction is followed by elaborated sections 
for each of the previously described overall trends. The chapter concludes by summarising the oppor-
tunities and challenges that the identified trends open up to inspire future research. Together with two 
other chapters from the 2013 Participatory Design handbook (on methods as well as on techniques and 
tools), the reader may obtain an authoritative overview of approaches, methods and techniques used in 
the field since the Participatory Design research area was established.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
166
Introduction
Participatory Design is a research area with a long tradition and an inherent focus on processes and 
process support: “Participatory Design can be defined as a process of investigating, understanding, 
reflecting upon, establishing, developing, and supporting mutual learning between multiple partic-
ipants in collective ´reflection-in-action’” (2013 handbook, p. 2). Since the publication of the 2013 
handbook, the field has extended and expanded application areas and engaged in rediscussing 
the foundations of the practice and the need for decolonised and alternative ways of thinking and 
practising Participatory Design. Participatory Design has undergone significant changes in terms 
of where and how it is practised, thus renewing and amplifying its commitments to empowerment 
and democracy by responding to current social, political and environmental challenges. This is 
reflected, for instance, in the themes of recent Participatory Design Conferences: Reflecting Con-
nectedness (PDC’2014), Participatory Design in an Era of Participation (PDC’2016); Participatory 
Design, Politics and Democracy (PDC’2018); Participation(s) Otherwise (PDC’2020); Embrac -
ing Cosmologies (PDC’2022); and Reaching Out: Connecting Beyond Participation (PDC’2024). 
Novel approaches, methods and techniques have been connected to adjoint research communities 
and appropriated to new application areas as well as to diverse and specific geographic, geopoliti-
cal and local cultural regions.
This chapter aims to provide an overview of how Participatory Design has evolved in the last 
decade in terms of approaches, methods, tools and techniques. We use the term approaches as 
an overall concept addressing concrete Participatory Design practices described through methods, 
tools and techniques as well as their inherently grounding perspectives. Grounding perspectives 
constitute the ideals, principles and philosophical points of view that inform epistemological en -
deavours and design practices. Ongoing movements in grounding perspectives are addressed by all 
chapters of this book, which contribute to an understanding of how and why Participatory Design 
has evolved during the last decade. This chapter specifically focuses on how guiding methods and 
techniques have been investigated, developed and evaluated to support and provide appropriate 
processes and outcomes. Methods are “generalisations from a vast amount of empirically based 
experiences on how to conduct Participatory Design” (2013 handbook, p. 118). A method may de-
scribe its application area (the scope of the method), perspective (the basis for guiding principles), 
guidelines (recommendations for carrying out the design process), principles for organisation (how 
to plan, distribute and coordinate activities and tasks) as well as techniques and tools supporting 
the method. A technique is defined as “a specific direction for performing a certain activity”, while 
representational tools are defined as “suggestions for graphics, figures, and models to support the 
processing and presentation of knowledge contributed by a technique” (2013 handbook, p. 146).
This chapter is based on a review of the Participatory Design literature published from 2012 to 
2023. The basis for this review is a scrutinisation of all Participatory Design conference proceed-
ings, special journal issues and books on Participatory Design issued during this period (for an 
overview of Participatory Design literature, see pdcproceedings.org). Our review identifies three 
overall and cross-cutting movements and trends in approaches within the Participatory Design 
landscape, described as follows:
• Approaches addressing new application areas : Participatory Design approaches have moved 
from initial design and development to embrace evaluation, sustainability and infrastructuring –  
in short, to post-implementation.
• Approaches in adjacent research areas: These approaches include Participatory Design re -
search and practice that takes place in areas adjacent to Participatory Design and develops 

New Approaches, Methods and Techniques
167
alongside new trajectories, addressing challenges within different application areas. We pro -
vide one such example here: the Interaction Design and Children research community.
• Approaches for a decolonial Participatory Design practice and research: Participatory Design 
researchers and researchers from other communities have engaged in the identification and 
discussion of practices and concerns of Participatory Design in the Souths, including Latin 
America, and in the inclusion of disregarded aspects in Participatory Design through decolonial 
thinking and concepts from the Souths.
The review in this chapter follows up on previous reviews from the 2013 handbook; specifically, 
Chapter 6 on methods and Chapter 7 on tools and techniques. The 2013 handbook’s Chapter 6 
on methods presents three examples of Participatory Design methods: STEPS, developed by re-
searchers from Hamburg University; MUST, developed by researchers from Roskilde University; 
and CESD, developed by researchers from Aarhus University. These methods are all characterised 
by addressing early design activities up until visions and prototypes with a focus on organisational 
and work-oriented contexts. Chapter 7 on tools and techniques addresses early design activities 
by helping different users and stakeholders (e.g., workers, tourists, citizens, children, elderly, etc.) 
envision, enact and experiment with ideas of the future. Chapters 6 and 7 of the 2013 handbook 
review Participatory Design research conducted since the first PDC conference held in 1990. This 
research represents a grounding perspective inspired by research conducted in typical Western 
cultures from North America, Europe and Scandinavia.
In the following sections, we describe each of the three overall trends identified by our review. 
The chapter concludes by outlining the opportunities and challenges they open and the need for 
further research and knowledge production.
Approaches Addressing New Application Areas
The first trend in Participatory Design that we describe is the application area moving beyond the 
initial design, development and implementation of information technologies. Participatory Design 
researchers remain preoccupied with developing and maturing appropriate approaches, methods 
and techniques that address new and evolving application areas and the complexities and chal-
lenges they encompass (Halskov and Hansen, 2015). In this section, we characterise how the Par-
ticipatory Design literature since 2012 has been increasingly addressing the new application areas 
of post-implementation. We start by reviewing the initial research (2012–2014) falling under these 
application areas. Then, we describe subsequent literature elaborating on these areas, including 
studies within evaluation, sustainability and infrastructuring. We finally describe a recent example 
of a Participatory Design method dedicated to post-implementation application areas.
The last decade of Participatory Design research is characterised by researchers increas -
ingly embracing application areas beyond the initial design activities that most of the earlier 
research-driven projects have traditionally focused on. Participatory Design have moved away 
from focusing on pre-implementation, that is, initial analysis and design, development of visions, 
prototypes and so on, to include post-implementation application areas where technologies are 
organisationally implemented and used and remain in operation for years or perhaps even decades. 
This reposition of application areas was initially recognised in the 2013 handbook and articu -
lated, among others, as a move “from tinkering and tailoring to appropriation” (2013 handbook, 
pp. 50f) – a move conceptualised as “design-after-design” and “design-in-use” (2013 hand -
book, pp.  57; 135; 138f.). These new application areas include continuous adaptation and socio -
technical reconfigurations of technologies and work practices after they have been implemented. 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
168
This also encompasses qualified evaluations of the benefits from Participatory Design activities 
and other investments in new technologies in general and infrastructuring activities of the web of 
multifarious and heavily interconnected systems that modern workplaces employ today. This trend 
is especially visible in a traditional field application of Participatory Design involving organi -
sationally implemented information technologies. Modern information technology has become 
increasingly configurable, which allows for ongoing changes, modifications and adaptations after 
initial implementation and use.
Initial Research Towards Application Areas of Post-Implementation
The repositioning towards post-implementation application areas was initiated by Participatory 
Design studies of organisational implementations, many within large-scale and commercial con -
texts (see Chapter 2 for a thorough discussion on the scaling of Participatory Design). Projects in 
commercial contexts often struggle to achieve successful organisational implementation (these 
struggles are further described in Chapter 8). Several Participatory Design projects from the start 
of the last decade, many of which are within the healthcare field (see, e.g. Kanstrup et al., 2017), 
address implementation application areas – sometimes referred to as pilot implementation (Hert-
zum et al., 2012).
One strand of Participatory Design research has investigated the experiences, challenges 
and conditions for Participatory Design within implementation contexts: The MUST method, 
described in the 2013 handbook (Chapter 6), was used in the commercial design and imple -
mentation of implantable cardioverter-defibrillators as well as to implement energy renovation 
and CO
2 reduction for buildings, as reported on by Bødker et al. (2014). Shidende and Mört -
berg (2014) investigated the role of Participatory Design implementation mediators in a project 
with distributed settings related to maternal and child health. The lack of proper Participatory 
Design techniques has been observed by Bødker et al. (2012), who criticised the use of per -
sonas (used as a substitute for Participatory Design techniques) in commercial e-government 
projects. Furthermore, Johannessen and Ellingsen (2012) discussed the challenges that arise 
when applying agile, bottom-up Participatory Design approaches in large-scale implementa -
tions supporting communication and laboratory analyses between general practitioners and 
hospitals.
Another strand of Participatory Design research has contributed by developing principles, 
approaches and methods. Mogensen and Wollsen (2014) engaged in a project involving co -
ordination and communication between alarm monitoring centres, ambulance personnel and 
emergency departments. They then developed Participatory Design principles and insights 
pertaining to Participatory Design in realisation of such large-scale projects. An approach 
extending Participatory Design iterations into organisational implementation has been out -
lined based on a large-scale commercial healthcare project (Simonsen and Hertzum, 2012). 
Finally, a methodological framework has been presented addressing pilot implementations 
that were defined as “a field test of a properly engineered, yet unfinished system, in its in -
tended environment, using real data, and aiming – through real-use experience – to explore 
the value of the system, improve or assess its design, and reduce implementation risk” 
(Hertzum et al., 2012, p.  314). This framework, which is manifested through three com -
mercial, large-scale healthcare projects, focuses on mutual learning that is interrelated to 
four implementation elements: planning and design, technical configuration, organisational 
adaptation and use.

New Approaches, Methods and Techniques
169
Post-Implementation: Evaluation, Sustainability and Infrastructuring
Over the past decade, Participatory Design studies within post-implementation application have 
been investigated through three review studies. These studies address post-implementation appli-
cation areas in terms of, respectively, evaluation, sustainability and infrastructuring.
Bossen et al. (2016) conducted a literature review on evaluation in Participatory Design fol -
lowing a workshop on this topic on PDC’2014 (Bossen et al., 2014). The aim of the workshop 
was to discuss how Participatory Design initiatives may outlive singular research projects and gain 
sustainability and long-term effects that can strengthen lasting outcomes. The workshop was fol-
lowed by a literature review addressing post-implementation that posed the following question: 
“What happened to the IT system and people’s work and life after the project?” (Bossen et al., 
2016, p. 151). Specifically, the authors investigated how explicit and systematic evaluations may 
achieve ambitious Participatory Design aims of enhancing workplace quality, democracy, mutual 
learning and empowerment. They contribute to the Participatory Design literature by proposing 
seven key questions to characterise evaluations in Participatory Design and by offering detailed 
discussions of theories, models, gains and benefits for conducting Participatory Design evaluations 
as well as strengthening efforts to evaluate Participatory Design. The review also notes that this 
is still an area that needs attention: Of 66 reviewed papers, only 13 papers provide an explicit and 
systematic evaluation of Participatory Design processes and outcomes. The review calls for more 
research on Participatory Design evaluations and inspires the use and elaboration of the frameworks 
and methods developed and described thus far. This call was later echoed by Nguyen (2022) in a 
paper contributing to a dialogue in the Participatory Design community on evaluation. These evalu-
ations contribute to the general development of Participatory Design and focus on learning and 
knowledge development as important and alternative supplements to standard project management 
models “where evaluations are required though primarily for the purposes of control and account-
ability [. . .] with little attention to learning, knowledge and value” (Bossen et al., 2016, p. 159).
Participatory Design research on evaluation advocates for projects and approaches that fos-
ter real and enduring change through summative or formative evaluations (Bossen et al., 2016, 
p. 152). Evaluations may address post-implementation by conducting summative evaluations of 
projects and the impact technologies and project processes may have resulted in (for a discus -
sion on Participatory Design results, see Bratteteig and Wagner, 2016). Evaluations may also be 
conducted as formative learning-based evaluations of iterations and interventions that address 
reconfigurations of technologies and accompanying work processes and practices such as, for 
example, through sustained iterations (Simonsen and Hertzum, 2012) and pilot implementations 
(Hertzum et al., 2012).
A literature review conducted by Poderi and Dittrich (2018) explores the relationship between 
Participatory Design and sustainability. The concept of sustainability is closely related to evalua-
tion, as described earlier, in terms of directing interest towards, creating an understanding of and 
supporting the long-term impacts and effects of Participatory Design. They note that the reviewed 
papers often used concepts such as “design-in-use” and “infrastructuring” when conceptualising 
the sustainability of Participatory Design practice and Participatory Design results. The review 
identifies and categorises 26 reviewed papers into three use patterns of the concept of sustain-
ability: (1) Participatory Design for sustainability (seven papers) – using Participatory Design to 
obtain sustainability in a classic understanding (sustainable development, living, transports, etc.); 
(2) Sustainability of Participatory Design practice (eight papers) – Participatory Design methods 
and approaches to continue Participatory Design practices after the timeframe of an initial Par -
ticipatory Design project. For example, Uchida et al. (2014) proposed a “powers of ten” model to 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
170
engage multiple participants to take ownership of social innovation projects by building autono-
mous, self-motivated and resilient communities; (3) Sustainability of Participatory Design results 
(11 papers) – achieving sustainable outcomes for Participatory Design projects by paying attention 
to mutual learning and the emergence of skills or expertise, which are highly relevant when ad -
dressing post-implementation. For example, building self-knowledge and increasing the capaci -
ties of Colombian weaving communities was a core aim for Pérez-Bustos and Franco-Avellaneda 
(2014) when they designed ICTs to sustain local skills, wisdom and experiences in this domain. 
Achieving sustainable design results has recently been discussed in the book Future-Proofing: 
Making Practice-Based IT Design Sustainable by Simone et al. (2022). This book also contains a 
number of case studies.
The sustainability concept has been used to broadly define the 17 UN sustainability goals (Buh-
mann, 2014) as well as to address Participatory Design approaches and the impact of Participa -
tory Design activities that reach out beyond solitary Participatory Design research projects. The 
latter comprise summative and formative evaluations, as mentioned earlier, along with various 
Participatory Design approaches that target post-implementation application areas focusing on 
long-lasting effects and results.
Karasti’s (2014) literature review on infrastructuring in Participatory Design from the 
PDC’2014 conference was received with great interest and has subsequently been highly cited. 
The “infrastructure” concept originates from research on information infrastructures introduced 
to Participatory Design by Neumann and Star (1996). Karasti (2014) observes that the verb “in -
frastructuring” was introduced to Participatory Design by Pipek and Wulf (2009) and was dis -
cussed in the 2013 handbook conceptually (e.g. Chapter 3, p.  57) and in relation to communities 
(Chapter 8; see, e.g., pp.  201ff.). Infrastructuring expands the notion of design-in-use into “a 
more inclusive approach where the boundaries between use, design, implementation, modifica -
tion, maintenance, and redesign are blurred”, where approaches try to “extend design towards 
more open-ended, long-term, and continuous processes” and support “creating socio-technical 
resources that intentionally enable adoption and appropriation beyond the initial scope of the 
design” (Karasti, 2014, p.  143f). Infrastructuring thus clearly includes post-implementation ap -
plication areas. Lee and Schmidt (2018) criticised the concept of “infrastructure” for being too 
broad and vague and “infrastructuring” as an approach that is too inclusive. Among others, they 
criticise “infrastructuring” for being a “placeholder for a host of interdependent and intersecting 
issues that only with difficulty can be investigated separately, if at all” (p.  28) and they “distin -
guish at least four different discourses and related meanings of the term ‘infrastructure’” (p.  30). 
However, infrastructuring seems to be used within Participatory Design in a fairly pragmatic 
manner, referring to design-oriented processes and activities. Bødker et al. (2017), for example, 
pragmatically observe that “most design projects are infrastructuring projects, because they build 
on technologies, competencies and practices that already exist” and continue by describing in -
frastructuring within Participatory Design as “horizontal co-design and local, mutual learning 
processes” (p. 245). Angeli et al. (2014) concisely described infrastructuring as an overall bridg -
ing of social and technical aspects and proposed a so-called “hourglass approach”, depicting their 
design and use process combining technical and social infrastructuring. Hansen et al. (2019, p. 7) 
generally referred to infrastructuring as “Participatory Design activities in which researchers and 
participants collaboratively establish the social, organisational and technical arrangements that 
will secure that the results achieved during the project can lead to sustainable outcomes”. Such 
infrastructuring Participatory Design activities have more concretely been defined and character -
ised as activities in which “heterogeneous groups of [users] strive to facilitate their collaboration 
by configuring, reconfiguring, developing, and establishing local guidelines and standards for 

New Approaches, Methods and Techniques
171
effectively using the available technologies and information systems as part of their joint col -
laborative practice” (Simonsen et al., 2020a, p.  116).
Information infrastructures – and infrastructuring as the verb addressing these infrastructures – form 
a research area with theoretical foundations in science and technology studies. Over the last dec -
ade, several special issues researching this area have been published in journals such as the In-
ternational Journal of Medical Informatics (IJMI, V ol. 82, 2013), the Scandinavian Journal of 
Information Systems (SJIS, V ol. 26, 2014), the Journal of the Association for Information Systems 
(JAIS, V ol. 15, 2014) and Computer Supported Cooperative Work (CSCW, V ol. 26, 2017; V ol. 27, 
2018). Participatory Design research on infrastructuring has attracted increasing interest and has 
particularly been based on healthcare studies, as expressed by the International Conference on In-
frastructures in Healthcare (InfraHEALTH), established as a biennial conference by Participatory 
Design and CSCW researchers in 2007.
A Method for Post-Implementation Participatory Design: Effects-Driven IT Improvement
A Participatory Design approach to post-implementation is Effects-Driven Information Technology  
improvement (EDIT), an approach recently discussed by Simonsen and Hertzum (2022). EDIT 
has been identified by Hansen et al. (2019) and in the aforementioned review articles (Bossen 
et al., 2016; Poderi and Dittrich, 2018) as exercising systematic evaluations and obtaining the 
sustainability of Participatory Design practice. EDIT has also been studied as a Participatory De-
sign approach to infrastructuring (Simonsen et al., 2020a). EDIT is a method as defined in the 
2013 handbook, that is, “a coherent set of organising principles and general guidelines” based 
on “generalisations from a vast amount of empirically based experiences on how to conduct Par -
ticipatory Design” (p. 118). EDIT may be compared to the MUST method, especially regarding 
its contrasting application area. The MUST method described in the 2013 handbook (Chapter 6) 
is based on a decade of research including more than ten action research projects. EDIT is cor -
respondingly based on a decade of more than ten action research projects. The MUST method ad-
dresses the traditional Participatory Design pre-implementation application area of early analysis 
and design activities and aims at coherent visions for change. On the other hand, EDIT targets 
post-implementation, which is conducted by users and other local actors. EDIT further presup -
poses an adequate understanding of current work practices, challenges and needs that often are 
obtained through ethnographic approaches, collaborative workshops and the like that are obtained 
through the MUST method.
EDIT offers a perspective that provides a basis for organising principles and general guide -
lines, as well as specific tools and techniques. The idea behind EDIT is to sustain Participatory 
Design iterations by specifying, realising and evaluating desired usage effects from operational 
systems. Effect specifications are followed by experimental interventions that aim to realise ef -
fects through reconfiguring systems, work practices or both. The following formative evaluation 
provides quantitative and qualitative data about whether the interventions have been satisfac -
torily realised, thereby facilitating learning with a sustained focus on effects. Hence, the itera -
tions combine experimentation with the data-driven realisation of effects (see Figure 7.1). The 
iterations’ effect evaluation might result in three potential outcomes, illustrated by the arrows 
in Figure 7.1: renewed effect realisation interventions (i.e., the effect has not been attained but 
is still deemed desirable and realisable); reopening effect realisation (e.g., because of unantici -
pated challenges or adverse side effects); or the interruption of the iterations either because the 
wished-for effects have been satisfactorily attained or because the window of opportunity to 
continue EDIT closes.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
172
The grounding perspective of EDIT is a pragmatic approach to disseminating Participatory Design 
into the post-implementation application area:
In our experience, post-implementation IT improvement is often a local initiative that 
exploits a temporary window of opportunity, is conducted by local actors in a single de-
partment, enjoys little or no attention from top management, and makes do with available 
competences and IT-configuration opportunities.
(Simonsen and Hertzum, 2022, p. 39)
The methods’ pragmatic principles can be summarised as being local, lightweight, data-driven, 
exemplary and meaningful, with the latter emphasising that the effects must be accepted and make 
sense to the users and other involved stakeholders (Simonsen and Hertzum, 2022, p.  41f). These 
principles, along with the three processes depicted in Figure 7.1, constitute the method’s organis-
ing principles. While EDIT specifically addresses information technology improvement, these 
organising principles are general to the extent that they might be applied to other improvement 
efforts.
EDIT’s general guidelines include a list of central questions to consider, a catalogue of locally 
needed competences and supporting tools and techniques. The most specific guideline is a list of 
36 significant questions to consider along the pathways depicted in Figure 7.1. For example, dur-
ing effect specification, an important question is: “How will the effects be measured? – Are evalu-
ation data easy to obtain?” (Simonsen and Hertzum, 2022, p.  44); while for the effect evaluation, 
it is important to consider: “Have the [quantitative] evaluation data been cleaned to bolster their 
quality?” (Simonsen and Hertzum, 2022, p. 48).
Often, locally Participatory Design improvement initiatives are difficult to establish because 
organisational change projects are traditionally governed top-down. Management might resist lo-
cal change projects because of the concern that this might violate attempts to standardise work 
processes (being oblivious to the fact that local work processes must adapt to overall standards and 
that this is exactly what local improvement contributes to). EDIT has thus been argued as a change 
approach that may adequately co-exist and support standardisation and top-down approaches 
Figure 7.1  Effects-driven information technology improvement (Simonsen and Hertzum, 2022).
Effects specification
Effects realization
Effects evaluation

New Approaches, Methods and Techniques
173
(Simonsen et al., 2018). The specification of local wished-for effects is supported by two tools, 
an effects template supporting effects specification and a means–ends hierarchy documenting the 
effects alignment with the organisations’ overall standards, strategies and change management 
initiatives (Hertzum and Simonsen, 2011).
Local improvement initiatives demand competence. To support this, a catalogue of the compe-
tences the project group needs to embrace has been identified (Hertzum and Simonsen, 2019). This 
catalogue includes 21 competence profiles with associated skills and knowledge areas. The devel-
opment of a catalogue of competences also reflects a research approach to the post-implementation 
area in which Participatory Design researchers undertake a facilitating role to support learning 
(see, e.g. Brandrup et al., 2017) and the “sustainability of Participatory Design results” mentioned 
by Poderi and Dittrich (2018): EDIT “focuses on the desired effects and leaves the process open 
for the user-participants to learn, understand and experiment in various ways to realise these ef -
fects without insisting on any specific methodological techniques or guidelines for how to do this” 
(Simonsen et al., 2020a, p. 142).
Approaches in Adjacent Research Areas
The second movement we have identified relates to Participatory Design research and practice 
that takes place in areas adjacent to it. More specifically, over the last decade, Participatory 
Design approaches have increasingly found their way into adjoining research communities, 
including, for example, User-Centred Design (Mallam et al., 2021), Responsible Research and 
Innovation (Holter, 2022) and Evidence-Based Practices (Becker-Haimes et al., 2022). This 
has led to a proliferation of Participatory Design practices and methods as well as to new de -
velopments in Participatory Design, as these approaches have been adopted and appropriated 
to serve new research areas. This tendency is arguably part of a larger trend where participa-
tory practices, to some extent, have become commonplace in civil society. Indeed, the theme 
of the PDC’2016 conference was “Participatory Design in an Era of Participation”, inviting 
researchers to reflect on the role of Participatory Design when participation itself moved into 
the mainstream. In this section, we explore one such research area in which Participatory De -
sign has come to play a prominent role during the last decade. As we dive into these research 
areas, we aim to explore both how Participatory Design practices and grounding perspectives 
have been adopted, as well as how these research areas have advanced our understanding of 
Participatory Design.
We have chosen the area of Interaction Design and Children (IDC) because it serves as a good 
illustration of how both concrete techniques and grounding perspectives have been adopted and 
further developed in a specific research area adjacent to established Participatory Design  commu-
nities. Indeed, IDC has arguably undergone a significant shift over the last two decades in terms of 
how the direct involvement of children is conceptualised and practised. The IDC conference series 
started in 2003 and yearly conferences have been held since then. In addition, research related 
to IDC has been reported in the Journal of Child-Computer Interaction  in several yearly issues 
since 2013. Broadly speaking, IDC is concerned with all aspects of designing and conceptualising 
the design of interactive technologies for children and how these technologies affect the lives of 
children. As technologies have made their way into the hands and homes of children, the research 
area has grown and brings together researchers and practitioners from design disciplines, learning 
sciences and human–computer interaction. Contributions span both the design of novel technolo -
gies and interaction concepts, issues related to technology and learning and critical approaches 
(see Hourcade [2015] for a general introduction to IDC).

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
174
In the last decade in particular, IDC has witnessed a surge in work focusing on the participation of 
children in design and on ideals of empowerment of children through technology design. However, 
issues regarding the roles children can and should play in research design can be traced back at least 
20 years, where Druin described how children can be users, testers, informants and design partners 
(Druin, 2002). Within this framing, a plethora of techniques have been described for how children 
can be involved in design and the kinds of tools, approaches and concerns needed for this involve-
ment. These range from techniques such as “mixing ideas” (Guha et al., 2004), which is aimed at 
supporting young children in collaborating during brainstorming processes to techniques using fic-
tion to spur children’s imagination when envisioning new technologies (Dindler et al., 2005). Indeed, 
the IDC community has in some ways been a leading venue for new techniques to foster engagement 
and participation, as the researchers and practitioners have had to build a repertoire of practices at-
tuned to the particular challenges of working with children. Broadly speaking, the nature of Partici-
patory Design in IDC in the first decade of the 21st century was characterised by commitments to the 
practical and methodological side of actively involving children inthe design process.
Within the last decade, there has been a noticeable shift as IDC has renewed its engagement 
with Participatory Design, with authors arguing that Participatory Design has more to offer IDC 
than methods, tools and techniques for collaborative design. This shift is reflected in several as-
pects, including a renewed focus on sustainability, empowerment, ethics and diversity, but with a 
common denominator being an increased interest in the underlying ideals and principles of Partici-
patory Design rather than the practicalities of participatory practices. In some respects, this devel-
opment echoes the earlier development in Participatory Design, where the focus on methods and 
techniques has been the subject of criticism and calls have been made for revisiting the underlying 
ideals of Participatory Design (Iversen et al., 2010). In IDC, a renewed uptake of Participatory 
Design can be found in several avenues of research. Here, we outline three of these to exemplify 
how Participatory Design approaches have developed in IDC: sustainability and empowerment; 
ethics and agency in Participatory Design with children; and computing education.
Sustainability and Empowerment
As noted, IDC has a historical relation to participatory practices dating back at least two dec-
ades. Beyond methods and techniques for design, Iversen and Dindler (2013) suggested that the 
grounding perspectives behind early Participatory Design trade union projects (Bjerknes et al., 
1987) provide a fruitful platform for IDC research to explore ideals such as empowerment and 
democracy when designing with children. They argue that, in some aspects, the important chal-
lenges relating to children’s wellbeing and education in a digitised society mirrors the concerns 
that originally motivated the Participatory Design tradition in the 1980s in terms of giving future 
users a say with regard to introducing new technology. Similar to developments in the PDC com-
munity, scholars in IDC have begun to explore how Participatory Design initiatives are sustained 
beyond project time and what children learn and gain from their participation (e.g., Schepers 
et al., 2018). For example, Bell and Davis (2016) present a study of the learning opportunities and 
outcomes experienced by high school students taking part in a Participatory Design project. This 
research focus echoes studies within PDC that focus on how participants experience and gain from 
their participation (Bossen et al., 2010; Bowen et al., 2013). Other IDC scholars have addressed 
the challenge of sustainability, exploring, for example, Participatory Design approaches to infra -
structuring in which the process centres on an on-going long-term participatory process. Again, 
this concern for sustainability and infrastructuring approaches in IDC somewhat mirrors the more 
general tendency in Participatory Design described earlier in this chapter. While this does suggest  

New Approaches, Methods and Techniques
175
a parallel development to Participatory Design, IDC’s unique focus on children has led to authors 
accentuating particular aspects such as the ethics of engaging with children in Participatory Design 
and a concern for Participatory Design as it relates to education. These are the subjects of the next 
two sections.
Ethics and Agency in Participatory Design With Children
Given that children play a primary role in IDC, ethical concerns pervade much of the literature. 
Some of the ethical concerns voiced in this area specifically relate to the question of how children 
participate in research and design activities. The commitment to ethics is reflected in a very tangi-
ble way in IDC research, as papers in the IDC proceedings series have a mandatory section called 
“selection and participation of children” in which the authors address consent, recruitment and 
any additional ethical considerations regarding the research. The concerns for ethics are reflected 
broadly in the IDC community with regular panels and workshops featured at conferences (e.g., 
Frauenberger et al., 2017a; Hourcade et al., 2023) and cover a range of topics related to ethics (see 
Van Mechelen et al. [2020] for an overview). In terms of conducting Participatory Design with 
children, Read et al. (2014) addressed the topic of how representation and participation become 
transparent for children by proposing the TRAck analysis method that traces how children’s ideas 
are used and represented in design sessions. In particular, the TRAck method focuses on making 
the impact of children’s ideas transparent and ensuring that individual input is given an equal 
chance. Moreover, Spiel et al. (2018) explored the often-overlooked “micro-ethics” of conducting 
Participatory Design with vulnerable children. On a more overarching level, several papers have 
argued for promoting design practices in which children are empowered to take on a larger degree 
of agency in design. Based on the political aspects of Participatory Design, Iversen et al. (2017) 
propose that children may take on the role of “protagonists”, focusing on how they developed 
knowledge and new perspectives on technology through their participation (see also Kanafi et al., 
2022). Chatlani et al. (2023) proposed that teens be engaged as “research apprentices” by focusing 
on giving teenagers the authority to deal with issues around online safety.
Another important and related trajectory in the last decade of IDC research on Participatory 
Design relates to issues of diversity and inclusion. One aspect of this trajectory is the engage -
ment of diverse children with special needs, which has been a growing concern in IDC for some 
time in terms of designing technologies and in terms of the nature and practice of participation. 
As an example, Frauenberger et al. (2017b) reflect on the need for re-interpreting, blending and 
combining building blocks from existing methods to accommodate the characteristics of a child 
in their project. Beyond the inclusion of children with diverse abilities, recent work has called 
for more generally “pushing the boundaries of Participatory Design with children” (Korte et al., 
2023) in a special issue of the journal of child–computer interaction. In the contributions to this 
special issue, the authors demonstrate, among other things, a hybrid and distributed Participatory 
Design process using a transcultural approach to Participatory Design involving children in Fin-
land and underrepresented children from Namibia and Malaysia in distributed co-design processes 
(Winschiers-Theophilus et al., 2022).
Concerns regarding the ethics of Participatory Design are certainly not exclusive to IDC. These 
concerns for ethics can be traced back throughout the PDC literature. IDC does, however, provide 
valuable resources and reflections both in terms of concrete methods (e.g. Read et al., 2014), con-
cepts that orient us towards issues of agency and empowerment (e.g. Iversen et al., 2017; Chatlani 
et al., 2023) and perspectives that help us better understand ethics in practice (e.g. Spiel et al., 
2018).

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
176
Computing Education
Given the focus on children, the issue of education has naturally played a central role in IDC 
research. Within this research, Participatory Design  has been used to inspire research, curricula 
building and educational activities at large. In terms of using Participatory Design to design educa-
tional technology concepts, IDC research showcases a variety of cases, ranging from co-designing 
search query tools (Fails et al., 2019) and intelligent tutoring systems (Mack et al., 2019) to the 
creation of a joint storytelling platform for children with mixed visual abilities (Cullen and Metatla, 
2019). In recent years, an increasing amount of work in IDC has begun to address the challenge of 
providing children with the skills and knowledge about technology for them to grasp the digitisa-
tion of society and how technology affects democratic processes and everyday life. Participatory 
Design has played a prominent role in this area as a means for creating learning experiences with 
a focus on empowerment and active participation of children (Kinnula and Iivari, 2021; Göbl et 
al., 2023). More broadly, researchers in IDC have argued that there is a notable resonance between 
IDC’s concern for empowering children to make informed decisions and live meaningful lives in 
a digitised society and Participatory Design’s decades-long concern to empower people to have a 
say in the introduction of technology (Iversen and Dindler, 2013). This affinity between IDC and 
Participatory Design has led to research agendas focusing on, for example, children’s “computa -
tional empowerment” (Dindler et al., 2020) that challenges traditional approaches to computing 
education that focus more explicitly on technology and programming as technical skills to be 
learned. Examples emerging from this line of work include Morales-Navarro et al. (2022), who 
demonstrated how youth are engaged in co-design activities to surface their critical perspectives 
of computing as being more than a technical issue.
In summary, across IDC research, we have seen a continuous engagement with Participatory 
Design across at least two decades. The last decade in particular has witnessed a renewed engage-
ment with some of the foundational issues that set Participatory Design apart from co-design 
or user-centred design, including the empowerment of children through design, issues of ethics 
related to children’s participation and the sustainability of outcomes for children in terms of their 
agency and education. The uptake of Participatory Design in IDC not only shows the former’s 
relevance but also how Participatory Design grows outside of PDC; indeed, issues around empow-
erment and ethics perhaps develop more rapidly in IDC as compared to PDC. For Participatory 
Design researchers and practitioners, IDC is an abundant resource of inspiration for how to prac -
tise Participatory Design; deep engagement with issues related to ethics, agency and empower -
ment; and – above all – demonstrations of how Participatory Design may be appropriated in other 
research areas. The influx of Participatory Design in IDC is, to some extent, fuelled by Participa-
tory Design researchers traversing into IDC and vice versa. Indeed, an examination of the authors 
and institutions in the IDC literature reveals that there is some overlap with the PDC conference 
series. As such, this section illustrates how Participatory Design research topics and researchers 
themselves are active in other research areas.
Approaches for Decolonial Participatory Design Practice and Research
The third movement in Participatory Design approaches and methods that we address is ena -
bled by researchers who have discussed practices and concerns of Participatory Design in the 
Souths and through a decolonial thinking perspective. “The Souths” is used here instead of 
Global South, since it is a word that, according to Santos (2018), refers to (and recognises) 
all alternative/non-hegemonic epistemological perspectives specific to a variety of different 

New Approaches, Methods and Techniques
177
countries and cultures that are disregarded when we use the expression “Global South”, which 
homogenises them. Over the last decade, Participatory Design scholars have increasingly re -
flected on the need to think about design and Participatory Design knowledge beyond the North 
European and modernist traditions and roots and Western/Westernised knowledge. In this case, 
the movement in grounding perspectives has been epistemological, worldview-related, and, 
partially, geographical. It has embraced aspects of both practice and research in Participatory 
Design.
Scholars have questioned dominant ways of understanding the practice and one-size-fits-all 
approaches by interrogating concepts that so far had been unchallenged and generalisations 
of the field, as well as related and existing approaches and methods, through a decolonising 
perspective and through other worldviews perspective (i.e., participation, participants, design, 
etc.). Researchers have pointed out the marginalising dynamics inherent in Participatory De -
sign approaches, methods and tools – for example, universal understanding of participation, 
exclusion of certain dimensions of life or aspects of an experience (e.g., feelings, affection, 
etc.), to mention a few (Akama and Yee, 2019; Del Gaudio et al., 2021) and sought alternative 
forms of world-making and knowledge production. These authors posited the need to em -
brace decolonial thinking to avoid perpetuating universalising narratives (e.g., Shepherd, 2018; 
Smith et al., 2020; Akama, 2021; see also Chapter 5).
According to scholars researching decolonial thinking and practice (Shepherd, 2018), univer -
salism is one of the main aspects of Western knowledge and manifests itself in two different 
ways: (1) discreet “cannibalisation” and appropriation of aspects of local/alternative knowledge 
and ways of thinking that are useful and compatible; and (2) subalternisation or destruction of 
local knowledge and traditions by labelling them “non-knowledge” (i.e., cultures, traditions or 
beliefs). Furthermore, these scholars perceive Western knowledge as being grounded on a binary 
way of thinking that results in a limited understanding of what knowledge is (Shepherd, 2018). 
Knowledge is understood as a matter of reason and mind, with subsequent rejection of everything 
that is not of reason and mind, such as emotions, affects, senses, memories, experiences, desires 
and imaginations.
Therefore, embracing decolonial thinking requires: (1) acknowledging practices of “cannibali-
sation” and appropriation that did not credit the original culture, (2) recognising processes involv-
ing the subalternisation of alternative and local traditions and engaging in valuing them, and (3) 
developing a wider understanding of what knowledge is.
Chapter 5 provides in-depth information about this discussion, how it emerged, the theo -
retical ideas that support it and the various key voices and topics addressed. Our review 
of PDC contributions clearly reveals that within the Participatory Design community, the 
Participatory Design Conferences of 2020 and 2022 have been cornerstones of the shift to -
wards decolonial thinking and practice in the Participatory Design process, with the themes of 
“Participation(s) Otherwise” and “Embracing Cosmologies: Expanding Worlds of Participa -
tory Design”, respectively. They held decolonial concerns at their core and addressed issues 
such as the implications of implementing Western design practices in non-Western contexts 
(Smith et al., 2020), the diverse meanings and ontologies that participation and design can 
take on (Del Gaudio et al., 2020) and forms of participation beyond the human including 
incorporating equitable design involving non-human entities (Vlachokyriakos et al., 2022). 
This is an emerging topic; thus, these conferences are where the majority of the contributions 
referenced here come from.
How specifically were these discussions put into practice? How have Participatory Design 
scholars tried to apply these ideas and concepts and address potential methodological gaps?

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
178
It is still too early to identify consolidated subareas of research, so we report existing scholarship 
through the following lenses: practices and concerns of Participatory Design in the Souths – mainly 
Latin America; and the integration of aspects that have been disregarded in Participatory Design.
Participation in Design as Practised in Latin America
Since 2020, the Participatory Design community has seen an increase in the participation of Latin 
American researchers in the academic debate. An analysis of their contributions has made it pos -
sible to identify some main areas of practice – and related approaches – that characterise partici -
pation in design in Latin America: (1) Participatory Design and participatory practices in design 
applied to address local needs that are often disregarded by and misaligned with mainstream design 
practices; (2) areas of concern and practice such as design education, intergenerational dialogue to 
preserve indigenous communities’ culture, and work with disregarded social groups; and (3) three 
main ways that local practitioners have used to promote participation in design – the development 
of local practices; development of hybrid practices that bring together inputs from Northern ap-
proaches to participation in the design and local ones; and the reinterpretation and practice of the 
emerging field of Design Anthropology.
“Design em Parceria” (a Portuguese expression whose literal translation in English is “Design 
in Partnership”) is presented here as a way of practising participation in design processes that have 
emerged and have been practised in the Souths in parallel and with no connection to Participa -
tory Design. It is an approach used as part of the pedagogical practice of Pontifícia Universidade 
Católica do Rio de Janeiro (Brazil), as described by Araujo et al. (2020). The approach was created 
in the 1980s both due to the influence of Papanek’s ideas on the need to design for individuals 
who usually disregarded (Papanek, 2011) and due to the understanding of the weaknesses inher -
ent in the implementation of Northern and Western approaches to design at the local level – the 
curriculum of the School of Ulm was implemented in local design schools at the time. Gradually, 
Design em Parceria became part of the regular curriculum in design education and is nowadays 
taught mainly within the first design studio of the undergraduate programme. First-year students 
are asked to design together with a partner that they have to identify. A series of activities ideated 
by local instructors guide students towards designing together with their local partners. Those 
activities focus on observation, listening, dialogue and co-creation. Prototypes guide, support and 
promote one-on-one conversation between the student and the design partner. Thus, there is a 
strong emphasis on listening and co-creation.
Design em Parceria has been used as a pedagogical approach to educating future designers in 
a design practice that not only counteracts mainstream design approaches but also contributes to 
informing socio-economic dynamics and systems that do not mirror Northern ones.
This is not the only case of implementation of participatory practices in design education in 
Latin America. Among the few studies reported, Dias et al. (2020) engaged students in partici -
patory processes to design games with marginalised social groups in the context of basic edu -
cation. In this case, Participatory Design is a way to foster societal dialogue between different 
socio-economical classes, therefore opposing classism and social exclusion.
Another area of application of participatory dynamics in design practice in Latin America is 
the preservation of local, generational, indigenous and ancestral knowledge – more broadly, Par -
ticipatory Design works with indigenous communities. A clear example is provided by Garcés 
(2020), whose research involves an action research project that took place in Ecuador in col -
laboration with the local indigenous community and aimed to support intergenerational exchange 
to preserve ancestral knowledge. More specifically, the study focused on collecting and sharing 

New Approaches, Methods and Techniques
179
personal histories between elders and young members of the community. Throughout the process, 
games were co-designed and used to recall and share them. In this case, the approach implemented 
emerged from the integration of “Western” Participatory Design principles and co-design tools/
techniques together with key concepts from “popular education” (PE). This is a clear example of a 
hybrid practice that brings together inputs from mainstream and local approaches to participation. 
It is important to note that Freire’s PE is one of the main theories and approaches informing partici-
patory practices in Latin America and that, over the last decade, it has inspired new Participatory 
Design practices (e.g., Calderón Salazar and Huybrechts, 2020). Drawing from Freire (2020), the 
theoretical foundation of Garcés’ practice was based on the principles of “dialogical subjects”, 
“levels of perception” and “generative topic”. The author merged these principles with co-design 
concepts and tools from the MIT Co-design Civic Media Group and the support of researchers 
from the University of the Arts Helsinki and from the Illinois Institute of Technology.
Intergenerational dialogue is also at the core of the work described by Martínez González 
(2020) – a seven-year design practice aimed at promoting horizontal dialogues between designers 
and artisans as well as dialogue between different generations since local indigenous populations 
were concerned about losing their culture. Martínez González’s (2020) work is one of many that 
points out a third way that Participatory Design researchers are beginning to practise Participatory 
Design in the Souths in a decolonial manner: Design Anthropology as a decolonising methodol -
ogy within long-term field work. Design Anthropology and long-term fieldwork are also at the 
core of Santos and Noronha’s (2020) work with local artisans in Northern Brazil. These authors 
focused on the concept and practice of “correspondence” (Ingold, 2012) and saw the exchange 
of experiences between designers and artisans on how to work with local materialsa as a way to 
reflect on what those materials mean in one’s life – therefore, the exchange is understood as a 
way to strengthen the understanding of one another’s human experience. This type of knowledge 
exchange is the practice of collaboration and enables the emergence of differences (Santos and 
Noronha, 2020).
Szaniecki et al. (2020) also engaged with Design Anthropology by combining its aspects with 
co-design to promote dialogue between different stakeholders and to strengthen designers’ politi-
cal actions at the local level. They developed and applied “dispositivos de conversação” (whose 
literal translation in English is “devices for conversation”) as a means for promoting dialogue and 
conversation on the use and possibilities of the public space (i.e., downtown Rio de Janeiro) in an 
academic symposium and during a panel discussion held in a favela.
These last works exemplify how in Latin America, researchers and practitioners have devel-
oped approaches that embrace the Western approach to Participatory Design and explore and 
evolve it according to local dynamics. They address the need to adapt Western approaches and 
methods according to contextual factors (Del Gaudio, 2014).
Sentipensar to Rethink Knowledge and Participation in Participatory Design Practice
Over the last few years, there has been increasing work done to reflect on and include aspects 
of practice and knowledge related to the act of designing, participation in design and research in 
Participatory Design that are disregarded within the mainstream binary and reason-based Western 
approach to knowledge. Often, concepts and theories from the Souths have been catalysts of this 
process and have been used to explore and inform new ways of practising Participatory Design. 
One of the most-explored concepts in this area is sentipensar.
“Sentipensar” (feeling–thinking) was introduced by Orlando Fals Borda, a Colombian soci-
ologist who set the foundations of participatory action research. This concept is rooted in the 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
180
episteme of riverside Colombians. As Calderón Salazar and Huybrechts (2020) indicated, the term 
combines the words sentimiento (feeling) and pensamiento (thought): the concept expresses the 
inseparability between reason and emotion, human beings and nature. It challenges the dichoto-
mic approach of modern science and research, worldview and knowledge production. Sentipensar 
points out that the mind is not the only way to know the world and gives relevance to the body, 
feelings, affects and non-rational interactions. Reflections on these topics have brought forward 
other concepts that, if different from sentipensar, share similar concerns. Examples of these con-
cepts include corazonar and ilkwatharra (described below), among others. In general, within the 
Participatory Design community, the concept of sentipensar, and similar terms has promoted both 
a rethinking of the Participatory Design process and a focus on designers’ positionality and bias.
Sentipensar to Rethink the Participatory Design Process
Several authors have explored the implications of the concept of sentipensar for the Participatory 
Design process. Albarrán González (2022) referred to the similar concept of corazonar: Escobar 
(2014), drawing from FalsBorda, translated sentipensar into coracionar, that is, “to reason with 
the heart”. Corazonar breaks with the reasons as the hegemonic centre for decision – making 
and prioritises affection and feeling (Guerrero Arias, 2011; Santos, 2018). According to Albarrán 
González (2022), as the latter were incorporated into the decision-making processes of several 
Andean cultures, they should become core aspects of the design process.
Feelings and affection are at the core of St John’s (2022) work as well. This author did not draw 
from the concept of sentipensar but from the concept of ilkwatharra from Western Arrarnta culture 
and Country in Australia. Ilkwatharra refers to a way of being with others that includes “concepts 
of friendships, connectedness, and doing things together” (p. 3), in general, “good feelings”. This 
concept is used as the starting point of exploration and reflection on the need to change the cur -
rent practice of acquisition of “ethical consent” within Participatory Design research and practice. 
A Participatory Design education experience in Western Arrarnta Country shows that to ensure 
meaningful consent, Participatory Design researchers need to engage as people first and to gener-
ate “good feelings”. “Good feelings”, drawing from ilkwatharra, can be considered a manifesta-
tion of consent. Participatory Design practitioners need to bring them at the core of their doing and 
as part of their consent practice; since these feelings constantly evolve, they need to constantly 
negotiate consent. In addition, St John (2022) points out the need to extend responsibility after 
fieldwork. The latter means extending the Participatory Design timeline and bringing up the need 
to develop approaches and methods for it.
Maccagnan and Meyer (2022) reflect on embodied and sentient ways of participating and prac-
tising Participatory Design. Drawing both from the concept of sentipensar and matters of care 
(Puig de la Bellacasa, 2017), these authors engaged in an experimental practice to include sentient 
design aspects that are usually excluded in Participatory Design. They designed a prototyping 
practice oriented by touch – a touch-oriented form of Participatory Design able to promote democ-
racy through storytelling and the ethic of care. These authors used manual embroidery to enable 
participants to access and share intimate, familiar, feminine and mundane aspects of everyday 
life. First, participants engaged with embroidery alone and accessed their own intimate sphere; 
second, they participated in collective open conversations on what they created and what touched 
them throughout the process. An interplay between individual and collective activities chracterises 
this approach. During the individual activities, this type of practice enabled participants to slow 
down and cultivate a distinct sensibility (Maccagnan and Meyer, 2022); while the collective ones 
encouraged participants not to become detached but to embrace correspondence. The final goal of 

New Approaches, Methods and Techniques
181
these authors’ study was to explore how feelings and knowing can be integrated when mobilising 
people.
Finally, according to Bittencourt and Freire (2022), a way to practise a sentipensante (feeling–
thinking) type of Participatory Design is for designers to incorporate core concepts of spiritual 
disciplines rooted in alternative ontologies into the design process. According to the authors, this 
can be done only by designers who are engaged with those disciplines authentically and in a dis -
ciplined manner. A strong identification with those values enables both designers and participants 
to relate differently: to overcome self-centredness, and to be open to listening, connection with the 
community and acceptance of others. To exemplify how this can be done, the authors present a 
case of the use and adaptation of the Management by Mandala methodology. Such methodology, 
co-created by Lama Padma Samten and the community of Bodhisattva Buddhist Studies Center 
(CEBB) to manage a large network of Buddhist initiatives and groups, is structured around the 
principle that “the reality that surrounds us co-emerges with our identity and our vision” (Bitten -
court and Freire, 2022, p. 59). Due to this understanding, the methodology focuses on developing 
certain skills and attitudes that can enable people to generate desired outcomes that need to be “for 
ourselves, for others and for the biosphere” (Bittencourt and Freire, 2022). The skills to be pro -
moted are deeply rooted in the core tenants of the spiritual practice and aim to develop a different 
approach and relationship to one’s reality – for instance, “calming our mind down to identify and 
develop freedom from our own thinking and behavioural patterns” (Bittencourt and Freire, 2022, 
p. 59). The methodology includes several tools for introspection, reflection and action. In the at -
tempt to implement this in a design setting, the authors identified four principles among the litera-
ture on Management by Mandala of what the authors define as a sentipensante form of co-design. 
These principles, which should not be approached as fixed steps, are at the core of the adapted 
version of the methodology to a Participatory Design process: “calming the mind, recognizing 
co-emergence, sitting in a circle, and accepting people in their context” (Bittencourt and Freire, 
2022, p. 59). In addition to all this, according to Bittencourt and Freire (2022), integral to a senti-
pensante type of Participatory Design is also the reflection on one’s own (i.e., the designer’s) po-
sitionality and biases and the integration of these reflections in the Participatory Design practice. 
The need for Participatory Design designers to reflect on positionality and biases had already been 
pointed out – beyond sentipensar – by Pihkala and Karasti (2016), who addressed it as “reflexive 
engagement”, and Akama et al. (2019).
On this topic, we can notice also the emergence of new Participatory Design approaches 
at the intersection between concepts from the Souths and the current field of Participatory 
Design. For instance, Ibarra (2020), drawing both from the understanding of sentipensar and 
from a Design Anthropology perspective, engaged in a self-reflexive process aimed at un -
derstanding her own (designer’s) experience in support of a collective of people engaged in 
strikes for better neighbourhood infrastructure in Brazil. According to her, Design Anthro -
pology is an approach that can support this type of reflection within Participatory Design 
practice.
In general, an in-depth look at the efforts implemented so far shows that, to date, to discuss and 
rethink existing Participatory Design approaches and methods from a decolonial perspective, Par-
ticipatory Design researchers have mainly: (1) identified and shared ways of practising participa -
tion in design that emerged beyond the Northern Participatory Design tradition – acknowledging 
and valuing alternative practices; (2) brought to the fore how researchers in (and from) the Souths 
have engaged with Participatory Design and adapted it to the local needs; (3) engaged with alterna-
tive concepts and theories (mostly from Latin America) that foster a different approach to knowl-
edge and participation that could generate new operationalising principles for Participatory Design 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
182
practice; and (4) finally engaged with aspects of practice, knowledge and participation disregarded 
within mainstream binary and reason-based approach to knowledge.
Conclusion: Opportunities and Challenges
This chapter reviewed Participatory Design literature in terms of its new approaches with a focus 
on the past decade’s trends (e.g., methods, tools and techniques and their inherently grounding 
perspectives). Participatory Design is a highly process-oriented research area, and many publica -
tions include research and projects describing various approaches addressing different issues. In 
this chapter, we identified and selected three recent movements and trends in approaches within 
the Participatory Design field: new application areas; research in adjacent areas; and decolonial 
Participatory Design practice and research. In this section, we conclude the chapter by pointing 
to opportunities and challenges to inspire future Participatory Design research for each one of the 
three movements addressed in this chapter. We refer the reader to other chapters of this book that 
review different contemporary trends and approaches within Participatory Design, as well as their 
implications for responding to current social, political and environmental challenges.
New Application Areas
The application area of Participatory Design methods has clearly advanced to embody what we 
have labelled as post-implementation, which focuses on Participatory Design practice beyond ini-
tial design activities. The trend is apparently a result of technological evolution, especially within 
information and communication technologies, as well as of a growing interest in whether Partici -
patory Design achieves its goals of mutual learning, empowerment and improving work life. Most 
users live in work environments today packed with information systems, some newly introduced, 
and others part of the existing installed base (Aanestad et al., 2017). These systems often poorly 
meet the users’ needs because efforts to adapt them to the processes and practices they affect are 
typically discontinued relatively shortly after their initial implementation. The need for and rel-
evance of Participatory Design to address organisational post-implementation application areas is 
becoming evident. This has opened many new research opportunities: while new systems continue 
to be developed and implemented, this only involves users in one organisation and for a limited 
period. The potential for improvements and the number of involved users might be much higher 
within the existing technology base in a post-implementation context rather than in another new 
system that is yet to be designed and developed. The exchange from temporary research-driven 
projects to collaboration and commitment to external, long-term, large-scale, public or commer -
cial initiatives and projects is reflected by the three discussed literature reviews inquiring into the 
research of evaluation, sustainability and infrastructuring.
Research into post-implementation application areas also poses challenges. The empirical work 
entails dependency on external realities, including conditions and partners that the researcher has 
very little or no power to influence (see Simonsen et al. [2020b] for a discussion on how this 
affects PhD studies). This dependency imposes risks, especially when undertaking an engaged, 
action research or interventionist approach aiming at real-life change – risks that also have been 
debated earlier (Simonsen, 2009). Bossen et al. (2016) observed that evaluation studies are time- 
and resource-intensive and that the evaluation of Participatory Design elements, such as mutual 
learning, empowerment, democracy and work life, requires engaging external participants and 
stakeholders. Finally, these challenges stem from the fact that the research yet is not fully matured: 
Poderi and Dittrich (2018) pointed to a “pervasive lack of a concrete, explicit, and operational 

New Approaches, Methods and Techniques
183
connotation of what ‘sustainability’ means” (p. 4), a concern that has been met with a recent book 
contribution by Simone et al. (2022). Karasti (2014) described challenges in researching infra-
structuring as a ubiquitous phenomenon with increased heterogeneities and complexities as well 
as scaling along multiple dimensions – an observation critically recognised by Lee and Schmidt 
(2018).
Research in Adjacent Areas
As is evident by an examination of the development in IDC, Participatory Design has grown in 
adjacent research areas that find inspiration in the methods, techniques and grounding perspectives 
of Participatory Design. This does not only serve to broaden the knowledge and application of 
Participatory Design; new research areas also add, reimagine and challenge traditional notions of 
participation and design. Supporting Participatory Design in adjacent research areas continues to 
be a great opportunity for Participatory Design. A main driver for this development is the tendency 
for Participatory Design researchers to broadly engage in other research communities. This is evi-
dent when looking at IDC and a series of conferences related to, among others, Human–Computer 
Interaction and Computer-Supported Cooperative Work, where it is common to find authors who 
also have a deep engagement in Participatory Design. Moreover, it remains important for Partici-
patory Design to invite other communities into traditional venues such as biennual Participatory 
Design Conferences to embrace new perspectives on participatory practices.
A challenge and dilemma for Participatory Design is remaining relevant when participatory 
practices have already, in some countries, found their way to practices in public administration 
and industry. As eloquently formulated in the PDC’2016 conference, what is “Participatory Design 
in an era of participation”? It might be argued that the proliferation of participatory practices is 
indeed a great success. On the other hand, concerns have been raised that, in some areas, participa-
tory practices are superficial and do not reflect the grounding perspectives of Participatory Design. 
Thus, questions regarding how Participatory Design should relate to more “light-weight” forms of 
participation and contribute to the research and development of this practice remain.
Decolonial Participatory Design Practice and Research
As addressed in the previous sections, epistemological and ontological discussions have character-
ised part of the last decade of Participatory Design research and have led to an exploration of how 
to rethink existing Participatory Design approaches and methods from a decolonial perspective. 
Even if this is an area of research that has recently received significant interest and a fast-growing 
number of Participatory Design publications, our review reveals that rethinking Participatory De-
sign from a decolonial perspective is a fairly new trend. This can be seen in the contributions that 
still present themselves as discrete explorations and experimentations with new topics in search of 
potential directions for research and practice. The contours of this trend are still in the making and 
will certainly be further formed and shaped in the future. As this field is an incipient area of work, 
it brings several opportunities for new research: the explorations described earlier can be embraced 
and further developed in new research directions (e.g., touch-oriented Participatory Design prac -
tices, sentipensante forms of Participatory Design and the integration of Northern and Southern 
approaches to participation). In addition, this area of research has already shown great potential 
for strengthening the diversity within the Participatory Design community by bringing together 
actors from the Global North and from the Souths. Drawing on Reynolds-Cuéllar et al.’s (2022) 
suggestion of a stronger collaboration between researchers from different geographical locations, 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
184
cultures and worldviews, is the path forward in this area and a process that can strengthen Partici-
patory Design practice and research. This is a key opportunity for current and future researchers 
in Participatory Design that can enrich and strengthen participatory practices and approaches to 
research through cross-fertilisation.
Several potential challenges have also emerged from our review. In spite of a general widespread 
attempt at rethinking Participatory Design from “alternative” concepts, only a few past, historical 
and alternative experiences of practising participation in design from the Souths were shared and 
brought to Participatory Design researchers’ attention. If there is a need for additional collaborative 
efforts between researchers from different geographical regions in the process of understanding a 
history of participatory methods in design, this might have been hindered by language and academic 
barriers – this became obvious at PDC’2020, the first multilingual PDC conference. Additional re-
search efforts able to capture the history of Participatory Design practices in Southern contexts are 
necessary, and creative efforts seem to be crucial for identifying venues and forms of communica-
tion that can embrace differences in knowledge production, academic systems and needs.

8
PARTICIPATORY DESIGN 
BEYOND ACADEMIA
Daria Loi, Penny Hagen and Raphael Arar
DOI: 10.4324/9781003334330-9
This chapter focuses on participatory practice in non-academic contexts, how such practice has evolved 
over the past ten years, and how this evolution has seen the rise, in many non-academic contexts. The 
core of the chapter discusses three themes central to the decade of non-academic Participatory Design 
practice: the critical impact that context has on practitioners’ ability to fully apply Participatory Design; 
key aspects surrounding the work itself (methods, strategy, tactics, and logistics); and implications of 
Participatory Design as a Western practice, alongside a reflection on emerging work at the intersection 
of Indigenous and Participatory Design practices.
In overviewing the historical tensions that exist between Academic Participatory Design versus In-
dustry Participatory Design, authors propose that new ways to describe the plethora of non-academic 
participatory practices that have emerged over the past decade are urgently needed. Additionally, they 
argue that criteria currently leveraged to estimate what is and is not Participatory Design practice 
should be re-evaluated to recognise the fundamental differences that exist between academic and 
non-academic Participatory Design practice.
The chapter proposes that new metrics would provide opportunities to recognise and invite a 
broader set of practices that would provide legitimacy to under-recognised non-academic Partici -
patory Design approaches. Additionally, the authors propose that over time deeply participatory 
practices and work have become invisible to academic-led communities (such as the Participa -
tory Design Conference) due to terminology divergence and the academisation of Participatory 
Design.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
192
Introduction
This chapter focuses on participatory practice in non-academic contexts, how such practice has 
evolved over the past ten years, and how such an evolution has seen the rise in many non-academic 
contexts. The chapter is divided into six sections. After this brief introduction, a reflection on key
