terminology and contextual aspects is offered, followed by a discussion of three themes that re -
flect key aspects of the past ten years of non-academic Participatory Design practice and a closing 
section.
The first theme focuses on the critical role of context in non-academic forms of Participatory 
Design and its impact on practitioners’ ability to apply Participatory Design consistently. Draw -
ing mostly from the enterprise as well as North American and European contexts, it discusses 
how and why practitioners struggle in applying the academic definition of Participatory Design in 
non-academic environments and what systemic phenomena arise as a consequence, including pro-
cess shortening, misuse of terms, renaming, co-opting, and a long list of damage-control activities.
The second theme centres on the work, including methods, strategy, tactics, logistics, and more, 
and how this work varies in diverse environments. Non-academic Participatory Design often finds 
itself embedded in existing design frameworks and approaches that organisations rely on and 
serves in distinct contrast to contemporary academic practice, where Participatory Design can 
often be an end in itself. Drawing mostly from the enterprise as well as North American and Euro-
pean contexts, this section reflects on the evolving practices of practitioners over the past decade, 
highlights how existing methods can be made more participatory, and provides suggestions on 
advocating for a continued transfer of agency to participants.
The third theme explores the implications of non-academic Participatory Design as a Western 
practice, and its relevance, particularly in the context of communities that experience the impacts 
of colonisation and where there are existing (but potentially marginalised) Indigenous participa -
tory practices. In recent years in places such as Australia and Aotearoa New Zealand (NZ) (as well 
as others), it has become common for Participatory Design (or rather co-design) to be applied in 
such settings as an “innovative” way to address complex social challenges, particularly within the 
public sector, and it is one of the key places in which Participatory Design practices are promoted 
outside of academia. Drawing specifically from examples across Australia and Aotearoa NZ, this 
third theme explores tensions and issues that are raised by this, as well as practice that is emerging 
at the intersection of Indigenous and Participatory Design practices, and poses some questions for 
Participatory Design practitioners (or about Participatory Design practice) in such settings.
The final section of this chapter offers closing remarks and recommendations.
Background
Before discussing the three thematic areas at the centre of this chapter, it is important to define 
key terminology in the context of non-academic participatory practice. Specifically, after offering 
reflections on the term Participatory Design from the perspective of non-academic practice, this 
section overviews historical tensions between Academic Participatory Design versus so-called 
Industry Participatory Design to ultimately propose the need for new ways to describe the plethora 
of non-academic participatory practice that has emerged over the past decade.
First, what does Participatory Design mean? Over the past decade, mainstream adoption of 
the term has shifted the meaning and expectations associated with the practice, to a point where 
Participatory Design is becoming (or arguably has already become) a fashionable trend, similar to 
Design Thinking. Design Thinking “has garnered into a cult that naively believes that it can create 

Participatory Design Beyond Academia
193
impactful change in larger systems via a reductive method” and “Design thinking marketing needs 
to stop enchanting industries with a diluted design process (Jen, 2018).” Arguably, Participatory 
Design as a concept seems to follow a similar trend (Arar et al., 2022).
In an effort to pursue the core ethos of Participatory Design, many contemporary practitioners have 
started using different terms to label their participatory practice. For instance, the term co-design has 
been frequently used (Auckland Co-Design Lab, 2018; Blomkamp, 2018; McKercher, 2020; Sand-
ers and Stappers, 2008; Szebeko, 2010) to describe participatory practice. Re-labelling has enabled 
many practitioners to better articulate, push for, and ultimately apply those precepts within contexts 
that are very different from academic ones. Indeed the term co-design is now commonplace in loca-
tions such as Australia and Aotearoa NZ where the term Participatory Design or its academic lineage 
would not be well understood – if known at all. In addition, many practitioners using participatory 
methods would refer to co-design without a connection to Participatory Design’s history or origins. 
Because of that, this chapter includes discussions of co-design as such a term is offered as a proxy 
for Participatory Design in non-academic contexts. Additionally, for the same reason, it is difficult to 
track Participatory Design practice as it is frequently disseminated with different labels.
Second, it is important to appreciate the Academic versus Industry Participatory Design di-
chotomy that has historically existed in the Participatory Design Conference community in the 
past couple of decades.
At a high level, one could argue that the dichotomy originates from different end goals: while 
academic Participatory Design is typically oriented towards generating research findings, Partici-
patory Design practice out of academia is more frequently outcome-driven.
1 Because of that, their 
measures of accountability and success differ.
A close look at Participatory Design Conferences (PDC) over time highlights a more complex story. 
In its first edition, the Participatory Design Conference’s goal was “to promote greater understand-
ing of Participatory Design in the U.S. and to explore its applicability to the design of ‘off-the-shelf’ 
applications” (Namioka and Schuler, 1990). To achieve such goals, the programme included invited 
talks by researchers, practitioners, and “representatives from computer labor organizations,” half-day 
workshops, a plenary talk, and “an open discussion to evaluate the conference and indicate some next 
steps” (Namioka and Schuler, 1990). A closer look at the 1990 programme shows a very balanced 
representation and no use of terminology indicating a distinction between academic versus industry 
research or practice.
After that first edition, while the Participatory Design Conference proceedings started show-
casing a growth in academic contributions, the conference continued having a mixed audience. In 
PDC2010 however a line started being drawn, as the programme started including a separate track 
called industry cases, which consisted of short case study papers by authors from non-academic 
backgrounds. This inclusion occurred to more intentionally create space for those practising out -
side of academia and without a historic connection to Participatory Design and the decision to 
support the submission of short case studies was intentional, to avoid a full academic paper sub -
mission, a barrier to many. While the Participatory Design Conference in 2012 followed suit, 
PDC2014 experimented with an industry-day format to offer practitioners a way to share and 
contribute without being constrained by academic paper formats. While the day was well attended, 
the event also set a spotlight on a clear fissure in the Participatory Design Conference community, 
with several academic researchers not participating and providing the feedback that the day had 
little to offer to them. PDC2016 resumed industry cases and, to include practitioners without paper 
submission requirements, nested those cases in the interactive exhibition track. For the 2018 Par -
ticipatory Design Conference, a decision was made to extend the same call for participation across 
all conference formats – since the Participatory Design Conference was a dominantly academic 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
194
conference by then, non-academic participants were therefore invited to share their knowledge 
yet do so within the constraints of academic practice. By 2018, the Participatory Design Confer -
ence Advisory Board had already tracked a general ongoing shrinking of the community and a 
need to attract new participants and audiences. There was a strong sense that the conference had 
to not only move beyond traditional Participatory Design Conference locations (North America 
and Europe) but also that it had to be extended beyond its dominantly academic territories. De -
spite the COVID-19 pandemic, PDC2020 was hosted in Columbia (and online), and, to re-engage 
non-academics, the Beyond Academia track was created to engage practitioners without having 
to follow traditional full academic papers requirements. In that edition of the conference, the 
requirement explicitly stated that an academic paper was not required – instead, practitioners had 
to submit an online form containing specific questions to structure the submission while provid -
ing enough freedom to fully describe the case or topic. While practitioners were also encouraged 
to include audiovisual material to complement their submission if they felt appropriate, a written 
submission was still a requirement for participation. PDC2022 was the first conference that broke 
the written submission requirement entirely. In that edition, the Beyond Academia track followed 
an invitational model, with sessions shaped as facilitated panels around preselected themes and 
collaboratively constructed with invited practitioners. Given the success of this new model (for 
audiences and participating practitioners) PDC2024 is scheduled to follow a similar format.
The previous historical summary shows how different the Participatory Design Conference 
is today compared with its 1990 edition and the journey of reconciling diverse Participatory De -
sign communities under the same roof and in an inclusive, equitable manner. While distinctions 
did not seem to exist in the early days of PDC, academic work has dominated the conference’s 
proceedings for almost two decades, and, parallel to and likely because of that, the inclusion of 
non-academic work has declined.
While the work discussed in this chapter has been frequently labelled within the Participatory 
Design Conference community as Participatory Design in Industry, it is here proposed that such 
labelling serves as a narrow lens of the plethora of participatory practice that has emerged over 
the past decade and continues to shape contemporary Participatory Design. Mirroring this sugges-
tion, in Participatory Design Conferences the title of the track focused on this type of work shifted 
over time from Industry (in 2010) to Beyond Academia (2020). Indeed Participatory Design has 
been and continues to be deployed across many areas, beyond what the term industry implies and 
more representative of the diverse range of practices that have and continue to occur outside of 
academia. Areas include (Blomberg, 2014):
• Participatory Design in commercial sectors. This realm includes institutions including cor -
porations, design consultancies, agencies, VC-backed startups, and more where Participatory 
Design practices coincide with capitalist, profit-generating ventures.
• Participatory Design in non-profit sectors. This sector includes entities such as operating 
non-profits, foundations, and other philanthropic organisations. These groups are organised for 
purposes other than generating profits.
• Participatory Design in the public sectors. Here we refer to the work of government and other 
governmental agencies and the way Participatory Design takes shape within those institutions.
As such the kinds of work that has been profiled in the Industry and Beyond Academia track 
in the last ten years are diverse. The 2020 track for example included talks on collaborative 
international learning (Anand and Weinstein, 2020), urban planning in the U.S. (Nautiyal et 
al., 2020), community-led lighting design in Puerto Rico (Vélez and Ortiz González, 2020), 

Participatory Design Beyond Academia
195
political foodscapes in Colombia (Prada, 2020), and hospital design in NZ (Wylie et al., 2020) 
to name a few.
While non-academic Participatory Design practice differs from academic Participatory De -
sign endeavours in many ways, non-academic Participatory Design practice cannot be described 
using one monolithic, stand-alone lens. The space of non-academic practice is vast and the mo -
tivations under which practitioners, organisations, and institutes seek to employ Participatory 
Design (or the value they understand it to bring) differs across the domains and could be seen 
to align, extend, and conflict with some of the original emancipatory values and rights-based 
motivations for Participatory Design. For example, this might include wanting to increase profits 
and usage through user involvement in commercial settings; ensuring better experiences and 
outcomes accessing products and services in health settings; wanting to ensure and foster more 
influence, voice, participation, or leadership of community members in civic, creative, and com -
munity settings; strengthening legislated consultation processes; reframing complex social policy 
issues; or building long-term partnerships and sharing governance and power with communities 
at different levels of government. To capture the breadth of this space we acknowledge these di -
verse areas and reference some throughout the chapter. It is however important to recognise that 
it is impossible to fully capture such a breadth – especially given that a number of practitioners, 
despite the participatory nature of their work, may not label their work as Participatory Design 
or even co-design.
As noted earlier, Participatory Design Conferences over the past decade have surfaced a ten -
sion between academic versus non-academic Participatory Design practice, which also makes it 
difficult to keep visibility of the diversity of Participatory Design beyond academia. This tension 
stems from a variety of factors worth considering. First, the purity of Participatory Design’s values 
as a more democratic and power-balanced approach to design can often feel at odds with for-profit 
contexts. Second, the exclusive nature of many academic contexts (including Participatory Design 
Conferences) frequently alienates commercial, non-profit, and public sector practitioners without 
an academic background or history, creating a sterile ground for participation, cross-pollination, 
and debate. Third, there is evident friction when it comes to the currency used to generate de-
bate around Participatory Design. While in academia the currency is written manuscripts and 
peer-reviewed publications, practitioners are interested in projects, cases, and outcomes – they 
rely on freely available and less formal methods of information dissemination (e.g. blogs and we-
binars), which implies that they get limited value when papers are the dominant tool used to spark 
debate and learn. It is important to also note that the currency is not only a written manuscript: 
it is a manuscript written in English, creating further barriers to a healthy, inclusive discourse. 
Because of these factors, the gap between those in academic versions of Participatory Design 
and those practising Participatory Design elsewhere has widened over time. This is particularly 
evident in the uptake of co-design as a design approach, with many non-academic practitioners 
being unaware of and disconnected from Participatory Design as a design discipline. This dy -
namic has ultimately warranted a context where powerful and important versions of Participatory 
Design outside academia become invisible and hard to track, and where their lack of academic 
lineage makes them discounted as non-Participatory Design. It is here argued that over time the 
academisation of Participatory Design has indirectly and inadvertently excluded many, to a point 
where it is almost impossible to index the full breadth of Participatory Design practice outside of 
academia – limitations that have had an impact on this chapter and should be acknowledged and 
recognised.
While, as discussed later in the chapter, applying Participatory Design in for-profit sectors 
brings a number of challenges to the surface, it is worthwhile considering and questioning whether 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
196
academia is fully immune from these for-profit dynamics, given how academia is itself a for-profit 
institution and part of the broader capitalist construct. Additionally, it is important to recognise 
that academia, like all other contexts, has its own ideology, which in turn drives priorities, modus 
operandi, and, ultimately, outcomes.
This chapter’s position is that contemporary participatory practice has little, and perhaps noth-
ing, to do with such a polarised dissection of the practice. Instead, it is proposed that contemporary 
Participatory Design practice has evolved, hybridised, and grown in multiple, equally meaningful 
approaches outside of academia. New metrics to legitimise those now concretised approaches are 
essential for continued growth in the scope of Participatory Design practice.
Theme 1: Critical Role of Context in Non-Academic Forms of Participatory Design
As mentioned previously, Participatory Design has been and continues to be deployed across many 
areas and this chapter borrows Blomberg’s (2014) approach to defining Participatory Design be-
yond academia to include practice that takes place in commercial, non-profit, and public sectors. 
Drawing dominantly from the enterprise as well as North American and European practice, we 
propose that the specific context in which non-academic Participatory Design takes place impacts 
practitioners as well as their output – at political, strategic, and tactical levels. This first theme 
therefore discusses three types of contextual factors having an impact on Participatory Design 
practice: practical, external, and internal.
Practical Factors
The first practical factor to consider relates to time. In commercial sectors, timelines are typi -
cally tight and stringent due to annual product releases, product development processes, organi -
sational patterns, and fiscal cycles. As a general comparison, a project that may take 12 to 18 
months in academic contexts would need to be closed within three to six months in a for-profit 
environment – at times within even shorter timeframes. While there may be intent and even an 
organisational buy-in for more participatory approaches, timelines have a massive impact on 
designers’ and researchers’ ability to complete work in these contexts, let alone stay within the 
boundaries of idealised Participatory Design practice. Consequently, steps may be compressed, 
activities outsourced, processes hybridised (Loi, 2008) and new methods developed (Romaine, 
2014). In public sector settings, the fast pace demanded by the need for visible outcomes, mile -
stones, and achievement of targets for public accountability often sits in conflict with the time 
needed to build or more often repair relationships with communities who need to participate 
(Shen and Charles, 2022; Wylie et al., 2020).
Entwined with timelines are budgets, budgeting decisions, and prioritisations. The relation -
ship between budgeting decisions and a designer’s ability to stay on top of their preferred process 
has been at the centre of numerous debates and how to guides and blogs (Riggs, 2015; Spence, 
2019). Non-profit organisations are frequently underfunded, resulting in prolonged timelines, 
hybrid practices, and an unreliable cadence of impact. Additionally, donations frequently bring 
to the forefront competing interests from funders, which in some instances cause organisational 
whiplash resulting in stakeholder flip-flopping among desired outcomes. While commercial sec -
tors generally allocate more funding, such funding is frequently at the whim of sudden corporate 
shifts – easily cancelled or dramatically cut. The public sector tends to have more stability yet 
is often impacted by political shifts and related re-prioritisations. Additionally, it is important 
to highlight that while the public sector may communicate an intent to share power and that it 

Participatory Design Beyond Academia
197
operates in a context where participation is often a requirement, such an intent is not always ac-
tualised in practice due to political factors and an unwillingness or lack of capacity to genuinely 
relinquish decision-making processes in meaningful ways (Mark and Hagen, 2020). Alternatively, 
terms such as co-design may be used to make a process of consultation sound more participatory 
than it really is.
A third practical factor to consider relates to the lack of stability in organisational structure 
and leadership makeup, which in non-academic contexts is frequently less stable and reliable, due 
to a variety of factors, including market and political dynamics. For example stakeholders and 
decision-makers may shift or disappear overnight and organisational priorities may suddenly and 
considerably take unpredictable turns; a top priority project may be deprioritised or cancelled; new 
decision-makers may suddenly institute strategic shifts that require complete project makeovers; 
or key team members may be redeployed overnight impacting the ability to successfully complete 
an activity due to sudden competency gaps. This lack of stability, which is less frequent in aca -
demic scenarios, often impacts practitioners’ ability to document and share complete Participatory 
Design efforts, hence stifling the broader community’s opportunity to benefit from key learnings.
A fourth practical factor to consider relates to alignment – cultural, political, and philosophical. 
In academic contexts a Participatory Design practitioner has typically the freedom to explore and 
work somewhat independently, provided work is grounded in credible and extensive literature 
and is methodologically solid. On the other hand, in non-academic contexts, a solid methodology 
and literature foundation have often limited value if compared with key stakeholders’ personal 
opinions, political strategies, or commercial plans. In relation to that, it is important to recognise 
that in many cases a Participatory Design practitioner may not be the final decision maker for 
aspects that are central to their own practice. For example, methodological decisions may be ques-
tioned and shifts imposed by executives, recommendations may be actively occluded when they 
inconveniently do not validate agreed strategies, and participant selection may be actively limited 
or invalidated to ensure a study conforms with executive mandates. Legal or corporate restrictions 
may also limit the pull of participants or the type of engagement. Similar to struggles experienced 
when engaging in any human-centred design practice, Participatory Design often “doesn’t fun -
damentally align with the incentives of the org” (Weaver, 2020), particularly in commercial or 
expert-led settings.
While both academic and non-academic institutions and organisations collaborate across other 
geographies and cultures, a fifth consideration is that, in commercial contexts, the workforce is in-
creasingly geographically dispersed and partially if not fully remote, which further impacts one’s 
ability to ensure, as well as maintain, alignment over the course of a project, due to time zones 
and cultural, political and philosophical tensions. It also could be argued that the geographic dis -
tribution of contemporary commercial organisations creates an opportunity for Participatory De-
sign practitioners to refine their cross-cultural competencies, making their participatory portfolio 
stronger and richer.
Last, but definitely not least, there are practical implications and numerous ramifications re-
lated to a key aspect at the core of Participatory Design: power sharing. Participatory Design or 
co-design practitioners outside academia often attempt to encourage greater power sharing with the 
engaged communities or users, (in big and small ways) even though this may run counter to the ac-
cepted underpinning and prioritised philosophy of the organisation. Practitioners in non-academic 
settings struggle to consistently execute processes based on power sharing in contexts where the 
notion of sharing power is antithetical or new to the organisation itself. In that sense, a full execu-
tion of Participatory Design in commercial, non-profit, and public sectors often calls for consider-
able shifts in how an organisation operates.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
198
External Factors
Related to the practical factors described in the previous section, Participatory Design practitioners 
frequently must engage in a series of activities to maintain the commitment and space for Partici-
patory Design within their organisations. This is required because within these organisations the 
day-to-day work of Participatory Design often is experienced or characterised as time-consuming, 
destabilising, and stressful.
Bringing diverse stakeholders along with the use of Participatory Design practices and the 
implications of this on standard project approaches is a typical competency and responsibility of a 
Participatory Design practitioner. Even when such Participatory Design advocacy occurs in con -
texts where stakeholders are open or willing to embark on the possibilities of the practice, the par-
ticipation of users or communities as experts able to contribute and participate in decision-making 
often is not familiar and can meet with strong opposition. Practitioners are questioned, and teams 
are siloed. Furthermore, while conceptually Participatory Design may be approved and considered 
important at face value, practitioners can receive similar opposition when a project moves from 
conceptual to practical stages.
Because of this dynamic, Participatory Design practitioners can end up directing much of their 
time and efforts toward justifying their craft and evidencing the value of a more participatory 
approach, instead of applying it. This may take the shape of countless marketing attempts to con-
vince others – including team members – that Participatory Design provides value and can be 
executed in diverse contexts. Again, a particularly contentious aspect relates to power sharing, 
as in commercial as well as governmental contexts the notion of sharing power is perceived and 
experienced as destabilising if not against corporate and legal guidelines.
Internal Factors
A final category relates to factors that are internalised by Participatory Design practitioners and 
are often the byproduct of their attempt at disentangling the practical and external factors we 
mentioned previously. These internal factors typically take the form of questionings, doubt, and 
endless hesitations.
Is this authentic?
Can this really be participatory?
Why should we do this?
Is this legitimate?
Who is deciding what?
Who should and can we include?
Authenticity and legitimacy hesitations are frequent, persistent, and even insidious phenomena 
for non-academic practitioners, who push themselves to meet standards that stem from academic 
Participatory Design practice even if such standards may have little relevance outside of academia. 
Because of that, practitioners may relabel their work, offer extensive disclaimers to legitimise their 
efforts or present their work outside of traditional Participatory Design circles. As noted in the ear-
lier section, in the context of the biennial Participatory Design Conference, for instance, organis-
ers have struggled to consistently attract a contingency of non-academic practitioners. Those who 
persevered by attending to be actively included in the programme had to conform to standards that 

Participatory Design Beyond Academia
199
did not represent their craft, reflect their modus operandi, consider their success metrics, and bring 
benefits to their professional careers.
Inclusivity is a theme that emerges also in the context of participant selection and that poses nu-
merous conundrums for non-academic practitioners. While standard practice requires the inclusion 
of diverse participants from diverse perspectives (e.g. age, gender, geography, socio-economic, or 
cultural diversity), application of such standards in non-academic contexts can prove difficult. 
Budgetary constraints may limit one’s ability to include participants from diverse geographies or 
with different linguistic backgrounds.
Additionally, while the public sector in many regions (e.g. Australia) shifted its approach from 
expert-led design of things for people to incorporating co-design by actively involving communi-
ties, power tensions remain. Questions that practitioners in those settings increasingly face include:
How much power can actually be shared?
How much decision-making can be distributed?
Do we have and can we leverage all the needed capabilities?
Is it really possible to commit to co-design in many of the public sector contexts? Or is it really a 
mere dressed-up consultation?
A deeper and more serious aspect of this question is explored in Theme Three with regard to the 
promotion and use of Participatory Design by public and community entities seeking to work with 
and involve Indigenous communities.
Dealing With Practical, Internal, and External Factors
Given the previous considerations, practitioners are encouraged to consider the following op-
portunities and strategies. It is important to acknowledge that the issues discussed in Theme One 
as well as the following recommendations can be applied beyond Participatory Design, to ben -
efit human-centric designers operating in non-academic contexts more generally. That said, it is 
equally important to recognise that issues discussed in Theme One are typically amplified in par -
ticipatory contexts due to one of the necessary conditions for Participatory Design to thrive: power 
sharing. The reader should also know that the following suggestions and strategies are pieces of 
wisdom that authors learned over decades of on-the-ground trials, errors, and successes. They are 
not proposed as the ultimate reference guide but as starting points for those wishing to bring Par -
ticipatory Design outside of academia.
Never Underestimate What Surrounds an Effort
To address issues related to alignment and power sharing, practitioners are called to allocate and 
spend additional time at the start of a project to gain deep insights into context, stakeholders, and 
likely allies. This may not only create the conditions for better alignment but also enable the iden-
tification of additional options, ways forward, and impact opportunities.
Prioritise and Consider Multi-Steps
To address issues that impact one’s ability to drive a participatory effort given aggressive timeline 
constraints, it is key that one carefully identifies which sections of a project are must-haves (versus 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
200
nice-to-haves). It is equally crucial that one crafts strategies as well as methodologies to enable 
multiple, complementary results that can be distributed over time.
Keep Key Goals in the Forefront
To be in a position to ensure that key participatory goals are kept at the forefront, practitioners 
should consider outsourcing nice-to-have sections of a project. This will ensure that prioritised 
areas can receive all the focus they need given constraints.
Compress Timelines But Do Not Compromise Quality
Given the pressure that practitioners receive and its impact on participatory goals, a good strategy 
is to compress timelines while challenging established organisational processes and ensuring that 
the overall quality of the must-haves is not compromised.
Underpromise and Overdeliver
Given likely organisational and political shifts, a key antidote is to build into timelines, budget re-
quests, and process outlines for extra buffers. This will enable practitioners to maintain full control 
over their ability to successfully complete the project regardless of sudden shifts, while ensuring 
they do not have to compromise their participatory goals and having a line of sight of what they 
promised in light of what they can deliver.
Be Clear on Timelines and Impacts
To ensure successful outcomes from a stakeholder as well as participatory perspective, one must 
ensure that stakeholders (especially business ones, such as sponsors) are clear from day one on 
what timelines are required for a successful outcome and, if such timelines must be shortened, that 
they are well aware of likely consequences and pitfalls – not only on the project but also on their 
business’ goals.
Do Not Underestimate Advocacy
In for-profit and policy sectors particularly, practitioners will likely (and often) find them -
selves in loops of participatory advocacy. Besides being fearful advocates of key processes 
and methods, they may have to devote considerable quality time to educating stakeholders 
and allies. While this role is crucial and unavoidable, practitioners are encouraged to equip 
themselves to avoid it becoming a full-time job impacting their ability to achieve their project 
goals.
Identify and Recruit Powerful Allies
To counterbalance likely pressure from a project’s main stakeholders and sponsors and in light 
of the previous point about advocacy, a good strategy is to recruit powerful allies and sponsors 
in complementary departments and teams, as they may provide practical and political support in 
exchange for gaining benefits from the effort.

Participatory Design Beyond Academia
201
Predict and Plan
Since the foundations of an effort are frequently shaken by many forces, practitioners should fore-
cast what negative impacts could emerge, based on prior patterns. This will enable them to have a 
line of sight and clarity on which factors and stakeholders may impact or shift a project and create 
alternative paths to achieve key goals ahead of time.
Adapt and Flex Processes
Since outside academia change and shifts are typically not an if but a when, practitioners are called 
to monitor the context surrounding their efforts on an ongoing basis and be open to adapting their 
methods and processes if needed, while ensuring their key goals and quality metrics are kept in 
the forefront.
Challenge and Stretch
Given described internal factors impacting practitioners on an ongoing basis, it is important one 
is prepared to challenge personal assumptions as well as to question, adapt or contextualise one’s 
established participatory processes, and to develop novel methodologies that may better fit the 
context.
Be Authentic and Open to Growth
Participatory Design practice is constantly evolving and so should those who fold Participatory 
Design in their work. For practitioners such growth is often a frequent and accelerated reality. 
Given that, they are encouraged to ask hard questions and to embrace hard questions in return.
Apply Participatory Design to Cross-Team Dynamics
Given that much of the pressure that practitioners experience originates from human-to-human 
dynamics, one can consider leveraging Participatory Design practice to create work conditions 
that will benefit their ultimate Participatory Design goals.
Theme 2: Practical Implications of Applying Participatory Design Approaches 
Beyond Academic Environments
While Participatory Design practice leverages diverse approaches, a number of contextual factors 
greatly impact their effectiveness, regardless of the approach. While we acknowledge the con-
stantly evolving nature of Participatory Design methods (Kensing and Blomberg, 1998), in this 
section we overview how common methods (Gibbons, 2018; Sanders and Dandavate, 1999) are 
applied in non-academic contexts; discuss how practitioners can best embody Participatory De -
sign’s inherent emancipatory goals when leveraging such methods; and offer a series of contextual 
considerations. Although we focus on Participatory Design in non-academic contexts, many of the 
considerations raised may also apply to academic contexts.
To document what people think and say, practitioners leverage methods that, largely akin to 
what one would find in ethnographic practice, include interviews, surveys, and focus groups. 
These all offer different possibilities for a Participatory Design focus. In interviews and focus 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
202
groups, open-ended, not leading questions, provide avenues for generativity and participant 
agency as well as an opportunity to distribute power to participants. Participatory Design 
approaches can extend these possibilities to cases where interviewers invite participants to 
co-create dialogue instead of a more structured interview process. While focus groups also 
have the potential to afford a more problem-posing structure (Freire, 2020), time and resource 
constraints often limit a truly liberatory think/say understanding phase, meaning that good 
intent to include more participatory power-sharing practices may run the risk of reinforcing a 
more conventional design power dynamic that places participants in the driver seat but with a 
pre-determined structure to ensure certain outcomes. In the case of surveys, due to their asyn -
chronous nature, extractive research practices are often reinforced, and open-ended dialogue 
is rare. This issue can be partially mitigated by providing the space for participants to provide 
feedback or input they deem relevant. Additionally, when it comes to insights analysis and 
use throughout the design process, the agency typically remains with the practitioner, and a 
shared power dynamic is rare.
To understand what participants do, experienced design researchers and Participatory Design 
researchers typically leverage field and usability studies. The former involves observing partici -
pants in the context in which the design will be used (Burgess, 2002) and may risk being one-sided. 
In more conventional design thinking practice, practitioner teams often dictate the terms of the 
engagement and assume reciprocity through compensation of participants’ time. While monetary 
compensation is a starting point, this is only just the beginning of levelling the power dynamic 
between practitioners and participants. To increase the participatory nature of a field study, design 
teams should consider involving participants in the design of the study including the criteria for 
observation, agenda setting, and so on. Usability studies, a method familiar to commercial product 
and service contexts, often involve gathering a group of participants and asking them to complete 
tasks or use a product or service in a controlled setting (Nielsen, 1994). In these settings, organisa-
tions have historically dictated the agenda and set of tasks. Practitioners interested in increasing 
participant agency can advocate to co-observe and co-analyse data with participants, and in effect, 
cultivate greater opportunities for mutual learning.
To uncover and understand what people feel to enrich the ideation process, design practition-
ers continuously explore and develop new tactics, tools, and techniques. The first well-known 
technique – Cultural Probes (Gaver et al., 1999) – incorporates a highly context-dependent 
and creative design effort in both creation and curation. This method can often be exclusive to 
expert-led design teams, leading to a lopsided power dynamic. While there have been discus -
sions (Loi, 2007) focused on Cultural Probe alternatives that shift the power dynamic, distribute 
agency, and question who should design them, these tools are traditionally not participatory in 
how they are developed in academic as well as non-academic contexts. However, when applied 
with a Participatory Design lens, cultural probe design can and should be a participatory act. 
Participants can be invited to co-create kits (artefacts and questions) and distribute of them (Loi, 
2007).
To document ideas, brainstorming is a common method to encourage participants to share 
ideas without fear of judgement, freely (Osborn, 1953). When applied as a Participatory Design 
technique, it is an opportunity to generate and gather the ideas and perspectives of a range of dif -
ferent people, who can then work collectively to both theme them through affinity diagramming 
(Pernice, 2018) and then build concepts or prototypes together. Unlike brainstorming, affinity 
diagramming is an activity that may more frequently fall on practitioners, sometimes by con-
straints but also by choice. It is not uncommon to find stakeholders unwilling to delegate power 
to participants in synthesising divergent ideas. The Participatory Design practitioner has a role 

Participatory Design Beyond Academia
203
in advocating to continue with participants in this step, since it often provides lenses into more 
diverse conceptual groupings.
To capture experiences, journey maps are typically used to describe an individual’s steps 
through a given event, such as completing a task or achieving a goal (Howard, 2014). Two com -
mon forms of journey mapping focus on the existing state and desirable, viable future states. The 
first, focused on identifying pain points, frustrations, and areas for improvement, is by its very 
nature a participatory one. Without participants, the practitioner would have to make assumptions 
for each step and its emotional effect based on prior data or research. The second, building off of 
existing journey maps, focuses on significant pain points, converting them into opportunities that 
enable the design of new solutions. It is often during this last step, when future states are imagined, 
where including participants may bear fruit, since it unlocks participants’ imaginations, inviting 
them into the ideation process.
Finally, to document opportunities, sketching and prototyping methods are used, leveraging a 
wide range of tools – from architectural models to physical or software-based paper prototypes. 
These methods are well-known in established design teams, and participatory approaches straight-
forwardly invite participants in as co-designers in sketching and prototyping processes. While 
participatory approaches may be more easily incorporated into these methods, Participatory De -
sign practitioners can continue to advocate for greater frequency and duration of them in design 
engagements.
Spectrum of Participant Agency
Good design is good business.
– quote from T.J. Watson (IBM, n.d.-b)
One could argue that Participatory Design is good business. If we displace design agency to the 
real people impacted or engaged in a design experience, they are more likely to want to take 
part in it. This mindset, utilised by some of the champions of Participatory Design practice in 
non-academic spaces, has proved only sometimes successful in employing Participatory Design 
methods in project work (V ogel, 2021). The transfer of agency in Participatory Design practice 
will always fall on a spectrum. Methods focused on understanding what participants think and say, 
by their very nature, have the potential to prioritise participant agency. This transfer of agency is 
often supported by stakeholders from many enterprises since organisations of all contexts have a 
vested interest in meeting participant needs or in civic contexts encouraging greater participation 
of citizens. On the other hand, the appetite for methods that fall under what participants feel and 
that draw upon their expertise and creativity such as ideation efforts, depends on the specific cul -
tural makeup of a design team and stakeholder interest.
The challenge for Participatory Design practitioners, however, often falls in the framing of 
these Participatory Design methods. Stakeholders in the for-profit sector are beholden to profit 
maximisation, which trickles down into quarterly goals and metrics for sales, adoption, and so 
on. Non-profit organisations are not immune to the pressures of capitalist forces either. Whereas 
for-profit organisations need to prove efficacy to shareholders, non-profit organisations often have 
obligations to donors, albeit sometimes less transparent. Despite these pressures, sharing power 
and influence with participants should be the ultimate goals to realise the emancipatory potential 
of Participatory Design practice. At a bare minimum, addressing participant needs should be pri-
oritised in all contexts since it’s rare to find products and services that do not do so and still remain 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
204
revenue-generating or effective. Actions taken in light of these pressures determine where on the 
spectrum of participant agency all methods fall.
As previously stated, organisational culture plays a large role in where design methods will fall 
on the discussed spectrum. A common trend in commercial contexts is to anticipate participant 
needs. One may even go so far as to say that for-profit organisations have a vested interest in gen-
erating desire to increase sales and profit (McGowan, 2017). Economic forces shape the organisa-
tional output in such a way that the for-profit sector produces products that not only seek to address 
needs but interpret them in more innovative and even disruptive ways. This way of thinking is 
perhaps best summarised by the tired quote designers often hear in self-described innovation sec-
tors: “If I had asked people what they wanted, they would have said faster horses” (Walsh, 2017). 
One can very well see how this interpretation by design teams provides a vast, ambiguous window 
where participation stops after a few brief interviews, focus groups, and so on. From our experi -
ence, Participatory Design methods can be stymied early in the process due to external pressures 
on the survival of an organisation, which do not place Participatory Design as part of the critical 
path for a design project.
Despite these pressures, tides may be changing. The Design Justice movement, which advo -
cates for ten core principles in line with many facets of Participatory Design practice, continues 
to gain prominence outside academia (Costanza-Chock, 2020). Designers from all contexts attend 
meetings and advocate for a greater embodiment of the core principles, which seek to transfer 
greater agency to participants. The momentum of this space has both an internal and external ef -
fect. Internally, it alters the interest of stakeholders in making hiring decisions for designers. If 
designers believe in greater participant agency that may mean they are less inclined to work for 
organisations focused on expert-led design. An organisation interested in pursuing the familiar 
course has the potential to negatively impact their workforce. Externally, Participatory Design 
becomes a vehicle for greater product or service adoption. As more individuals gain awareness 
and concern over how things are made, adoption values may shift to align with enterprises that are 
employing greater Participatory Design practice in the design process itself.
Goal-Setting, Project Planning, and Success Measurement
Both external and internal constraints will determine the trajectory of a design effort and the de-
gree of Participatory Design practice that will be supported. As previously discussed, timelines 
and budgets are the first set of hard constraints, which determine project scope, staffing, research 
budgets, and so on.
In most settings, teams align on project outcomes, and in best-case scenarios, outcomes are 
co-created with participants, or at the very least, derived from methods involving what participants 
say and do. However, outcomes are instead, in some projects, derived from stakeholder hypotheses 
or hunches. Even if an organisation’s governance and decision-making structure will ultimately 
determine which outcomes are approved and how, in these “stakeholder hunches” cases, practi -
tioners can leverage curiosity as a tool to strategically realign teams to consider participants’ inclu-
sion. Questioning the origin of a stakeholder’s hunch or rationale can be a fruitful practice to raise 
stakeholder awareness of gaps or blind spots.
Project plans and schedules often unfold from these agreed-upon outcomes and contain milestones 
and deliverables that are punctuated with artefacts to drive convergence on a design solution. Com-
monly used frameworks and design processes used by practitioners include the Design Council’s 
Double Diamond (Design Council, 2022), IDEO’s Design Thinking framework (IDEO, n.d.), and 

Participatory Design Beyond Academia
205
bespoke design processes shepherded by various enterprises and organisations (IBM, n.d.-a; Knapp, 
2016; Knapp et al., 2016). Typically, these processes follow distinct up-front research, ideation, and 
deployment/testing phases. While the past decade has seen an increase in more equity-driven design 
frameworks, such as Equity-centred Community Design (Creative Reaction Lab, n.d.) and Libera-
tory Design (National Equity Project, n.d.), non-academic Participatory Design practice often infuses 
itself within conventional design practice and not the other way around. Thus, the responsibility often 
falls on the shoulders of Participatory Design practitioners to advocate for greater transfers of agency 
to participants – not just in up-front research phases but also through the solutioning process itself. 
This intentionality should begin when setting outcomes to ensure that those outcomes have been 
voiced by participants through real-world mutual learning. This has greater potential to cascade into 
Participatory Design-oriented milestones and success metrics.
As previously mentioned, “feel” methods leave room for organisational interpretation, and 
ideation methods are often reserved for expert design teams in the infamous ivory tower (Shapin, 
2012). To mitigate lightweight co-design approaches or, even worse, participant omission from 
ideation phases, we advocate for Participatory Design practitioners to get more deeply involved 
in project planning and milestone setting. The construction of specific goals and milestones that 
involve adequate participant involvement in ideation phases can provide greater clarity to stake-
holders and help curb misunderstandings around what is meant by co-design.
Advocating for Participatory Design
Designers are used to advocating for the user, which often goes hand-in-hand with the argument 
of having a seat at the table. While the prominence of designers in executive roles has increased 
(Ireland and Giudice, 2013), incorporating Participatory Design approaches in the design process 
may still be a fringe set of activities.
To better advocate for spaces of mutual learning, Participatory Design practitioners should first 
understand the governance structure of the spaces in which they operate. A good initial question 
to consider is: where is power centred and who yields it? Knowing where decisions are made is 
key to impacting stakeholders. A second strategy that Participatory Design practitioners should 
consider is illustrating and stressing how organisational goals should/could align with participants’ 
needs and how such an approach can lead to improved quantitative and qualitative evaluations of 
success, such as net promoter scores and testimonials. Third, Participatory Design practitioners 
can demonstrate and stress the growing acceptance of Participatory Design as a vehicle for ex -
perience design discovery phases (Pobiner and Murphy, 2018). While experienced Participatory 
Design practitioners know that Participatory Design is not limited to the up-front part of a con -
ventional design process, the inclusion of Participatory Design at the start serves as an entry point 
and mechanism for the progressive gains of its adoption. Lastly, Participatory Design practitioners 
should better understand the specific design frameworks that their organisations rely upon. Since 
there are many flavours of the design process, a better understanding of an organisation’s unique 
approach can help highlight lightweight ways to increase degrees of participation and serve as an 
avenue for continuous improvement of liberatory processes.
Equitable Outcomes
Once Participatory Design is accepted as a go-to approach for a given project, practitioners need 
to embrace a number of considerations to ensure equitable outcomes for all parties. In this section, 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
206
we briefly cover important considerations in relation to participant selection, study compensation, 
and intellectual property (IP) implications. Given the complexity and richness of each of these 
areas, we introduce each to raise awareness and encourage Participatory Design practitioners to 
delve deeper on their own terms.
Bias can easily creep into any design and research process and participant selection is a classic 
process step where biases might emerge. Participatory Design approaches are not immune from 
this risk and there are numerous sources to consult when selecting participants (Sherif, 1998). The 
most common forms of bias that arise in participant selection are:
• Selection Bias, which occurs when selected participants are not representative of a target popu-
lation, likely skewing the results of the engagement. An example of this is a Participatory 
Design practitioner selecting friends and family as opposed to participants who may be more 
representative and appropriate.
• Homogeneity bias, which occurs when selected participants are similar in some way (e.g. age, 
gender, culture, education level, and socio-economic status). The effect of this bias is limited 
diversity in perspectives and ideas, leading to limited or narrow outcomes, which may com -
pound dominant ideas and worldviews.
• Confirmation bias, which occurs when information is gathered in ways that confirm preexisting 
beliefs or assumptions, ultimately limiting the types of ideas that are generated and even the 
ability to address participant needs. Stakeholders facing external pressures often fall victim to 
this bias and select participants who confirm their existing hypotheses.
Being mindful of how bias can arise during participant selection helps Participatory Design prac-
titioners mitigate skewed outcomes, increase their ability to develop equitable outcomes, and help 
promote bias awareness to benefit broader teams.
In any effort to ask for people’s active involvement, an important ethical consideration is 
to remunerate participants for their time. Participatory Design practice can be quite demand -
ing of participants and compensating them appropriately for their efforts is very important. 
While remuneration will vary depending on organisational context, to be equitable, consider 
compensating participants at the rate of an entry-level designer. Pay equity in the design 
field is a topic of much debate (Smith, 2018), yet those conversations do not often extend to 
participants for their contributions. Regardless, for an equitable design process, participants 
should be compensated appropriately for their time and effort since they are helping shape 
desired outcomes.
Participatory Design and design more broadly are rife with ethical, legal, and IP implications. 
When practitioners seek to transfer greater agency to participants, who should ultimately receive 
credit for outcomes? How should that credit be distributed? These questions get particularly com-
plex in the face of IP conversations. Some for-profit enterprises seek to patent their ideas leaving 
participants uncredited, unmentioned, and unable to receive royalties from their contributions. 
While practices vary by company and geography and some firms have a more equitable IP ap -
proach, it is unlikely that these circumstances will change in many contexts, as patent-seeking 
for-profit organisations desire to maximise their ideas’ earning potential. However, Participatory 
Design practitioners, armed with the awareness of these outcomes, can seek to shift conversations 
internally. The next era of Participatory Design practice in non-academic spaces has the opportu-
nity to shift power dynamics in ways that may level the playing field in service of both desirable 
and equitable outcomes.

Participatory Design Beyond Academia
207
Theme 3: Issues and Questions Surrounding Western Participatory Design 
Approaches in Existing Indigenous Innovation Practice Settings
Previous sections of this chapter explored some of the strengths, challenges, and evolutions of Par-
ticipatory Design beyond academia, particularly in not-profit, public sector, and commercial do-
mains. This third theme continues to look at the use of Participatory Design with emphasis on the 
public, health, and social sectors, specifically looking at ethical implications and questions raised 
by applying what can be described as Western or Eurocentric Participatory Design and co-design 
approaches (like those discussed earlier) in contexts of existing Indigenous innovation practice. 
In particular, the section focuses on the tensions of applying such approaches where Indigenous 
practices have been oppressed or historically dismissed by Western lenses through colonisation.
As previously noted, Participatory Design (or co-design) has been rapidly adopted in re-
cent years – this is particularly true within the public sector in contexts such as Aotearoa NZ, and 
Australia. In these regions co-design is currently and frequently a requirement for new policies 
and services and when working with Indigenous communities in social, environmental, and health 
policy and service settings there is an expectation that co-design will be the go-to approach. Given 
the rich documentation that exists from these regions, this chapter’s third theme focuses primarily 
on practices and experiences in Australia and Aotearoa NZ to explore a number of important con-
siderations that may likely benefit Participatory Design practitioners in other regions.
The theme starts with the broader context in which Western Participatory Design and co-design 
in Australia and NZ needs to be considered. Second, it highlights some of the specific issues that 
have arisen in the application of Participatory Design and co-design. Third, it explores practice 
that operates at the intersection of Indigenous and Western participatory approaches, including 
how Indigenous and non-Indigenous practice evolved by integrating different perspectives and 
ways of knowing, or superseded co-design altogether in reclamation of Indigenous approaches. 
The theme concludes by posing some questions for consideration for those wishing to apply Par -
ticipatory Design and co-design in such contexts.
The Broader Context for Participatory Design
Firstly, it is important to understand why co-design is so often applied in public, health, and so-
cial sectors as a way to work with Indigenous communities around complex social and economic 
challenges. As stated by Wakefield (2019) when reflecting on co-design within Māori spaces, 
Indigenous communities have been the subject of past (and ongoing) acts of racist violence and 
oppression and are also frequently the focus of innovation and co-design efforts ostensibly aimed 
at “lifting the health and social outcomes” of these communities. The risk is for co-design to oc -
cur as an attempt to appear like power sharing and as if action is being undertaken, but without 
governmental shifts or acknowledgements of the underlying behaviours or structures that caused 
harm in the first place. In the words of Nyikina and Nyul Nyul woman Sara Bergmann, “As a 
result, Indigenous people get the same outcomes as before under the disguise of new inclusive 
practices, and a better public perception for those businesses and organizations. Co-design is con-
sultation, rebranded” (Bergmann, 2021). In a similar vein, Indigenous communities in NZ and 
Australia have been the subjects of research for many decades, often resulting in inaction or further 
harm (Cram, 2012 in Wakefield, 2019). There is a justified mistrust of those coming from Euro -
centric and Western perspectives to offer help or to ask for input/feedback/time and labour from 
Indigenous communities, organisations, and families (NSW ACI, 2021; Shen and Charles, 2022; 
Wakefield, 2019). Those seeking to apply and evolve Participatory Design and co-design with 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
208
and within Indigenous communities and on behalf of government teams must do so with a critical 
awareness of this broader context. Without such an awareness, any attempt to bring participatory 
value is likely to contribute to further harm.
The potential confluence between the values and the relational, participatory emphasis of 
co-design and Indigenous ways of being and doing has been recognised (including by Indigenous 
practitioners). Referencing Davis (2018), Wakefield (2019) refers to the potential for co-design 
to occupy a nexus in which Western and Māori knowledge around the engaging community can 
be synergised. Wakefield (2019) notes that while co-design is not an Indigenous methodology, “it 
can be seen to confer a Pākehā [NZer of European descent] meaning to practices that are implicit 
within Māoritanga [Māori way of life/culture/practices]” and adds that there are “distinctive har -
monies in the values which underpin both which translate into the practical considerations in the 
application of co-design.”
At the same time, significant caution and wariness remain (NSW ACI, 2021; Schollum-  
Whaanga et al., 2020; TACSI, 2020; Wren, 2019). Depending on how and by whom it is practised, 
“Co-design risks being an imported process that perpetuates colonial and Eurocentric mindsets and 
values” (Mark and Hagen, 2020). Rather than supporting communities, poorly practised co-design 
has the potential to further marginalise people, and by increasing the use of co-design the risk for 
its misuse also increases (Schollum-Whaanga et al., 2020). Co-design brings value only if prac-
tised genuinely and with respect, if one acknowledges histories of harm and mistrust as a result of 
historic action, and when Indigenous processes are the basis of engagement. Meaningful efforts 
to co-design with Indigenous communities must be centred on existing wisdoms, knowledge, and 
strengths and serve to further self-determination (Davis, 2018; Shen and Charles, 2022; Tangaere, 
2021). This sentiment is strongly articulated in Bergmann’s piece (Bergmann, 2021), Co-design or 
Conspiracy. An important aspect of understanding Participatory Design beyond academia is criti-
quing the adoption and enthusiasm for co-design within governments and organisations from this 
broader context.
Participatory Design in Public and Social Sectors: Issues and Tensions
In reviewing discussions, blogs, presentations, and publications by Indigenous practitioners and 
communities as well as those working with them, a number of issues and challenges can be identi-
fied, all demonstrating how the enthusiasm for applying co-design and Participatory Design has 
been problematic. These include:
• The problematic use of co-design by non-Indigenous practitioners to research or organise In -
digenous communities’ participation and practitioners’ inability to support culturally appropri-
ate protocols and perspectives (Wehipeihana et al., 2018).
• The use of co-design to re-brand what is a mere consultation process or good initial intent fol-
lowed by an inability to share power or decision-making when appropriate (Bergmann, 2021).
• Timing, project, and financial constraints that are not compatible with prioritising relationships, 
rebuilding trust, or responding in the context of trauma and harm (Mark and Hagen, 2020; Shen 
and Charles, 2022; Wehipeihana et al., 2018).
• The “dressing up” of Western concepts and methods to appear Indigenous through the use of 
Indigenous terms and concepts (Schollum-Whaanga et al., 2020).
• Use of co-design methods without cultural grounding or context, including emphasising the 
co-design process over kaupapa [purpose] or relationships, or the use of culturally unsafe or 
harmful spaces or practices (Shen and Charles, 2022).

Participatory Design Beyond Academia
209
In addition to these issues, Western co-design processes are often focused on the human and indi-
vidual experience, omitting or ignorant to dimensions and perspectives that are central to Indig-
enous world views. For example: relationship to land, country, and place; ensuring Te Taiao [the 
environment] is at the centre; and connection to tūpuna [ancestors], whakapapa [connections], 
history, customary practices, knowledges and wisdoms. As Bergmann (2021) emphasises, “When 
Indigenous people are part of the creation process, have all the information and understand the 
problem, they can tap into thousands of years of knowledge to create appropriate, fit-for-purpose 
solutions that work for everyone.” This speaks to the cultural knowing and depth of knowledge 
that may not be recognised or understood by Participatory Design or by Western practitioners 
generally.
Problematic again is the presentation and promotion of co-design and Participatory Design and 
their associated processes of systems thinking and approaches as new, without recognition of the 
existing innovation and participatory practices already present (and with long histories) in Indig-
enous communities. As Shen and Charles (2022) states, “We already think in complex systems 
and family systems.” Much of what co-design seeks to introduce is understood as the natural way 
of working with whānau [family] (Schollum-Whaanga et al., 2020) – or as Materoa Mar (Ngati 
Whātua, Ngati Porou) well puts it: “Indigenous communities in New Zealand have a long history 
of doing this work” (Mar and Walden, 2021).
This discussion highlights some of the tensions that emerged for practitioners seeking to under-
stand the role of Participatory Design and co-design in places such as Australia and Aotearoa NZ. 
There is also extensive work to develop participatory approaches that more effectively balance 
and draw upon Indigenous and Western world views. Many of these approaches involve govern-
ment teams working with Indigenous practitioners (internally or externally to the organisation) to 
develop processes and frameworks that better centre Indigenous worldviews (including cultural 
values, practices, and protocols) to ensure the integration and use of culturally grounded method-
ologies as the starting point or to bring specific cultural expertise into the design process. There 
is no given set of Participatory Design techniques that can be universally applied, place and the 
knowledge and practices of place matters.
One example, shared in the Beyond Academia track of PDC2020, is the work of Ara Manawa, 
a health innovation team based in Tāmaki, Auckland. The team notes: “Methods honouring 
bi-cultural values are especially relevant in public health care, as government bodies recognise 
our colonial history and work to change its legacy of inequitable health outcomes for Māori” 
(Wylie et al., 2020). Their project to redesign the whānau rooms at the hospital was an opportu -
nity to apply a co-design framework that not only enabled genuine enactment of the government’s 
commitment to Māori and to partnership with Māori but also highlighted the challenges created 
by timeframes, fiscal constraints, and the need to regain trust with Māori communities previ -
ously harmed by government actions. In particular, the philosophical conflict between authentic 
co-design and the requirements of business processes in public institutions (Wylie et al., 2020). 
Both Te Morenga et al. (2018) and Wehipeihana et al. (2018) describe the integration of Participa-
tory Design and kaupapa Māori and other Indigenous approaches in the development of different 
health initiatives with Māori and Pacific communities, demonstrating the need to rework Western 
methods for them to become useful in these settings. Emerging from this is a need to ensure that 
the expectations on what “co-design” means are clear for design teams, Māori communities, and 
providers. Linked to this, Māori practitioner Debbie Goodwin (2021) has developed an evalua -
tion framework that looks at participation and co-design through the lens of Māori communities 
and practitioners and provides criteria for whether the things that matter to Māori communities 
have been upheld within a design process.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
210
The Agency for Clinical Innovation (NSW Government), supported by Indigenous team mem-
bers, has recently shared its approach to working together with Aboriginal communities (NSW 
ACI, 2021), in which the integration of Aboriginal ways of being, doing, and knowing is under -
stood as critical to building health care with and for Aboriginal communities. Their approach 
works across the intersection of Indigenous and Western knowledge and approaches drawing on 
the Aboriginal pedagogical framework developed by Tyson Yunkaporta (NSW ACI, 2021). Indig-
enous team members emphasise for those wanting to co-design with Aboriginal people the impor-
tance of bringing your whole self (not your skill set); knowing who you are; making clear your 
own role and where you fit in; working from values and relationships; and demonstrating your 
commitment to working with Aboriginal people – for example, by truly acknowledging the people 
of the land where you are meeting, and being true to the words spoken in that commitment.
2 These 
aspects are all emphasised as ways to demonstrate that the commitment to co-design is authentic 
and that power sharing and listening are not token gestures.
The Australian social innovation organisation TACSI is also working at the intersection of 
co-design and Indigenous knowledges and uses co-design in ways that acknowledge the harm 
done to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities and the context of Australia’s colonial 
history (TACSI, 2020). Guided and led by Aunty Vicky, a cultural leader at TACSI, their tools help 
to forefront the kinds of questions and capabilities that need to be developed by those seeking to 
work with Indigenous communities. Key aspects of this include the role of allyship: what it looks 
like, what it means, and how it is threaded through one’s work whether the focus is on Indigenous 
communities or not.
Reclamation of Indigenous-Led Innovation and Design Practices
There is a growing body of literature about Participatory Design in the context of Indigenous com-
munities and more specifically decolonisation and Participatory Design (Charlotte Smith et al., 
2020; Kambunga et al., 2021; Klaveren, 2018; Talhouk and Armouch, 2022; Wilde et al., 2022), 
including Chapter 5 of this book. Alongside the development of co-design approaches that are 
localised and culturally grounded, within non-academic settings there is also growing visibility 
of practices that supersede Western Participatory Design or co-design, by returning to or starting 
within culture and cultural practice. Such participatory processes reclaim existing Indigenous in-
novation practices and ways of knowing, doing and being.
For example, Māori practitioner Karl Wixon (Waitaha, Kati Mamoe, Kāi Tahu, Ngati Toa Ran-
gatira, Moriori) talks about the Western cultural constructs from which co-design originates, and 
the balancing act needed between tikanga [customary practices and protocol] and design tools, ul-
timately moving past this to encourage whakapapa-led design where for example the kawa and ti-
kanga of marae [the protocols of traditional meeting houses] are the process (Wixon, 2022). These 
ways of being, doing, and designing recognise and make visible (again) Indigenous-led methods 
and reclaim practices that start in place, culture, and country draw from existing knowledge and 
wisdoms and are more rightly used in these contexts than Western-led co-design methods.
Tangaere (2021) also describes a design process that, while initially informed by co-design 
methodologies, is now firmly grounded and driven by Indigenous knowledge and approaches, led 
by whānau Māori [Māori families] themselves, held by tikanga [cultural protocols] and grounded 
in place. Her work emphasises that cultural values and customary practices are inherently about 
complexity, innovation, and learning and she links such approaches to mana motuhake and ran-
gatiratanga [autonomy, self-determination, sovereignty, agency] (Tangaere and Hagen, 2023). 
Tangaere stresses it is not about including Māori voices or whānau Māori as simple participants, 

Participatory Design Beyond Academia
211
but about whānau leadership. This imperative for leadership by Indigenous people and via Indig-
enous knowledge systems is reinforced by Shen and Charles (2022) who affirm that ultimately for 
responses to be meaningful and sustainable they need to come from Indigenous communities who 
have the experience and understand what is required – they need to be Indigenous-led. This has 
significant implications for government or health and social organisations seeking to “co-design 
solutions” with Indigenous communities.
Tokona te Raki, the innovation arm of iwi [tribe] Ngāi Tahu, is another group visibly sharing their 
Indigenous-led design practices having returned to these roots after exploring other Western approaches. 
In describing their Indigenous practice Te Korekoreka, they write that “the four realms of Te Kore-
koreka are an opportunity for us to apply our traditional knowledge of creation to the complex chal-
lenges we face today. Te Korekoreka is a way to reconnect with our own mātauraka [Māori knowledge] 
and to reclaim the future-making mindset of our ancestors. Te Korekoreka is a way to use our own 
cultural knowledge to help us imagine and navigate towards a new future” (Tokona Te Raki, 2022). 
The group is explicit about the limitations of Western models to achieve meaningful transformation:
It is no longer credible to keep using imported Western frameworks to try to fix the harm 
done by imported Western systems within Aotearoa. Instead, we need to trust our own In-
digenous knowledge and use these to create our own systems that work for Māori. Te Kore-
koreka is our way of doing this.
(Tokona Te Raki, 2022)
Such approaches are also reflected in the work of Barbarich et al. (Barbarich et al., n.d.), who 
reject Western tools, prioritise designing through an Indigenous lens, and claim that as design 
strategists, researchers and practitioners they find that “design methodologies are euro-centric 
and homogenising,” that they “don’t allow for cultural rights, perspectives, knowledge or ways 
of being” and that “conventional design methodologies are colonising and exclusionary.” Among 
many other similar examples, Shultz a Gamilaraay man of Aboriginal Australian and European 
Australian descent describes Decolonising Design as a space for design working outside of the 
confines of the Anglo-European one world system (Shultz, 2021). Shultz’s work starts outside 
of these Western concepts and begins instead with Indigenous-led methods that centre on cul-
ture and peoples. In a hui [gathering] that brought together practitioners from across Aotearoa 
to discuss Māori Co-design Ethics, it was agreed that existing Māori cultural practices hold 
the why, who, and the how for process within co-design in Aotearoa (Schollum-Whaanga et 
al., 2020). A key focus of the discussion was also on the need to grow Indigenous capability 
and recognition of Indigenous processes and practices across government as well as provid -
ers, practitioners, and participating whānau and community. At the same time, there is a need 
to “quality control” non-Indigenous practice and cast a critical lens over whether it is useful 
(Schollum-Whaanga et al., 2020).
Considerations and Questions for Participatory Design and Co-Design Practitioners
To complete the discussion of this third theme we note some key considerations and reflective 
questions for practitioners operating beyond academia, with an emphasis on non-Indigenous 
practitioners.
The first consideration is a recognition of multiple world views. Shultz (2021) highlights the 
fact that Indigenous folks and practitioners are always operating in (at least) two worlds, drawing 
on the concept of border thinking. This requirement to understand that there are different worlds 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
212
operating and that we might need to move beyond, negotiate across, and certainly give more bal-
ance to Indigenous worldviews is work for Western thinking to do.
The second is a greater understanding of being and creating relationships in the context of pain and 
loss. Communities are often working within the context of multiple burdens and, as Shen describes it, 
are “holding such loss and pain, and then trying to make a system work” (Shen and Charles, 2022). 
Participatory Design and co-design practitioners working alongside Indigenous communities need 
the capability to hold and operate from a cultural context and this wider context of trauma and pain.
A third key consideration is about actively ensuring safe spaces. This refers to safe spaces for 
Indigenous practitioners to do and be in cultural ways, as well as safe spaces for non-Indigenous 
and Indigenous people to do unlearning, recognising, positioning, and letting go. This includes 
non-Indigenous and allies having honest and challenging conversations. Creating time and space 
for these things needs to be a priority even though it might clash with factors like time constraints 
as noted earlier in the chapter.
A fourth consideration is about allyship. Shen generously offers several points of guidance for 
non-Indigenous co-design practitioners (Shen and Charles, 2022). Firstly, that allyship means: “work 
to support the self-determination of aboriginal people in the co-design process and in true partner-
ship.” Such work requires “a deep willingness to really work in partnership with people, to ensure 
they deeply listen and learn and seek guidance and direction on the right protocol and ways of work-
ing” (Shen and Charles, 2022). These efforts imply a need for Participatory Design practitioners to be 
self-reflective; have cultural humility and respect; challenge the barriers to structural racism as well 
as individual and organisational white privilege; reflect on our own bias, privilege, and how what 
we are saying, doing, and the language we use may be reinforcing the systems that get in the way.
Questions to support a reflective practice for Participatory Design practitioners operating be -
yond academic contexts:
• What are the implications for Participatory Design and co-design practitioners for how we talk 
about and conceive of Participatory Design practice in the context of existing Indigenous in -
novation and participation practices?
• What does it mean to see Eurocentric Participatory Design as only one of many relational,
