participatory, and values-led design and innovation traditions?
• How might we ensure we are aware enough to know when Participatory Design isn’t the right 
process or when teams are not equipped for the work?
• How are we paying attention to what is needed to grapple with positionality as inherent in Par-
ticipatory Design work?
• What is our personal work to do alongside the design process?
• Is there sufficient readiness to actively commit to allyship, personal discomfort, the work of 
challenging racism and the personal cost this might have?
• How might we ensure the creation of safe spaces for this work becomes part of the Participatory 
Design process?
• If Participatory Design isn’t led by Indigenous communities, or walking its way there, and 
it isn’t an explicit act of allyship – then is it helpful/meaningful/relevant/justified in these 
contexts?
Conclusions
The core of this chapter discusses three themes central to the decade of non-academic Par -
ticipatory Design practice. Theme 1 focuses on the critical role of context in non-academic 

Participatory Design Beyond Academia
213
forms of Participatory Design and its impact on practitioners’ ability to fully apply Participa-
tory Design. Theme 2 is centred on the work itself – from methods to strategy, tactics, and 
logistics – and how it contextually varies. Theme 3 explores the implications of Participatory 
Design as a Western practice and reflects on emerging work at the intersection of Indigenous 
and Participatory Design practices to pose key questions about Participatory Design practice 
in such contexts.
Among the many reflections and points made in the chapter, a number should be reiterated.
First, non-academic practitioners interested in embedding Participatory Design in their organi-
sations need to appreciate and come to terms with the complexities that exist when trying to recon-
cile Participatory Design’s sharing of power where such a sharing may be anti-ethical to how their 
organisations are constituted and wish to operate.
Second, it is important to recognise that even in organisations that are willing (and even ex -
cited) to fold Participatory Design in their work, the output of such willingness and excitement 
may disappoint, due to a number of factors. The reality is that in non-academic contexts there is 
frequently a gap between stating willingness to do Participatory Design and actually doing Par -
ticipatory Design. While participatory practice in non-academic contexts has greatly evolved over 
the past 10 years and an increasing number of organisations are adopting Participatory Design 
values, it is proposed that such an evolution has seen the rise of what is referred to as “Participa -
tory Design Light.”
Third, doing Participatory Design in non-academic contexts requires more than Participa -
tory Design expertise and willingness, as it also requires organisational readiness – from poli -
cies to clear mandates and organisational backing to name a few. The Co-design Capability 
and Conditions Framework (Auckland Co-Design Lab, 2018) offers valuable insights in this 
regard.
Fourth, even when there is institutional support for Participatory Design in settings such as 
the public sector, practitioners must reflect critically on the motivations for Participatory Design, 
the wider cultural and historic context and impact of colonisation in particular, and how Western 
conceptualisations of Participatory Design may have the opposite effect to the emancipatory and 
empowering intentions Participatory Design might have intended.
Fifth, variations of participatory and co-design practices are wide and varied and operate 
strongly without the input or contribution of academic Participatory Design practice. What work 
might academic Participatory Design practice do to create greater recognition and space for these 
practices to be celebrated and acknowledged?
As mentioned at the start of this chapter, it is important to acknowledge and deeply appre-
ciate the historical tensions that exist between Academic Participatory Design versus Industry 
Participatory Design and an urgent need for new ways to describe the plethora of non-academic 
participatory practice that has emerged over the past decade. Additionally, it is fundamental to 
realise that criteria currently leveraged to estimate what is and isn’t Participatory Design practice 
require a re-evaluation that recognises the fundamental differences that exist between academic 
and non-academic Participatory Design practice.
Consequently, the chapter proposes that new metrics are needed, as they are key to providing 
overdue and adequate legitimacy to important and under-recognised non-academic Participatory 
Design approaches – work that is essential for continued growth in the scope of Participatory De-
sign practice. Additionally, it is proposed that terminology divergence and the academisation of 
Participatory Design have over time created the conditions practitioners, practice, and work that 
are deeply participatory to be excluded and become invisible to academic-led communities such 
as the Participatory Design Conference.

SECTION II
Exemplary Participatory Design



  
9
CO-DESIGNING DEMENTIA 
CULTURE(S)
Yanki C. Lee, Niels Hendriks and Andrea Wilkinson
  DOI: 10.4324/9781003334330-11
This chapter shares two case studies on design with dementia in two different cultural contexts: start-
ing from studies initiated by a university-based research lab in Western Europe (Belgium) and a series 
of experiments conducted by a social design collective/an independent action-based charity in Asia 
(Hong Kong). The authors aim to raise the fundamental questions to the Participatory Design commu-
nity on who our target groups are and how to engage them in different levels of participation.
An in-depth examination of these case studies brings to light various aspects of designing participa-
tory experiences, including challenges in ensuring full participation. For these cases, the role of design-
ers, in collaboration with people living with dementia, extends the notion of “resource weak stakeholder” 
(Ehn et al., 2008
, p. 162) and considers them as “life experts” on the condition. Both cases advocate for 
integrating lived experiences into design and co-creating dementia-friendly cultures. The Belgian case, 
titled “Dementia Lab – Why We Stopped Worrying About Participation”, describes their shift from focus-
ing on participation to prioritising relationship-building and human connections and discusses four key 
aspects of their approach: (1) long-term, embedded work, (2) prioritising human connection over design 
identity, (3) viewing participation as a process, and 4) adapting to specific situations. The Hong Kong 
case, supported by social innovation funding, defines three stages of Designing Participation in dementia: 
(1) design by people living with dementia – leveraging insights from dementia experiences, (2) collabora-
tive design with service providers and students – innovating in dementia services, and (3) public-focused 
design – raising dementia awareness. Spanning from social activism to academic application, both ap-
proaches aim to influence the lives of those affected by dementia and their supporters, impacting various 
stages from societal debate to redefining participation in social innovation and higher education.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
220
Introduction: Who Participates in Design?
As the definition of Participatory Design is ever changing, fundamental questions of the practice 
still arise within the community: who participates in design processes and in what capacity, who 
are the co-creators, and how does one ensure that everyone is brought to the collaborative table? 
This leads to the question of what the actual role of the designer is.
In the introduction to the book Making Futures: Marginal Notes on Innovation, Design and 
Democracy, Making Futures, Ehn et al. (2014) refer to situated practices of making “multiple 
futures imagined and made locally, in heterogeneous communities, and with marginalised pub -
lics”. Looking back on his first steps in practice, Ehn reflected on the fact that “Participatory 
Design sided with resource weak stakeholders” (Ehn, 2008). Initially, workers in factories were 
considered “resource weak stakeholders” as they were unable to take control of the design and 
implementation of new tools within their workspace. They were either not heard or not enabled 
to raise their own concerns or desires. In 40 years, Participatory Design practice has shifted from 
a political interest-through-democratic systems development in the workplace to a more encom -
passing notion of accountability in design. With this shift, the “resource weak stakeholders” 
are not only workers but a diverse group: inhabitants of a town, caregivers, children, and so on.
In this chapter, two case studies look at dementia from different contexts who were brought together 
to explore the process of redefining “resource weak stakeholders” and reflect on the Participatory De-
sign process – similar to discourse around redefining the term “Alzheimer’s disease” and refocusing 
on the state of “dementia”. In this way, the term “dementia” describes a state, not a specific disease. 
In a similar manner, designing effective responses to each of these definitions requires more than a 
broad definition (Herrup, 2021, p. 10). Referring back to resource weak stakeholders, the person with 
dementia can be perceived as resource weak not only through these cognitive, psychiatric and physical 
limitations but also due to the societal perception of them. As a group, they have a multitude of psy-
chiatric, cognitive and often physical ailments that do or will eventually impact their daily lives as well 
as impede their participation in design. Solutions are often sought from medicine, but this fails to take 
into consideration other factors: the context of care and living, the way relationships are established and 
evolve or how social networks can support or maintain a person’s independence. Although in design 
those impacted by a design are often referred to as “users” and thus in these cases this could be assumed 
to be “People with Dementia (PwD)”, the authors have expanded this term to designing with “People 
Living with Dementia (PLwD)”, which includes the social context of the situated research state.
New Roles of Designers: Designing for Participation, Design as Participation
Looking specifically at both the co-creators and the role of the designer, the interventions de -
scribed here work with the concept of “designers as participants”, which indicates a new role for 
designers (Ito, 2017) in which they are “aware of and able to use all of (their) lenses by being 
aware of the systems that (they) are in and being continuously perceptive”. The collective A. Tel-
ier, in the book Design Things (Binder et al., 2011), describes this as designers having a democratic 
role that is akin to the definition of design.
The discussion on the role(s) of designers and the differing relationships between “designers” 
and “users”, or how Slavin (2016) defines the relationship between “designers” and “others”, is 
related to discourse within Participatory Design, challenging the idea of the designer as the sole 
creator, artist, and celebrity (Szebeko and Tan, 2010).
The first designer versus others model of “design for users’ participation” is collectively referred 
to as user-centred design (UCD). In UCD the designer’s imagination shifts from their own centre to 

Co-Designing Dementia Culture(s)
221
one in which the centre is that of the user. This challenges the heroic sensibility of the modern de-
signer and contributes to there being better-defined roles of “designers” and “users”. Instead of “us-
ers” or designing for use, the second model promotes the concept of “designing for participation”. 
In this model, the designer’s role is to create or orchestrate spaces for participation to take place.
Finally, the model presented here progresses even further. Design participation is about de-
signers/design researchers immersing themselves to the point that they become participants in the 
systems that have been created. Both case studies adopted this approach but in different ways. The 
design researchers of both cases have identified different combinations of design and participation 
within their own cultures that shape and inform how immersion (designer as participant) plays out 
in design research.
The Cases: When Design Meets Care
The following two case studies highlight the role(s) of the designer within these wider sys -
tems and the role that participation (in whatever form it takes) can engage individuals. This 
participation enables industries, communities, systems, and even new cultures to reflect on 
how the processes that are created impact the quality of life of PwDs, their caregivers, and 
the communities in which they live. Although both cases stem from a common position that 
prioritises participation and co-creation, they exist within two divergent dementia cultures: 
from studies initiated by a university-based research lab in Western Europe (Belgium) and 
a series of experiments by a social design collective/an independent action-based charity in 
Asia (Hong Kong).
Case 9.1
Project Title: Dementia Lab – Why We Stopped Worrying About Participation
Authors: Dr. Niels Hendriks and Dr. Andrea Wilkinson
Country/Region: Belgium, EU
Period: Since 2011
Operation Model: Research cluster based on an art and design faculty. Funding partly provided by the 
university’s own funds and external, regional, and European funding
Keywords: Relational Design, Dementia and Design, Designing for One, Design Research, Social 
Design, and Inclusive Design
Organisation: LUCA School of Arts (Caring and Design Research Cluster, Inter-Actions Research Unit)
Project Lead: Dr. Niels Hendriks and Dr. Andrea Wilkinson
Partners:
• Local care centres and care organisations, that is, OCMW Genk, Expertise Centre Dementia Flan-
ders, Alzheimer League, and local residential care facilities
• International research groups; Leuven Centre for Health Humanities; Digital Society Institute Uni-
versity of Leuven; HOMEDEM Marie Curie Doctoral Network
• National/international funding partners; philanthropic organisations (Alzheimer’s Society, Inno -
vate UK, Robert Bosch Stiftung, etc.); Flemish Ministry of Innovation, Flanders Innovation and 
Entrepreneurship, Interreg, Marie Curie, and so on.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
222
Contact Information/Website:
• http://caring.anddesignresearch.com
• www.dementialabresearch.com
• www.dementialabconference.com
Over a decade ago, a collaboration among academic, small and medium enterprises (SME), and 
residential care partners initiated our design and dementia journey. Advocating for participation, we 
ventured to involve PwDs in the design process – an unconventional approach at the time. Initially 
challenging, with tools falling short and results seeming irrelevant, our perspective on Participa -
tory Design has evolved. Fast forward to now and we feel that Participatory Design might not be as 
“important” as we once thought, or to say it less provocatively in a handbook on Participatory Design: 
we stopped worrying about participation. Although this position may not resonate with everyone, 
this shift towards relation instead of emphasising process has provided us a liberty that continues to 
impact our research practice – from working with design students in care facilities to contributing to 
European projects and ongoing PhD research exploring ways to engage carers with residents.
Dementia Lab Research is a group of designer-researchers, a research programme and a net -
work that takes an inclusive, participatory approach. Each project involves the person with demen-
tia as a valued contributor while not ignoring the important actors (friends, family, formal carers) 
surrounding them. Ultimately the lab wants to impact the everyday life of a person with dementia, 
with the mission being: “How will this design make this person’s life more pleasant”, while ex-
perimenting and exploring not only what the role of design can be for care and dementia but also 
by developing design methods that go for radical inclusive participation (collaborating with those 
who we can’t or don’t want to collaborate with). By documenting, reflecting on, and sharing these 
processes and outcomes, there should be an agonistic effect that centres the conversation on design 
and dementia but also challenges the way we perceive a person with dementia as a “full” person.
As we develop and critically engage with theoretical concepts, our international impact extends 
beyond academic texts. Through the Dementia Lab Conference platform, we connect with inter -
national design researchers, critical designers, industry partners, care organisations, and advocacy 
groups. Originating in 2016 as an event involving student designers and PwDs, the platform has 
evolved into an international community prioritising human-centredness and agonistic design over 
solutionist or technology-centric approaches. The bi-annual Dementia Lab Conference, now in its 
7th edition in 2025, serves as a crossroads for care and design research, bringing together practi -
tioners, PwDs, and caregivers.
While not explicitly stated, the foundational theoretical framework of this work draws from 
Husserl’s phenomenology. This is evident in the adopted situated and relational approach, empha-
sising understanding the world as experienced by individuals, particularly PwDs. Phenomenology 
prioritises direct experience over abstract concepts or theories, aligning with this work’s focus on 
the experiences of PwDs within their care and living contexts. The approach also underscores the 
significance of relationships between individuals and their environment.
Participatory Design has always been central to the way we work. Even before we began, the 
challenge of involving PwDs was tied to the problematisation of dementia at a societal level. In 
short, when society agrees that it is too difficult to involve PwDs, then participation will either 
not be successful or perhaps not even be considered. This unwillingness to challenge this societal 

Co-Designing Dementia Culture(s)
223
Figure 9.1  Care facility in Stuttgart, Germany, 2016 (image credit: Andrea Wilkinson).


Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
224
position at the start of our work (in 2012/13) was evidenced by the lack of papers that described 
participation and inclusion of PwDs (Span et al., 2013). Papers stated, seemingly self-evidently, 
that participation with PwDs was impossible and this was echoed in practice. Project partners 
stated that it was unnecessary to allocate funding to participation efforts and care partners who 
had been involved in previous projects were shocked that we found value in engaging with PwDs; 
especially engagement that was over time and in a personal manner.
The issue here was not only the societal perception of PwDs but our own definition of partic -
ipation. Although we had experience in participatory practices, we were struck by the inability 
of our collaborative setup to work in the way we were expecting. Based on a simple mapping 
(Hendriks et al., 2013), PwDs were questioned about their lives and the challenges they were 
facing and used stickers to visually and (if possible) verbally allow them to express their an -
swers. In spite of discussions (with caregivers) and well-thought-out and established settings, it 
didn’t work: the questions, as well as the participatory tasks, did not deliver results. If there was 
a response, it was often unexpected or didn’t fit our intention. The combination of these things 
caused us to abandon our workshop configurations and to fundamentally question the feasibility 
of Participatory Design with PwDs; that maybe participation just didn’t “work” (see Hendriks  
et al., 2014).
Although this appeared to confirm the literature, we responded to this sense of resignation 
by questioning the way we approached Participatory Design; we stopped worrying about par -
ticipation. One of the most decisive moments of this research experience (that continues to 
inform our practice to this day) happened while meeting a woman with dementia who lived 
alone in her apartment yet was heavily supported by her daughter. On our first encounter, we 
left heavy-hearted as she was very nervous and could not overcome this during our time with 
her. The reason for this nervousness, we later understood, probably came from the position 
we took: introducing ourselves as academics, asking her to be part of this research, and so 
on. On our second visit to her apartment, however, we did what we started to call “The Pie 
Thing”. We brought along a large pie and had coffee with her and her daughter, we talked 
about a trip to the US we were about to make and chatted about the woman’s lovely and 
very inquisitive dog. Although this may sound trivial, this was decisive in shaping how we 
now frame participation. In the following section, these reflections will be divided into four 
characteristics:
Work embedded (and for a longer time) : Our own work with PwDs brought us to residential 
care facilities, apartments, and day care centres where we taught, tinkered, laughed, and learnt 
from within the care-based living spaces of PwDs. Our becoming part of the person’s care and 
living context, alongside formal and informal caregivers, partners, and friends, allowed us to em-
brace an embedded role. This deliberate choice counters the prevailing practice of time-limited, 
meticulously planned Participatory Design sessions, much like the sessions we had set up in our 
previous case (see, e.g., Hendriks et al., 2013). Embeddedness, as showcased in Figure 9.2, en-
hances comprehension of an individual with dementia – revealing habits, behavioural patterns, 
daily challenges, and more. It bridges the gap between theory and the lived reality of care, enabling 
researchers to connect with the person with dementia and their care context. This engagement is 
not a one-time occurrence but a long-term commitment, demanding designer flexibility and a 
people-oriented approach unconstrained by strict timing.
Be a human, don’t be a designer : When stepping into the care-based living spaces of PwDs 
one cannot step in as a goal-driven, distant other. Engaging as a human who is trying to connect 
(without the goal of designing something) is crucial. Designers then are able to change their ac-
tions. They help out with eating, sing along in an afternoon choir, dance together, support someone 
A family of eight is seated at a dining table, three of them are playing with a kid holding a doll 
and others are discussing among them.

Co-Designing Dementia Culture(s)
225
who wants to go to a religious service, or simply keep someone company. These aspects of being 
human lead to a form of relational expertise.
Relational expertise is acquired by desginer-researchers  through their close relationships with 
individuals and encompasses the extensive knowledge and expertise accumulated during frequent 
interactions (Dindler and Iversen, 2014). This serves as a foundation for the designer researchers 
to judiciously select, adapt, and employ existing tools and techniques that facilitate effective col-
laboration. These decisions are often guided by envisioning decisions from the perspective of the 
person with dementia. The emphasis on relational work within this research provides designers 
with a framework or mindset to cultivate relational expertise. It provides designer researchers the 
agency to speak on behalf of the person with dementia and to engage with carers from the position 
of a sort of understanding of a person’s identity and not from the position of their condition which 
in turn releases many constraints that participation calls for (Wilkinson and Hendriks, 2022).
See participation as a stage: As mentioned earlier, our open definition of participation sees the 
context of the person with dementia as a metaphorical stage in which the researcher steps into the 
subjective world of the person with dementia and enters the “frame of reference of the individual 
and understanding the world from their point of view” (Brooker, 2003, p.  218). The stage is the 
daily context of care and asks the researcher to step into the “lived reality” of the person with de-
mentia, the way the person with dementia, at that point, perceives the world (see this in action in 
Figure 9.3). This means that a designer might be perceived as a volunteer, a family member, or a 
Figure 9.2  Care facility in Berlin, Germany, 2016 (image credit: Niels Hendricks).


Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
226
visiting neighbour, and they will have to perform in line with the vision the person with dementia 
then has. The participatory setup or “script” is then a loosely defined working scenario that defines 
the actions between the actors and the props (a doll, a painting, a prototype, a joke, a religious 
belief, . . .). It is based on these narratives of the now and then that are important to the person 
with dementia. In this way, the involvement of the person with dementia goes beyond traditional 
cognitive externalities such as verbal or visual utterances, and this “acting” allows the designer to 
take design decisions based on the explicit and implicit participation of a person with dementia: 
explicit “in use” (Bratteteig and Wagner, 2014) in which a person with dementia tinkers with an 
unfinished design and implicit through their paying close attention to the small, potentially banal 
elements on this stage.
Respond to the situation: Although some of these characteristics may sound self-evident, giv -
ing up a specific format of Participatory Design asks for the designer to be capable of reacting 
to the situation at hand, the “situated” character of each design moment (Chiu, 2003). To engage 
individuals with dementia in the design process, it is essential for the researcher to align each 
action with the evolving state (moments of clarity/restlessness), condition (spans of rapid cogni-
tive decline/additional health factors), or mood (not willing to cooperate due to toothache  . . .) 
of the person with dementia. Reacting to the situation asks for a novel set of capabilities from 
Figure 9.3  Home participation session, Winterslag, Belgium, 2014 (image credit: Niels Hendriks).


Co-Designing Dementia Culture(s)
227
the Participatory Design researcher, such as empathic responsiveness (“I see that this discussion 
is making them sad”), critical self-reflection (“What am I taking away from this engagement”), 
and sensitivity towards potential power relations (“What the husband says about her doesn’t 
seem to be what I am experiencing once he leaves”). While it could be contended that design -
ing from within situations requires a designer to be always actively designing empathetically, 
these actions are intricately woven into the fabric of both the relationships and the situations 
(Wilkinson and Hendriks, 2022).
We primarily stopped worrying about participation because we began investing strongly in 
relationship-building and connecting as humans and this has become essential to our way of 
working. Questions such as whether such an approach is a genuine form of participation or 
valuable participation or whether it is enough participation have become irrelevant in that sense. 
Closely connected to the political tradition of Participatory Design (Robertson and Wagner, 
2012), this form of Participatory Design has a broader ethical reflex in (participatory) design 
practice (van der Velden and Mörtberg, 2014). Next to this, we have successfully applied a 
similar approach in contexts beyond PwDs in design projects collaborating with persons with 
profound intellectual and multiple disabilities and people in palliative care and end-of-life de -
sign, as well as on taboo subjects such as residents with high care needs living in an elderly care 
centre on the topic of sexuality and intimacy. Future challenges for the Participatory Design 
domain will then be how to define and prepare for this form of relationship-building, resulting 
in designers who are better prepared for diverse situated actions and who design for inclusive 
participation.
New challenges in future participatory work with PwDs will deal with (a) moving away 
from a person-centred perspective to a relational perspective (the person with dementia in rela-
tion to the others – family, friends, caregivers – not only the designer) and how this will influ -
ence the participatory process and results (thinking about integration in rituals and routines of 
a caregiver, a specific culture, or family context); (b) the use of adapting and enabling adoption 
of designerly participatory ways of working in care and how caregivers will be able to foster 
stronger relationships with PwDs from this; (c) the (material) position of the designer in the 
relational participatory way of working (questioning how certain methods, techniques, and 
tools are not only “working” for a person with dementia but should be adapted to a designer’s 
preferences, idiosyncrasies, abilities, and challenges); (d) how the valuable but time-intense 
and resource demanding process of Participatory Design can be translated to contexts that are 
limited in resources (SME to name one); (e) how specific participatory approaches can cater to 
diverse care constellations (e.g. the different definitions of family – blood vs. chosen family) 
and the blending of different health care cultures (e.g. various frame of references on dementia 
care from expats or migrants).
Case 9.2
Project Title: OK Dementia: Designers as the Culture Creators/Co-creating Dementia Things
Author: Dr Yanki C. Lee, founder of Enable Foundation
Country/Region: Hong Kong, China
Keywords: Design Speculations, Design Research, Social Innovation, Topic – Dementia, Cross-  
disciplinary, Types of Participation/involvement

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
228
Period: Since 2017 – project-based
Operation Model: Social Design Collective and Education Charity with public funding on social 
innovation
Organisation: Enable Foundation – A Social Design Collective and Education Charity
Project Leads: Dr Yanki C. Lee, Ire Tsui, and Pascal Anson, Research and design team of Enable 
Foundation
Partners:
• Funder – Social Innovation and Entrepreneurship Development Fund (SIE Fund)
• Collaborators – 10 NGOs providing dementia care services under the Hong Kong Government’s 
Dementia Community Support Scheme (DCSS)
Website: www.enable.org.hk/en/projects/dementia-design
Key Theoretical Concepts: Design Participation (DP) rather than Participatory Design
In April 2020, we started our Second Capability Building Programme, entitled Social Innova -
tion Design Lab in Places (SI.DLab II’s Dementia Hong Kong), a 14-month capacity-building 
programme with a focus on cross-disciplinary collaboration and investigation of different forms 
of participation, between design (design researchers and professional designers) and over 100 
social service providers (from both medical and social models) including all key-workers on 
dementia support services. Instead of direct participation with PwDs, we worked on three types 
of engagement/ways to build capabilities/participation to develop social innovative ideas for 
dementia by working with PLwD. First of all, we developed cross-disciplinary participation 
to engage ten NGOs, the social service providers that joined the “DCSS”, initiated and funded 
by the Hong Kong Government and operated by the Social Welfare Department and Hospital 
Authority. Secondly, cross-generational participative tactics were conducted with university 
students to co-create new meanings of dementia in our society. Finally, the third type of par -
ticipation was through disseminating the results from the two stages of engagement. A series of 
“dementia things” were prototyped and invited public participation to reimagine dementia and 
explore future possibilities with the public. Here are the three stages of Designing Participation 
in dementia: Design by PLwD (inspirations of dementia); Design with service providers and 
university students – social innovation on dementia services; and Design for public (awareness 
building of dementia).
According to the 2017 Mental Health Review Report, Hong Kong Government estimates 
put the population of PwDs at 100,000, representing almost one-tenth of the elderly popula -
tion in Hong Kong. While public policy makers and the social service sector address de -
mentia challenges from medical and social perspectives, numerous large-scale programmes 
exist with diverse application methods. Yet, a gap persists between service needs and the 
provided services, necessitating a new, integrated service model that combines various 
approaches.
Seeing dementia as a form of disability and referring to the debates on the medical and social 
models of disability, we are advocating for a new model, the cultural model of dementia. While the 
medical and social models are in conflict, the new model acknowledges both the traditional mod-
els. The medical model is the dominant one, which allows medical experts to lead the discussions 

Co-Designing Dementia Culture(s)
229
and major operation models. At the same time, those working with the social model continue to 
provide direct services to make sure the lives of PwDs are better and their rights are protected. In 
addition, it attaches more importance to capturing how people tackle their own medical and social 
issues (Lee, 2020).
Many designers addressing social issues aim to solve problems by working directly with af -
fected individuals, exploring their roles in Participatory Design processes. If issues are deemed 
“wicked” – considered impossible to solve – it’s reasonable to design for better understanding rather 
than solely aiming for solutions. This was our journey in social innovation projects with diverse 
dementia “users” and Participatory Design processes.
Instead of direct participation with PwDs, we worked on three types of engagement/ways to 
build capabilities/participations to develop socially innovative dementia ideas. We began with a 
speculative design question/condition: What if the subject experiencing dementia was not a per -
son but rather an everyday object or the city around us became “demented”? Our approach was to 
design objects that conveyed aspects of having dementia and then allow people without dementia 
to interact with them observing the interactions. We focused on creating well-designed items 
to attract others’ attention. Unlike other people-centred designs we were attempting not only to 
include the needs and wants of PwDs but to translate their experiential struggles in a meaning -
ful way, allowing the people around them to understand and act from a place of empathy. In this 
phase, a design researchers’ and designers’ role is to articulate PwDs’ unimaginable somatic and 
cognitive experiences and to carefully create design artefacts and environments to help others 
(especially those people who are totally unaware of dementia) to feel and even be in the experi-
ence of a PwD. Figure 9.1 shows the Dementia Home (first launched in Hong Kong in 2018), 
which was refined into the Dementia Show Flat (first launched in Hong Kong in 2019). The home 
is the place where many PwDs struggle with their family members who are their caregivers. 
Many familiar things and situations become unfamiliar and even strange. By creating different 
“demented” objects including the “Dementia Light Switches Corner”, “Dementia (Upside Down) 
Toilet”, and “Dementia Broom” at home environment, our goal was to raise public awareness of 
dementia happening to their family members and to provide a stimulating environment for car -
egivers to empathise with PwDs and encourage them to develop new tactics to solve their own 
everyday problems.
Figure 9.4  Dementia Toilet, researched, designed and installed by Enable Foundation, 2018, at Social In -
novation Market, Hong Kong. (Photo credit: Ire Tsui)

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
230
The project, Dementia Things allowed us to articulate a 3-S process to explain our methodology:
• Stories: collect stories from PwDs and their carers (professionals and family members)
• Symptoms: match the stories to the common dementia symptoms
• Situations: illustrate/visualise the situation by creating a corresponding Dementia Object
For the participation of different disciplines and generations, there is a need to develop Participa-
tory Design works with professional carers from both medical and social models. Through these 
professionals, we met caregivers whose experiences with dementia were inspiring. As part of our 
ongoing work with these caregivers, we are unfolding everyday tactics from different dementia 
communities and from that developing corresponding design briefs. The briefs fall into three areas:
1. Dementia and Bodies – Could we develop tangible tools for us to express our body preferences 
and awareness before dementia?
2. Dementia and Realities – Could we translate tactics of “Reality Orientation” (developed by 
Occupational Therapy) into new tools to enable us to navigate the realities with PwD?
3. Dementia and People – Could we create tools that introduce new ways of interaction to allow 
caregivers different methods of communication with their family members with dementia?
We invited different designers to interpret these briefs and to create tools to prepare the public for 
dementia. In one of the design examples, we learnt from carers that many PwDs withdraw from 
communal activities after making mistakes during these activities. This inspired us to write a brief 
about new ways to say hello using bodily gestures. In response, a group of young designers from 
Zürich interpreted the brief and developed the “wave index”: a new body language used to say 
hello by following the numbers on the mirror.
Our reflection is that it is crucial for us to reconnect to our bodies and learn new ways to com-
municate. This should be part of the preparation for better communication with caregivers when 
someone develops symptoms of dementia.
Our practice with dementia is about articulating design tactics by interrogating dementia ecolo-
gies (PwD, family, and friends) and then translating this rich material into design briefs for designers 
to design for others: Design by People (Living with Dementia) for People (no experience of Demen-
tia). This form of participation is about empowering PwD by developing a common language for us 
to participate in the world of dementia. Among these ideas inspired by Dementia, we think the most 
controversial is the concept of “OK De Cafe”. While the other ideas are working within the social 
model by providing new ways into socialisation. “OK De Cafe”, a visualisation (2D/3D tool), is 
inspired by the Montreal Cognitive Assessment Test, and its goal is to unfold the medical assessment 
to public awareness by engaging the public to understand the seven strengths related to dementia.
Figure 9.5  Wave Index, designed by Jonas Shriqui, David Lüthi, and Mia Seulmi, designed in Zürich for 
Hong Kong, 2020. https://youtu.be/06Weitw_gYQ


Co-Designing Dementia Culture(s)
231
Unlike innovative service concepts for dementia such as the “The Restaurant of Mistaken Orders” 
in Japan and “Dementia Tour” in Hong Kong, which aims to re-train PwD to work, our next mis-
sion is to engage and empower ex-dementia caregivers and co-create with them the Dementia 
Culture for our city.
Since 2015, we have explored the potential for collaboration between different professionals 
and generations on the topic of dementia. During this process, we found that it is more essential 
and effective to develop a common “language” to discuss matters from dementia, and this makes 
participation with PwD difficult.
This is why we created the collection of Dementia Jackets. Putting a jacket on is such an eve -
ryday task, but would you imagine it could become a problem? “I can’t tell the difference between 
the front and back of my dress and what is inside and what is outside of the dress. This makes it 
difficult to put on”. This is a quotation from a citizen of Copenhagen who has dementia and was 
collected by our collaborator, Center of Demens. We find this is a universal problem for PwD to 
put on their clothing, and we created five jackets to explain five different possible design responses 
for dementia:
• Everyday Jacket – Do Nothing
• Do-Re-Mi Jacket – Understanding dementia
• Diagram Jacket – Trying to develop solutions to solve the problems
• Empathy Jacket – Practising empathy
• Everyday Dementia Jacket – Co-creating an inclusive society
The collection was first shown at the Dutch Design Week in 2019 where we asked the design 
community, “What can design do to super ageing societies?” Many responses were collected and 
we brought them back to Hong Kong and used them to ask the general public, “What action and 
how Participatory Design process could you carry out after interacting with our designed objects 
with dementia and understanding more about the condition?”
How can we articulate the experience of dementia as a culture? With Dementia Things for dif-
ferent forms of participation, our vision is one day we can create a network of convenient pop-up 
stores for dementia where dementia is OK, a culture to be accepted and embraced by the public, 
in everyday interactions. A city accepting dementia! Part of the everyday culture in our future 
super ageing society. We do not wish to claim that PwDs are part of a single culture, like the D/
Figure 9.6  (Left) OK De Cafe, researched by Enable Foundation and designed by Matthew Perchard, de -
signed in London for Hong Kong, 2020. (Right) Dementia Jacket Collection, researched and 
designed by Enable Foundation and Pascal Anson, designed and made in London, launched in 
Eindhoven, 2019.


Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
232
deaf culture (Padden et al., 2009). Even though PwDs do experience their own reality, they have a 
subjective interpretation and an understanding of everyday life unique to themselves. Each person 
with dementia has their own ways of behaving that are rooted in the past and a relation to and 
interpretation of the present. Dementia culture captures the ingenuity of these patients’ everyday 
lives and can inspire design and innovation to reduce stigmatisation of the disease. We hope for a 
new role for designers, to become the culture creators, to enable public participation to reimagine 
dementia together.
Similarities and Differences Between the Two Case Studies
As well as cultural differences, the two cases are working on different social situations. The 
European case study focuses on the importance of grounding Participatory Design in deep, 
empathetic connections with the individuals affected and their care environment. It heralds a 
relational perspective and approach to bring a nuanced understanding of the lived experiences 
and changing needs of the target audience. The Asian case study experiments with design-driven 
approaches to materialise the experiential struggles of individuals with dementia and share this 
insight with a broader audience, by promoting awareness and empathy through the creation 
of “demented” objects and environments. It does so in close collaboration with professional 
caregivers, forging new methods and tools for dementia care. The two cases offer a range of 
possibilities to rethink/reflect on future Participatory Design practice by asking deep questions 
of WHO and HOW, from “resource weak stakeholders” to “Issue-insiders”. The latest Participa -
tory Design developments merge with other initiatives, such as social innovation, and the notion 
of involving “resource weak stakeholders” in the process is being challenged. Instead of helping 
the needy, the Hong Kong case study approach refers to the speculative design and challenges 
the notion of traditional human-centred design practice by seeing them as the problem-owner 
who can provide insiders’ solutions. All the tools that were developed for different purposes for 
dementia, were inspired by the People with Dementia concept. This notion shined a new light 
on the practice; that is, could Participatory Design be inspired by “issue-insiders”? With a focus 
on the caregivers, those who are caring for PwD, the specific practice is defined as “design by 
people, for people”; that is, the Do-Re-Mi Jacket and Diagram Jacket are the design articulations 
that represent the caregiver’s wisdom of how they cope with the issues from dementia.
This new practice focuses on the “issue-insiders”, challenges the problem-solving nature of 
design disciplines, and expands to the social science discourse of a solution-focused approach. The 
Hong Kong team is based on public funding and aims to achieve social impact with experimental 
practice by intentionally working on solution-focused processes, while the Belgian case study 
is a cross-disciplinary practice between caring and design research, and the latest development 
is a doctoral network to bring together design and dementia caregiving with different levels of 
involvement and multiple approaches.
From social innovative experiments/activism to academic implementation, while both 
have similar goals, to impact the lives of those affected and those that support PwD, their 
impact is visible in different stages. The Hong Kong case seeks to create societal impact by 
short-termed experimental projects and provoking discussions in the society, while the Euro -
pean case is part of the bigger notion to highlight the role that participation can have in driv -
ing change both within the landscape of social innovation and development and with design 
academia and education.

Co-Designing Dementia Culture(s)

10
COLLECTIVE CAPABILITIES IN 
LIVING LABS
Liesbeth Huybrechts, Pablo Calderón Salazar,  
Katrien Dreessen and Mela Žuljević 
De Andere Markt (DAM) started in 2015 as a Living Lab in the neighbourhood of Winterslag in Genk, 
Belgium. It was founded by researchers of LUCA School of Arts, UHasselt and the city of Genk, to 
research and shape an alternative – more participatory – approach to the transition of the work land -
scape that the city was undergoing, after the progressive shut-down of its mining and manufacturing 
industries. In line with the early Participatory Design tradition dealing with democracy at the workplace 
(Ehn,1988), DAM was founded with the goal of repoliticising the conversation on this evolving work 
landscape. This process started by designing and putting in place a series of soft interventions. These 
interventions were not so much directed at disturbing the status quo but rather aimed at carefully under-
standing the local context and its actors, as well as getting the researchers and their agendas known by 
the local inhabitants. The capabilities present among the people of Genk were identified and mapped, as 
a way of reshifting the focus from the loss of jobs to highlighting the existing capabilities that could sup-
port the collective transition of the socio-environmental landscape. The chapter will first explore how 
the Living Lab allowed an understanding of the rich and complex interdependencies between the ca -
pabilities of human (designers, inhabitants, organisations and institutions) and more-than-human actors 
(the landscape, the built and the digital environment) in shaping the past, current and future landscape. It 
will then zoom into how the lab shaped and employed these interdependencies into collective capabili-
ties to articulate and prototype alternative work and living spaces in Genk. We will finally discuss how 
the approach was – and can be – extended to other urban, suburban and rural contexts and themes such 
as food production and consumption, material exchange, mobility, energy or water.
  DOI: 10.4324/9781003334330-12

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
236
The Living Lab in the Context of Socio-Environmental Transitions
In December 2014, Ford Genk (a car manufacturing plant and the city’s largest employer) closed 
down after two years of progressively decreasing its operations. The plant had opened 50 years ear-
lier, after the coal mines which powered the city’s development began to shut down. DAM was ini-
tially founded with the support of the local city administration and the doctoral trajectory of an Early 
Stage Researcher within the Marie-Curie ITN project TRADERS (under the FP7 framework). This 
continued within a Horizon2020 MSCA Training Network on Critical Heritage Studies and today 
the MSCA Doctoral Network REWORLDING, which deals with designing socio-environmental 
transitions. Today the lab is not solely limited to the city of Genk but works within multiple project 
contexts, such as the one discussed in this article: a large road transition project between Hasselt 
(BE) and Eindhoven (NL), called Noord-Zuid Limburg, that has been going on for four years. All 
the studied contexts share a difficult experience of transition from a predominantly industrial land-
scape, with a palimpsest of transformations in the environment, towards developing more sustain-
able relations with that landscape. These kinds of processes involve transitioning to a post-carbon 
economy/context, yet trying to ensure the well-being of the actors involved – or what is known as 
just transitions (Abram et al., 2022). This was particularly relevant in Genk, considering that its 
economy was initially based on coal mining and later on vehicle manufacturing, and any process of 
transformation had to be centred on principles of socio-environmental justice.
With the goal of studying and co-designing these transitions, from an early start DAM was an-
chored within Northern-European Participatory Design discourses, which allowed it to build upon 
notions, methods and approaches developed within the Participatory Design community – such 
as that of Living Labs. Living Labs have been defined as environments for open innovation that 
support experiments with real users in concrete contexts and long-term strategies (Følstad, 2008). 
In Participatory Design, Living Labs are considered open innovation milieus where new groups, 
issues and ideas emerge from bottom-up, long-term collaborations between diverse actors (Björg-
vinsson et al., 2012, p. 41). We were particularly informed and inspired by a previous experience in 
Malmö with Living Labs (Björgvinsson et al., 2012; Kommonen and Botero, 2013). However, this 
influence was also addressed through a critical lens, to expand the understanding of Living Labs 
within Participatory Design, as well as of different practices associated with them (interventions, 
capacity building, long-term engagement, embeddedness, etc.), and adapting them to the local real-
ity of Genk. This required care and attention to how the politics of Participatory Design were ar -
ticulated in both the Living Labs in Malmö and Genk (Huybrechts, Devisch, and Tassinari, 2022b).
Collective Capabilities
The Living Lab DAM in Genk developed an approach that engaged closely with reframing the politics 
of Participatory Design in a situated way. It responded to the particularities of the socio-environmental 
circumstances it was confronted with and devoted particular attention and efforts to developing col-
lective capabilities in transitioning contexts. This early approach and focus on collective capabili-
ties in Living Labs takes into account the role of more-than-human actors (de la Cadena, 2018). 
Participatory Design research engaging with more-than-human actors involves projects that include 
animals, insects, plants and elements as research partners (Akama et al., 2020). This particular Living 
Lab approach was motivated by two reasons that emerged from the local context: firstly, the histori-
cal setting of Genk and other cities that the Living Lab engaged with, which were (or still are) in the 
middle of a significant turmoil in terms of its social, environmental and economic conditions and, 
secondly, their spatially dispersed urban organisation (similar to a ‘sprawl city’).

Collective Capabilities in Living Labs
237
First, the type of projects DAM engages with is controversial, insofar as they deal with polarised 
socio-environmental transitions. One of the central concerns of the lab was to support and enable 
a shift from a focus on built infrastructure for industrial work practices (coal extraction and later 
car manufacturing), towards other ways of being and working that make room for biodiversity, and 
sustainable uses of water and energy. This implies creating space for the more-than-human (de la 
Cadena, 2018), which also results in changing the relations with – but also reducing – the built 
environment for people. This forced us to think closely about building relations not only between 
worlds – between human and more-than-human worlds – but also between the different worlds of the 
very diverse actors within the context, living together with various experiences of the environment.
This process of closely crafting relations between worlds was further backdropped by the south-
ern background of two of DAM’s researchers (one from a South-Eastern European country and 
another from Latin America) and the mixed ethnocultural composition of the population in Genk. 
Southern perspectives on design and research put much emphasis on a relational practice that sup-
ports the self-realisation of communities (Calderón Salazar et al., 2018). These perspectives inspired 
us to articulate the individual capabilities of inhabitants, policymakers, local organisations and de-
sign researchers, to move towards developing collective capabilities that could give shape to future 
self-organised socio-environmental changes. Southern perspectives build upon an ontological un-
derstanding of design that focuses on the politics of radical interdependence amongst human and 
more-than-human actors – making legible how people relate to other human and more-than-human 
actors, as well as helping them act upon the possibilities and politics of shaping these relations in 
alternative ways (Anastassakis and Szaniecki, 2016; Mol, 1999; Calderón Salazar et al., 2018; Huy-
brechts, Devisch, and Tassinari, 2022a, 2022b). This concretely implied looking into the capabilities 
of each actor and how they relate to their environment (e.g. people, organisations, neighbourhood, 
water, energy), as well as what they could do together in close relation to the urban and natural 
landscape, to use their collective capabilities to organise their environment in alternative ways. In 
doing so, we framed the Living Lab as a pluriversal space (Escobar, 2018; Calderón Salazar and 
Huybrechts, 2020), an environment that opened spaces of possibility to a ‘world of many worlds’.
The introduction of both a Scandinavian and a Southern approach to Participatory Design in 
our Belgian context was not without struggles. In 2015 the participatory approach to spatial plan-
ning in Belgium was dominated by a neoliberal logic (Kuhk et al, 2019), focused on demonstrating 
the gains and reducing costs in spatial planning processes. This represented a challenge for us, as 
researchers, to show how a relational way of working – slowly building a network – could eventu-
ally lead to a more just way of organising (urban) space in the long run. This meant emphasising 
how all actors would have a place to thrive, instead of only more efficient spatial planning and less 
juridical procedures. This motivated us to put a strong focus on visualising these slowly knitted 
networks and advantages through our web platform DAM (https://deanderemarkt.be/).
Second, due to the low-density and sprawled urban context of Genk, DAM had to invest signifi-
cantly in revealing the relations that exist between human and more-than-human actors – which 
are at first sight often invisible – and then bring them together in collective activities (Goyens 
and Huybrechts, 2021). The space and the dynamics responded to the particular socio-economic 
context of Genk: it started as a low-density rural environment, later evolved with industrial infra-
structure and labour, and today presents itself as a post-industrial landscape. These historical peri-
ods can be traced in the environment today, as they coexist with the transition landscape of Genk 
(Zuljevic, 2022; Metalidis et al., 2018). These particularities made us realise that no ‘Living Lab’ 
and ‘work’ approaches or concepts could be copied from high-density urban contexts like Malmö 
and, in attempting to adapt these to the reality of Genk, we set out initial focus on discovering 
the rich and diverse capabilities present in the local context. The choice for nurturing collective 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
238
capabilities in Living Labs was thus driven by a desire to connect expertise between different, scat-
tered worlds, which could enable groups to self-organise around socio-environmental transitions 
(Huybrechts, Devisch, and Tassinari, 2022a). Working in dispersed contexts required time and 
an intensive ongoing engagement of our researchers, which would not have been possible in the 
context of a conventional spatial planning assignment. In the first years, this approach was very 
dependent on the EU funded projects that allowed for researchers to engage in the Participatory 
Design work with sufficient budgets.
Our aim to reveal and shift the politics of radical interdependence amongst human and 
more-than-human actors in the transitioning landscape of Genk demanded us to reflect 
on – and propose – the collective capabilities required by inhabitants, organisations, design -
ers and researchers living and working in these settings in particular ways. Based on previous 
research work on these capabilities (Huybrechts, Dreessen, and Hagenaars, 2018; Dreessen 
et al., 2021; Huybrechts, Devisch, and Tassinari, 2022a, 2022b), we identified four directions 
for collective capabilities : (1) tracing, (2) connecting, (3) imagining and (4) institutioning 
interdependencies, which were, in turn, defined collectively between designers, collectives of 
inhabitants, organisations and institutions in society. These represented a working structure 
for our research, which was shaped as a pluriversal and heterogeneous process historically 
associated in Participatory Design with a Living Lab (see also the Malmö case). We began 
by revealing  the relations that were already present in the transitioning spatial context (e.g. 
food initiatives), followed by how they could be articulated together  (commoning; see Mart -
tila et al., 2014), to then collectively think and work on how they might be reimagined and 
taking into account their relation to institutional planning  projects (institutioning; see also 
Huybrechts et al., 2017). This protocol was, on the one hand, not linear and could therefore 
run parallel or in reversed ways and, on the other hand, in service of facilitating a (work land-
scape) transition within the city. Over the years our online platform has enabled the Living 
Lab to both mediate and trace the relations that were built and the projects that evolved from 
it across scales and time periods. This digital tool – which we have called a relational network 
tool – has also allowed the Living Lab to remain active, even without access to the physical 
space and shopfront (which was open from 2015 to 2019), as well as make visible the actors 
and initiatives in the contexts where we have operated (Calderón Salazar and Huybrechts, 
2020).
Tracing
In our work with the Living Labs in different locations, we learnt together that in designing 
socio-environmental transitions we need to avoid generalising, which demanded an effort to be 
as specific as possible in tracing the particular relations that are developed on a daily basis in 
the studied locations. This implied tracing different specific actors and the locations they use and 
transform regularly, to start imagining futures from there. This could be clearly evidenced when 
DAM collaborated in the ‘North-South project’, a project concerned with a large road transition 
in Limburg, connecting the Dutch North with the Flemish South. We worked mainly in the for -
mer coal-mining municipality of Houthalen-Helchteren, where we traced the diverse relationships 
people had with the road and its environment. We observed how the road infrastructure was built 
for connecting industrial sites and had changed its relation to the surrounding communities and 
landscape over the years. To nurture the collective capabilities in rediscovering this environment, 
self-organised platforms emerged over time by designing together new dynamics around shifting 

Collective Capabilities in Living Labs
239
types of relations. For instance, one platform involved groups of people concerned with ensuring 
safe, slow, car-free environments. This was a type of relation with the road that many people shared 
from different perspectives. Young families were worried about the safety of their children and the 
elderly with safe crossings without being surprised by fast cars or bikes. Nature protection organi-
sations were concerned with clean air and reducing paved road space, as well as enhancing green 
space by promoting a mobility shift from car-dependency to biking, walking and public transport. 
All these actors have developed their own capabilities in dealing with these concerns. Opportunities 
can thus arise from these relations but also require an active, continuous engagement by us – as de-
signers/researchers – as well as inhabitants and different organisational and institutional actors. By 
building the collective capabilities of different actors and sharing their experiences via maps, vid-
eos, interviews and relational interventions, the Living Lab aimed to complement expert views on 
the need for slow pedestrian and cycling connections, with these diverse experiences of the world 
traced through design anthropological approaches. This was enhanced by our strategy of explicitly 
visualising the diverse experiences of people but also concrete accounts on green spaces, trees or 
water areas, which were documented on a map and on DAM’s website (Figure 10.1), so people 
could learn from each other (e.g. how they dealt on a daily basis with avoiding fast riding cars) 
and see the potential of the natural and built environment (e.g. the potential of reducing car space 
in favour of bicycle paths or the interaction with water in their daily lives, such as the reduction 
of flooding risk). This enabled collective learning in the process of researching and representing 
diverse experiences and perspectives (Huybrechts, Devisch, and Tassinari, 2022a).
Figure 10.1 Screenshot from the DAM website on 26 November 23.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
240
Connecting
In our working approach with DAM, we paid particular attention to developing the collective 
capabilities needed in the design process to create particular relations. For example, connecting 
the necessary capabilities for providing a safe and slow road environment between multiple ac-
tors, disciplines and angles (thematic, location-based or historical) allowed for diverse groups 
to reflect together on the things they care for. At a certain point, a group was formed around the 
shared concern for a more ‘slow’ environment. They asked our project team to support them in 
appropriating an old heritage building, left neglected for years, where they could start developing 
activities that align with their ideas of ‘slowing down’ (e.g. mobility, but also food production), 
in close relation to the road study (Figure 10.2). In this group – but also in other platforms that 
were developed within the North-South project – actors started designing translations between 
their different worlds: they developed their capabilities and supported their partners in organis-
ing gatherings where they could share experiences via workshops, markets or interventions. This 
enabled these actors to create new interdependencies between speaking, silent and silenced actors, 
which became evident with the group that formed around the old heritage house. They translated 
their ambition – supported by our research team – into a manifesto for discovering and activat -
ing slow roads in their village. Posters depicting this manifesto were made. They communicated 
and asked for feedback on these, by organising markets in the garden of the house and through 
walks in the surroundings of the building. These markets and walks were very successful on dif -
ferent counts: they brought diverse actors together around a shared concern (‘the road’), com-
municated the ambitions around slow roads by visualising them on posters and walking on them 
Figure 10.2 Pastorie overtaken by nature.

Collective Capabilities in Living Labs
241
and gave a new life to their village centre by nurturing a closer relation between different human 
and more-than-human actors and their surrounding environment. With time, a wider diversity of 
people started to come to these events (people of different ages, cultural and class backgrounds and 
institutional associations), and through the walks they also became familiar with the value of walk-
ing and biking on the slow roads, discovering their particular flora, fauna, water areas and overall 
natural environment, instead of privileging the use of cars and fast roads. In this way, the platform 
around the old heritage house expanded from a group of engaged supporters for a more green and 
connected environment for cyclists and pedestrians, to a group of inhabitants looking for a place to 
meet different neighbours or to discuss their concerns around the transitions in their environment.
Imagining
As design researchers, a greatly valued collective capability is to reimagine – together with diverse 
groups of actors – the relations between themselves and their environment. This was initially fa-
cilitated by DAM’s organisation of a first series of relational interventions (ephemeral) and the set-
ting up of the shopfront (permanent), which functioned as a fixed and concrete physical space that 
stayed active for four years. Since then, with DAM we have nurtured this capability through the 
use of maps, maquettes and built interventions that have allowed us to make future imaginations 
tangible. In the case of the heritage house, we were able to imagine it as a new hub for transitioning 
the paved, polluted environment into a soft, slow context, by repurposing the building, its garden 
and the surrounding roads together (Figure 10.3). To facilitate this, a collaboration was developed 
between the local and supralocal government, a group of inhabitants and a group of architecture 
students from one of our universities (UHasselt). The different actors engaged for two subse -
quent years inhabiting the house, working and workshopping in and around it; from this daily oc-
cupation and collective engagement, an image of its future emerged. This image was represented 
via a digital montage that was shared online and travelled across inhabitants and institutions.
Institutioning
Through our experience with DAM, we have learnt about the importance of nurturing and sustaining 
the relations created between different actors, by articulating the work done ‘in the field’ to diverse 
institutional actors operating in different contexts (academic, public, private and third sectors) and 
scales (municipal, provincial, regional and European). In these settings, designers, inhabitants and 
Figure 10.3 Digital visualisation of what the Pastorie could be.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
242
organisations are trained in shaping projects into new types of organisational forms. In the case of 
the Noord-Zuid project, the old house was transformed into a temporary Living Lab (‘The Pasto-
rie’), collectively shaped by inhabitants and different local and supralocal organisations (collec-
tives such as environmental organisations, music and recreational groups, municipality, different 
departments of the Flemish government, the university, etc.). This was also evidenced in another 
project, FunghiLab, where we supported a network of actors in Genk in testing and implementing 
the infrastructure and process for growing mushrooms out of local waste and resources (described 
in Calderón Salazar et al., 2018). Besides the material and methodological support, we supported 
the transition from an experimental process facilitated by DAM to an autonomous organisation, 
which, in their case, took the shape of a cooperative initiative called Fungimama. In supporting 
these sorts of institutional articulations, we distribute responsibilities – and power – across the dif-
ferent actors, which also results in our role and presence becoming less prominent and essential.
Discussion
Besides the development and nurturing of collective capabilities, several questions and tensions 
have arisen throughout our years of personal and professional engagement with the actors in 
Genk and other situated contexts. These deal mainly with the dilemma between keeping the open-
ness of the relational process to facilitate the emergence of potential collectives and that of the 
pre-structuring process through a collective capability approach that would enable us to define a 
clearer timeline and role division in the research process.
One of these issues has to do with the fact that the researchers – involved through affilia-
tions with local and regional universities – did not live in the studied contexts, which implied 
that we arrived every day from outside of the city (Diepenbeek, Hasselt, Leuven or Brussels). 
Additionally, being considered as paid, hired or subsidised by public bodies at different levels 
(local, regional and European) creates a distance in relation to the actors who live and work in 
the city. A case can be made for structuring the research process to allow us to take a profes -
sional ‘distance’ – both physical and symbolic – from the place where we work, but criticism 
regarding the extent of our engagement is both timely and necessary. Are we really embedded 
in a place that we professionally structure, yet ‘check out’ on the evenings and weekends, and 
where we do not endure the same conditions of its inhabitants? In discussing this question, we 
gained some insights into issues of power imbalance in Participatory Design projects and set-
tings. This allowed us to understand that – even if we were not elected officials – we had some 
level of responsibility to ‘open up’ our space and initiatives to everyone, even the ones who 
might not be on board from the beginning. One of the things we had to come to terms with in 
doing so was the fact that some did not agree with our process – or the regional and city admin -
istration’s, for that respect – in the neighbourhood. Accepting such agonistic space to develop 
dissensus (DiSalvo, 2012) without attempting to ‘convince’ the sceptics implied inhabiting the 
conflict that our presence represented.
Another issue we encountered was that of the ethics of representation in the collective capabil-
ity approach of our research process, which was amplified by our decision to have the Living Lab 
be a space as open as possible. One of the main tactics we used to map the capabilities present 
within the city (tracing interdependencies ) was to initiate discussions with the inhabitants, but 
also policymakers or the city administration, on their capabilities to transform the city in sustain -
able ways – either at the Living Lab or in public space through one of our relational interventions 
(Calderón Salazar et al., 2018; Huybrechts et al., 2016). Portraits of different actors holding a 
poster with a text describing (one of) their capabilities were posted in our blog, as well as printed 

Collective Capabilities in Living Labs
243
as postcards and presented at the Living Lab. This mapping activity served as a way for us to ‘set 
the ground’ for future conversations and collaborations. However, people – and their life experi-
ences with their complexity – were represented through a single portrait with a phrase. Later in 
the process, the actors we were able to further collaborate with, decided how they wanted to be 
represented and the extent to which they would remain involved in the process. These sorts of 
representations – present in many participatory projects – demand an acute awareness of the posi-
tion of the researchers, in relation to the position of the participants involved in the process. They 
require a process of critical positioning that acknowledges that no presence is ever neutral and that 
we are all located ‘somewhere’ in the axes of discrimination (Vázquez, 2020). Design/research 
projects are situated – they are time and site-sensitive, and they emerge from the particularities of 
the context (Kaethler and Calderón Salazar, 2020). In our case, this motivated us to shift from the 
conventional role of design researchers who study the contexts from an expert position towards 
being researchers who are but one actor with a particular set of situated capabilities, being part of 
a diverse group of actors with other situated capabilities.
Both discussed tensions represent for us a revisiting of the notion of design interventions, as 
we formulated at the beginning of the text, as well as the continuous investigation of a situated, 
decolonial and therefore relational design/research approach, aiming to support the self-realisation 
of communities (Calderón Salazar, 2021). In our process of appropriating Living Lab approaches 
and interpreting the literature on the more-than-human, pluriversality and decoloniality, we have 
learnt that there might not be ‘a Belgian way’ to do Living Labs or a way to do Living Labs in 
scattered urban areas. What we have learnt – especially when dealing with recent projects such as 
Noord-Zuid – is the importance of the choice of words and concepts, thus the articulation of how 
we name things. In our projects, we continuously needed to revisit the words we used in our design 
and research: space, work, ethics, representation, intervention and so on, depending on how we 
embody them with the particular actors we work with. As a result, our take on collective capabili-
ties has not disappeared but moved more and more toward articulating how they are embodied, 
inspired among others, by Mol (2021) and Ghosh (2021). Designing with such an attitude enables 
another relation to design’s politics, what, for example, Ghosh (2021) calls a politics of vital -
ity. Here the relationship between nature and human beings is defined beyond ownership, driven 
instead by harmony and co-existence, and where otherwise considered inert objects, such as the 
green spaces in neighbourhoods, are lively actors within a complex network. The further explora-
tion of these politics takes solace on a day-to-day basis in the work of DAM and our engagements 
with multiple socio-ecological challenges in different contexts.
Summary of Challenges and Opportunities
• This case shares the challenging experience of transitioning towards more sustainable relations 
with a landscape that is in the middle of turmoil in terms of its social, environmental and eco -
nomic conditions and in a spatially dispersed urban organisation (similar to a ‘sprawl city’).
• The case explores the potential and pitfalls of Participatory Design processes through a situated 
approach to Living Labs.
• The case shows how a Living Lab can focus on collective capabilities, taking into account the 
role of more-than-human actors as research partners. These are tuned towards revealing the 
relations that are present in the space (e.g. food initiatives), followed by how they could be 
articulated together (commoning), to collectively think and work on how they might be reim-
agined, and lastly connected within institutional planning projects (institutioning).

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
244
• It investigates how Western and Southern perspectives come together in building upon an on -
tological understanding of design focusing on the politics of radical interdependence amongst 
human and more-than-human actors – making their relations visible and legible.
• We have discovered the need to keep the openness of the relational process to facilitate the 
emergence of potential collectives, at the same time as pre-structuring certain aspects of the 
process through a collective capability approach, enabling us to define a clearer timeline and 
role division in the research process.
• We have explored the importance of the choice of words and concepts in relation to how we 
embody them with the particular actors we work with.
• To continuously reflect on the aforementioned challenges and opportunities, we have seen the 
advantages of putting a strong focus on visualising these slowly knitted networks through our 
web platform DAM (https://deanderemarkt.be/)
