11
RECONCILIATION THROUGH 
DIGITAL TEXTILES
Tania Pérez-Bustos, Laura Cortés-Rico, and Andrea Botero
This chapter provides a critical reflection on the geopolitics of knowledge mobilisation within an 
interdisciplinary research project called Mending the New – Reconciliation through digital textiles, 
which was carried out by a consortium of researchers from Colombia and the United Kingdom 
working together with four women’s textiles collectives located in different rural areas of Colombia 
(Bojayá, Quibdó, Mampuján, and Sonsón). This project aimed to generate meeting points and con -
nections between these collectives to understand their use of textiles as a language of memory and 
care of life during wartime. Through the research, the team used Participatory Design (PD) methods 
to explore this collective and material mode of documenting and narrating the conflict through tex-
tile making and introduced digital technologies as a strategy for engaging the participants in unusual 
material dialogues; this, in turn, triggered challenging conversations about war and reconciliation 
from new perspectives. This case presents rich information on the role of Participatory Design in 
reconciliation, peace, and armed conflict contexts; however, constituting the focus of this chapter, 
the specific setting of this project shaped and sustained research design work in such a way that 
geopolitics of knowledge practices considerably marked participation. Awareness of the politics of 
knowledge production and mobilisation within Global North–Global South research collaborations 
brings a set of critical challenges that, while not necessarily new to Participatory Design, reconfig -
ure what counts as participation, who participates, and how.
DOI: 10.4324/9781003334330-13

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
248
Introduction
Mending the New – Reconciliation through Digital Textiles (MtN) was a transdisciplinary research 
project funded by an international call seeking to promote research on sustainable peace in Colom-
bia. The call was framed by the peace process between the Colombian government and the guer -
rilla group FARC, signed in 2016. The research (2018–2020) included the participation of social 
scientists and design researchers who worked hand in hand with four women’s textile groups who 
practice textile craft as a language for documenting war and peace: Artesanías Guayacán in Bojayá, 
Chocó; Artesanías Choibá in Quibdó, Chocó; Tejedoras de Sueños y Sabores de Paz in Mampuján, 
Bolívar; and Costurero Tejedoras por la Memoria de Sonsón in Sonsón, Antioquia. The main goal 
of the research was to think about the craft of these collectives as a material language of reconcilia-
tion and, importantly, to imagine, together with others, ways in which their experiences and knowl-
edge could be brought to public discussion with the participation of digital textiles.
The research proposed a bottom-up understanding of reconciliation in the phase after the 
peace agreement in 2016 of Colombia as a mechanism to establish reconciliation practices as 
long-lasting and collective acts of communication, making, and learning. The transdisciplinary 
nature of the research used a combination of design-based ethnographic and creative methodolo -
gies that contributed to give continuity and visibility of the political agendas of communities at the 
regional and national levels. In this sense, communities must be understood as active participants 
in the research, who benefited from it in political terms, but also financially, given that their time 
and work were symbolically and economically recognised. The project also favoured the mutual 
recognition of women’s textile collectives, who did not know each other before the project.
1
As we will see, a central concept for understanding this case is the idea of collaboration as a knowledge 
dialogue. This concept is borrowed from the Latin American critical pedagogy proposal of Paulo Freire 
(1990, 2000) and Orlando Fals-Borda and Montis (1985), which closely aligns with the long-standing 
commitment of Participatory Design (PD) to mutual learning (Bratteteig et al., 2013; see also Chapter 5 
for a short overview of Freire’s impactful ideas on early Participatory Design developments). In this case, 
besides mutual learning between designers and users, knowledge dialogue underlines the possibility of 
intercultural encounters – as mutual learning, yes – but also continuous and critical learning encounters 
that are aimed at transforming conditions of inequality and power, between communities and researchers, 
as well as between researchers in transnational collaboration. We also think alongside authors such as 
Arturo Escobar (2018) and Lucy Suchman (2011, 2002) about the importance of acknowledging the local 
and geopolitical situatedness of knowledge practices. Therefore, our reflection aims to contribute to the 
urgent need for the Participatory Design practice to be more attuned to situatedness (Agid, 2016; Clarke et 
al., 2022). In particular, for this case, we will focus on geopolitics pertaining to relations of power between 
peer researchers rather than between researchers and communities. In MtN, researchers from both coun-
tries were sensitive to how privileges and knowledge differentials operated between them and local actors 
and worked toward deconstructing those structures of power in their practices. However, this sensibility 
was not as attuned to the differential of knowledge and resources between those considered peers in the 
research process, at least not at a more institutional level.
2
In what follows, we present a more detailed description of the project and its methodology. 
Then, we focus on two dynamics that shaped participation in the development of the research and 
that were shaped by the geopolitics of knowledge. We close the case by presenting lessons learned 
that are relevant for similar Participatory Design research projects.
General Description of the Project and Methodological Approach
The project used a methodological approach that embraced the conjunction of ethnographic and 
Participatory Design-based practices to dive deep into the textile material collective modes of 

Reconciliation Through Digital Textiles
249
documenting and narrating the conflict used by the women of these groups. The research also intro-
duced digital technologies as a strategy to engage women in textile collectives in unusual material dia-
logues but also to trigger challenging conversations about war and reconciliation with them and with 
the broader public (Patarroyo et al., 2019; Cortés-Rico et al., 2020). These different forms of research/
design enabled the creation of the Digital Archive of Testimonial Textiles and an exhibit that included 
textile pieces embroidered by the women to which a series of digital components were weaved using 
textile techniques (Villamizar-Gelvez and Pérez-Bustos, 2020; Sánchez-Aldana et al., 2020).
During the first year of the project, the research team collected information for the digital archive 
and the digital textile exhibit. For this collection, the team met communities and conducted ethno-
graphic work on their territories four times throughout the year. These visits lasted two weeks, each 
week including a workshop where communities and the research team met around textile and digital 
materials to reflect and craft together. Between these ethnographic encounters with communities, the 
project held two digital mingas (an Andean Indigenous tradition of collective work events to involve 
others in mutual support), one in Bogotá, Colombia, and the other one in Nottingham, UK. In these 
collaborative spaces, designers, textile artists, and social scientists not participating in the fieldwork 
met, speculated, and created in conjunction with the research team and, in the Colombian minga, with 
some representatives of the communities. In what follows, we describe in greater detail the workshops 
in women’s territories and the digital mingas to show how they contributed to the design process.
Each visit to women’s territories entailed a workshop (four with each collective, sixteen in to -
tal) led by at least one anthropologist with long-standing relationships with the communities, one 
person from the design team, and one postdoc from the UK with social science training. One of the 
workshops, oriented toward working with each collective about the digital archive, invited them to 
think materially with one of their emblematic textile pieces as an example of the story of their po-
litical work. Hence, with the companionship of researchers, communities collected and reflected 
upon the material characteristics of the piece, how it was made, who had crafted it, and what di -
mensions of the internal conflict it was documenting. This collective reflection allowed us to think 
together, with each group, about the database structure of the archive (González-Arango, 2019; 
González-Arango et al., 2022). The design of the digital platform stands as a collective memory of 
this process, bringing to the public the communities’ voices (audio) regarding needlework and how 
this work materialises political agendas, giving additional details for their craft pieces. The back 
and front end of the archive’s design presents each collective story, as well as the story of one of 
their textile pieces, the story of the conflict that it documents, the political agency that each textile 
object has had, and the ways it has been preserved. Each community entry is also complemented 
with related documentation about its history.
In addition to this workshop, which was central in the design process of the digital archive, 
during fieldwork, three other workshops were planned. In each of these workshops, a digital tex -
tile artefact was proposed to prompt conversations around topics of interest to the research. In 
Figure 11.1, we share details of some of the explorations. The image on the left, for example, was 
a small warp and woof textile created with conductive threads brought to communities in the first 
workshop. They were invited to touch it and see how that touch triggered the lighting of a series of 
LED connected to it. The design of the artefact was simple: if only one person held the piece, the 
LED lighted softly, but if there were many holding hands and sustaining the digital textile object, 
the LED would shine more brightly. This artefact allowed for conversations and reflections about 
community and the power of collective being together. For the second workshop, the idea of being 
more powerful with others was explored through a carrier bag (shown in the central image) that 
was connected to a series of electronic components that allowed the bag to send SMS messages to 
those who had previously received the bag. This explorative artefact was thought of as a carrier of 
gifts between communities, which, in turn, contributed to a process of mutual recognition between 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
250
them. Through the bag, the collectives sent small stories, seeds, and recipes as offerings for the 
others. The collectives were informed, through an SMS on their phones, when the bag had been 
opened and which collective had received the gifts. This created a sense of collectivity between 
the groups that was central to their self-recognition as political actors and that also strengthened 
their commitment to the research process. The image on the right shows a member of one of the 
collectives listening to an audio testimony from a speaker she had stitched herself out of a kit that 
was designed with the help of other collaborators at the digital mingas. In this case, the artefact 
was thought of as a process, as women had to craft their own speaker (which takes time) to listen 
to the testimonies.
The mingas gathered a wide variety of participants who interacted with textile crafts and sto -
ries coming from communities, as well as with electronic components and digital devices made 
available to them by the researchers to imagine possible forms that the artefacts to be designed 
for the exhibition could take, as ways to materialise feelings and thoughts about reconciliation. As 
in the case of the embroidered speakers in Figure 11.1 (right), some artefacts initially designed in 
the mingas went back to the communities through the workshops, as a way of prompting material 
dialogues to think/craft together possible artefacts. As learning devices, they connected people 
in mingas with communities, materially as in the case of speakers, by the very act of stitching a 
listening textile object. The idea of taking the time and labor for listening condensed in the em-
broidered speakers became then central to the concept of the exhibition and the digital textiles it 
included (Patarroyo et al., 2019; Sánchez-Aldana et al., 2020).
During workshops and in the mingas, the evolving digital textile artefact central to the exhibit 
invited communities to think, through their making, about their feelings regarding the conflict 
and the possibility of reconciliation. The combination of materials familiar to the communities 
(threads, fabrics, needles) with unknown components (sensors, microcontrollers) generated cu-
riosity and activated spaces for experimentation, speculation, and reflection about these topics 
through continuous and critical learning (Freire, 1990, 2000). This process, also seen as an inter -
cultural encounter, highlights the horizontality of learning and its political and transformative po-
tential. Between one fieldwork visit and the next, communities were invited to continue thinking 
materially about the conversations prompted during the encounters. To do so, the team proposed 
that the women create a textile piece that could express their feelings about reconciliation and that 
would also become central to the final exhibit.
During the second year of the project, from December 2019 to early April 2020, the research 
team worked with the information and materials collected during the first year, through the work-
shops and the digital mingas as collaborative spaces threaded by ethnographic work.
3 The initial 
configurations of the database and the exhibit continue to be developed in this period in Bogotá 
and Medellín. The idea was to bring these advances to textile collectives in May 2020 to con-
tinue with the Participatory Design process. However, lockdowns due to the COVID-19 pandemic 
started in late March of that year, and the team had to adapt to continue working with the women’s 
textile collectives in the design process across some distance.
These two main products of the research (Figure 11.2), the digital archive (Digital Ar -
chive of Testimonial Textiles
4) and the digital textile exhibit (Time(s) to Listen 5), together 
with a collective book and a series of podcasts telling the soundscapes and the stories of 
each textile collective, were launched in a virtual event that gathered the four collectives in 
September 2020. After the project’s formal closing, the digital archive has continued to be 
used and nourished by researchers and communities. It has contributed to the political vis -
ibility of these collectives and the positioning of textile activism in the country. For its part, 
once mobility restrictions due to the pandemic were over, the exhibit was taken to Medellín 

Reconciliation Through Digital Textiles
251

and then to Quibdó in 2022. These public exhibitions, close to some of the communities, al -
lowed new encounters between collectives, enabling them to interact with their textile pieces 
which now were part of the digital textile exhibit. Hence, in both cities, women from the

and Artesanías Choibá  in Quibdó. The meetings contributed to strengthening the community 
bonds between these groups.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
252
Geopolitics of Participation
As initially described, the project started and was originally possible, significantly, through a generous 
binational grant from the Newton-Caldas Fund that joined the efforts of the national research councils 
of Colombia and the United Kingdom. The call required Colombian research groups to collaborate 
with UK researchers in a proposal oriented toward thinking about peace and reconciliation, given the 
signature in 2016 of the peace agreement between the Colombian government and the guerrilla group 
FARC. It implied that although the resources came from two contexts, they should both contribute 
to local peace processes in Colombia. The project’s initial idea came from the Colombian anthro-
pologists who were part of the team, who thought that the call could give continuity to communities’ 
processes, which they had supported for more than ten years. This original team invited Colombian in-
teraction; designers and  textile designers to join the project and contacted the UK researchers, known 
to one of the Colombian anthropologists, to be part of the consortium. As we mentioned, all research-
ers, no matter their location, were sensible and acknowledged through their research practices the role, 
knowledge, and interest of communities as part of Participatory Design transdisciplinary research. 
Thus, communities beyond being engaged in design practices in horizontal terms were provided by 
the research budget with the financial resources that they needed to continue with their political work. 
Having said this, this sensibility was not extensive to a recognition of the different conditions of possi-
bility for doing research at the institutional level between both teams. Somehow it was assumed by all 
parties that researchers in both countries were peers and that funding agencies provided equal condi-
tions for developing the research. As we will show, this naive understanding of the conditions of possi-
bility for research between locations did not contribute to artful integration (Suchman, 2002) between 
parts, but underscored power relations that are shaped by the geopolitics of institutional knowledge.
In this section, we concentrate on two dimensions of the project that were shaped by this 
general geopolitical dynamic and that in turn configured participation. First, we present how 
different levels of knowledge of researchers on the dynamics and conditions of existence of 
communities contributed to the emergence of disparate understandings of their location and role 
in strengthening communities’ actions and the role that communities could play in research and 
design practice. Second, we will show how the distribution of resources generated a dynamic of 
division of labor at international and local levels, which shaped the scope of the impact of the 
designed artefacts. As we will argue, geopolitics of knowledge is molded, in this case, by North–
South tensions on an international level, as well as by the configuration of centres and peripheries 
at the local level.
Figure 11.2  Left: screenshot of the Digital Archive of Testimonial Textiles. Right: photography of the digital 
textile exhibition, Time(s) to Listen. Copyright holder: Mending the New Project.

Reconciliation Through Digital Textiles
253
Participation Is Shaped by Differentials in Knowledge of Communities
A central resource that made the project possible was the long-standing relationships and previous 
knowledge that some Colombian anthropologists had about women’s textile collectives and the 
dynamics of fieldwork with these local communities. Hence, before MtN was launched, textile 
collectives knew the work of these anthropologists and trusted them because their work had mate-
rial and political implications for them. Collectives of women appreciated the documentation of 
their work to which these researchers had contributed. Hence, communities accepted to be part of 
MtN as a way of giving continuity to this work done together with these particular researchers. 
This knowledge and engagement with communities situates local and international researchers 
differently. These differences also shape our understanding of who participates in research and the 
role of research more generally in a Participatory Design process.
Colombian anthropologists who were part of the team, including the principal investigator, had 
fieldwork experience of more than fifteen years, including five to ten years with textile artisans. 
This experience was central to the writing of the research proposal and the development of the 
project, especially considering that Colombian anthropologists saw the funding as a possibility 
to continue their work, not just on textile crafts as a political language but also on community 
engagement. Hence, MtN did not establish a relationship with the communities but contributed to 
strengthening an ongoing and previous process of collaboration between the collectives of women 
and the anthropologists of the team. Thus, questions about how textile crafting was a language to 
speak of internal conflict, memory, and reconciliation were not only to be answered to widen com-
prehension of the role of materiality in political action but, in themselves, were forms of inquiry to 
be thought with the communities as a way to understand together the possibilities, conditions, and 
potentialities of their ongoing political action and that action’s material dimension.
Let’s focus on an example. As previously mentioned, Time(s) to Listen, the digital textile exhi-
bition that resulted from MtN, included a series of textile pieces created by each women’s collec-
tive in which they materialised how they understood and what they felt about reconciliation. In the 
exhibit, each of these creations includes a series of embroidered speakers, some stitched by com -
munities themselves, which softly amplify their voices regarding the figures they had embroidered 
in relation to their experiences during the armed conflict. The crafting of each piece emerged as 
part of the fieldwork and its embroidering by each collective was suggested by one of the anthro-
pologists that had been working with communities over the years.
The UK social researcher visiting the country and the communities for the first time raised 
concerns about the process of asking local communities to embroider pieces for an exhibition. She 
felt that this could imply extra labour for communities, which should be recognised in economic 
terms. Moreover, she was concerned that researchers inviting communities to embroider the pieces 
and accompanying them when doing so could be patronising and potentially biasing the findings. 
For the Colombian designers participating in fieldwork, with no previous similar research experi-
ences, that was an important reflection, which also raised a red flag for the designers and prompted 
them to reconsider how initially they had assumed that the labour was part of what communities 
already crafted on a daily basis, and thus unproblematic. However, as Colombian researchers, we 
contend that what is at stake in this case is more subtle. Embroidering the pieces for the exhibition 
entailed extra labour for the communities and recognising the economic value of the time invested 
on their part is important; in fact, that was assumed in the Colombian budget for the project. 
However, what is also important to recognise and work with is the fact that the women of these 
collectives not only inhabit their territories and open their doors so that researchers can approach 
their realities and material creations to inspire design processes. Instead, participating in MtN 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
254
was an opportunity for textile collectives to think about why they do what they do and how that 
strengthens their political action. For those researchers who had been working with the communi-
ties for years, this was clear, after accompanying these political processes, engaging with their 
problematic realities, and staying with their troubles, as Haraway would say (2016).
Inviting communities to participate in a process of participatory creative research is not just a 
matter of recognising that their work is important; it is also about recognising that communities 
are themselves engaged in their own practice-based research and that this work takes place in 
contexts of precariousness and therefore needs collaboration (Fals-Borda and Montis, 1985). This 
is collaboration not in the sense of generating relations of dependence but instead of making a 
commitment to community processes, of participating, through research, in generating conditions 
of possibility (see also Chapter 5 and Agid, 2016; Harrington et al., 2019). In this case, it was not 
only about crafting a textile piece for others (i.e. for a design process with community input) but 
rather about creating a textile piece (collectively) through which they could pause to think about 
themselves and their political and collective practices through making (Vega et al., 2023).
In projects such as MtN, the difference in knowledge between researchers, whose links with 
the communities are recent or whose fieldwork experience in these territories is limited, meant 
that strengthening the work of the collectives, as a horizon for research and the labour that this 
entails, was understood as a patronising practice and not as a long-term process of self-shaping by 
the collective in which research and design were other of the participants. In the case of Colom-
bian anthropologists, they have become part of the community and its problems thanks to their 
long-term involvement. This is what allowed researchers and the project in general to engage in 
a more accountable dialogue, leading to the process of continuous and critical learning (Freire, 
2000; Agid, 2016), when accompanying the design processes, and what made the exhibition and 
the archive be perceived by the community as their own work and not just as a work in which they 
participated (Winschiers-Theophilus et al., 2010). This said, MtN emerges as an example of how 
communities invite researchers into their own processes of active creation and political work as 
a way of crafting research (as has been suggested by Fals-Borda and Montis, 1985), an invitation 
that is not always visible or recognised by all (see also Chapter 3). Understanding the location of 
the researchers (as inviting, as being invited, or part of) and their knowledge differentials, is thus 
relevant for other Participatory Design projects in which the research team cannot be understood 
only as speaking “for” the community or “accompanying” the community or collective.
Participation Is Shaped by Distribution of Resources
In this section, we focus on the ways in which the distribution of financial resources for research 
in international collaboration shaped forms of collaboration in Participatory Design. It is impor -
tant to emphasise again that communities were financially supported throughout the research and 
that researchers from all disciplines and locations were sensitive to power differences that could 
undermine the role of women’s collectives and, with it, reinforce the inequalities they have lived. 
The discussion on financial resources proposed here addresses, then, the geopolitical differences 
between research partners that were accentuated due to how resources were allocated and its im -
plication for design practices.
Due to the way the grant of each funding agency was defined, each country allocated its 
budget to fund the project separately, and the administration of resources was done accordingly 
(RCUK-Colciencias Research Partnerships Call, 2017). The project’s original resource distribu-
tion relied also on the experiences of the PIs from both countries. They had broad experience 
in leading social inquiry but less knowledge in resourcing design projects. Thus, in the UK, the 

Reconciliation Through Digital Textiles
255
allocation was mainly to fund social research in Colombia, with a proportionally smaller budget, 
the allocation was to support both social and design research. This meant that resources for Partici-
patory Design had to be continually sourced and worked out in the creation of the exhibit and the 
archive. We argue that this implied ways of rebusque – an expression that in Colombian Spanish 
slang means to “make do with” within the socioeconomic context of precarity. This implies that 
extra labor was not equally shared between the teams and had implications for how participation 
was constituted in at least three ways: in the fieldwork, when mobilising resources for design, and 
in the sustainability and maintenance of the resulting artefacts.
Regarding fieldwork, the project proposal conceived that it would be carried out mainly by a 
Colombian anthropologist with a long-standing and trusting relationship with women and a social 
scientist from the UK. In that plan, the design team would collaborate with these social researchers 
rather than operate directly with the women in the territories. However, during the project imple-
mentation, it became imperative to have the design team actively participate in the on-site col-
laborative work. The resources needed for this to happen were added by the Colombian team into 
their budget and represented a first form of research (“make do”) rebusque. Specifically, for the 
design component of the fieldwork, sixteen new trips were funded for one Colombian designer to 
participate in each workshop on the communities’ territories. This administrative accommodation 
was carried out only in Colombia, as the UK team did not have a field design researcher as part of 
their component of the partnership. In addition to highlighting the financial inequity between the 
two teams, this situation confused the Colombian team with respect to the role of the UK team in 
the design process. That led to a continuous wondering about how autonomous they (the Colom -
bian team) were in the decision-making regarding the design of both the archive and the exhibit. 
Thus, even when unexpected needs and decisions were made, the way it was done accentuated the 
local differences and international divisions in the project.
The distribution of resources also affected the possibilities of mobilising more speculative de-
sign. The budget contemplated for the design was tight and, as mentioned, was mainly charged 
to the Colombian funds. Although initial planning included speculative processes such as those 
enabled by the two digital mingas, it did not consider the need to draw connections between these 
events during the workshops in the territories. Therefore, materials and resources were allocated 
for the digital mingas but not for the design process with the collectives between the mingas. 
However, it was these workshops that constituted the settings of most of the participatory creative 
practice with communities, in conjunction with fieldwork in the territories. Thus, to create the con-
ditions of possibility for the design process to be part of those workshops, one of the Colombian 
universities involved mobilised additional local resources to provide materials, tools, design re -
searchers’ additional time, and final capstone projects from design undergraduate students. These 
additional resources allowed material speculations and dialogues in the field, oriented mainly to 
the exhibition. However, it also reinforced the burden of Participatory Design on the Colombian 
team and its limited budget.
Finally, the two resultant artefacts, the archive and the exhibition, have had very different con-
ditions of sustenance, also shaped by resource distribution. First, the archive design was con-
ceived to continue to grow over time. For this, long-lasting IT infrastructure support was needed, 
something which is difficult to provide for institutions in the South, given the precarity of their 
resources but also considering that the costs of these services must be paid in dollars and not in the 
local currency suffering from constant devaluation. Despite this, the hosting, web services, and do-
main of the archive were funded by the project in Colombia but for no longer than three years. The 
feeding of the archive, which requires the work of web technologists, has not been possible, given 
that maintaining aesthetic harmony, quality in the photographs, or revision of the text style implies 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
256
human resources that are no longer available. On the other hand, “Time(s) to Listen,” the resulting 
digital textile exhibition, benefited from resources from the project and the additional funds given 
by one university in Colombia. This additional institutional support, based in Colombia only, has 
provided continuity for the travelling of the exhibition, which requires the mobility of heavy and 
delicate elements, a careful assembly process from someone able to solve technical difficulties, 
and, very importantly, the presence of someone to mediate the interaction between the public and 
the exhibition, aimed at encouraging the public to connect with the communities’ stories rather 
than being distracted by the visual and interactive elements (Pérez-Bustos, 2024).
The maintenance and mobilisation of these artefacts highlights the importance of the resources, 
care, and mediation they require. Securing this possibility was only possible through institutional 
support and could not only rely on team motivation once the project ended. The archive, which 
was initially intended to grow, has faced challenges in maintaining continuity due to limited re -
sources. On the other hand, initially conceived as contemplative and static, the exhibition has 
benefited from institutional resources that have enabled its mobility and promoted new exchanges. 
In summary, the distribution of resources (financial and institutional) affected the sustainability 
of these artefacts and created an additional burden for the Colombian counterpart of the project.
Challenges and Opportunities
MtN contributed to giving continuity to the political agendas of communities and created links 
between collectives. In this, both the archive and the exhibition, with their limitations, raised 
awareness among other audiences about the issues with which the women’s collectives live and 
how they continue to care for life in the middle of armed conflict. Along with this, the project 
also represented a professional growth scenario for the research team in general. For the design 
team, participating in the research was an opportunity to strengthen concerns related to socially 
responsible design. For the ethnography team, it opened up new forms of creative research that 
transformed the way they do fieldwork.
That said, this case of Participatory Design-based research allows us to recognise the partial 
possibilities of transdisciplinary research work and international collaboration. The limitations 
mentioned concerning the distribution of resources and knowledge differentials on both a local 
and international geopolitical scale lead us to underline the importance of conceiving Participatory 
Design research processes paying attention to geopolitics and its material implications. Assuming 
that interdisciplinarity and transnational collaboration can emerge in the research process has costs 
that affect creative practice and create tensions within teams. These costs, in turn, can contribute 
to entrenching workloads that tend to operate according to a more structural logic of inequality.
In addition, it is important to recognise that there are differences in knowledge when working with 
communities in Participatory Design processes. Those differences cannot only be understood and ex-
pected to be overcome, in terms of mutual learning (Agid, 2016). Projects like MtN highlight the need 
for the Participatory Design process to serve as a platform for continuous learning and, importantly, 
for knowledge dialogues (Freire, 1990). However, while this dialogue can be profoundly transforma-
tive for creative research, such transformation entails workloads for those who undertake the ongoing 
accompaniment and mediation that ensures that work with communities is not appropriated or instru-
mentalised for creative practice (Agid, 2016). It is important that this accompanying design work can 
be properly valued and recognised so that it does not perpetuate its invisibility as a care work.
Finally, one of the main lessons learned from this case is the need to continuously open up to 
the question of the reasons that motivate participation in this type of creative research process with 
communities. As we have already pointed out, for the seed team of this project, participating in calls 
for proposals of this magnitude represents the opportunity to give continuity to long-term processes 

Reconciliation Through Digital Textiles
257
that are difficult to sustain given the scarcity of resources and the precariousness of local institu -
tions. In these cases, the mobilisation of knowledge is subordinated to the process of strengthening 
grassroots work. Research must take advantage of these processes, not the other way around. When 
local and international alliances are created to promote this type of political involvement, they 
should not only be an opportunity to broaden knowledge about these territories and their problems. 
Those who do not have a history of working with communities and are invited to participate in these 
processes and who are also in centres of knowledge with certain institutional privileges and stability 
should ask themselves why they should participate, if not to strengthen these dynamics in a deci-
sive and sustained way. If this is not achieved, the logic of academic institutions will mean that the 
rebusque (“make do”) of resources, required to sustain knowledge dialogues, continuous learning, 
and strengthening processes will end up reinforcing inequalities of a geopolitical nature (both at the 
international and local levels) and that the South (periphery), which is used to performing rebusque, 
will end up doing so to sustain its processes, while the North (centre) continues to produce the 
knowledge that its institutions demand. How this rebusque practice can also be distributed in con-
texts of Participatory Design with grassroots communities will depend on whether local problems 
become everyone’s problems and not just of those of the few who are close to them.
