12
LIVING LABS FOR OPEN-ENDED 
PARTICIPATORY DESIGN
Per-Anders Hillgren, Per Linde, Alicia Smedberg,  
Elisabet M. Nilsson, Pelle Ehn and Mette Agger Eriksen
Malmö Living Labs (2007–2017) built on a Scandinavian Participatory Design approach and aimed 
to explore how processes of change in the City of Malmö could be further democratised. In this chap-
ter, as a community of remembrance, Participatory Design researchers of different ages, roles and 
duration of involvement recall and revitalise memories of lab engagements not previously told. The 
main challenge addressed concerns how to navigate Participatory Design processes with an aim of 
open-endedness. The chapter is structured as follows. First, the main source of inspiration is intro-
duced: Umberto Eco’s metaphor of the forest as a narrative place of potential transformation. Next, 
comes a brief introduction to the context of Malmö Living Labs including its core theoretical foun-
dations and ideas of democratisation, infrastructuring and heterogeneity. Then, at the centre of the 
chapter, four reflective stories of lab engagements are shared in the form of “Wanderings”. The aim 
of the stories is not to give voice to all people who participated but rather to reflect upon influential 
moments that made big imprints on each researcher. The Wanderings encounter the aftermath of a 
women’s association; a decade of moving in the “academic jungle”; intensities around a game jam; and 
embodied gatherings around a king’s chair. Lastly, the aim of the chapter is to learn from the challenges 
and opportunities fronted in the Wanderings and to propose points of attention for future open-ended 
Participatory Design practices. In addition to arguing for the value of storytelling as an approach to col-
lective remembrance and learning, the three main contributions, proposed are; (1) to acknowledge and 
work with different intensities and paces in infrastructuring (2) to recognise the complex boundaries in 
heterogeneous networks, and (3) largely inspired by a dissertation from 2022 by one of the authors, to 
be carefully aware of the sensitised labour of infrastructuring.
  DOI: 10.4324/9781003334330-14

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
260
Introduction
In folklore and mythology, the forest is a place of both wonderment and danger, a place for getting 
lost or finding refuge, a place for unanticipated encounters and meetings with the other. The act of 
Wandering there is often narrated as a rite of passage including both the experience of ambiguity 
and the potential for transformation. Conceptually, this bears a strong resemblance to the concept 
of participation. Also familiar to the Participatory Design researcher is the strong link to narration, 
storytelling and anecdotalisation, which are common formats for both communicating and report-
ing (Smedberg, 2022). Umberto Eco, in “Six Walks in the Fictional Woods” (Eco, 1994), shares 
his life as a reader and author and reflects on the complex interplay between authors and readers, 
in which the entanglement of voices blurs the borders between sender and receiver and where 
meaning is emerging rather than being at beforehand understood. A fundamental characteristic of 
Participatory Design is the complex network of relations and different voices in which researchers 
wander, at times finding unknown forest springs, at times getting lost.
In this chapter, six researchers will use the forest as a metaphorical frame to articulate and re -
flect on some of the key characteristics and theoretical concepts of Malmö Living Labs. Similar to 
Eco’s accounting of the wanderer straddling between the imaginary and the real, they search for a 
point of intersection between democracy and innovation. A long time has passed, and the revisit -
ing of stories makes configurations of remembrance possible in a way not always accessible in the 
very moment at “project reporting time”. The reflections come in the form of short wanderings, 
that is, stories, and personal memories of lab events that as forest walks run the risk of getting lost 
while still maintaining the ambition to restore and regenerate collaboration. They will circulate 
around some of the characteristics of the labs such as an ethos emphasising open-ended processes, 
heterogeneity and a long-term perspective on working relations and the labour of infrastructuring.
Malmö Living Labs
Malmö Living Labs was initiated in 2007 and active for approximately ten years, with no official time 
of closure. It was established at Malmö University in southern Sweden as a core part of the research 
platform MEDEA. Based on various fundings, overall Malmö Living Labs was organised in three labs: 
the Factory, the Stage and the Neighbourhood (see Figure 12.1). This chapter mainly builds on stories 
from the Neighbourhood lab (to get a fuller picture of all lab engagements, see Ehn et al., 2014).
With historical roots in Scandinavian Participatory Design, Malmö Living Labs gathered research-
ers, public and grassroots organisations, companies and citizens in processes of joint democratic design 
experiments (Ehn et al., 2014). The aim was to explore how processes of change in the City of Malmö 
could be further democratised. More specifically, the lab aimed to empower and give voice to groups 
and citizens with fewer resources and in close collaboration with these explore how new technology, 
collaborative services or social innovation could provide value for them within their everyday engage-
ments and lives. The notion of democratisation related to who should take part in the lab, what kind 
of value production to engage in and strive for and how to work with design and processes of change.
This pushed the lab into a rather open journey and, instead of starting to frame, plan and initiate 
projects and then invite citizens or grassroots organisations into these, the lab set out to first find 
actors that were not in the immediate proximity of the creative class or academic world – basically, 
actors who were less visible and considered less powerful. The idea was then to articulate the what 
and how in close collaboration with these actors.
This openness married well with the concept of infrastructuring as developed by anthropologist 
Susan Leigh Star and colleagues (Star and Ruhleder, 1996), which during this time had started to 

Living Labs for Open-Ended Participatory Design
261
Figure 12.1  An overview of Malmö Living Labs as a landscape inspired by Umberto Eco’s metaphorical for-
est. As this chapter mainly builds on stories from the Neighbourhood lab we have provided map 
cut-outs later in this chapter, see Figures 12.2 and 12.3. Illustration created by Alicia Smedberg.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
262
influence the Participatory Design community (Karasti, 2014). Infrastructuring has become a rich 
and elaborated concept (see Chapter 3), especially as an approach that brings attention to ongoing 
socio-material complexities and power issues in Participatory Design projects. In our case, this 
attention supported us to be more open regarding the exact course of our engagements. It allowed 
opportunities for change to emerge in relation to the needs that different groups articulated and 
the socio-material conditions that occurred along the way (Hillgren et al., 2011). This process was 
also accompanied by an emphasis on establishing long-term working relations that offered good 
opportunities to build trust and support mutual learning (Simonsen and Robertson, 2013).
Another key trait that distinguished the labs was their heterogeneous character. One theoreti-
cal inspiration to nurture this came from the political philosopher Chantal Mouffe (2009) and her 
concept of agonism which stresses that a vital democracy needs radical plurality. According to her, 
plurality could be achieved by bringing together actors with opposing views in agonistic (instead of 
antagonistic) struggles. Her core idea is that despite their disagreements actors should respect each 
other as adversaries rather than enemies. However, as it became clear and what we hoped to show 
in our stories, achieving this mutual respect turned out to be hard. We will return to these concepts 
and the key traits of the labs in the final discussion, but, first, we will wander into the forest.
Stories From Wanderings Through the Forest of Malmö Living Labs
The following personal stories, framed as four Wanderings, do not follow a chronological order 
but rather the logic of how our distant memories revisit us. The authors are Participatory Design 
researchers of different ages, with different lengths of their careers and who have been engaged in 
Malmö Living Labs, particularly in the Neighbourhood lab or in the aftermath of it. Their aim is 
not particularly to give voice to all people who participated in the lab but rather to share and reflect 
upon influential moments and processes for each researcher that made big imprints on them.
Wandering 1: The Story of the “Mothers of Invention”
It is 2016, I am sitting at a café with J, the coordinator of Herrgårds Women Association, a group 
of officially unemployed immigrant women. As a non-governmental organisation (NGO) these 
“Mothers of Invention” had created catering services, worked with refugee children, counselled 
on violence in the home and explored new ways of collaboration with the municipality as well as 
with private companies (Figure 12.2a). Our meeting takes place some years after the end of a long 
collaboration to discuss the storyline for a joint chapter in a book for prospective teachers.
It was first at this moment, in the aftermath of our joint work, that the intricacy of their networks 
became clear to me. My colleagues and I had very quickly become impressed by their creativity, com-
munity spirit and generosity and saw them as a very potent organisation with a capacity to create pro-
found social change. What we had not realised at that time was that their agency and ability to act as an 
independent women-based organisation had come from quite an elaborate and extensive effort. When 
J articulated their origin, I realised that long before we started to collaborate, they had been engaged in 
complex infrastructuring labouring (Smedberg, 2022). They were situated within a heterogeneous and 
multiethnic community, where power to a large extent resided among prominent men. The agency of 
these women was therefore quite limited, and many actions (that seem ordinary for others) were un-
thinkable. For example, to travel outside their neighbourhood by bus or to ride a bike – or for that matter 
to start an organisation for and with women. To increase their agency these women initially spent a lot 
of time supporting the men in the community. This included everything from contacts to authorities, 
translations, arranging weddings and helping with kids’ homework. Step by step they gained the trust 

Living Labs for Open-Ended Participatory Design
263
of these men, and, at the same time, they earned more and more emancipation and agency. This prior 
infrastructuring labour was a crucial factor in how they could engage in our joint experiments.
Looking at this from a perspective of heterogeneity, we had at that time not understood that the 
lab’s extended networks reached into groups whose conservative values were very far from our 
own (and of course also far from the women). Still, it was this heterogeneity that (paradoxically) 
also produced concrete emancipation for women. If we had better understood the complexity of 
their networks during our collaboration, this would probably have helped us to better explain to 
the city representatives why this group of women had a unique capacity to engage the local com -
munity and therefore should be seen as an important partner.
During our collaboration, in 2012, we initiated another path with them that went in a differ -
ent direction and revealed a less successful act of infrastructuring. We thought that we had found 
a valuable glade in the forest, a place that opened up for a rich encounter between two different 
organisations, Herrgårds Women Association and a group of business women and entrepreneurs, 
both intriguing in their own way. However, it turned out that this place was of a different character. 
This became evident when two of my colleagues and I were invited to a meeting at the local library 
with J where she was very resigned. She explained that they could not continue the collaboration 
with the other group. Initially, they were very positive about the collaboration, and several prom-
ising ideas emerged, for example, the development of catering services or children’s stories in 
different languages. However, now the women felt very uncomfortable because the female entre-
preneurs had asked them to step forward as individual business women instead of as a collective. 
They were not ready for that, not yet. Also, J told us that someone had put their premises on fire 
and that this probably was an act of men within their own community who regarded the women as 
too radical in their emancipation process.
The collaboration included two groups (Herrgårds Women Association and the business women) 
with very different worldviews and ideas of how to understand and value the collective versus the 
Figure 12.2  These map cut-outs connect to left: Wandering 1 and right: Wandering 2. Illustration created 
by Alicia Smedberg.


Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
264
individual, but no process was initiated to bring these worldviews together as respectful adversaries. 
This was a pivotal moment that changed my research focus, and both brought my attention towards 
the role of worldviews in design processes and to a high degree redirected my engagements towards 
supporting people in power in rethinking taken-for-granted assumptions and worldviews.
Wandering 2: The Story of Knowledge in the Making in the “Academic Jungle”
While the previous Wandering largely took place in “the wild”, this Wandering moves around in the 
academic jungle, where I both get lost and find refuge in the making of knowledge (Figure 12.2b). It 
spans more than a decade and three venues at our university – a classroom, a lecture hall and a studio.
Our first visit is to a classroom, the very place where academic knowledge may be transformed 
into future practices. For almost the entire duration of our labs and with other lab members, I have 
been teaching a class on design, democracy and participation. Through our teaching, we have 
inspired a diversity of students to do democratic design interventions with local actors. Together, 
we have shared and reflected upon Participatory Design theory and practice and especially experi-
ences from the labs, not least from the long-term collaboration with the courageous women from 
Herrgårds Women Association.
In 2019, I am teaching together with A, our new PhD student and the youngest member of the 
labs. We share a growing interest in the political philosophy of Hannah Arendt (2013) and her con-
cepts of human activity, labour, work and action, as well as in her narrative style of writing. As we 
interpret Arendt, the concept of labour concerns the repetitive and reproductive toil of keeping the 
household afloat and staying alive. To her, labour is a private and social activity that is a necessary 
human condition, but the household is not a place of freedom or a platform for human inventions. 
Freedom and inventions ideally take place as political actions among “free men” (freed from 
private and social toil and interests), as participation in open debate and as heroic interventions in 
agonistic public spaces. To Arendt, work is neither labour nor action. In our vocabulary, it is liter-
ally craft and design, neither reproduction nor political action, but the making of infrastructure, 
of things and institutions, that over time connect people and have a certain durability. We thought 
that Arendt’s human conditions challenged Participatory Design in several fundamental and po -
tentially constructive ways, even if we as researchers with a Marxist inclination (A’s contemporary 
and mine somewhat faded and outworn since 1968) felt a bit uneasy with Arendt’s hierarchy of 
human action and with her exclusion of the social from the political.
The next stop on this Wandering is in December 2022 in a fully packed lecture hall: A is defend-
ing her doctoral thesis. Here another kind of infrastructuring is going on – the qualifying process of 
transforming research efforts into the best knowledge we have on a certain issue. She is engaged 
in a vivid conversation with her opponent and the international grading committee on the virtues 
of affect, care and anecdotalisation. With her concept of affective infrastructuring she has done 
with Arendt what Marx did with Hegel, turned the theory of human activity on its head. A argues 
that labour and the social are not obsolete or redundant in relation to design as work and politi -
cal action. The caring and affective activity that is carried out by those in the margins of a design 
intervention is fundamental for positive achievements. By attending to these actors and listening 
to their stories, A has (as Arendt by the way) refined a set of anecdotes, for example, about the 
(re)productive labour of the (heroic) “Mothers of Invention”, which highlights the importance of 
social affective infrastructuring for Participatory Design.
This brings us to the end of this Wandering, back to the early days of the labs and yet another 
transformative place – a studio hosting an event in which gold can be converted into research. It 
is springtime in 2010, and I fail as that kind of sorcerer. I am by far not the most central design 

Living Labs for Open-Ended Participatory Design
265
researcher in the labs but as a professor and the most senior participant I am representing us at a 
meeting with the guardian of the gold, the venerable Knowledge Foundation. A year ago they had 
conditionally awarded us a substantial 10-year grant to do research on co-production with our liv-
ing labs as the main asset. Now, it was judgement day and the foundation’s scientific expert com-
mittee came to our studio for a review. So far the most promising design and innovation activities 
have been carried out with and by Herrgårds Women Association. Given the inspiring labour and 
deeds of these “Mothers of Invention”, it should not be too difficult to argue for a continuation 
of the grant. This belief came to an abrupt end when one of the highly esteemed experts in affect 
exclaimed, not as a question but in a condescending tone: “I cannot see what these housewives 
have to do with innovation”. No design work, no inventive action, just reproductive labour. No 
gold. End of story.
This happened back in the days when neoliberalism and new public management were at their 
highest. The professors of the expert committee and the Knowledge Foundation clearly subscribed 
to this worldview of control. In the decision document terminating the funding for the labs, it was 
stated that we did not have a good enough “quality control system that could grant research on 
co-production of good scientific quality”, that “the environment was lacking functioning and reli-
able co-production” and that “lack the ability to transform this into robust and long-term collabo-
ration with industry”. The fundamental wisdom of Aristotle that the household is the fundament 
of economy was rejected. I wish A and also her faculty opponent and grading committee, from 
a decade later, had been by my side in the studio that day. Maybe they could have found a route 
through the academic jungle, a passage where knowledge trumps profit where the gentle voices of 
the “Mothers of Invention” can be heard through the cacophony of entrepreneurial roaring.
Wandering 3: The Story of Arabic Game Jam
The Wandering through the Terrain of Arabic Game Jam can act as a contrast to the other stories 
about the lab as being questioned in terms of the “innovativeness” and capacities of the involved 
actors and the quality of the outcome of their actions (Figure 12.3a). In comparison, the Arabic 
Game Jam was situated in a context with strong connections to an industry holding great commer-
cial potential as well as an aura of being the “future”, namely the games industry.
In 2012, when the Arabic Game Jam took place, there were still few computer games developed 
targeting Arabic-speaking markets despite the evidence of a strong and growing Arabic game cul-
ture across the world, including the Arabic-speaking communities in Malmö.
Malmö had (and still has) a strong cluster of game developers as well as a large immigrant 
population with Arabic cultural backgrounds and language skills. During this period, the City of 
Malmö and the Neighbourhood lab were in contact to discuss the development of urban areas. In 
one of the many meetings, my colleagues and I launched the idea of bringing the game developers 
and the Arabic-speaking community together to co-design game concepts directly targeting the 
growing Arabic-speaking game markets. What alternative stories, game mechanics, aesthetics and 
values systems would such a mix of competencies, skills and experiences generate? What if this 
initiative could contribute to widening the still somewhat homogeneous selection of game titles 
available on the market and even generate new work opportunities within the game industry? This 
was the starting point for a development process involving actors from the City of Malmö, repre -
sentatives from immigrant groups, the games industry, academia and NGOs. A series of workshops 
and meetings were organised to discuss the potential from business and cultural perspectives, and 
the idea of hosting a game jam was born. We all seemed to share the view that this was a brilliant 
idea and a win-win situation for everybody involved.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
266
After an intense planning period, the Arabic Game Jam finally took place over a weekend 
and involved six design teams consisting of game developers and people with Arabic back -
grounds. At the end of the jam, they pitched their game concepts in front of a jury consisting of 
business developers and people from the games industry. All in all, the game jam was perceived 
as a great success and received massive media coverage in both local and national press. We 
saw a clear potential for merging competencies and creating conditions for people from dif -
ferent domains to be creative together and challenge the norms of how media content could be 
produced.
The whole process was indeed intense and, on paper, successful, but then what? After the game 
jam, we had to move on to new assignments and there was limited time left to reflect upon the 
insights gained. Most of the resources allocated to the project had been spent on the initial phases 
and on getting it all going, which was also necessary to mobilise the forces needed. When it was 
time to harvest the learning experiences gained and bring the ideas to the next level, both time 
and resources were out. The importance of building long-term relations with stakeholders and 
including long-term perspectives was at large neglected and many of the potentials discovered 
were never explored or realised. Again, the Arabic Game Jam was by many perceived as a success. 
Yet a game jam was organised in Malmö the year after, and the Arabic Game Jam concept even 
travelled to Beirut and engaged game developers in that part of the world. Since then, the Arabic 
Game Jam has become a beautiful memory of how an idea can turn into an empowering event with 
lots of promises, which hopefully have been picked up by someone else and brought to life in other 
contexts. But about this, I do not know.
Wandering 4: The Story of the King’s Chair
When I enter the forest, it has been over 10 years since the ignition of Malmö Living Labs. Neither 
the forest, the labs nor the intrepid explorers are the same as they once were. I know, because I 
Figure 12.3  These map cut-outs connect to (left) Wandering 3 and (right) Wandering 4. Illustration created 
by Alicia Smedberg.


Living Labs for Open-Ended Participatory Design
267
have read the stories from the forest, from the adventures of yore, battles lost and battles won. The 
meaning of the word open-ended has changed, as I follow the trails into the forest, made by others 
who have come before me – meaning that I don’t have to lose myself in the thicket every time I en-
ter the forest. There are maps at my disposal, taxonomies for things that grow around me, and I can 
make educated guesses as to what my explorations will bring me. The forest is, I admit to myself, 
not without some disappointment, somewhat tamer, today than it was when the labs began. From 
where I am standing the labs were a way to start and build a relationship with the municipality. 
Instead of making isolated visits – returning to the ivory towers of the university at the end of each 
day, the lab established a presence and gave the researchers a face. This allowed them to conduct 
research in an embodied way and to familiarise themselves with the city and its inhabitants.
I have seen the effect the city has had on the lab-makers as well: there have been things 
growing inside them that we never intended to grow there – seeds attached to us as we made 
our way through the bushes and sprouted inside the lab. The labs were never clinical, they 
were always infected. Infrastructuring is the perfect term for this presence, as the work is not 
on the city it is of the city. Like the city the labs have extended far beyond any event: they are 
infected with ideas inherited from previous projects, with knowledge from a parallel process, 
with skills gained in a different field, or aims informed by an external vision. The people we 
engage in these processes are rarely, if ever, only engaged in the one project and are rarely, if 
ever, reducible to the role that the project has anointed them. The participants’ understandings 
of the projects that we conduct together will differ from the co-designers, as will their under -
standing of the worth of the project. This long-term engagement made the term “design process” 
clunky and unfitting in my ears. In 2019, I confessed to P that I struggled to come to terms with 
the connotations of prestige that the words held and that I felt more like a housekeeper in the 
infrastructuring practice than a show-stopper. Arendt came up, and from her, I learned that the 
underlying human condition is that we share the world with others (Arendt, 2013) but that there 
are many ways of doing so. Infrastructuring is a way of interacting with the world that takes 
time, like keeping something alive over generations.
In 2017, when I began working on a new three-year city planning project, there was a young 
woman in the team who had previously worked with my supervisors and was familiar with Par -
ticipatory Design. I didn’t know her work specifically, but I knew the project that she had been 
part of, and I knew of some of the projects that had followed that one. I had heard the stories, as 
had she. There was a shared history, in a way. This sets me apart from the earlier generations of 
lab members, I never had to prove myself in the same way my colleagues did when they started 
working with the labs. This woman vouched for me, let me in the door and allowed me to initiate a 
number of very open-ended processes without question. As a result, the project was busy with ac-
tivities, everything from panel discussions to ethnographic exercises in the area to carpet-making 
workshops taking place there in the first few months. The project caught the municipality’s atten-
tion and was selected as a site for the upcoming state visit from the Swedish king.
The project’s management team was flattered by the court’s attention and was eager to show 
off all of the initiatives, in particular the ones that had been citizen-led. It was agreed that the king 
would visit our venue and we were told to display “evidence” of our activities and provide back -
ground information. Neither the team nor our citizen collaborators would be allowed to be there 
when the king arrived. Instead, the presentations of the project would be held by people in higher 
positions in the municipality. Determined to make the honour of being crowned a flagship project 
into something more than a disruption (venue closed for a day, mandatory dusting and scrubbing 
before the king’s arrival), two of our citizen groups were roped into making a project out of the 
visit itself. They invited a bunch of kids from the local school to have a throne-making workshop, 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
268
promising the kids that they would later receive a photo of the king on the throne they made. A 
group of enthusiastic second-graders set to work, armed with glitter glue and yellow-and-blue 
streamers, flags and a most tasteful collection of stickers. Ornaments they deemed fit for a king.
After the visit, the management group was excited to share a photo of the king sitting on the 
throne with the children. They hoped to continue working with the school and believed that a 
trophy such as this photo would be an incentive to carry on the collaboration. So the management 
group rushed back to the second-graders with the photo but did not receive the cheers they had 
hoped for. The kids were deeply unimpressed by the only man sitting on their throne – who was 
he? “It’s the king” explained the management group but to the children “the king” obviously meant 
the Malmö-native football star, Zlatan Ibrahimovic. It was for him they had made the chair, not the 
old man in the picture (Figure 12.3b).
In the anecdote about the king’s chair, at least a dozen different minds are deciding and evalu-
ating the work we did together. Each of them makes sense of it in relation to their worlds. The 
engagement of each was not guided, not purely, by whatever task the management group had ar -
ticulated. During our conversation in the classroom in 2019, P expressed his appreciation for 
the way Arendt narrated history through anecdotes about historic and contemporary figures. 
This was something that I had not considered before but he was very right, and so the doing 
of anecdotes – anecdotalisation  – in relation to infrastructuring became a key aspect of my 
doctoral thesis work (Smedberg, 2022).
Remembering the Wanderings: Challenges and Opportunities Fronted in the 
Stories From Malmö Living Labs
Communities of Remembrance and Storytelling
With Eco (1994), we started relating Malmö Living Labs to a forest, a place for getting lost or 
finding refuge and with the potential for both unanticipated encounters and meetings with others. 
The forest was also referred to as a fictional space where stories are the main means of wayfind -
ing. This metaphor helped open up our process of collective remembrance, and, indeed, the open-
ness in the labs made us get lost, for example, within the complex infrastructuring processes with 
Herrgårds Women Association. Yet, many years later it also allowed us to find refuge again in an 
academic dissertation defence or by writing a joint book chapter.
Further, Eco’s forest metaphor has helped us understand different paces of storytelling. Like 
the processes in the labs, some stories such as the Arabic Game Jam were swift and then gone. 
We still hear echoes of the successful game jam but, in these, our part is forgotten. Yet, once 
again we have found ourselves lingering in our storytelling around Herrgårds Women Associa -
tion. Often, we tell ourselves that we must write about other events and processes, but we are 
still coming back, lingering around the complex imprints that were made on us in our joint 
ventures, and again new perspectives appeared in the process of writing the first and second 
Wanderings.
As unfolded in the second and fourth Wandering, Hannah Arendt’s philosophy increasingly 
inspired our thinking during the later years of the labs. By telling the stories of historical and 
contemporary figures, Arendt showed us, many times over, how “the anecdotal account” is 
larger than the sum of its words. Alongside Eco, she argues how meaning emerges as we walk 
and write with others. Based on this, from Smedberg’s doctoral defence and thesis (2022), we 
propose emphasising storytelling and anecdotalisation  as central to infrastructuring in Partici-
patory Design.

Living Labs for Open-Ended Participatory Design
269
We see a strong value in revitalising and passing on these different stories, for example, to 
elaborate on how the labs engaged in a plurality of voices, aspirations and actions. The Wander -
ings depict some of the more existentially and defining moments in our research life. Events and 
processes that made big imprints on us regarding how to understand Participatory Design, how 
to believe in change and what to hope for. Hence, as Participatory Design researchers thinking 
with Eco and Arendt, we may also participate as narrators who, with the benefit of hindsight, can 
put actions and deeds into perspective, make them come alive again and inspire future actions in 
Participatory Design as a community of remembrance.
Intensities and Pace in Infrastructuring
As stated in the introduction, the concept of infrastructuring helped us challenge the boundaries 
of our co-design projects, both regarding a temporal perspective, for example, allowing longer 
time frames, and as a way to democratise the design processes by opening them up for other more 
marginalised actors. It also played another role that has become clearer for us now when we look 
back on our engagements, namely that the infrastructuring also created energy and intensities. 
Especially since it allowed us to continually provide space in the design work to include new ac -
tors, perspectives and ideas along the way. The route forward was open and welcomed surprises 
and opportunities we had not thought of beforehand. This fuelled the processes even more; energy 
started to sparkle and attracted a wider diversity of people, higher engagement and more resources 
and triggered attention from the research community, media and other actors in the city.
Knowledge-wise these processes could not easily be grasped, understood or categorised. In 
some ways, we see a resemblance with what John Law and Vicky Singleton describe as fire ob -
jects (Law and Singleton, 2005). These are objects that are generative and productive, that cannot 
be domesticated but rather create the unknowable and the unexpected. They bring some otherings 
to the foreground, while simultaneously othering something else. Law and Singletons´ particular 
metaphor is not the fireplace where “the fuel that feeds it can be limited and the ashes raked out” 
but instead the bushfire that “jumps, creatively, destructively and more or less unpredictably from 
location to location” (Law and Singleton, 2005, p. 347).
Although this figure might sound a bit extreme, it is also fitting to describe the intensity, pro -
ductivity and high number of design experiments that energised not only the processes but also 
us when we put our faith in the performative potential of curious, unexpected and serendipitous 
encounters. You could also argue that the labs may have become too productive since it often was 
hard to find enough time to bring sensitive attention and care to the many options and actors that 
were brought together. The intensity made it difficult to ensure full accountability for all of the 
experiments and their potential consequences. This could be seen in the process around Arabic 
Game Jam, which quickly aggregated many stakeholders and resources, but where our resources 
were exhausted too soon. Similarly, the dynamic between the two different groups of women 
described in the first Wandering quickly mobilised high engagement and many opportunities 
that we could not control and that eventually led to a breakdown. A key question following this 
is: how we could become more sensitised and find a way to continuously balance between more 
generative versus more cautious and careful processes?
The Complex Boundaries in Heterogeneous Networks
Other important concepts in the Neighbourhood lab were heterogeneity and agonism, but they 
were also followed by complications. Although an ethos emphasising heterogeneity in labs that 

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
270
strives to democratise design can be seen as theoretically desirable, it is much more complex as 
a practice. This came to the forefront when we followed the “Mothers of Invention” in the first 
and second Wanderings, encountering everything from a funding body’s evaluation committee, a 
businesswomen network, conservative men and a doctoral defence committee. Although we made 
attempts to bring together adversaries with radically different perspectives in respectful agonistic 
encounters, the powerful actor often opted out of the process or the weaker actor’s worldview 
was not seen as legitim. For example, the business women could not respect a different world -
view regarding how to understand individuality versus collectives. And the evaluation commit -
tee expressed profound disrespect towards the “Mothers of Inventions” as a legitimate partner in 
innovation.
As demonstrated in the incident with the evaluation committee in the second Wandering, fund-
ing also played a significant role in how the heterogeneity revealed itself. Especially since it some-
times was accompanied by agendas that manifested hegemonies that the labs and its actors wanted 
to challenge. These complex entanglements certainly contributed to the heterogeneity but not in a 
way that allowed the agency to be distributed or that opened up new alternatives. This leaves us 
with the questions: How to understand the boundaries and dynamics of a heterogeneous design 
network? When does it become too heterogeneous, or heterogeneous in a form that limits its 
democratic agency?
The Sensitised Labour of Infrastructuring
In contrast to the early processes, ten years later our least senior co-writer of this chapter initi-
ated her doctoral research with more caution, by trying to understand how to nurture a sensibility 
towards agency (Smedberg, 2022). This work was closely aligned with the notion of care that has 
pervaded the Participatory Design field in recent years (Light and Akama, 2014), and she paid 
careful attention to questions of when to act or when to step back. Still, as seen in the fourth Wan-
dering, in the story of the king’s chair, the care work and maintenance work that infrastructuring 
entails is affective as well as practical. How to best care for someone can be understood radically 
differently by others. If there is no guarantee that our care practices are right the first time around, 
the one thing we can do is to be consistently present and accountable. Paradoxically, we could say 
that we moved a bit too fast when we first entered the forest, now that we know the forest better, 
we move gentler. This is also because we have learned more about the necessary effort of labour 
within infrastructuring (Smedberg, 2022). Processes require not only creating but to maintain -
ing paths and relations in design engagements and caring for affect that emerges among all the 
involved actors – including our own (Smedberg, 2022).
At this time of closure, many questions still haunt us, such as: while we invested a lot of en -
ergy, aspiration and hope in the collaboration with “Mothers of Invention” and they invested in 
us – were we too naïve to believe that a funding body’s expert committee would regard this col -
laboration as innovative, legitimate and relevant in co-production? Would we dare to engage in 
the same way today? Would we allow care and hope to accompany us to the same extent? Now, 
almost 20 years later, if the forest is less feral, how can we then understand that? How do our 
work and attention differ when the surrounding landscapes are tamer? If we were able to re-do 
our democratic design experiments, in some respects, the results would have been different and 
hopefully better. However, some of the results and effects would not have emerged because they 
required certain intensities.
Finally, to conclude our collective process of remembrance, we ask ourselves: what have we 
learned from remembering and revisiting these stories from the Malmö Living Labs? We have 

Living Labs for Open-Ended Participatory Design
271
learned that care and caution are a necessary foundation for Participatory Design but also that 
intensities and bushfires have their place when a diversity of actors are brought together sur -
rounded by an ethos of openness. This calls for Participatory Designers to develop the skills and 
competencies to artfully and sensitively handle different paces, rhythms, durations and intensities 
in open-ended Participatory Design processes and writing.
