13
TEACHING PARTICIPATORY 
DESIGN
Vincenzo D’Andrea, Betsy DiSalvo, Giacomo Poderi  
and Jesper Simonsen
This chapter is written for scholars who may be teaching Participatory Design for the first time but 
have an understanding of, and possibly concrete experiences with, Participatory Design work. This 
chapter will also give experienced Participatory Design teachers a chance to reflect upon their practice. 
Based on our own teaching experiences and the contributions of several scholars and colleagues, we 
place strong emphasis on the need to base the teaching of Participatory Design on the continuous com-
bination of practice and reflection. The chapter discusses the implications of this approach, the chal-
lenges it entails, and how to address them. We argue for the possibility of students engaging in “real” 
Participatory Design processes outside the classroom. The aim of this chapter is also to contribute to 
the development of a pedagogical framework for teaching Participatory Design. This direction centres 
teaching practice on two pedagogical modes: mutual learning and reflection-in-action. In discussing 
the practice of teaching Participatory Design, the chapter highlights three main aspects. The first is 
supporting students’ awareness of the relevance of the social dimension in Participatory Design prac -
tice and engaging them in reflection on related issues. To this end, questions that can promote students’ 
critical thinking are discussed. Given the relevant role of workshops in many Participatory Design 
processes, a second aspect is providing students with guidelines to consider the materiality in facilitat-
ing workshops, as well as opportunities to practise and combine practice with reflection. The chapter 
provides some concrete steps to consider for this purpose. The third aspect is guiding students in 
analysing Participatory Design outputs, a critical practice that is not easy and sometimes overlooked. 
The chapter ends with an annex, providing nine cases-examples, complementing the text and inspiring 
future teachers of Participatory Design. The cases-examples comprise teaching Participatory Design to 
bachelor-, master-, and PhD-students and to practitioners engaged in NGOs living labs.
  DOI: 10.4324/9781003334330-15

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
274
Introduction
In this chapter, we address the topic of Teaching Participatory Design by leveraging our concrete 
and long-standing experiences in teaching and practising Participatory Design. We do this primar-
ily through a reflective and practice-based rationale rather than building upon previous literature. 
This approach is, first and foremost, consistent with the practice-based and reflective orientation of 
Participatory Design (DiSalvo et al., 2017). A reflective approach is also a way to contribute to a lack 
of a substantial, comprehensive pedagogical knowledge base for the field. Many scholars involved in 
teaching Participatory Design might find the arguments of this chapter familiar to their pedagogy, and 
we do not seek to advance any normative stance on how Participatory Design should be taught, nor 
do we claim that the chapter will solve the whole argument of Teaching Participatory Design. Instead, 
we offer this reflection on our teaching practices as an initial step in building a Participatory Design 
pedagogy and as an inspiration for educators who consider or practise teaching Participatory Design.
Participatory Design is an orientation and approach to design that often appeals to students eager 
to conduct design projects in close collaboration with users, citizens, and other external stakehold-
ers. Many courses imply that the students leave the university and exercise Participatory Design 
techniques by involving and engaging external participants – for example, through different Partici-
patory Design workshops (as exemplified in the Annex, Cases 1 to 4: they include initial and “safe” 
classroom experiments training specific techniques and then practising by using these techniques 
in activities and workshops with external partners) followed by classroom evaluations. The aspira-
tion of combining theory, practice, and reflection this way is motivated as a pedagogical approach; 
as a desire to work in more inclusive, collaborative, or democratic ways; or to design on behalf of 
groups overlooked and marginalised in decision-making processes. Some students might initially be 
suspicious or concerned about the challenges and threats that designing with others poses to their 
designerly expertise, vision, agency – and comfort zone. This juxtaposition illustrates a key aspect of 
teaching Participatory Design. Students will need to learn both: how to inhabit, tackle, and solve the 
challenges of doing things together and understand the ethical, historical, political, and theoretical 
underpinnings of why a participatory democratic practice in design is warranted, desired, and, more 
often than not, needed. To meet this challenge, we encourage educators to provide students with 
authentic contexts for learning since Participatory Design practice is deeply tied to concrete, situ-
ated challenges and to close collaborations with potential users and other stakeholders. At the same 
time, teachers need to provide students with proper guidance and framing for the learning-by-doing 
process. Indeed, literature on teaching Participatory Design highlights the tension between a pure 
constructivist and practice-based learning pedagogy and the need for scaffolds to make sense of the 
experienced process (Andrews et al., 2014; Christiansson et al., 2018). Additionally, teachers and 
students cannot avoid the clash of courses and institutional settings with the ideal of a “real-life” 
practice-based learning experience, which draws attention to various pedagogical challenges: (i) the 
struggle to align the course and students’ learning pace with the pace that is required to build the nec-
essary trust and expectations alignment with the course’s live-project stakeholders; (ii) the inherent 
conflict between the teachers’ and students’ pedagogical focus on the process and the stakeholders’ 
desire to achieve an actual outcome; and (iii) the students’ expectation for “traditional” explanations 
and teaching session and the teachers’ commitment to a learning-by-doing practice-based approach 
(Agger Eriksen et al., 2022; Andrews et al., 2014; Hecht and Maass, 2008; D’Andrea and Teli, 2010).
This chapter is written for scholars who may be teaching Participatory Design for the first time, 
but have an understanding of, and possibly concrete experiences with, Participatory Design work. 
In the next section, we bring to the fore mutual learning and reflection-in-action as fundamentals 
underpinning the teaching of Participatory Design. In the section “The Practice of Teaching Partic-
ipatory Design”, we dive into aspects such as the social and material dimensions of Participatory 

Teaching Participatory Design
275
Design activities, the materialities involved in such activities, and the reflective, analytical chal-
lenge of analysing Participatory Design outcomes. In the Annex, the readers will find nine exam-
ples that showcase past and present Participatory Design courses and teaching cases.
Teaching Mutual Learning
The 2013 Participatory Design Handbook defines Participatory Design as: “a process of investi -
gating, understanding, reflecting upon, establishing, developing, and supporting mutual learning 
between multiple participants in collective ‘reflection-in-action’” (Robertson and Simonsen, 2013, 
p. 2). The pedagogical approach of reflecting in (and on) action is rooted in the work by Schön 
(1987). Because Participatory Design is a reflective process “between multiple participants” (Rob-
ertson and Simonsen, 2013, p. 8), students need to engage in group-based reflections rather than 
individual ones. Training collective reflection-in-action is supported by many Participatory De -
sign tools and techniques, including different workshops to engage in telling, making, and enact -
ing (e.g. Brandt et al., 2013), as well as within design and evaluation of design visions, artefacts, 
and prototypes (e.g. K. Bødker et al., 2004, S. Bødker et al., 2022). In this chapter, we emphasise 
the relevance of engaging students in practising Participatory Design but to complete the learning 
process, it is paramount to combine practice with reflection continuously.
When teaching the importance of mutual learning in Participatory Design, one can recognise 
it as an inherently and fundamentally situated process. As such, it calls for a variety of teaching 
modes and settings. For instance:
• Student group work done at the university reflects the peer-to-peer collaboration and mutual learn-
ing situations staging, for example, the Participatory Design of simple artefacts such as process mod-
els, storyboards, mock-ups, prototypes, and scenarios (e.g. Bødker et al., 2022). See, for example, 
Annex, Case 2: The students’ results from this course are presented in a final expo open to the public.
• Training to learn the realities of the users’ situation and context requires the students to do field 
work outside the university using ethnographic techniques (Blomberg and Karasti, 2013). This 
can be supplemented by techniques to collectively analyse the obtained qualitative data (Simonsen 
and Friberg, 2014). See, for example, Annex, Case 1: The students conduct, analyse, and model 
as-is processes and present and evaluate them with participants from the external organisation.
• Situations where different users and domain experts learn from each other and strive to articulate 
their desired aims, can train students to facilitate workshops with external participants, for ex-
ample, using collective modelling techniques such as dead sea scrolls, prompted reflection, diag-
nostic, or virtual maps (Bødker et al., 2004). See, for example, Annex, Case 8: The participants 
document, comment, and assess collaborative work processes using dead sea scrolls models.
There are a range of approaches to teaching Participatory Design, from a socio-political perspec-
tive to a pragmatic “how to run a Participatory Design workshop”. In all cases, the teacher in a 
Participatory Design classroom takes on the role of facilitator. As the facilitator, the teacher focuses 
on practice and methods that help students lead mutual learning with stakeholders about the design 
objectives. Vygotsky’s theories on cooperative learning highlight how learning with others assists 
us in constructing new and more critical theories about the world around us (Brame, 2016). Key to 
engaging students in developing this critical perspective on design is engaging them with stakehold-
ers in real-world settings, echoing Dewey’s emphasis on authentic learning context (Dewey, 1903). 
An authentic context also provides opportunities to assess students to gauge if they can take abstract 
ideas, such as socio-political perspective, and transfer them to real-world application. While this 
may seem daunting, practitioners of Participatory Design can build their pedagogy on the skills they 
use to facilitate groups to actively engage in design, collaborate, and critically reflect.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
276
The Practice of Teaching Participatory Design
The Social Dimension in Designing Participatory Design Activities
The design spaces we work in always have social components. However, in Participatory Design, 
social considerations, and interactions are part of the entire process, from conceptualising the 
design space to determining how to communicate the outcomes. When teaching Participatory De-
sign, we can convey the importance of social interactions between participants and the researchers 
or designers and how social elements of design spaces interact with collaborative work. Yet, we 
cannot anticipate and prepare students for every social nuance. When teaching Participatory De-
sign, we suggest that establishing and facilitating key moments of reflection on social engagement 
will help plan, implement, and evaluate these interactions. This starts with developing (formal or 
informal) partnerships and continues through awareness of social-cultural aspects during analysis, 
design, and implementation.
When planning a participatory process, students must concern themselves with multiple 
social considerations and learn how to deal with the day-to-day messiness and unpredictability 
of project work. It is helpful to remind students that they will encounter several challenges, 
many of which are difficult to anticipate (e.g. partners or participants not following through 
with what they initially agreed upon). Such encounters can also be appreciated as rewarding 
teaching and learning moments (see Annex, Case 6). The following broad questions can be 
used to articulate teaching moments and promote students’ thinking.
What Is the Design Context That is of Concern?
The design context may initially be identified in classrooms through pre-established partnerships 
and may engage civic, non-profit, or corporate interests. In this initial planning stage, students 
can reflect on what the partners might be expecting, what the partners may not have considered, 
and what the goal is for the partners. For example, in a course on participatory community design 
DiSalvo taught, she brought in multiple non-profits to introduce themselves to the class with a 
question-and-answer session. After each presentation, students talked about the spoken and un-
spoken goals of the organisations and how Participatory Design might be used to help them reach 
those goals. At other times, a student may hope to work in a particular design context and need 
to build partnerships. Guiding learning through a partnership-building process is essential to Par -
ticipatory Design. In courses including projects following the MUST method (see Annex, Case 
1), Simonsen asked the students to prepare their project establishment with an external partner 
organisation by thorough document analysis, and by making an initial Business Model Canvas and 
SWOT analysis. This could be presented as their initial interpretation of the organisation, later to 
be supplemented by a stakeholder analysis.
While each Participatory Design teacher might have different guidelines for working with part-
ners, we lay out our primary considerations in the following list – each of which may be supported 
by project establishment as described in the MUST method (Bødker et al., 2004):
• How can you encourage students to establish their relationship as a partnership rather than as a 
client and designer?
• How can students build mutual trust by attending to and learning about the organisation or 
design space beyond the issues the partner raised?
• What are approaches to identifying goals for the Participatory Design sessions with partners? 
(One can even create specific sessions to help identify those goals.)

Teaching Participatory Design
277
• How can students work with their partners to find approaches to recruiting participants, secur-
ing space, and providing other material or staff support?
• How will students set expectations for outcomes, and how will those outcomes be shared? 
Who Is a Participant in the Design?
While we may be in contact with one organisation, there are many different stakeholders in any 
given organisation, and typically, there are stakeholders outside the organisation. Students should 
reflect on who is invited into the design process by identifying and analysing relevant stakehold-
ers. This means pushing your learners to think beyond the first set of participants a partner might 
present. Primary considerations for students to reflect on in identifying participants include:
• Which groups of people will be impacted by the outcome of the Participatory Design goals?
• What are the different motivations for different stakeholders?
• How might different stakeholders interact with each other?
• Who is currently left out or not engaged in the design space?
How Can One Facilitate Participation?
Throughout these early stages, we think it is valuable to remind students that working with people in a 
democratic process requires empathy and care. Students should reflect on their own bias and the bias 
different participants bring to the process. Nurturing a Participatory Design process requires not only fa-
cilitation skills but also a specific attitude and a political (as well as an ethical) position. This calls for an 
attitude of acknowledgement of all the participants’ perspectives and the skill to identify, for instance, 
when the few are excluding the many, and train to navigate that. As with many aspects of Participatory 
Design, experience and practice are the best ways to develop social skills. However, there are several 
ways to help prepare students to engage in such social interactions. Students can be asked to:
• Read case studies of Participatory Design sessions, focusing on the challenges and social 
interactions.
• Practise facilitation skills in the classroom by leading group activities or even in-class work -
shops (see Annex, Case 4).
• Observe social interactions in their design context, such as meetings, staff lunchrooms, or so -
cial events.
• Test design prototypes with classmates, friends, or family.
• Have regular reflection opportunities about the design process and focus on aspects such as 
“genuine participation”, quality, or relations with external partners (Simonsen and Storm Jensen, 
2016).
The Materiality in Designing Participatory Design Activities
The social interactions outlined earlier are the crux of the “participation” in Participatory Design 
practice. However, if there is one illustrative element of the practice, it is the workshops that comprise 
the backbone of many Participatory Design projects. The Participatory Design workshop is pivotal in 
materialising the principles and goals of a design outcome pursued through participatory ambitions. 
Encourage students to think about what they want to accomplish with these workshops and attend to 
the planning and execution, including the location, materials, timing, and recruiting of participants.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
278
Teachers can help students structure their very first Participatory Design workshop session, for 
example, by providing a detailed list of practical steps guiding their first workshop session. Below 
is an example of an initial workshop process structure by considering ten relevant steps:
Step 1 Gather Information:
Through initial work with partners and independent research, the students may gather information 
to identify design goals and the imagined future in abstract terms. Sometimes, this will be about a 
specific goal, such as “designing an interface to teach financial technology skills to the elderly”. 
In other cases, the design goal may be more abstract or formative, such as “identifying what role 
technology plays in elderly care facilities”.
Step 2 Identify Goals:
Students can write out their goals and hereby share these with the class for open discussion. There 
are common pitfalls that students make that instructors should keep in mind when guiding stu -
dents. The most relevant examples are when the design goal is:
• Too specific – activities will be more similar to user studies than Participatory Design.
• Too broad and cannot be achieved in the frame of the course.
• Activity-driven rather than goal-driven.
• Not related to any specific problem or need.
• Not aligned with the values of (often differing) stakeholders.
Step 3 Brainstorm:
Students can brainstorm ideas and sketch out promising initial activities. Students should be en -
couraged to think creatively and broadly about what types of activities can contribute insights to 
the design goals. These brainstorm ideas and sketch outputs can be presented and discussed using 
peer groups or discussions to help students narrow down.
Step 4 Iterate:
Students can elaborate and iterate upon sketched ideas to create a workshop session. Helping stu-
dents structure the whole workshop can be challenging because each context calls for a different 
structure. However, it is often easiest to have students start with a warm-up activity, then move 
into a design activity that helps the participants reflect broadly on the design space, and then move 
to a more and more narrow focus on the design goal. A workshop may consider including relevant 
materials such as visual presentations (e.g. SWOT posters, freehand drawings, and diagnostic 
maps; see Bødker et al., 2004) supporting reflection and the focus and the participants’ interactions 
(see Frølunde, 2014).
Step 5 Prototype:
Students can prepare a prototype of their design workshop and conduct it with their peers. 
Peers offer critiques and provide feedback on what they observe. Each student could make a 
presentation about what they learned conducting their prototype, so the peer “participants” can 

Teaching Participatory Design
279
confirm their findings or help them see what might have been missed in their observation. Such 
prototype steps can be repeated until students are comfortable conducting their workshop with 
external partners. The main point is to train genuine participation: “to step up, take the pen in 
hand, stand in front of the large whiteboard together with fellow colleagues and designers, and 
participate in drawing and sketching how the work process unfolds as seen from their perspec -
tives” (Robertson and Simonsen, 2013, p. 5).
Step 6 Session structure:
Students often jump to developing activities without considering the structure of the sessions. 
Identifying the logistical options for Participatory Design sessions, such as the location, the dates, 
duration, and other logistical items is part of the social interaction students need to learn to conduct 
Participatory Design. In many cases, these elements are decided by the practitioners’ ability to 
engage and build trust with their partners. Students can consider their options for multiple logisti-
cal concerns:
• What locations can be secured, and are they easily accessible to the participants?
• Is the space suitable for the planned activities, or should the activities or space be revised?
• How can you recruit participants, and what incentives can be used?
• Should refreshments (food and beverages) be secured and served?
• What dates and times work best for participants?
Step 7 Session goals:
Students might need to revisit their goals at this time – to keep these objects at the forefront of 
the design process. Students, particularly if they do not have a visual design background, are often 
unaware of the power of the material and aesthetics of the workshop materials. Ask the students to 
compare different experiences with high-quality and low-quality materials. Prompt students to think 
about the socio-cultural context they will be working in, making sure the language and request will 
be respectful to the values of their participants. This can help to finalise the workshop plan and create 
relevant materials for it.
Step 8 Workshops:
Encourage the students to conduct the workshops in an authentic external setting. There are several 
learning objectives for using an authentic context. For example, logistical considerations are many, 
from transporting materials to and from a location to ensuring the space is clean and inviting. These 
logistical concerns are important to emphasise to students until they experience them first hand. 
Similarly, the challenges of facilitating a Participatory Design workshop will be more apparent in 
an authentic context. During the workshop, students should take notes and make sketches, similar 
to any participant observer in a research setting (Blomberg and Karasti, 2013).
Step 9 Reflection:
There are several ways to conduct reflection at the end of Participatory Design work. However, 
similar to any qualitative data collection, we encourage students to document their reflec -
tions as soon as possible while the workshop is still fresh in their minds. A typical reflective  

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
280
practice is for each workshop leader to spend 30 min to an hour making notes on what hap -
pened during the workshop. These can be organised around the participants or the activity but 
should include observations and insights. A second method is to have a group reflection at the 
end of a session where everyone talks through the workshop, sharing and piecing together an 
understanding of what happened. It is typically best to audio record and transcribe these re -
cordings and for workshop leaders to keep notes.
Step 10 Reporting:
Teaching students how and when to communicate with external partners is important. As with any 
partnership, this should be an ongoing collaboration rather than a client-and-consultant relation -
ship. A report can address the workshop outcome as well as the process. If students have invited 
external partners to participate in the workshop and stay for the group reflection, a report might be 
a short summary with bullet points. At other times, a partner may not be part of the workshop or 
the group reflection, and a more detailed report might be needed.
Analysis of Participatory Design Outputs
Analysis of Participatory Design outputs is one of the more challenging elements of Participatory 
Design to teach. As with much of design research, there is a less systematic approach to analysing 
artefacts than speech or text. However, there are a number of techniques to help students learn to 
analyse the process and outcomes of a workshop. and
Observations Notes – As noted earlier taking time to record reflections on the Participatory De -
sign workshop is important to do as soon as possible. These observations can then be used as 
primary or supporting data for analysis. Observation notes most often benefit from being sup -
plemented by photos and video-recordings.
Audio recordings/Transcripts of Workshop – Typically, Participatory Design practitioners do not 
audio record and transcribe full workshops. The sessions generally create poor recordings be-
cause activities can be noisy and participants move around. In addition, sometimes, a recording 
in such a setting, unlike a more intimate one-on-one interview, can be off-putting for par -
ticipants. However, in some cases, perhaps when conducting sessions virtually, a recording 
transcript can be valuable data for analysis. For some languages, transcriptions may be done 
automatically.
Artefacts – Artefacts can range from somewhat refined prototypes that participants create to scrape 
notes or digital photos that participants create as part of their design process. At the end of a 
session, students should consider how to organise these artefacts for analysis.
Analysis – There are many ways to conduct analysis on Participatory Design outputs. Traditional 
ways include creating collaborative or affinity notes and then taking those notes to create af-
finity diagrams (Simonsen and Friberg, 2014). With a smaller group of participants, one can 
create biographies of each participant, noting their background, design process, and the topics 
and concerns they raised through their dialogue in the session. Other methods include user 
journeys (Gudiksen and Svabo, 2014), mind maps (Burgess-Allen and Owen-Smith, 2010), or 
the development of diagnostic or virtual maps (e.g. Bødker et al., 2004; Simonsen and Friberg, 
2014) – the latter have been used as a mandatory technique in the bachelor course described in 
Case 1 of the Annex. Each of these approaches to analysis has multiple resources for a teacher 
or learner to explore. For some students starting out with analysis, using a grounded theory 

Teaching Participatory Design
281
(Glaser and Strauss, 2017) approach of open coding and comparative practices is a concrete set 
of steps they can take to learn how to code their data. As they gain experience, they will likely 
use different approaches based on the context and data they have.
There are fewer resources on analysis of artefacts (Bratteteig and Wagner, 2016). One approach 
is to take each participant’s artefact(s) and create a set of notes on each that can then be organised 
similarly to typical qualitative coding practices. Another approach is prompted reflection (Kens-
ing, 1998) used for complex work settings where participants make, present, and discuss models 
representing their respective processes and practices. Once the learner starts engaging with the 
artefacts, they will find that coupled with observations, these provide a rich source for analysis.
Participatory Design outputs vary in form and content. Often outputs represent a part of a pro-
cess that the participants engage in. Representations and models made by students demonstrate the 
students’ interpretation of Participatory Design sessions and their output. They may be presented 
and communicated to the participants for evaluation and to inform subsequent sessions and itera -
tions. This corresponds to the Participatory Design principle of “anchoring visions” described in 
the MUST method (Bødker et al., 2004). Simple models outlining processes in the focus of a 
Participatory Design project may play an important role as a common reference point for the 
participants: This was the case for as-is and envisioned to-be models of processes analysed in the 
master’s thesis described in Annex, Case 6 (depicted Simonsen et al. (2020)) and the dead sea 
scrolls modelling collaborative processes illustrated in Annex, Case 8.
Summary
In this chapter, we systematise our experiences as Participatory Design teachers (and practitioners) 
and provide case-examples for inspiration in the Annex. The distinguishing trait of the learning 
path we presented is the key role of practice in connection with practice-based reflection (Schön, 
1987). Whenever possible, students should experience a “real” Participatory Design process, 
rather than classroom exercises only. This requires a dedicated effort from teachers to provide 
suitable connections and guidance for establishing the possibility for the students to work on real 
cases. Such an approach will provide students with significant contextualisation of all the guide-
lines and examples provided in this chapter.
As a final note, we consider the situation of researchers and practitioners who do not have the 
possibility of attending a specific course on Participatory Design. Although this chapter could pro-
vide valuable suggestions to designers seeking to enrich their practice as self-learner practitioners, 
we have to warn that kind of readers that this is not enough. Advice or collaboration from experi-
enced Participatory Design practitioners would be a significant resource to consider (see Annex, 
Case 8). Chapter 7 in Bødker et al. (2022) provides general guidelines on how to autonomously 
approach Participatory Design practice. Chapter 7 in this book reviews the Participatory Design 
approaches, methods, and techniques supporting practitioners. Finally, we also refer to Chapter 8 
in this book for a better understanding of the implications of starting a Participatory Design pro -
cess in a non-academic context.
Annex – Cases and Examples
The following nine cases are meant to provide inspiration and suggestions. In accordance with the 
Participatory Design approach, they should be revised, contextualised, and reshaped rather than 
“applied”.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
282
Cases-examples comprise the following levels and application areas:
• Bachelor
• Master
• PhD
• Labs and NGOs
Bachelor
Participatory Design in an Organisational Context Case 13.1
Half-day lectures, project work, and group supervision. 10–14 weeks.
Divide students into groups of 4–6 students. Each group establishes a Participatory Design infor -
mation technology-project in collaboration with a local organisation, which can be a private company, 
public organisation, or NGO. The main literature is a textbook on the MUST method, a method for 
Participatory Design in an organisational work context (Bødker et al., 2004). The students follow the 
four principles and four phases and use selected tools and techniques from the method. The book and 
the method help the students to organise a Participatory Design process and experience the theory in 
practice. The student projects typically support communication, collaboration, or knowledge sharing 
between a group of employees and management in an organisation.
The course form is a blend of lectures, workshops, and group work in collaboration with the chosen 
external organisation. The lectures introduce the MUST methods’ phases one by one and the students 
organise their projects accordingly. Specific tools and techniques are trained and subsequently applied 
at student activities and workshops in the organisation. The students receive supervision from the 
course teacher(s) in preparing and evaluating activities with the organisation.
The student’s Participatory Design project produces a MUST design report that may work as a 
point of departure for a subsequent procurement or other organisational change process. The course 
often results in relatively professional design reports highly appreciated by the participating external 
partners. The course has been offered regularly at five Danish universities since 2000, currently among 
others as a mandatory course at Roskilde University.
Participatory Design for Human–Computer Interaction (HCI)  
Students Case 13.2
Half-day lectures, portfolio work, and group supervision. 10–14 weeks.
Divide students into groups of 4–6 students. The course introduces one common design case for 
all groups. For example, “How can you design an interactive prototype that supports citizens’ critical 
and constructive understanding of emerging technologies?” The groups work individually with this 
design case through three iterations: exploration, intervention, and prototyping. The main literature 
is a textbook aimed at HCI students introducing Participatory Design in a straightforward and ac -
cessible way (Bødker et al., 2022). The book defines and introduces four strong commitments of 
Participatory Design covering core values of democracy, empowerment, emancipatory practices, and 

Teaching Participatory Design
283
Master
Course Including an Empirical Participatory Design Project in the  
“Real World” Case 13.4
One semester (3 months)
Students taking the Participatory Design course at the master in Human–Computer Interaction 
(University of Trento) are required, in small groups, to engage in a project involving an external entity. 
Before using the various techniques “outside”, they experiment with their peers in the classroom. In 
particular, they design, plan, facilitate, and critically analyse a 2-hour workshop. The instructors also 
supervise this activity. All this is quite demanding in terms of class time, with the risk of losing the 
possibility to present, discuss, and reflect on theory.
To solve the issue, the theme of each “classroom” workshop is one of the chapters of the 2013 hand-
book. The content of the chapter is briefly introduced in one class, in the following class one student 
Course “Design for People: Laboratory of Design and Social  
Innovation” Case 13.3
In this 60 hours studio course for the Bachelor in Design (UTFPR, Brazil), students discuss and 
realise the role of design in increasing or decreasing social inequalities. To achieve this, they must 
develop a design project with a disenfranchised community. However, before joining a community, 
they must learn how to design together. Hence, the course adopts a participatory approach to the 
collective learning journey grounded on Paulo Freire’s book “Pedagogy of the Oppressed” (Freire, 
1985), which inspired Participatory Design pioneers in the 1970s and continues to be an inspiring 
reading for young design students of today. Readings and discussions around parts of the book ac -
company the participatory process, organised around the Rumsfeld Matrix: an artefact representing 
the eventual mismatches between student knowledge and student consciousness on self-selected 
topics (the known knowns, known unknowns, unknown knowns, and unknown unknowns). Peda -
gogical principles supporting this course are discussed in (Angelon and van Amstel, 2021). A syn -
thesis of the 2019 edition is at https://fredvanamstel.com/teaching/designing-for-social-innovation
mutual learning in the design of future practices. It is organised in chapters, each discussing answers to 
frequently asked questions to Participatory Design, providing historical accounts, cases, methods and 
tools, and reading lists for further studies. The students use the book as a resource and practical means 
to conduct – and reflect upon – an iterative and situated design process combining inquiry, interven-
tion, and construction.
The course form blends lectures, practical exercises, fieldwork, and student presentations. The 
lectures introduce the design case, and the students investigate this case through portfolio work com -
prising design sprint, fieldwork, workshop with users, prototyping, and evaluation. The groups work 
with the case and interact with potential users, for example, people at a public library, schoolchildren, 
or employees in a local organisation. The groups present the results in a final expo open to the public.

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
284
group run a workshop they prepared on the chapter topic, and finally, in the next class, the instructors 
provide feedback on the workshop and answers to chapter-related questions coming from the workshop. 
The various activities are organised in a sort of chain, so each week there is a “chapter workshop”.
Figure 13.1  Grounding exercise (contact dyad) at a master course at Roskilde University. Photo and il -
lustration by Jesper Simonsen.
Advanced Participatory Design Case 13.5
Half-day lectures, 10 weeks.
The course is organised by the 2013 handbook, with one chapter for each lecture. The book pre -
sents an authoritative overview of Participatory Design, and its history and discusses contributions and 
challenges within central themes, including ethics, ethnography, methods, tools and techniques, and 
community involvement. Individual chapters are thoroughly read and examined for each course week. 
At each lecture a short introduction to the chosen chapter is given along with a series of discussion 
questions provided by the course teacher. The students discuss each chapter in small groups and the 
lecture is concluded by a general discussion.
Each course day is introduced by 30 minutes of physical exercises (i.e. grounding exercises), to 
exercise integration of body awareness and personal contact. The point of these exercises is two-fold: 
First, the students experience being grounded, thereby being relieved from performance pressure or 
anxiety (the book represents a rather complex text aimed at a Ph.D. level). Hence, they engage in the 
discussions with an open mind, and discuss what they do not understand well from the text. Second, the 
grounding exercises (see Figure 13.1) form a training platform to investigate open-minded contact and 
authentic meetings: A Participatory Design competence needed to practise and qualify human contact, 
human relations, and cooperation (Simonsen and Storm Jensen, 2016).

Teaching Participatory Design
285
Specialising in Participatory Design – Thesis Work Case 13.6
One semester, 5 months, master’s thesis.
Students may specialise in Participatory Design through their master’s thesis. Most often this in -
clude empirical work in the form of a case analysis of a Participatory Design project or a design and 
action-research-oriented Participatory Design project conducted by the student(s).
The latter was the case of a master’s thesis project that resulted in a lasting change in the 
visitation process within a hospital ward in Denmark. The project (described in Simonsen et al., 
2020) was completed within five months and included analysis, design, pilot implementation, and 
evaluation of a new information technology-supported visitation process. The student conducted 
the project in close collaboration with a nurse information technology specialist, medical sec -
retaries, and the chief physician. The empirical activities during analysis and design comprised 
observations of medical secretaries and physicians handling the visitation, workshops with medi -
cal secretaries, specifications of wished-for effects, and the design of a detailed clinical guideline 
for the new visitation process. These activities were followed by a pilot implementation where the 
clinical staff initiated a new visitation process with the students providing information technology 
support to the medical secretaries. The evaluation comprised effects assessments conducted by 
the student, including observations and quantitative analysis based on data from the healthcare 
system.
PhD
Designing Human Technologies (a Participatory Design Summer School) –  
and PDC Doctoral Colloquium Case 13.7
Two-day seminar, held both as Ph.D. course and PDC Doctoral Colloquium.
Ph.D. students submit a position paper elaborating on their research problem, research ques -
tions, theories, methods, and selected achieved and/or expected outcomes. Also, students are asked 
to relate their work to a chapter of their choice from the 2013 handbook. The course is a blend of 
lectures and discussions in small groups (see Figure 13.2). Invited lectures by senior academic staff 
present key theories, methodological reflections, and novel approaches within the field. Discussions 
occur in groups of five doctoral students and two faculty members, discussing the students’ posi -
tion papers. Group discussions will dedicate one hour to each position paper. The course provides 
opportunities for networking with other doctoral students and senior faculty in the field. At the 
PDC Doctoral Colloquium, the students have also made posters of their work to be presented at the 
conference.
The PDC Doctoral Colloquium is offered at the biennial PDC conferences. The Designing Hu-
man Technologies course has been held as a Participatory Design summer school yearly since 2013 
(pdcproceedings.org).

286
Figure 13.2 Student group discussions at a Ph.D. seminar. Photo and illustration by Jesper Simonsen.
Labs and NGOs
Participatory Design Start-up as a Learning Experience  
With an NGO Case 13.8
A large NGO was to procure a shared electronic case and document management system (DMS). 
The purpose of the DMS was to standardise procedures and documentation of all their applications, 
funding, and projects. The NGO had several autonomous departments, and the management and 
employees were concerned about how the DMS standardised workflows would support their inter -
nal processes. A project group of three employees (a project manager, an analysis consultant, and a 
method consultant) was appointed to the task of making a bid, procuring the DMS, and managing the 
technical and organisational implementation of the DMS system. An external Participatory Design 
researcher was hired as a consultant to supervise the project group. The supervision included monthly 
two-hour meetings.
Over a five-month period, the project group held intensive Participatory Design workshops with 
representatives from each of the departments in the NGO. The workshops used the MUST method’s 
dead sea scrolls (Bødker et al., 2004), where the project group with participants from a department 
drew and documented current workflows (see Figure 13.3). The wished-for effects from using the 
DMS were noted as systems needs without specifying technical requirements. The workflows con-
tributed to a shared picture of the work processes the DMS should support and which effects from 
using the system the different departments requested. The bid included the combined set of effects 
specifications and the vendors were asked to justify how their solution could meet them. During the 
implementation, the project group used the effects specifications to configure the DMS and evaluate 
how the system’s use satisfied the effects.

Teaching Participatory Design
287
Figure 13.3  Photos from the workshops with work process modelling with dead sea scrolls (Bødker et 
al., 2004). Wished-for effects from using the DMS were noted with yellow Post-its and docu -
mented in numbered effect specifications (inspired by the EDIT method described in Chapter 7 
in this book). Photo by Jesper Simonsen.
Participatory Design and Architecture Through Live Lab Case 13.9
Living Lab as a pedagogical platform for participatory and socially sustainable architectural 
practice
Supported by the University of Hasselt, Belgium, and targeted primarily but not only at master stu-
dents in Architecture, the Live Lab provides a pedagogical platform where students work on externally 
initiated design assignments and projects. In recent years, Live Projects, Design and Build projects, 
and Building Beyond Borders projects have emerged under the umbrella of Live Lab, which started as 
an initiative by 15 student volunteers with a Live Project in 2015. Nowadays, several different learn -
ing and working methods are linked together in and through long-term educational partnerships with 
societal actors and societally relevant issues in Live Lab.
The Live Projects nurtured within the Live Lab are closely linked to principles of environmental edu-
cation to enable socially and ecologically sustainable ways of life. Live Projects enable civic education and 
research at Hasselt University, and they go hand in hand with the innovative cooperation model between 
the university and society. Live Projects link the development of students’ employability skills (stake-
holder awareness, multidisciplinary collaboration, focus on realism and manufacturability, communication 
and presentation, self-managing action) to social engagement. They serve as a model for the interconnect-
edness of inclusive, participatory architectural practice and education together with actors from society.
Pedagogically, the work on Live Projects is supported through “Developing an Inclusive 
Definition, Typological Analysis and Online Resource for Live Projects” (Priest and Anderson, 
2014).
An overview of Live Lab and various Live Projects can be found at https://deanderemarkt.be/

AFTERTHOUGHTS FOR AN 
EMERGENT FUTURE
Statements by Susanne Bødker and Pelle Ehn
By way of an ending, and to bring the handbook full circle, the editors asked some of the founding 
members of the Participatory Design community to reflect on the role of contemporary Participa-
tory Design, based on their long engagement in the field and their knowledge of the handbook. 
It became clear that, rather than projecting hopeful visions for the future, they felt the need to 
re-emphasise the foundations of Participatory Design in the service of enabling deeper local im -
pact, based on mundane, everyday, and socio-material and political engagements. In the uneasy 
contemporary global condition, they struggled to position themselves or to set out a direction for 
the coming generation of researchers for how to address participation and technology design at 
global scales, in decolonial ways, with multiple species, and so forth. The sentiments they express 
at once draw attention to the nurturing of hopeful democratic design experiments (Björgvinsson 
et al., 2010) and Utopian future-making design practices (Ehn et al., 2014) that have been core to 
Participatory Design. Reaching far back to the early Utopia, we see this attendance to the mundane 
everyday acts of caring as a thoughtful reminder that even when facing the big issues and condi-
tions at scale (Bødker and Kyng, 2018), the potentials of participation continue to emerge and 
unfold in the contemporary moment:
Participatory Design Alternatives: Facing the “Big Issues” at Work
A statement by Professor Susanne Bødker
Participatory Design as a research field is alive and thriving after more than fifty years. For all 
those years it has played an important role in doing critical research and pointing out alternatives. 
By alternatives I mean both alternative processes and designs. In the last many years Participatory 
Design has extended its reach to many different types of fields and methods and that is great. With 
this handbook we get an updated set of methods and discussions to address a wider set of contexts 
and participants, both culturally and in new forms of (mainly outside mainstream work) settings. 
These are often contexts that are less regulated by legal and regulatory frameworks than work, and 
often technology in those contexts is managed through people “voting with their feet” (see Bødker, 
2006). As pointed out in (Bødker, 2003) it is important for researchers to use our curiosity and 
  DOI: 10.4324/9781003334330-16

Routledge International Handbook of Contemporary Participatory Design
292
creativity to question solutions that come out of large development projects and help ordinary us-
ers raise questions about the specific technologies proposed to them.
Bannon et al. (2018) raise the concern that Participatory Design is spread too thin because “it 
has spread itself across geographies, ideologies, methods, and time itself – losing definition or 
political teeth,” which seems to still be true. In an era where computing is powerfully under the 
control of multinationals such as Apple, Google, and Meta, and soon OpenAI, Participatory De -
sign does not seem to have much to offer in terms of specific methods and activities to the decision 
processes in everyday organisations where users (and management) struggle with empowering 
and infrastructuring to make the most of the technologies that are available. Many suggestions for 
data-driven and activist agendas seem very far away. Hence, where “Participatory Design That 
Matters – Facing the Big Issues” by Bødker and Kyng (2018) suggested facing the big issues, I am 
suggesting here that Participatory Design may actually also need to return to some of the small and 
everyday issues of technology use at work.
Participatory Design as Peace-Making Experiments in the Small
A statement by Professor emeritus Pelle Ehn
I belong to the privileged 1968 generation that grew up in a post-war Scandinavian welfare state. 
As researchers and activists we took peace for granted and engaged in activities expanding democ-
racy beyond mere representation towards more collaborative bottom-up forms of participation and 
civic engagement. Democracy-making and core ideas of Participatory Design, if you like. What 
some of us later came to describe as “Participatory Design experiments in the small”. Indeed, those 
were times filled with hope.
“Utopia where workers craft new technology. Today Scandinavia, tomorrow maybe the rest of 
the world”. This very optimistic quote from MIT Technical Review in the mid-1980s was a com-
ment on these kinds of democratic design engagements. Inspiring as this Utopia may have been, 
we also know that it did not come through, but as witnessed by the many examples in this book, 
not least from the Global South, there are still good reasons to be hopeful about possible “demo -
cratic design experiments in the small”.
However, as an old Participatory Design activist and researcher from the privileged North, 
I cannot help but also feel despair. In the West, the expansion of democratic participation has 
in many places been overruled by strong tendencies towards illiberal democracy or outright au-
tocracy. The “democracy as parenthesis” thesis may be the reality we have to confront, and so 
we must.
And then there is war – a human condition we, perhaps naively, never anticipated. But what 
if war is the normal state of human affairs, and peace is something we always have to fight for? 
Maybe as heroic political action replacing warfare, or as miracles you cannot predict, but grace -
fully may make possible. That is how I interpret the political and ethical thinking of refugees and 
activists Hannah Arendt and Simone Weil, not least in their different accounts of war and annihi-
lating violence in the Iliad, the Western epic poem par excellence. I am far from clear here, not 
least on the work of compromise, reconciliation, and grace. But this is where I think there is an 
emerging relevant space for Participatory Design as “democratic design experiments in the small”.
Without peace, there is no democracy, and without civic public engagement, there is no 
peace. So, I am tempted to suggest that Participatory Design activists should join forces with the 
peace movement. Certainly, this has to be a humble act. Most of us know much too little about 
peace-making activities before, during, and after actual violent war. At least I do. But local civic 

Afterthoughts for an Emergent Future
293
engagements across parties and borders, even in agonistic contexts, are an area where Participatory 
Design theories and practices may contribute. Maybe we could, with a little help from the think -
ers and activists from earlier dark times in Europe, form a new Utopian vision for Participatory 
Design where “the banality of evil” is met by the “grace” of participation and design. But as in the 
early days of Participatory Design, this has to be concrete and specific. In Sweden, where I live, it 
would mean aligning with the work of the 135-year-old peace organisation “Svenska Freds”. Just 
as in the early days of Participatory Design we aligned with the work of trade unions. This could 
for example mean engaging with initiatives towards transforming the Swedish weapon industry 
into socially useful production (like the efforts of the Lucas Aerospace workers in England in the 
1970s), supporting civic democracy projects in Russia, or reinforcing local cross-border peace 
initiatives between people from Israel and Palestine.
So, my suggestion is not that Participatory Design could or should play a role in summit meet-
ings, but, in the spirit of Participatory Design theory and practice, to find a new long-term orienta-
tion towards local peace-making engagements. I do not know if this is yet another Utopian dream, 
and it is certainly not to replace democratic design experiments, decolonial, more-than-human, 
and climate design activism, but maybe to make them possible.
